[STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app enterprise distribution channels MUST implement managed configuration interfaces: (1) The super-app enterprise portal allows IT administrators to define JSON schema-validated configurations per corporate mini-app; (2) The native container bridges 'navigator.managed.getManagedConfiguration()' to local MDM/EMM policy storage (e.g. Android Managed Configurations / Apple Managed App Configuration); (3) Dynamic policy pushes from the enterprise MDM server dispatch change notifications directly to active mini-app webviews.

title: Managed Device Origin Sandboxing: Zero-Trust Policy Scoping & Enterprise Fleet Integration
standard_reference: WICG Managed Device Web API (Device Attributes & Security Considerations)
summary: Establishes cryptographic origin boundaries, policy allowlisting, and zero-trust verification for enterprise-managed web and mini-app deployments.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Because enterprise configuration data and device attributes (such as directory device ID, annotated asset ID, and serial number) represent highly sensitive operational metadata, the WICG Managed Device Web API enforces strict sandboxed access controls. The API is exclusively available to 'managed applications'—origins explicitly allowlisted by device policy (e.g. 'DeviceAttributesAllowedForOrigins' and 'ManagedConfigurationPerOrigin'). The API is strictly forbidden in normal unmanaged consumer browsing sessions. Furthermore, configuration values are isolated strictly per origin: a mini-app on 'https://corp-app1.company.com' cannot read or enumerate configuration data assigned to 'https://corp-app2.company.com'. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app B2B enterprise stores MUST implement origin-scoped configuration sandboxing: (1) Public consumer mini-apps are denied access to 'navigator.managed' interfaces by default; (2) Enterprise tenant applications must present cryptographically signed enterprise distribution certificates to bind to MDM configuration namespaces; (3) Device identifiers and tenant credentials and configuration parameters are strictly segregated per mini-app origin, preventing lateral data movement or tenant impersonation across the shared super-app container.

title: WICG Idle Detection API: Dual-State Model & Permissions Policy Containment
standard_reference: WICG Idle Detection API Specification (§2.1 Dual Presence Model & §2.2 Permission Gate)
summary: Establishes the two-dimensional user presence model ('userState' and 'screenState') and enforces granular 'idle-detection' permission policy boundaries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WICG Idle Detection API defines an interface for observing system-wide user presence across two distinct dimensions: user idle state ('userState': 'active' or 'idle') indicating whether the user has interacted with the keyboard, mouse, or touchscreen; and screen idle state ('screenState': 'locked' or 'unlocked') indicating whether the host OS has activated a lock screen or screensaver. The feature is controlled by the powerful feature identifier 'idle-detection'. WebIDL interfaces 'IdleDetector' require Secure Context execution, are exposed to Window and DedicatedWorker environments, and mandate explicit permission via 'IdleDetector.requestPermission()' or Permissions Policy delegation ('allow="idle-detection"'). Calls to 'start(options)' reject with SecurityError if executed from non-fully active or cross-origin documents lacking permission. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app containers MUST enforce strict policy sandboxing for idle detection: (1) Mini-apps must declare the 'idle-detection' permission in their mini-app manifest, subject to store audit; (2) The container webview defaults 'idle-detection' to disabled, only delegating the capability via iframe 'allow="idle-detection"' to trusted first-party or certified enterprise domains; (3) The native shell binds 'IdleDetector' to system display listeners (e.g. Android DisplayListener / ACTION_SCREEN_OFF).

title: Coarse Threshold Clamping & Keystroke Timing Side-Channel Neutralization
standard_reference: WICG Idle Detection API (§2.4 IdleOptions Threshold Clamping & Privacy Considerations)
summary: Mandates minimum 60,000ms threshold clamping on IdleDetector.start() to prevent micro-timing side-channels, behavioral biometrics profiling, and cross-origin tracking.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Observing system-wide user interaction poses critical privacy hazards, including inferring user daily routines, cross-origin co-presence correlation (determining if two distinct apps are used by the same person), and keystroke dynamics side-channels. To neutralize these vectors, the WICG specification enforces strict coarse threshold boundaries: 'options.threshold' defines the idle duration in milliseconds, and user agents MUST enforce a normative floor of at least 60,000 ms (1 minute). If a script requests a threshold below 60,000 ms, the user agent clamps it to 60,000 ms or throws a TypeError. Furthermore, the API provides no historic event timestamps, providing only monotonic state transitions via the 'change' event to prevent inter-keystroke interval reconstruction. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app stores MUST audit mini-app idle detection configurations: (1) Static analysis review flags any mini-app specifying custom thresholds below 60 seconds; (2) Mini-app containers enforce global threshold quantization (clamping all thresholds to multiples of 60 seconds) to prevent subtle timing fingerprinting; (3) Background mini-apps are prevented from receiving idle state transitions unless actively engaged in an authorized background capability (such as an active audio worklet or VoIP call).

title: Event-Driven State Synchronization: Battery Conservation & Polling Elimination
standard_reference: WICG Idle Detection API (§2.4.6 Reacting to State Changes & Battery Preservation)
summary: Replaces CPU-intensive JavaScript setInterval/requestAnimationFrame polling loops with native OS event-driven presence notifications.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Legacy web applications historically implemented presence detection by listening to mousemove, keydown, and scroll events on the window, combined with continuous 'setInterval' or 'setTimeout' polling loops. In multi-tenant environments like super-apps where tens of mini-apps may run concurrently or stay cached in memory, script polling prevents mobile CPUs from entering deep C-states, causing severe battery drain and thermal throttling. The WICG Idle Detection API delivers an asynchronous, event-driven architecture: scripts instantiate 'new IdleDetector()', attach an 'onchange' listener, and invoke 'start({ threshold, signal })'. The host runtime offloads state evaluation to native OS power managers, firing DOM tasks on the idle detection task source strictly when transitions occur, achieving zero JavaScript CPU utilization while the user remains in a continuous state. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app performance review guidelines MUST enforce native presence primitives: (1) Mini-apps exhibiting continuous DOM input polling loops or timer-based idle trackers during automated dynamic inspection are flagged for battery optimization; (2) Mini-apps requiring presence awareness (e.g. real-time chat, collaborative document editing, active gaming lobbies) must migrate to 'IdleDetector'; (3) The native bridge suspends all idle dispatching when the hosting super-app enters OS background standby.

title: AbortSignal Cancellation Lifecycle & DedicatedWorker Thread Offloading
standard_reference: WICG Idle Detection API (§2.4 IdleDetector Interface & AbortSignal Integration)
summary: Governs deterministic cancellation of idle monitoring via standard AbortController signals and DedicatedWorker execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'IdleDetector.start(options)' method accepts an 'options.signal' member taking a standard WHATWG DOM 'AbortSignal'. When 'abortController.abort()' is invoked, the user agent immediately resets internal slot '[[state]]' to 'stopped', unregisters host-level presence listeners, and ceases event dispatch. In addition to Window environments, 'IdleDetector' is explicitly exposed to 'DedicatedWorker'. Offloading presence detection to a DedicatedWorker enables complex state reconciliation (e.g. flushing unsaved offline changes or computing presence heartbeats) without contesting main UI thread frame rendering. If the associated worker or document becomes discarded or navigated away, the user agent automatically runs the abort steps to prevent orphaned background memory leaks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDKs MUST wrap presence lifecycle within deterministic abort patterns: (1) Mini-app frameworks must bind 'IdleDetector' to mini-app page lifecycle hooks (e.g. 'onHide', 'onUnload'), triggering immediate signal abortion upon page exit; (2) SDK runtime checks verify that workers cleanly abort active detectors before worker termination; (3) Super-app container watchdogs monitor background threads and forcibly abort un-signaled idle detectors if a mini-app remains detached from visible views for more than 30 seconds.

title: Financial Session Auto-Locking, Enterprise Kiosk Governance & Store Review Criteria
standard_reference: Super-App Security & Governance Standard: Presence-Triggered Re-authentication & Kiosk Compliance
summary: Establishes mandatory automated session invalidation for financial/healthcare mini-apps and kiosk auto-reset upon user departure.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In regulated domains such as mobile banking, enterprise leasing, healthcare records, and public unattended kiosk terminals, regulatory frameworks (e.g. PCI DSS, HIPAA, banking IT circulars) mandate automatic session termination or re-authentication after specified periods of inactivity. Integrating the WICG Idle Detection API allows web applications to detect when a user walks away or locks their screen ('screenState === "locked"' or 'userState === "idle"'), instantly clearing in-memory cryptographic keys and sensitive tokens before OS memory dumps or physical shoulder surfing can occur. On public smart terminals and retail kiosks, detecting user departure triggers instantaneous session sanitization ('Clear-Site-Data') and navigation back to the welcome catalog. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store review guidelines MUST enforce presence-based security controls: (1) Financial and high-risk mini-apps MUST integrate idle detection to trigger automated session masking or biometric re-authentication after a maximum of 5 minutes idle; (2) Shared kiosk and retail super-app distributions must register an idle listener to purge local storage and clipboard states upon user exit; (3) Store reviewers evaluate the justified business purpose before granting the 'idle-detection' permission entitlement.

title: IETF RFC 7643 SCIM 2.0: Core User/Group Schemas & Extensibility Framework
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7643: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Core Schema (§3 SCIM Resources & §4 Core Schemas)
summary: Establishes standardized JSON-based resource models for 'User' and 'Group' identities, attribute mutability, and enterprise extensions across distributed domains.
detail: [SPEC FACT] IETF RFC 7643 defines a platform-neutral, attribute-based schema model for cross-domain identity management using JSON. The core resource schemas are identified via standardized URNs: 'urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User' and 'urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:Group', along with the Enterprise User extension 'urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:enterprise:2.0:User' (defining employeeNumber, costCenter, organization, division, department, and manager). RFC 7643 specifies strict attribute characteristics including mutability ('readOnly', 'readWrite', 'immutable', 'writeOnly'), cardinality, uniqueness, and returnability ('always', 'never', 'default', 'request'). Metadata attributes ('meta.resourceType', 'meta.created', 'meta.lastModified', 'meta.version') ensure cryptographic versioning and caching support via HTTP ETags across multi-tenant gateways. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Enterprise super-app stores MUST adopt RFC 7643 schema compliance for corporate tenant management: (1) Super-app tenant identity directories expose native SCIM 2.0 User and Group schemas; (2) Enterprise mini-apps declare required identity attributes via standard SCIM URNs rather than proprietary vendor fields; (3) The super-app directory gateway enforces attribute mutability rules, rejecting client attempts to overwrite server-managed identity keys.

title: IETF RFC 7644 SCIM 2.0 Protocol: Standard Endpoints, PATCH Semantics & Discovery
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7644: System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Protocol (§3.2 Endpoints, §3.5.2 PATCH & §4 Discovery)
summary: Specifies canonical RESTful endpoints (/Users, /Groups, /Me, /ServiceProviderConfig), granular PATCH modifications, and programmatic feature discovery.
detail: [SPEC FACT] IETF RFC 7644 defines the application-level HTTP protocol for exchanging SCIM schemas using media type 'application/scim+json'. The specification mandates standard endpoints: '/Users', '/Groups', '/Me', and self-describing discovery endpoints '/ServiceProviderConfig', '/Schemas', and '/ResourceTypes'. To prevent full-object overwrites that overwrite concurrent administrator updates, RFC 7644 §3.5.2 establishes granular HTTP PATCH operations ('add', 'remove', 'replace') targeting specific attribute paths (e.g. 'Operations: [{"op": "replace", "path": "active", "value": false}]'). The protocol enforces optimistic concurrency control using HTTP 'If-Match' and 'If-None-Match' headers carrying ETag entity versions, guaranteeing deterministic state synchronization across distributed identity providers and consumer applications. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app B2B operator platforms MUST expose certified RFC 7644 service provider interfaces: (1) Super-app identity servers support RFC 7644 endpoints for automated integration with enterprise IdPs (e.g. Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Ping Identity); (2) Tenant management APIs strictly support atomic PATCH operations for granular role, license, and entitlement assignments; (3) Feature negotiation via '/ServiceProviderConfig' explicitly advertises supported capabilities (patch, bulk, filter, changePassword, sort, etag).

title: Automated Corporate Lifecycle Provisioning: Instant Offboarding & JIT De-authorization
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7644 (§3.5 Modifying Resources & §3.6 Deleting Resources) & Zero-Trust Architecture
summary: Orchestrates instant, synchronized account suspension ('active=false') and resource deletion across all installed enterprise mini-apps upon employee departure.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A critical security vulnerability in enterprise SaaS and super-app ecosystems is 'orphaned access'—where former employees retain active sessions or stored tokens inside third-party mini-apps after corporate termination. Under RFC 7644, user deactivation is achieved instantaneously via an HTTP PATCH setting '{"Operations": [{"op": "replace", "path": "active", "value": false}]}' or an explicit HTTP DELETE to '/Users/{id}'. When the corporate IdP triggers this operation, the SCIM Service Provider is normatively required to immediately terminate all active sessions, invalidate issued bearer tokens, and cease authenticating that subject. This decouples user lifecycle management from authentication ceremonies, enabling automated, zero-latency deprovisioning across dozens of federated services. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Enterprise mini-app stores MUST enforce automated SCIM deprovisioning cascades: (1) When a tenant's SCIM client deactivates a user, the super-app platform immediately revokes all OAuth tokens, refresh tokens, and passkey registrations bound to that user; (2) The super-app host dispatches backchannel de-authorization webhooks or Shared Signals (SSF/CAEP) events to all mini-apps installed within that tenant; (3) Mini-app backends must process deactivation events within 60 seconds, purging local cached credentials and active websocket connections.

title: RFC 7644 Bulk Operations & Search Pagination: High-Scale Multi-Tenant Synchronization
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7644 (§3.4.2 Filtering/Pagination, §3.4.3 POST /.search & §3.7 Bulk Operations)
summary: Governs high-volume identity synchronization using /Bulk transactional batches, failOnErrors thresholds, and RFC 7644 filtering expressions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Large-scale enterprises managing tens of thousands of corporate seats cannot synchronize directory state through individual sequential HTTP calls without encountering rate limits and network degradation. RFC 7644 §3.7 defines the '/Bulk' endpoint, enabling clients to submit a single HTTP POST request containing multiple create, modify, and delete operations across different resource types. The bulk request includes a 'failOnErrors' integer specifying the maximum error count before the server aborts processing, alongside 'bulkId' references to resolve inter-resource dependencies (e.g. creating a User and immediately adding it to a Group within the same batch). For queries, RFC 7644 defines robust filter expressions (supporting operators 'eq', 'ne', 'co', 'sw', 'ew', 'pr', 'gt', 'ge', 'lt', 'le', 'and', 'or', 'not') and standardized pagination ('startIndex' and 'count'), preventing denial-of-service through bounded response limits. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app B2B directory gateways MUST implement bounded bulk and search capabilities: (1) The super-app SCIM gateway supports '/Bulk' requests with configurable transaction caps (e.g. max 500 operations per bulk payload); (2) Directory search queries enforce mandatory pagination caps (default 50, maximum 200 items) to protect gateway memory; (3) Complex filter queries must be indexed across core attributes ('userName', 'externalId', 'emails.value', 'groups.value') to maintain sub-100ms response latencies during large tenant sync cycles.

title: Enterprise Group-to-Mini-App Entitlement Mapping & Dynamic License Allocation
standard_reference: Enterprise Super-App Marketplace Architecture: SCIM 2.0 Role-Based Entitlement & Seat Allocation
summary: Architects automated mini-app license provisioning and departmental entitlement synchronization by mapping enterprise SCIM Groups to mini-app catalog visibility.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern enterprise super-apps, catalog visibility and in-app functional entitlements must be strictly governed by employee role, department, and software license quotas. Manually assigning mini-apps to individual employees is unscalable and error-prone. By implementing SCIM 2.0 Group synchronization ('urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:Group'), enterprise IT administrators can manage mini-app access entirely from their centralized identity governance platform (Okta, Entra ID, Ping). When an employee is added to an Active Directory / Okta group such as 'Finance-Field-Auditors', the corporate IdP pushes a SCIM group membership update to the Super-App Operator Gateway. The gateway automatically matches the group to store entitlement policies, instantly provisioning the user's seat, activating the required mini-app in their host launcher, and injecting tenant-specific configuration. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app enterprise store administration consoles MUST support automated group-based entitlement: (1) Administrators can map corporate SCIM groups directly to specific mini-app catalog bundles and license tiers; (2) The client launcher dynamically renders authorized mini-app icons based on real-time SCIM group memberships; (3) Removing a user from a corporate group immediately de-provisions their seat and revokes runtime launch tokens, maintaining license compliance and preventing unauthorized corporate data access.

title: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0: Decoupled Consumption & Authentication Device Architecture
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication Flow - Core 1.0 (§3 Core Architecture & Device Separation)
summary: Establishes decoupled authentication across independent Consumption Devices (POS, Kiosk, Smart TV, Web) and Authentication Devices (Super-App Native Client).
detail: [SPEC FACT] The OpenID Connect Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) Flow Core 1.0 defines an authentication model specifically designed for decoupled interaction patterns where there are no browser front-channel HTTP redirects through the user's browser. The architecture formally separates the client into two distinct endpoints: the 'Consumption Device' (CD)—where the user interacts with the Relying Party (such as a merchant point-of-sale terminal, public interactive kiosk, call center agent, smart TV, or desktop mini-app)—and the 'Authentication Device' (AD)—typically the user's personal smartphone running a trusted super-app native container. In CIBA, the Relying Party directly contacts the OpenID Provider via a backchannel HTTP POST, initiating user authentication out-of-band without exposing credentials or session tokens to the Consumption Device. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app identity platforms MUST implement CIBA decoupled profiles for cross-surface ecosystem integration: (1) The super-app acts as the authoritative OpenID Provider (OP) capable of dispatching interactive authentication challenges to the user's registered mobile device; (2) Mini-apps running in shared POS, desktop, or kiosk environments authenticate as CIBA Relying Parties; (3) The native super-app shell handles biometric authentication (e.g. FIDO2/Passkey/FaceID) and explicit consent, returning tokens to the merchant backchannel.

title: CIBA /bc-authorize Endpoint: Client Authentication & Cryptographic User Hints
standard_reference: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0 (§7 Backchannel Authentication Endpoint & §7.1 Authentication Request)
summary: Governs direct server-to-server authorization requests to /bc-authorize using private_key_jwt / mTLS and privacy-preserving user hints.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In CIBA, the Relying Party initiates authentication by sending an HTTP POST request to the provider's '/bc-authorize' endpoint. Because this is a direct backchannel call, client authentication is mandatory: public clients without authentication are prohibited, and confidential clients must authenticate using robust methods such as 'private_key_jwt' (RFC 7523) or mTLS (RFC 8705). To identify the target user without collecting their password or biometric on the consumption device, the client MUST provide exactly one user hint parameter: 'login_hint' (e.g. phone number, email, or loyalty ID), 'id_token_hint' (a previously issued ID token), or 'login_hint_token' (an encrypted or signed opaque container). If valid, the OP returns an HTTP 200 containing 'auth_req_id' (a cryptographically secure, high-entropy transaction handle) and 'expires_in' (lifetime in seconds). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer backchannel APIs MUST adhere to strict /bc-authorize constraints: (1) Mini-app backend servers must authenticate to the super-app authorization server using registered asymmetric public keys ('private_key_jwt'); (2) Front-end mini-apps are forbidden from prompting for master super-app passwords, passing only federated customer identifiers (e.g. phone or user handle) in 'login_hint'; (3) The super-app authorization gateway enforces strict replay protection on 'auth_req_id', expiring unacknowledged transactions after a maximum of 120 seconds.

title: CIBA Token Delivery Modes: Poll, Ping, and Push/Notification Protocol Profiles
standard_reference: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0 (§8 Token Delivery Modes: Poll, Ping, and Push)
summary: Defines the three normative token settlement models (Poll, Ping, Push) and enforces 'slow_down' / rate-limiting backoff algorithms.
detail: [SPEC FACT] CIBA Core 1.0 specifies three mutually exclusive token delivery modes established during client registration: (1) 'poll': the Relying Party repeatedly queries the standard token endpoint using grant type 'urn:openid:params:modrna:grant-type:backchannel_request' and 'auth_req_id'. The OP responds with error 'authorization_pending' until the user decides, or 'slow_down' if the client polls faster than the mandatory 'interval' parameter (increasing the interval by 5 seconds); (2) 'ping': the OP posts an asynchronous notification containing 'auth_req_id' to the client's registered callback endpoint once user interaction completes, prompting the client to make a single call to the token endpoint; (3) 'push': the OP directly delivers the ID Token, Access Token, and optional Refresh Token to the client's 'client_notification_endpoint' via HTTP POST, authenticated using a high-entropy 'client_notification_token' bearer secret. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app partner architectures MUST support standardized token delivery contracts: (1) High-throughput merchant integrations are provisioned for 'ping' or 'push' delivery to prevent polling amplification on the identity gateway; (2) Clients implementing 'poll' mode MUST strictly respect HTTP 400 'slow_down' responses, immediately increasing polling intervals to avoid IP-level throttling; (3) All callback endpoints must enforce TLS 1.3 with valid CA certificates and authenticate incoming bearer tokens.

title: Transaction Binding & Anti-Phishing Context: 'binding_message' & Cryptographic Proofs
standard_reference: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0 (§7.1 binding_message & §13 Security Considerations)
summary: Mandates human-readable transaction binding strings and cryptographic context verification to neutralize out-of-band phishing and relay attacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Because CIBA decouples the point of initiation from the point of authorization, malicious actors could attempt social engineering or 'push fatigue' attacks by triggering unauthorized backchannel requests to a victim's smartphone. To mitigate cross-session impersonation and relay attacks, CIBA defines the 'binding_message' parameter: a human-readable string (such as an order code, short confirmation text, or invoice summary) sent by the client. The OP MUST display this exact 'binding_message' on the user's Authentication Device alongside the consent prompt. The user verifies that the code on their mobile screen matches the code displayed on the physical POS or kiosk terminal before authorizing. Furthermore, when coupled with FAPI CIBA profiles, the request may include 'user_code' (a secret entropy string known only to the user at the consumption device) or cryptographic request objects signed by the client. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app omni-channel payment and authorization flows MUST enforce transaction binding: (1) Any commercial payment or data delegation request initiated via CIBA MUST provide a non-empty, clear 'binding_message' detailing merchant name and transaction amount; (2) The super-app native authorization dialog prominently displays the binding message alongside transaction metadata; (3) Biometric consent (FaceID/Fingerprint) is cryptographically signed and bound to the specific 'auth_req_id'.

title: Omni-Channel Retail POS & Kiosk Super-App Architecture: Decoupled Checkout & Settlement
standard_reference: Super-App Commercial Architecture Blueprint: Decoupled POS Integration & Instant Settlement
summary: Architects end-to-end contactless checkout for partner retail kiosks and POS terminals via super-app backchannel authorization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern retail and physical service environments, customer checkout friction is minimized by avoiding physical card swipes, paper slips, or scanning complex dynamic QR codes in poor lighting. Under the CIBA architecture, a merchant's POS system or self-service kiosk mini-app captures a lightweight user identifier (such as tapping an NFC membership card, entering a phone number, or scanning a static member barcode). The POS backend dispatches a CIBA '/bc-authorize' request with 'scope=payment' and detailed order data in 'binding_message'. Within milliseconds, the super-app pushes an urgent high-priority authorization sheet to the user's phone. Upon local biometric verification, the super-app OP releases an authorization token directly to the merchant's payment gateway, completing payment settlement without customer-merchant credential handover. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app retail partner ecosystem standards MUST establish omni-channel CIBA specifications: (1) The developer portal provides standardized CIBA SDKs for merchant point-of-sale and unattended kiosks; (2) Decoupled payment flows must execute end-to-end within a target p95 latency of <3 seconds; (3) The super-app ledger generates synchronized digital receipts delivered simultaneously to the user's transaction history and the merchant's settlement console.

title: Web Bluetooth Scanning API: navigator.bluetooth.requestLEScan & Filter Semantics
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Specification (§ Scanning and Advertisements)
summary: Standardizes raw Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) advertisement scanning via navigator.bluetooth.requestLEScan() with declarative service and manufacturer filters.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Web Bluetooth Scanning specification defines 'navigator.bluetooth.requestLEScan(options)', allowing web applications in secure execution contexts to passively receive advertising packets from surrounding BLE peripherals without establishing a GATT connection. The scanning options dictionary accepts 'filters'—specifying target 16-bit or 128-bit 'services', 'name', 'namePrefix', or 'manufacturerData' (with optional companyIdentifier, dataPrefix, and mask)—and a boolean 'acceptAllAdvertisements' flag. The method returns a Promise resolving to a 'BluetoothLEScan' object with an 'active' state and a '.stop()' method. Invocation requires transient user activation and is gated behind the 'bluetooth' Permissions Policy. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app containers MUST strictly regulate raw BLE scanning: (1) 'acceptAllAdvertisements: true' is strictly prohibited for standard third-party mini-apps and reserved exclusively for authorized system diagnostic utilities; (2) Mini-apps requesting 'requestLEScan()' MUST declare exact 16-bit/128-bit service UUIDs or registered Bluetooth SIG manufacturer IDs in their manifest capability profile; (3) The host container intercepts requestLEScan and displays an explicit, persistent system permission dialog showing the developer's entity name and justification before hardware radio activation.

title: BluetoothAdvertisingEvent: Parsing manufacturerData, serviceData & UUID Arrays
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Specification (§ BluetoothAdvertisingEvent Interface)
summary: Defines the 'advertisementreceived' event interface exposing device identity, RSSI, txPower, serviceData, and manufacturerData map structures.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a matching BLE packet is observed by the radio, the container dispatches an 'advertisementreceived' event of type 'BluetoothAdvertisingEvent' to 'navigator.bluetooth'. This event payload exposes: 'device' (a BluetoothDevice handle with an origin-scoped unique ID), 'uuids' (DOMString list of advertised service UUIDs), 'name' (local name string), 'rssi' (received signal strength indicator in dBm, as an integer), 'txPower' (calibrated transmit power at 0 meters in dBm), 'serviceData' (a Map of UUID strings to DataView binary payloads), and 'manufacturerData' (a Map associating 16-bit unsigned integer company identifiers to DataView binary slices). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDKs and super-app runtime bridges MUST enforce binary sanitization on advertisement processing: (1) The host container verifies that all DataView objects in serviceData and manufacturerData do not exceed 255 bytes (standard BLE advertisement limit) or 1650 bytes (Bluetooth 5.0 Extended Advertising PDU), truncating malformed frames; (2) Mini-app event listeners for 'advertisementreceived' MUST process frames asynchronously or in Web Workers, preventing main-thread UI jank during high-density beacon bursts (e.g. exhibition halls or smart retail malls); (3) The super-app static scanner audits mini-apps for buffer over-read vulnerabilities when parsing proprietary beacon formats (such as Apple iBeacon, Eddystone, or AltBeacon).

title: RSSI Proximity Metrics & Distance Estimation: Host-Mediated Noise Smoothing
standard_reference: Bluetooth Core Specification / Super-App Proximity Engineering Guideline
summary: Establishes path-loss log-distance attenuation formulas, RSSI jitter filtering, and host-mediated proximity thresholding for retail beacons.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In Bluetooth Low Energy systems, proximity is mathematically derived from the Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) and advertised Transmit Power (txPower) via the log-distance path loss model: Distance = 10^((txPower - RSSI) / (10 * n)), where 'n' represents the environmental path loss exponent (typically 2.0 in free space, 2.5-4.0 in cluttered indoor environments). Because multipath interference and body attenuation induce rapid high-frequency RSSI jitter (often +/- 10-15 dBm), raw RSSI readings cannot reliably determine instantaneous physical distance without algorithmic smoothing (such as Kalman filtering or exponential moving average). [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app proximity engines MUST standardize beacon telemetry and proximity triggers: (1) When mini-apps register for proximity-triggered actions (e.g. smart aisle coupons or automated turnstile check-ins), the super-app native core executes OS-level Kalman filtering across 5 consecutive advertisement packets before passing smoothed distance metrics to the mini-app; (2) Mini-apps are forbidden from polling raw RSSI at frequencies >10 Hz; (3) Automated store review enforces minimum threshold hysteresis (e.g. entering trigger at -65 dBm, exit trigger at -75 dBm) to prevent oscillation loops and excessive UI re-renders.

title: Hardware Duty Cycle Governance: Scan Window/Interval Arbitration & Battery Preservation
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Security & Privacy Architecture / Android BLE ScanSettings Specification
summary: Regulates BLE radio scan window and scan interval duty cycles, preventing rapid mobile battery depletion through host-mediated throttling.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Active Bluetooth scanning can deplete up to 5-15% of a mobile device's battery per hour if configured with a 100% duty cycle (where Scan Window equals Scan Interval, e.g. continuous 1000ms listening). Operating systems such as Android (via ScanSettings SCAN_MODE_LOW_POWER vs SCAN_MODE_LOW_LATENCY) and iOS strictly throttle background or non-focused BLE scanning to preserve battery and coexistence with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radios. The Web Bluetooth Scanning standard mandates that the user agent controls the underlying radio scan parameters, with the right to suspend or reduce duty cycles dynamically without notifying the application. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container runtimes MUST enforce strict BLE radio power governance: (1) The host container sets the default BLE scanning mode to low duty cycle (e.g. scan window 50ms, scan interval 500ms = 10% duty cycle); (2) High-duty-cycle scanning (100% continuous) is automatically clamped to a maximum duration of 30 seconds per session, after which the scan is automatically throttled or stopped; (3) If the mini-app transitions from 'active' to 'passive' or 'hidden' (per WICG Page Lifecycle), the super-app immediately suspends the BluetoothLEScan object via an implicit stop() signal, resuming only when foreground focus is restored.

title: Anti-Tracking Sandboxing: MAC Address Randomization & Ephemeral Device Scoping
standard_reference: Web Bluetooth Security Model (§ Privacy and Device Identification)
summary: Mandates client-isolated ephemeral device IDs and shields physical IEEE MAC addresses to prevent cross-app user tracking via BLE beacons.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Physical Bluetooth hardware addresses (48-bit MAC addresses) represent permanent, immutable hardware identifiers that can be abused for persistent cross-site and cross-physical-location tracking. To neutralize this threat, the Web Bluetooth specification explicitly forbids exposing the physical MAC address to web applications. Instead, the 'device.id' property contains an opaque, cryptographically random, origin-scoped pseudo-persistent identifier. Furthermore, peripherals utilizing Resolvable Private Addresses (RPAs per Bluetooth Core Spec) are tracked only within the active session, preventing long-term correlation across different sessions or disparate origin boundaries. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app security architecture MUST implement three-layer anti-fingerprinting defenses for BLE: (1) The BluetoothDevice.id MUST be generated using an HMAC of the peripheral's address keyed with a per-mini-app ephemeral salt, ensuring that two different mini-apps (or the same mini-app across cache resets) cannot correlate the same physical device; (2) The container scrubs non-standard manufacturerData payloads that leak user PII (such as device serial numbers or unencrypted phone numbers); (3) Mini-apps detected scanning continuously across background tabs or aggregating BLE beacon arrays for geo-triangulation without an explicit location permission are immediately flagged for security revocation.

title: W3C ImageCapture Interface: VideoTrack Binding & Still Capture Decoupling
standard_reference: W3C MediaStream Image Capture (§ 3 ImageCapture Interface)
summary: Establishes programmatic still photo capture bound to an active video MediaStreamTrack via new ImageCapture(videoTrack).
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C ImageCapture API defines 'new ImageCapture(track)', binding directly to an active 'MediaStreamTrack' whose 'kind' attribute is 'video'. Unlike drawing standard <video> frames to an HTML5 canvas (which is constrained to the video track's live streaming resolution, e.g. 720p or 1080p, and compressed preview stream), ImageCapture decouples the viewfinder stream from the camera sensor's high-resolution still capture pipeline. It exposes 'track' as a readonly attribute and provides asynchronous methods to inspect camera hardware capabilities, retrieve live video frame buffers, and capture full-resolution uncompressed still images directly from the camera hardware. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app frameworks MUST provide native bindings to ImageCapture for media workflows: (1) Developers must pass a valid, un-muted video track acquired via host-gated camera permissions; (2) The container enforces that if the underlying track is stopped (e.g. user minimizes the mini-app or switches tabs), all outstanding ImageCapture operations immediately reject with an 'InvalidStateError' DOMException; (3) The native shell isolates hardware camera locks, ensuring mini-apps cannot lock the device camera driver indefinitely.

title: takePhoto() Lifecycle & PhotoSettings: High-Resolution Artifact Capture
standard_reference: W3C MediaStream Image Capture (§ 4 takePhoto() & PhotoSettings)
summary: Standardizes full-sensor still photo capture returning a Blob encoded in image/jpeg or image/png with granular PhotoSettings controls.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'imageCapture.takePhoto(photoSettings)' method triggers the underlying camera hardware sensor to capture a still frame, returning a Promise that resolves to a 'Blob' object formatted as an encoded image (defaulting to MIME type 'image/jpeg' or 'image/png'). The optional 'photoSettings' dictionary allows granular parameter overrides, including 'imageWidth', 'imageHeight', and 'fillLightMode' (enabling values 'off', 'auto', or 'flash'). The capture process suspends preview frame generation momentarily to expose the physical sensor at its maximum native resolution (e.g. 12MP, 48MP, or 108MP) rather than the preview resolution. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platforms MUST regulate 'takePhoto()' in mini-app store review and runtime: (1) High-resolution image capture must enforce maximum memory buffer ceilings—the container automatically rejects photo requests if device available RAM is below 150MB, returning an 'OperationError' to protect against Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes; (2) The container strips sensitive EXIF metadata (specifically GPS coordinates and camera hardware serial numbers) by default, requiring an explicit 'geolocation' permission from the user before preserving geo-tags in the resulting Blob; (3) The native container plays a mandatory shutter sound or visual flash indicator to comply with regional privacy regulations (e.g. Japan/South Korea mandatory camera sound laws).

title: grabFrame() Stream Snapshots: Zero-Copy ImageBitmap Extraction for Real-Time CV
standard_reference: W3C MediaStream Image Capture (§ 5 grabFrame() Method)
summary: Governs low-latency frame buffer extraction via grabFrame(), returning an ImageBitmap for high-speed client-side computer vision.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'imageCapture.grabFrame()' method captures a snapshot of the live 'MediaStreamTrack' video stream, resolving to an 'ImageBitmap' object. Unlike 'takePhoto()', 'grabFrame()' does not trigger a hardware still photo exposure or encode to a JPEG/PNG compressed blob; instead, it extracts a direct, uncompressed GPU/CPU memory bitmap of the latest displayed frame. This ImageBitmap can be transferred zero-copy to a Dedicated Web Worker or rendered onto an 'OffscreenCanvas' or WebGL context, making it the normative standard for client-side barcode scanning, optical character recognition (OCR), face tracking, and augmented reality (AR) pipelines. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app computer vision runtimes MUST govern 'grabFrame()' resource consumption: (1) Mini-apps executing continuous real-time analysis MUST offload ImageBitmap processing to Web Workers via Transferable objects, preventing main UI thread blocking; (2) The developer must explicitly invoke 'imageBitmap.close()' immediately after processing each frame to prevent catastrophic GPU memory leaks; (3) The super-app static analyzer audits mini-apps for continuous grabFrame loops without an exit condition, enforcing maximum frame processing rates (e.g. 15-30 fps cap) to avoid device overheating and thermal throttling.

title: getPhotoCapabilities(): Hardware Telemetry, Optical Zoom, ISO & Exposure Limits
standard_reference: W3C MediaStream Image Capture (§ 6 PhotoCapabilities & MediaSettingsRange)
summary: Exposes camera hardware optical limits (zoom, ISO, exposure, white balance) via PhotoCapabilities and MediaSettingsRange structures.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'imageCapture.getPhotoCapabilities()' method returns a Promise resolving to a 'PhotoCapabilities' object detailing the exact physical and digital capabilities of the underlying optical sensor. This includes: 'imageWidth' and 'imageHeight' ranges ('MediaSettingsRange' exposing min, max, and step attributes), 'fillLightMode' (array of supported lighting modes: 'off', 'auto', 'flash'), and optical parameters such as 'zoom', 'exposureCompensation', 'colorTemperature', and 'iso'. The 'MediaSettingsRange' interface guarantees that applications query mathematically validated hardware constraints before requesting arbitrary image dimensions or exposure values. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app device abstraction layers MUST enforce range safety on camera hardware manipulation: (1) The host bridge validates all custom photo capture parameters against the active device's PhotoCapabilities ranges before dispatching calls to native camera APIs (Android Camera2 / Apple AVFoundation); (2) Mini-apps attempting to set values outside [min, max] or non-multiples of 'step' are automatically normalized or rejected with an 'OverconstrainedError'; (3) Automated store review flags applications that query PhotoCapabilities continuously without capturing media, preventing malicious sensor-based hardware fingerprinting.

title: Super-App eKYC & Optical Scanning Sandboxing: Document Framing & Anti-Spoofing
standard_reference: Super-App Financial Security Blueprint: Native Optical eKYC & Liveness Isolation
summary: Establishes host-mediated document framing, hardware flash illumination, and client-side anti-spoofing for high-assurance financial onboarding.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern fintech and banking super-apps, electronic Know-Your-Customer (eKYC) onboarding and identity document verification require capturing high-resolution still images of national ID cards, passports, and driver's licenses, alongside facial liveness verification. Relying on raw client-side HTML canvas grabs frequently introduces motion blur, lens glare, and inadequate resolution (preventing microprint and guilloche pattern verification). By leveraging ImageCapture with hardware 'fillLightMode: flash' and optimal focal distance constraints, client runtimes achieve cryptographic-grade document artifacts suitable for automated MRZ (Machine Readable Zone) parsing and liveness fraud detection. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Financial mini-app store standards MUST enforce optical eKYC security architectures: (1) Identity verification mini-apps MUST utilize the super-app native eKYC bridge or W3C ImageCapture with minimum imageWidth >= 1920px (1080p) to guarantee readable security micro-text; (2) The container overlays a native bounding box (viewfinder stencil) that guides user alignment and automatically triggers 'takePhoto()' only when on-device sharpness and document-contour algorithms confirm zero blur; (3) All captured document images must be encrypted in memory using WebCrypto AES-GCM-256 before disk caching or network transmission to backend verification services.

title: WebAuthn Multi-Device Credentials (Passkeys): Synced Authenticator Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (§ 5.4.3 Multi-Device Credentials) / FIDO2 Architecture
summary: Defines multi-device discoverable WebAuthn credentials (Passkeys) synchronized across user ecosystems via secure end-to-end encrypted keychains.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebAuthn Level 3 and FIDO2 standards define 'Passkeys' as multi-device discoverable credentials ('resident keys') where the asymmetric private key is generated within a secure hardware boundary and synchronized across a user's ecosystem of devices (e.g. via Apple iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, or Microsoft Entra) using end-to-end encryption. Unlike legacy single-device hardware security keys (FIDO U2F / Security Keys) which are bounded to physical USB/NFC tokens, synced passkeys ensure cryptographic key availability across desktop and mobile form factors without degrading security against credential stuffing, phishing, or server database leaks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app identity platforms MUST standardize passkey support across all micro-app authentication flows: (1) The super-app acts as a passkey Relying Party (RP) supporting passwordless registration ('navigator.credentials.create') and conditional UI autofill ('navigator.credentials.get' with 'mediation: conditional'); (2) The client runtime sets 'residentKey: required' and 'userVerification: preferred' (or 'required' for high-assurance financial operations); (3) Mini-apps can authenticate users through the super-app's native passkey bridge without handling master biometric raw data or private keys.

title: Relying Party ID & clientDataJSON Cryptographic Origin Binding
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 2/3 (§ 5.1.1 Relying Party Entity & § 5.8.1.1 Client Data Used in Signatures)
summary: Mandates strict cryptographic origin binding in clientDataJSON and rp.id scoping to mathematically eliminate phishing attacks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The fundamental anti-phishing guarantee of WebAuthn resides in the cryptographic construction of 'clientDataJSON'. During credential creation or assertion, the client user agent constructs a canonical UTF-8 JSON object containing: 'type' ('webauthn.create' or 'webauthn.get'), 'challenge' (base64url-encoded high-entropy nonce provided by the server), 'origin' (the fully qualified, browser-verified calling origin), and 'crossOrigin' (boolean indicating iframe context). The authenticator signs over a SHA-256 hash of this clientDataJSON alongside the authenticator data ('authData'). The Relying Party ID ('rp.id') MUST be equal to or a registrable domain suffix of the calling origin. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app security gateways MUST enforce strict RP origin verification when serving mini-apps: (1) When a mini-app initiates passkey authentication, the super-app verifies that 'rp.id' exactly matches the developer's registered domain (or the super-app root domain if delegated); (2) Super-app backends verifying WebAuthn assertions MUST strictly validate that 'clientDataJSON.origin' matches the authenticated container origin and that the cryptographic signature validates over the server-issued challenge; (3) Cross-origin iframes embedded within mini-apps are forbidden from invoking WebAuthn unless explicitly granted via the 'publickey-credentials-get' Permissions Policy.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.0/2.1: Client-to-Authenticator Protocol & pinUvAuthToken Architecture
standard_reference: FIDO Alliance Client to Authenticator Protocol (CTAP) Implementation Draft (§ 5 Authenticator Commands)
summary: Standardizes raw message framing (CBOR over USB/NFC/BLE) and pinUvAuthToken cryptographic permissions between host and authenticator.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The FIDO Client-to-Authenticator Protocol (CTAP) defines how the host user agent (client) communicates with roaming authenticators (via USB HID, NFC, or BLE) or platform authenticators (built-in biometric sensors). CTAP messages are encoded using Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR). In CTAP 2.1, user verification is governed by the 'pinUvAuthToken' protocol: an ECDH key exchange establishes a shared ephemeral secret between the host and authenticator, deriving a session token used to authenticate subsequent 'authenticatorMakeCredential' and 'authenticatorGetAssertion' commands without exposing the raw user PIN or biometric template to the host platform. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app native containers wrapping WebAuthn and CTAP primitives MUST enforce hardware boundary protection: (1) The super-app core interfaces with platform authenticators using native OS frameworks (Apple LocalAuthentication / Android BiometricPrompt) to bind passkey operations to hardware Secure Enclaves or StrongBox Keymasters; (2) The client ensures that ephemeral ECDH keys used during CTAP key agreements are zeroized in RAM immediately after assertion signing; (3) Third-party mini-app code is strictly sandboxed from accessing low-level CTAP CBOR pipes or raw authenticator descriptors.

title: Passkey Conditional UI: Form Autofill Mediation & Zero-Friction Credential Picker
standard_reference: WebAuthn Conditional Mediation Specification / Google-Apple Passkey UX Guidelines
summary: Governs 'mediation: conditional' integration with HTML <input autocomplete='username webauthn'> for seamless browser-native credential autofill.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Passkey Conditional UI streamlines user authentication by integrating passkey selection directly into standard browser and system autofill dropdowns. By setting 'mediation: conditional' in 'navigator.credentials.get({publicKey: ..., mediation: 'conditional'})' and adding 'autocomplete="username webauthn"' to the login form's username input field, the user agent prepares an asynchronous assertion request without displaying an intrusive modal popup. When the user taps the input field, the platform's autofill suggestion UI displays available passkeys alongside traditional saved passwords. Selecting a passkey triggers biometric verification and resolves the Promise immediately. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app UI frameworks MUST support Conditional UI: (1) Partner login and checkout interfaces must adopt the standard 'autocomplete="webauthn"' attribute to enable native passkey suggestions; (2) The super-app WebView container MUST properly propagate 'PublicKeyCredential.isConditionalMediationAvailable()' checks to prevent runtime JavaScript crashes on legacy devices; (3) The native shell prevents clickjacking and UI redressing around conditional autofill prompts by enforcing visual overlay integrity checks during passkey presentation.

title: Multi-Tenant Passkey Delegation: Super-App Root RP vs Subdomain Micro-App Architecture
standard_reference: Super-App Passkey Architecture Blueprint: Multi-Tenant Delegation & Token Exchange
summary: Architects multi-tenant passkey authentication enabling third-party mini-apps to leverage super-app passkeys via token exchange.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In a super-app ecosystem hosting hundreds of third-party merchant mini-apps, individual micro-apps running on distinct domain origins cannot directly access passkeys registered under the super-app root domain (e.g. an e-commerce mini-app at 'store.partner.com' cannot access a passkey scoped to 'rp.id: superapp.com' due to strict WebAuthn origin enforcement). To provide seamless biometric single sign-on across the ecosystem without violating WebAuthn origin boundaries, the super-app platform acts as an Identity Provider (IdP) executing passkey authentication natively at the root origin, and then issues down-scoped, cryptographically signed OAuth/OIDC tokens (or RFC 8693 Token Exchange tokens) to the calling mini-app. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app enterprise architecture standards MUST establish the multi-tenant passkey model: (1) Third-party mini-apps request user authentication via the super-app JavaScript SDK ('superApp.auth.loginWithPasskey()'); (2) The super-app native container performs WebAuthn assertion verification against its own root RP identity with hardware-bound user verification; (3) Upon success, the super-app identity gateway generates an ephemeral, audience-restricted JWT signed by the super-app authorization server and passes it to the mini-app backend for session establishment.

title: WebXR Device API: Immersive AR Session Lifecycle & XRSystem Handshake
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API Specification (§ 3 The XRSystem Interface & § 4 XRSession)
summary: Governs immersive augmented reality session initialization, feature negotiation, and user activation handshakes in mini-apps.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C WebXR Device API establishes a hardware-agnostic runtime interface for accessing augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) devices on mobile and spatial computing platforms. The entry point 'navigator.xr' (an XRSystem instance) provides 'navigator.xr.isSessionSupported(mode)' to query capability support for session modes, notably 'immersive-ar' (blended digital content over physical passthrough) and 'inline' (monoscopic canvas rendering). Requesting an immersive session via 'navigator.xr.requestSession('immersive-ar', { requiredFeatures: [...], optionalFeatures: [...] })' MUST be triggered by transient user activation (user gesture) and resolves to an 'XRSession'. The session exposes an animation loop driven by 'session.requestAnimationFrame((time, frame) => ...)' synchronized with native display refresh and hardware vsync. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host containers embedding mini-apps with AR capabilities (e.g. retail furniture visualization, virtual makeup, wayfinding) MUST enforce strict XR session governance: (1) 'xr-spatial-tracking' Permissions Policy directive MUST be explicitly declared in the mini-app manifest and delegated to the container iframe; (2) The container enforces a single active immersive session limit across all background and foreground tabs, automatically invoking 'session.end()' when the host app is backgrounded or minimized; (3) The native shell renders a persistent spatial tracking privacy indicator (visual icon) whenever the host camera sensor feeds the WebXR AR pipeline.

title: WebXR Hit Testing & Anchor Persistence: Real-World Geometry Sandboxing
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Hit Test Module & WebXR Anchors Module Specifications
summary: Defines raycasting against real-world physical surfaces, plane detection, and anchor pose tracking without exposing raw spatial mesh data.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebXR Hit Test API enables augmented reality applications to cast mathematical rays into the physical environment and determine intersections with real-world planes and geometry. Developers negotiate the 'hit-test' optional feature during session setup and create an 'XRHitTestSource' via 'session.requestHitTestSource({ space: viewerSpace })'. During each animation frame, 'frame.getHitTestResults(hitTestSource)' returns an ordered array of 'XRHitTestResult' objects, from which an 'XRSubImage' or matrix pose can be derived via 'result.getPose(referenceSpace)'. To prevent drifting over time, the companion WebXR Anchors API allows applications to pin virtual content to physical coordinates using 'hitResult.createAnchor()', yielding an 'XRAnchor' whose tracking pose is continuously updated by native SLAM / ARKit / ARCore subsystems. Crucially, the API isolates physical room meshes: the web app receives only ray intersection points and surface normal quaternions, shielding raw point clouds from rogue tracking. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app AR store review requirements MUST mandate privacy-preserving hit-testing: (1) Mini-apps MUST NOT attempt to reconstruct 3D topological meshes of private user environments from high-frequency raycasting arrays; (2) The super-app host container enforces a maximum hit-test raycast query rate (e.g. 30 Hz) and sanitizes hit result matrices against micro-vibration telemetry; (3) All active XR anchors MUST be destroyed and cleared from volatile memory upon session termination or navigation away from the mini-app.

title: WebXR Input Sources & Haptic Actuation: Spatial Interaction & Gesture Safety
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API Specification (§ 8 Input Sources & XRInputSource)
summary: Standardizes multi-modal spatial input sources (hand tracking, screen taps, 6DoF controllers) and haptic pulse feedback in immersive sessions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] WebXR represents interactive entities through 'XRInputSource' instances exposed via 'session.inputSources'. Input sources categorize interactions by 'targetRayMode': 'gaze' (head-mounted cursor), 'tracked-pointer' (6DoF handheld spatial controller with laser pointer ray), or 'screen' (touch gesture on mobile AR display). User activation events 'selectstart', 'select', and 'selectend' map directly to primary trigger actions or touchscreen taps. When physical 6DoF controllers or advanced haptic actuators are available, 'inputSource.gamepad' exposes standard analog thumbsticks, buttons, and 'gamepad.hapticActuators' supporting 'pulse(value, duration)' vibration feedback. This abstraction allows mini-apps to deliver tactile feedback during virtual object manipulation without interfacing with vendor-proprietary Bluetooth or USB SDKs. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container standards for AR interaction governance mandate: (1) Touch-based screen interactions in 'immersive-ar' mode MUST NOT bypass standard host navigation gestures (such as edge-swipes to return to the super-app dashboard or access the security menu capsule); (2) Controller haptic actuation MUST be clamped to a maximum duration of 1,000 ms and duty-cycle limited to avoid thermal throttling and battery exhaustion; (3) Mini-apps MUST provide non-spatial accessibility fallbacks (e.g. standard screen-reader compatible 2D UI controls) for all core transactions, ensuring users unable to perform AR gestures can complete purchasing and viewing workflows.

title: WebXR Lighting Estimation & Raw Camera Access: Environmental Privacy Controls
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Lighting Estimation & Raw Camera Access Module Specifications
summary: Regulates ambient lighting reflection probes, spherical harmonics, and raw optical passthrough camera access under strict privacy sandboxing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To realistically composite virtual objects into physical environments, WebXR defines lighting estimation via 'XRLightProbe'. Light probes calculate spherical harmonic coefficients and directional light vectors from the physical scene, allowing WebGL / WebGPU PBR (Physically Based Rendering) shaders to match physical room lighting. Because high-resolution reflection maps could inadvertently leak sensitive visual data (e.g. text on a computer monitor or reflections of human faces in a physical room), WebXR lighting estimation quantizes specular reflection cubemaps and restricts texture resolutions. Where raw camera feed access ('camera-access' feature) is explicitly requested for specialized computer vision, the platform restricts access to Secure Contexts, enforces camera indicator LEDs, and limits pixel buffers to ephemeral GPU textures that cannot be extracted via 'toDataURL()' without explicit user consent. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app store security specifications for AR mini-apps mandate: (1) Mini-apps requiring raw camera texture access ('camera-access') MUST undergo Tier-3 security and privacy audits prior to store publication; (2) The super-app host container displays a high-visibility security dialog explicitly notifying the user if a mini-app requests direct camera feed inspection versus standard lighting estimation; (3) Container runtime monitors verify that camera pixel textures are not serialized into IndexedDB, OPFS, or exfiltrated across external network endpoints via WebSockets or WebTransport.

title: WebXR Mobile Thermal Budgets & Adaptive Display Refresh Governance
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebXR Device API Specification & W3C Compute Pressure API Integration
summary: Enforces frame-time budgets, dynamic resolution scaling, and thermal throttling watchdogs for mobile AR container execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Immersive AR rendering simultaneously exercises the mobile device's camera ISP, computer vision SLAM engine, GPU rasterization, and display subsystem, generating substantial thermal heat and rapid battery drain. WebXR addresses this by exposing 'session.supportedFrameRates' and 'session.updateTargetFrameRate(rate)', allowing applications to dynamically adjust target rendering between 30 fps, 60 fps, 90 fps, or 120 fps depending on hardware capability. Furthermore, pairing WebXR with the W3C Compute Pressure API enables runtime observation of CPU and thermal pressure states ('nominal', 'fair', 'serious', 'critical'). When pressure reaches 'serious', mini-apps can dynamically downscale rendering viewport resolutions via 'XRWebGLLayer.requestViewportScale(scaleFactor)' (e.g. scaling from 1.0 to 0.75 or 0.5) to maintain steady framerates without triggering hardware thermal throttling. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mobile platform performance guardrails MUST enforce AR resource ceilings: (1) Mini-apps running in 'immersive-ar' mode MUST NOT sustain frame drops exceeding 15% over a continuous 60-second window; (2) If the host device reports a 'critical' thermal condition, the super-app container MUST automatically downclock the session framerate to 30 fps or prompt the user to pause AR visualization; (3) The container enforces a continuous AR session timeout (e.g. 10 minutes) with an explicit user confirmation prompt to prevent unintended camera and GPU drainage in unattended states.

title: WebCodecs VideoFrame Architecture: Hardware Zero-Copy Frame Allocation & GPU Texturing
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Specification (§ 6 VideoFrame Interface)
summary: Standardizes low-overhead hardware-accelerated video frame allocation, pixel format abstraction, and zero-copy GPU memory mapping.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C WebCodecs API provides low-level, high-performance access to hardware video and audio encoders/decoders, replacing heavy JavaScript Wasm software decoders (e.g. ffmpeg.js). At the heart of WebCodecs video processing is the 'VideoFrame' interface, which represents an individual raw video frame backed directly by hardware media buffers (e.g. Android GraphicBuffer / HardwareBuffer, Apple CVPixelBuffer / IOSurface). A VideoFrame can wrap HTMLVideoElement, OffscreenCanvas, or raw pixel data, exposing metadata including 'format' (e.g. 'I420', 'NV12', 'RGBA'), 'codedWidth', 'codedHeight', 'displayAspectRatio', and microsecond 'timestamp'. Crucially, a VideoFrame can be directly uploaded to WebGL or WebGPU textures via 'gl.texImage2D(..., videoFrame)' or 'device.queue.copyExternalImageToTexture({ source: videoFrame }, ...)' without CPU round-trip copies, achieving genuine zero-copy hardware graphics pipeline efficiency. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app native containers hosting video streaming, live commerce, and video editing mini-apps MUST standardize WebCodecs support: (1) The host container exposes hardware-backed WebCodecs primitives inside both Dedicated Web Workers and Window contexts; (2) The container enforces secure context execution (HTTPS / local sandbox origin) for all WebCodecs APIs; (3) Memory leak watchdogs monitor allocated VideoFrame handles across mini-app lifecycles.

title: VideoFrame Deterministic Disposal (close()): Native RAM Allocation Ceilings & Leak Defense
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Specification (§ 6.1 Memory Management & videoFrame.close())
summary: Mandates explicit deterministic disposal of unmanaged hardware frame buffers to prevent catastrophic out-of-memory crashes on mobile devices.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Unlike standard JavaScript heap objects which are automatically reclaimed by the garbage collector, each 'VideoFrame' instance wraps a heavy native hardware buffer allocating between 2 MB and 16 MB of native VRAM / shared memory (e.g. a single 4K NV12 frame consumes ~12 MB). Because JavaScript garbage collectors operate purely on JS heap pressure and cannot perceive underlying native GPU/VRAM exhaustion, relying on garbage collection to free VideoFrames causes catastrophic mobile out-of-memory (OOM) process termination within seconds of processing high-framerate video. To ensure memory safety, the WebCodecs specification mandates explicit disposal via 'videoFrame.close()'. Once closed, the underlying hardware buffer is immediately returned to the system pool, and any further operations on the VideoFrame throw an 'InvalidStateError'. The companion 'videoFrame.clone()' creates an explicit reference-counted clone, incrementing the native handle counter. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app static analysis and automated review gates MUST enforce deterministic VideoFrame lifecycle management: (1) Mini-app review pipelines inspect video processing loops to verify that every allocated or decoded VideoFrame is wrapped in a try/finally block or stream pipeline terminating in an explicit '.close()' call; (2) The super-app runtime container injects a watchdog tracking unclosed VideoFrame instances: if an active mini-app accumulates more than 30 unclosed frames (representing ~150 MB native VRAM), the container triggers an automated memory purge and records a reliability fault; (3) When a mini-app tab transitions to the background, all unclosed VideoFrames are forcibly closed by the host container.

title: VideoDecoder & EncodedVideoChunk: Hardware Codec Negotiation & Low-Latency Demuxing
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Specification (§ 4 VideoDecoder Interface & § 5 EncodedVideoChunk)
summary: Governs asynchronous hardware video decoding pipelines, codec profile validation (H.264, VP9, AV1, HEVC), and backpressure queue management.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'VideoDecoder' interface provides an asynchronous event-driven pipeline for decoding compressed video bitstreams into raw VideoFrames. Instantiated with an 'output' callback and an 'error' callback via 'new VideoDecoder({ output: handleFrame, error: handleError })', the decoder is configured using 'decoder.configure({ codec: 'avc1.42001E', codedWidth: 1280, codedHeight: 720, hardwareAcceleration: 'prefer-hardware' })'. Codec support and configuration validity are asynchronously queried beforehand via 'VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported(config)'. Incoming compressed packets are wrapped as 'EncodedVideoChunk({ type: 'key' | 'delta', timestamp, data })' and queued using 'decoder.decode(chunk)'. Hardware backpressure is monitored via 'decoder.decodeQueueSize': when the queue size grows excessively, callers must throttle demuxing or drop non-reference frames to prevent latency spikes. Asynchronous state transitions ('unconfigured', 'configured', 'closed') are synchronized using 'decoder.flush()' and 'decoder.reset()'. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app multimedia platform standards for video playback and live broadcasting mandate: (1) Mini-apps MUST probe 'VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported()' before initiating custom video streaming sessions and fall back to baseline codecs (e.g. H.264 Baseline Profile / VP8) if advanced codecs (AV1 / HEVC) lack hardware decoding support; (2) The container limits maximum active VideoDecoder instances to 2 per mini-app to avoid exhausting native hardware decoder chip instances (e.g. Qualcomm / Apple SoC hardware codec limits); (3) Codec configuration strings MUST adhere strictly to RFC 6381 syntax, with validation performed prior to passing parameters to native decoder components.

title: AudioDecoder & AudioData: Low-Latency PCM Decoding & AudioContext Synchronization
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Specification (§ 7 AudioDecoder Interface & § 8 AudioData)
summary: Standardizes raw planar and interleaved audio sample decoding (AAC, Opus, FLAC) and presentation timestamp synchronization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Alongside video, WebCodecs provides 'AudioDecoder' and 'AudioData' for hardware/system-level audio decoding. Configured with codec strings such as 'opus' or 'mp4a.40.2' (AAC-LC), sampleRate, and numberOfChannels, the AudioDecoder processes 'EncodedAudioChunk' packets and outputs 'AudioData' instances representing uncompressed PCM audio buffers. AudioData exposes 'format' ('f32', 'f32-planar', 's16', 's16-planar'), 'sampleRate', 'numberOfFrames', 'numberOfChannels', 'timestamp', and 'duration'. Samples can be copied out using 'audioData.copyTo(destinationBuffer, { planeIndex })' or piped directly into an AudioWorklet or Web Audio API node. Crucially, like VideoFrame, AudioData holds native memory allocations and provides 'audioData.close()' for deterministic memory reclamation. Presentation timestamps (PTS) in microseconds enable precise A/V sync algorithms to align audio playback with video display intervals. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app VoIP, podcast, and gaming mini-app standards mandate: (1) Audio decoding pipelines MUST explicitly synchronize AudioData timestamps against VideoFrame presentation timestamps using drift-correction filters with an allowable skew tolerance not exceeding ±40 ms; (2) Mini-apps MUST call 'audioData.close()' immediately after forwarding PCM buffers to audio render queues or AudioWorklet nodes; (3) Audio sample rates MUST be dynamically resampled to match the host hardware output rate (typically 48,000 Hz or 44,100 Hz) to eliminate native OS audio mixer CPU overhead.

title: Dedicated Web Worker Codec Offloading: Thread Concurrency & Zero INP Degradation
standard_reference: W3C WebCodecs Specification & W3C High Resolution Time API Integration
summary: Enforces execution of heavy video decoding and rendering loops within background Dedicated Web Workers to guarantee responsive UI.
detail: [SPEC FACT] While WebCodecs interfaces are exposed on the Window object, running VideoDecoder callbacks, canvas drawing, and frame parsing on the main browser thread introduces severe UI jank, long tasks, and catastrophic degradation of Core Web Vitals (specifically Interaction to Next Paint / INP). Because VideoDecoder, VideoEncoder, AudioDecoder, AudioEncoder, and OffscreenCanvas are fully transferable and constructible inside 'DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope', entire media pipelines can be decoupled from the UI thread. The worker receives compressed chunks over a MessagePort or WebSocket/WebTransport, decodes them via hardware-accelerated VideoDecoder, performs WebGL/WebGPU compositing on an OffscreenCanvas, and transfers finished frames or rendered results without ever blocking the main thread event loop. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app performance and review standards for media-rich mini-apps mandate: (1) Mini-apps performing real-time video processing (live streaming, video filters, video calling) MUST execute all WebCodecs decoding and encoding pipelines inside Dedicated Web Workers; (2) The main UI thread MUST NOT spend more than 16 ms per frame handling media synchronization events, maintaining INP within the 'Good' threshold (<200 ms); (3) Container performance telemetry continuously samples Long Animation Frames (LoAF) and flags any mini-app executing video decode loops on the main thread for automated developer remediation.

title: MediaStreamTrackProcessor: Camera & Audio Track Ingestion via WHATWG ReadableStream
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Media Capture Transform Specification (§ 5 MediaStreamTrackProcessor Interface)
summary: Transforms live camera and microphone MediaStreamTracks into readable streams of raw VideoFrames and AudioData.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Media Capture Transform specification (historically known as 'Breakout Box') bridges standard WebRTC / getUserMedia media tracks with modern streaming and WebCodecs primitives. The 'MediaStreamTrackProcessor' constructor takes an existing video or audio 'MediaStreamTrack' and an optional 'maxBufferSize' integer parameter. It exposes a single attribute 'readable', which is a WHATWG 'ReadableStream'. When connected to a video track, reading from the stream yields individual 'VideoFrame' objects containing live optical camera frames; when connected to an audio track, it yields 'AudioData' objects containing PCM microphone samples. Backpressure is natively managed by the WHATWG Streams API: if the consumer stream reader does not read quickly enough and the queue exceeds 'maxBufferSize', the processor automatically drops the oldest frames to maintain low real-time latency without exhausting device RAM. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app native containers embedding video calling, barcode scanning, and vision processing mini-apps MUST support MediaStreamTrackProcessor: (1) The processor readable stream MUST be transferable across Web Worker boundaries, allowing live video tracks to be piped directly into background worker threads; (2) The container enforces a default 'maxBufferSize' clamp (between 1 and 3 frames) to prevent uncontrolled memory accumulation in video processing pipelines; (3) Access to the underlying MediaStreamTrack remains strictly subject to user camera/microphone permission grants and Permissions Policy directives.

title: MediaStreamTrackGenerator: Synthetic MediaStreamTrack Creation via WHATWG WritableStream
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Media Capture Transform Specification (§ 6 MediaStreamTrackGenerator Interface)
summary: Enables creation of custom MediaStreamTracks fed dynamically by writing VideoFrames or AudioData to a WritableStream sink.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Serving as the complementary counterpart to the processor, 'MediaStreamTrackGenerator' inherits directly from 'MediaStreamTrack' and provides a 'writable' attribute conforming to WHATWG 'WritableStream'. Instantiated via 'new MediaStreamTrackGenerator({ kind: 'video' | 'audio' })', developers can write processed 'VideoFrame' or 'AudioData' instances directly into its writer. The resulting generator object can be attached to standard HTMLVideoElement instances for playback or added to an 'RTCPeerConnection' via 'peerConnection.addTrack(generator)' for live WebRTC transmission. This architecture enables developers to construct end-to-end media manipulation pipelines: raw frames from MediaStreamTrackProcessor are piped through a custom TransformStream (e.g. background blur, green screen replacement, watermark overlay) and output into a MediaStreamTrackGenerator, completely bypassing clumsy intermediate HTMLCanvasElement drawImage pipelines. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app video conferencing, live-streaming, and beauty-filter mini-apps MUST adopt MediaStreamTrackGenerator: (1) Video processing pipelines MUST utilize MediaStreamTrackGenerator rather than Canvas.captureStream(), achieving up to 4x reduction in GPU rasterization overhead and battery consumption; (2) Frames written into the generator's writable sink MUST match the declared kind and format; (3) The generator must propagate mute/unmute events correctly to connected WebRTC peers when upstream processing is paused.

title: TransformStream Web Worker Processing: Parallelized Computer Vision & Machine Learning
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Media Capture Transform & WHATWG Streams API (§ 4 Transform Streams)
summary: Standardizes zero-overhead stream composition connecting track processors, WebAssembly/WebNN filters, and track generators in Web Workers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] By combining MediaStreamTrackProcessor and MediaStreamTrackGenerator with the WHATWG 'TransformStream' interface, media processing becomes a pure composable stream pipeline: 'processor.readable.pipeThrough(transformStream).pipeTo(generator.writable)'. Inside the TransformStream's 'transform(frame, controller)' method, developers can inspect or modify individual VideoFrames (e.g. passing pixel buffers to WebAssembly OpenCV or W3C WebNN neural network inference models) and enqueue modified frames. Because both ReadableStream and WritableStream instances are transferable objects, the entire stream pipeline can be transferred to a Dedicated Web Worker using 'worker.postMessage({ readable: processor.readable, writable: generator.writable }, [processor.readable, generator.writable])'. This executes high-throughput computer vision and AR filtering entirely in the background, completely isolating heavy ML matrix computations from the main UI thread. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app architecture standards for AI-powered camera filters and eKYC mini-apps mandate: (1) All custom frame transformations (e.g. real-time liveness detection, face mesh estimation, background segmentation) MUST be executed inside Web Workers via TransformStream pipelines; (2) Inside the transform handler, developers MUST ensure that input frames are explicitly closed ('frame.close()') after generating the output frame to avoid catastrophic memory leaks; (3) The container monitors worker execution latency, triggering automatic frame-skipping if transform handling exceeds 33 ms (the 30 fps budget).

title: WebRTC Encoded Transform (Insertable Streams): End-to-End Media Encryption & Frame Sandboxing
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform Specification (§ 3 RTCRtpScriptTransform & Encoded Frames)
summary: Regulates insertion of cryptographic transforms directly into WebRTC sender and receiver pipelines for end-to-end encryption (E2EE).
