detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebRTC Encoded Transform specification provides programmatic access to encoded video and audio frames ('RTCEncodedVideoFrame' and 'RTCEncodedAudioFrame') after codec compression but immediately prior to RTP packetization and network transmission. By instantiating an 'RTCRtpScriptTransform(worker, options)' and assigning it to 'rtpSender.transform' or 'rtpReceiver.transform', developers can execute custom cryptographic algorithms inside a dedicated worker. This enables custom end-to-end encryption (E2EE) using WebCrypto AES-GCM or MLS (Messaging Layer Security) where intermediate super-app media routing servers / SFUs (Selective Forwarding Units) cannot decrypt video or audio payloads. The transform preserves RTP packet headers and codec metadata while encrypting only the frame payload, allowing SFUs to route packets intelligently without compromising user privacy. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app confidential communications and enterprise collaboration mini-apps MUST adhere to WebRTC Encoded Transform standards: (1) Enterprise mini-apps providing private video/voice communications MUST implement client-side E2EE using RTCRtpScriptTransform; (2) Encryption keys MUST be derived through hardware-backed WebCrypto / WebAuthn PRF protocols and never transmitted in plaintext to the super-app cloud infrastructure; (3) The container sandbox prevents encoded frames from being duplicated or diverted to unapproved external endpoints.

title: Camera Capture Privacy Sandboxing: Ephemeral Stream Scoping & Instant Hardware Revocation
standard_reference: W3C Media Capture and Streams & Media Capture Transform Security Considerations
summary: Governs permission scoping, hardware indicator synchronization, and immediate pipeline teardown upon permission revocation or app backgrounding.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Capturing raw camera frames via MediaStreamTrackProcessor presents heightened privacy risks compared to standard video display, as individual raw pixels can be covertly analyzed for facial recognition, iris scanning, or physical environment reconnaissance without user awareness. The W3C specification mandates that stream processors must immediately cease emitting frames and close the readable stream whenever the underlying MediaStreamTrack ends or is muted ('track.stop()'). Furthermore, user agent security architectures require that the native platform's hardware privacy indicators (e.g. green status bar dot on iOS and Android) remain actively illuminated throughout the entire lifespan of the MediaStreamTrack, regardless of whether frames are consumed on the main thread or inside an off-screen Web Worker. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container security and compliance policies for camera-capturing mini-apps mandate: (1) When the user switches away from a mini-app or locks the mobile screen, the host container MUST immediately invoke 'track.stop()' on all active camera and microphone tracks, instantly terminating the MediaStreamTrackProcessor stream; (2) The container displays an ambient, non-dismissible banner indicating that camera capture is active and identifying the mini-app name and developer entity; (3) Store review audits strictly verify that mini-apps do not persist raw captured frames into persistent storage without explicit, contextual, secondary user authorization.

title: WICG Soft Navigation Heuristics: Single-Page Application Route Detection & Heuristic Lifecycle
standard_reference: WICG Soft Navigations Specification (§ 3 Heuristic Detection Algorithm)
summary: Standardizes browser heuristics to detect user-initiated single-page application (SPA) client-side route transitions as discrete navigations.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern super-app mini-apps heavily utilize Single Page Application (SPA) architectures where views and pages transition dynamically via client-side routing frameworks without initiating native multi-page HTTP HTML document loads. The WICG Soft Navigations specification introduces a formal browser heuristic algorithm to detect when a 'soft navigation' has occurred. A soft navigation is recognized when three sequential conditions are satisfied: (1) A user interaction (click, keypress, or navigation tap) initiates a task; (2) The URL is modified via the HTML5 History API ('history.pushState()' or 'history.replaceState()') or the WICG Navigation API; (3) A meaningful DOM mutation occurs where content is added, replaced, or rendered into the viewport. Upon meeting these criteria, the browser synthesizes a discrete navigation lifecycle event, resetting Core Web Vitals attribution metrics. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host runtime containers and performance telemetry SDKs MUST support Soft Navigation heuristics: (1) Container instrumentation MUST listen for soft navigation lifecycle signals to accurately segment per-screen telemetry and user journey flows; (2) Mini-app SPA frameworks MUST ensure that route transitions update the document location and render new DOM nodes within the same task or microtask cascade to ensure accurate detection; (3) The store review portal rejects mini-apps that simulate route changes solely through CSS display toggles without updating URL routing states.

title: PerformanceSoftNavigationTiming: Programmatic Telemetry & Entry Segmentation
standard_reference: WICG Soft Navigations & W3C Performance Timeline (§ 4 PerformanceSoftNavigationTiming)
summary: Defines the PerformanceSoftNavigationTiming entry type exposed to PerformanceObserver for real-time client-side route performance monitoring.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Soft Navigations specification extends the W3C Performance Timeline by introducing the 'soft-navigation' entry type, represented by the 'PerformanceSoftNavigationTiming' interface inheriting from 'PerformanceEntry'. Developers and monitoring agents observe these transitions using a standard PerformanceObserver: 'const observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => { for (const entry of list.getEntries()) { console.log(entry.name, entry.startTime, entry.duration); } }); observer.observe({ type: 'soft-navigation', buffered: true })'. The entry provides high-resolution performance properties including 'name' (the resolved target URL of the navigation), 'startTime' (DOMHighResTimeStamp of the initiating user interaction), and 'duration' (time elapsed until the DOM mutations settled). This eliminates reliance on proprietary monkey-patching of History API methods across heterogeneous mini-app frameworks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app observability standards mandate: (1) Mini-app client runtimes MUST ingest 'soft-navigation' performance entries to calculate per-view latency, time-to-interactive, and navigation transitions; (2) Telemetry reporting pipelines MUST buffer and transmit soft navigation performance entries to the super-app APM gateway asynchronously without blocking the main rendering loop; (3) Store performance dashboards aggregate soft navigation durations as primary latency KPIs alongside hard initial load timings.

title: User Interaction Task Attribution & DOM Mutation Correlation
standard_reference: WICG Soft Navigations Specification (§ 3.2 Task Attribution & Script Execution)
summary: Regulates causal linking between initiating user gestures, asynchronous fetch cascades, and subsequent DOM mutations.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Accurately attributing a client-side navigation requires tracking execution context across complex asynchronous boundaries, including Promises, setTimeout callbacks, and fetch/XMLHttpRequest network responses. The Soft Navigations heuristic engine relies on browser Task Attribution mechanics to propagate the context of the initiating user interaction (e.g. pointerdown/click) through the asynchronous call tree. When an asynchronous network request resolves and triggers DOM insertion, the engine verifies whether that DOM update originated from the tracked user gesture task. If the URL changed and meaningful content was injected as a result of that tracked causal chain, the navigation is successfully committed. If an update occurs autonomously (such as background polling or banner rotation), it is correctly rejected as a soft navigation. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app architectural guidelines enforce clean asynchronous route boundaries: (1) Route transitions MUST be directly triggered from user gesture events and maintain unbroken Promise chains through API requests; (2) Background data prefetching MUST NOT inadvertently trigger DOM mutations that could cause false-positive navigation attributions; (3) Automated linting rules in the developer CLI verify that navigation routing handlers maintain clear causal links between user taps and view replacements.

title: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) & Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) Reset Governance
standard_reference: WICG Soft Navigations & W3C Event Timing / Core Web Vitals Guidelines
summary: Establishes Core Web Vitals windowing and resets, partitioning INP, CLS, and LCP across individual SPA view transitions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In traditional SPAs without soft navigation integration, Core Web Vitals degrade over long user sessions: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) only measures the very first page load, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) continuously accumulates across multiple hours of usage, and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) reflects the single worst interaction across all visited views combined. The Soft Navigations standard resolves this by formally resetting metric windows upon each recognized soft navigation: (1) A new LCP candidate is identified and tracked for the newly rendered view; (2) CLS is segmented, attributing layout shifts strictly to the specific view in which they occurred; (3) INP calculations are isolated per-view, preventing a sluggish interaction on a secondary screen from penalizing the entire application session. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app Quality of Service (QoS) and store certification standards mandate: (1) Store telemetry pipelines MUST evaluate mini-app Core Web Vitals per soft navigation segment rather than on aggregated multi-hour session summaries; (2) Mini-app developers MUST maintain an INP <= 200 ms and CLS <= 0.1 across >= 75% of soft navigation route transitions; (3) Mini-apps exhibiting severe rendering freezes during route transitions (> 500 ms INP) trigger store automated performance warnings and search ranking downgrades.

title: Store Automated Review & Quality Gating for SPA Navigation Health
standard_reference: W3C Navigation Timing Level 2 & WICG Soft Navigations Implementation Standards
summary: Mandates synthetic end-to-end testing and CI/CD validation of client-side routing transitions prior to marketplace publishing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The combination of W3C Navigation Timing Level 2 (for hard document bootstrap) and WICG Soft Navigations (for in-app view routing) enables complete, end-to-end visibility into mini-app performance. In automated headless testing environments (e.g. WebDriver BiDi / Chromium test runners), test harnesses can simulate user navigation paths, verify that 'PerformanceSoftNavigationTiming' entries fire deterministically at expected milestones, and measure DOM settlement durations. This provides objective, reproducible benchmarks comparing initial cold-boot time against warm route transitions. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app submission and verification pipelines MUST incorporate soft navigation audit criteria: (1) Pre-release automated verification suites simulate core user flows (e.g. catalog -> product detail -> cart -> checkout) and assert that each screen transition registers a valid soft navigation entry; (2) Soft navigation transition latency (startTime to DOM mutation settled) MUST NOT exceed 1,000 ms on standard mid-tier mobile hardware profiles; (3) Mini-app submissions failing to register soft navigations due to broken History API integration or unhandled Promise rejections are flagged for remediation before public catalog indexing.

title: Visual Viewport API: Dual Viewport Architecture & Coordinate Space Decoupling
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch & App Identity Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Visual Viewport Specification (§ 3 The VisualViewport Interface)
summary: Decouples the dynamic visual viewport from the fixed layout viewport for accurate mobile geometry and scaling.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern mobile browsers and webview runtimes, the screen geometry is bifurcated into two distinct viewports: the 'Layout Viewport' (which defines the fixed CSS coordinate space against which elements like 'position: fixed' are positioned and media queries are evaluated) and the 'Visual Viewport' (the portion of the page currently visible on screen, which changes dynamically during pinch-to-zoom and virtual keyboard invocation). The Visual Viewport API exposes 'window.visualViewport', providing real-time geometric attributes: 'visualViewport.width', 'visualViewport.height', 'visualViewport.pageLeft', 'visualViewport.pageTop', 'visualViewport.offsetLeft', 'visualViewport.offsetTop', and 'visualViewport.scale'. Traditional properties like 'window.innerWidth' or 'document.documentElement.clientHeight' fail to reflect zoom transformations or dynamic UI chrome contractions, leading to broken mobile layouts. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app container standards mandate: (1) Mini-app frameworks MUST utilize 'window.visualViewport' dimensions rather than static window client measurements when calculating full-screen overlay bounds; (2) The container WebView MUST expose standard VisualViewport bindings across both Android (Chromium WebView) and iOS (WKWebView) environments; (3) Store review linters check that mini-apps do not hardcode fixed pixel heights that assume the layout viewport matches physical display dimensions.

title: Virtual Keyboard Dynamic Adaptation: Viewport Resize Events & Input Focus Preservation
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch & App Identity Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Visual Viewport Specification (§ 4 Events & Window Resize Handling)
summary: Governs visual viewport resizing when mobile software keyboards emerge, preventing input occlusion and form breakage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When an on-screen software keyboard (virtual keyboard) opens on a mobile device, the layout viewport typically remains unchanged while the visual viewport height ('visualViewport.height') shrinks drastically to accommodate the native keyboard. The Visual Viewport API fires a 'resize' event on 'window.visualViewport' immediately whenever keyboard emergence, orientation rotation, or browser UI collapse occurs. By registering 'visualViewport.addEventListener('resize', handleViewportChange)', applications can compute the exact keyboard height ('window.innerHeight - visualViewport.height') and adjust form scrolling dynamically. This allows the active input element or payment submission button to be scrolled smoothly into the remaining visible viewport without causing full layout recalculation thrashing ('reflow') across the entire document. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app form and checkout UX guidelines require: (1) Checkout and input-heavy mini-apps MUST listen to 'visualViewport.onresize' to guarantee that focused input fields, SMS OTP verification boxes, and submit buttons remain fully visible above the virtual keyboard; (2) Mini-apps MUST NOT pin checkout submission buttons using 'bottom: 0' fixed positioning without compensating for 'visualViewport.height' contractions; (3) Automated store review testing validates keyboard emergence across simulated 300px keyboard heights without clipping critical call-to-action buttons.

title: Pinch-to-Zoom Scale Invariance: Floating Elements & Security Capsule Positioning
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch & App Identity Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Visual Viewport Specification (§ 3.1 Geometric Coordinate Translation)
summary: Enforces scale-invariant positioning for floating toolbars, security indicators, and dialog overlays during pinch-to-zoom.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a user performs pinch-to-zoom gestures, 'visualViewport.scale' increases while 'visualViewport.pageLeft' and 'visualViewport.pageTop' track the pan offset within the larger layout viewport. Traditional CSS 'position: fixed' elements remain attached to the layout viewport, causing them to scale up and pan off-screen, obscuring critical content or disappearing completely. Using the Visual Viewport API, developers can achieve true visual anchoring by dynamically adjusting CSS transform matrices: 'element.style.transform = `translate(${visualViewport.pageLeft}px, ${visualViewport.pageTop}px) scale(${1 / visualViewport.scale})`'. This keeps floating controls, notification banners, and modal dialogs anchored perfectly to the user's visible frame at standard visual dimensions regardless of magnification level. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host container architecture rules mandate: (1) Super-app host security capsules, back buttons, and close menus rendered inside the WebView MUST remain scale-invariant, using Visual Viewport coordinate transforms or native out-of-process overlays; (2) Critical regulatory disclosures and Terms of Service acceptance modals MUST remain fully accessible and visible when users zoom in for accessibility reasons; (3) Mini-apps are strictly prohibited from disabling viewport zooming ('user-scalable=no') unless granted an explicit store accessibility exemption.

title: Visual Viewport Scroll Dynamics: Compositor Synchronization & Jitter Elimination
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch & App Identity Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Visual Viewport Specification (§ 4.2 Scroll Event Timing)
summary: Regulates scroll event dispatch and compositor-driven transform updates to eliminate visual tearing and rubber-banding lag.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'scroll' event on 'visualViewport' fires whenever the visible viewport's offset changes relative to the layout viewport. Unlike traditional document scroll events which occur on the main script thread and can be delayed by heavy JavaScript execution, visual viewport scroll events are tightly synchronized with the browser's compositor thread. The offsets 'visualViewport.offsetLeft' and 'visualViewport.offsetTop' represent the visual viewport coordinate relative to the layout viewport's origin. Monitoring these values allows developers to implement high-performance sticky headers, floating bottom navigation bars, and parallax headers that update smoothly even during high-velocity fling gestures and rubber-banding overscroll effects. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Performance criteria for super-app mini-app scrolling mandate: (1) Scroll synchronization scripts MUST execute within requestAnimationFrame callbacks scheduled from 'visualViewport.onscroll' without blocking main-thread touch dispatch; (2) Mini-apps MUST avoid synchronizing DOM positions during touchmove if visual viewport scrolling can be handled via declarative CSS 'position: sticky'; (3) Automated review audits verify that mini-app scroll pipelines maintain a stable 60 fps rendering throughput without layout thrashing.

title: Host Capsule & Native Chrome Inset Arbitration: Safe Area Integration
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch & App Identity Contracts
standard_reference: WICG Visual Viewport & CSS Viewport Safe Areas Integration Guidelines
summary: Establishes unified coordinate mediation reconciling host native menu capsules, hardware insets, and mini-app canvas bounds.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In a super-app ecosystem, a mini-app rarely operates with unconstrained full-screen access: the host app superimposes native header capsules (e.g. WeChat capsule button 'wx.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect()'), gesture navigation bars, notch/island camera cutouts, and bottom navigation bars. The Visual Viewport API bridges native shell geometry with webview layouts. When the super-app native shell expands or collapses header banners, or when keyboard insets change, the webview visual viewport reflects the exact remaining renderable area. Combining Visual Viewport geometric telemetry with CSS environment variables ('env(safe-area-inset-top)', 'env(safe-area-inset-bottom)') ensures that mini-app interactive surfaces never collide with native chrome controls or physical display hardware boundaries. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host UI integration standards mandate: (1) Host container webviews MUST synchronize native shell insets with the webview layout and visual viewport bounds; (2) The mini-app developer framework MUST provide responsive layout utilities that bind visual viewport geometry with native capsule bounding rectangles; (3) Store pre-submission checks verify that mini-app interactive elements (such as navigation icons or close buttons) do not overlap with the host super-app top-right capsule button or bottom gesture bar.

title: WHATWG Shared Workers: Cross-Tab Execution Lifecycle & Origin Sandboxing
category: Cross-Context Isolation, Bridge Security & Concurrency Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§ 10.2 Shared Workers & SharedWorkerGlobalScope)
summary: Establishes multi-context background thread execution, same-origin lifecycle management, and sandbox boundaries across tabs.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML Living Standard specifies 'SharedWorker', a background execution context accessible from multiple browsing contexts (windows, tabs, or iframes) that share the exact same origin (scheme, host, and port). Instantiated via 'const worker = new SharedWorker('worker.js', 'shared-name')', the worker remains active as long as at least one connected browsing context maintains an open MessagePort. The global scope 'SharedWorkerGlobalScope' executes on an independent operating system thread decoupled from any single window's DOM lifecycle. Same-origin policy strictly gates SharedWorker instantiation: attempts to spawn or connect to a SharedWorker across different origins are rejected with a SecurityError. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app multi-instance and multi-window runtime standards mandate: (1) SharedWorkers MUST be strictly isolated per mini-app origin; cross-mini-app sharing is prohibited by origin sandboxing; (2) When a mini-app opens secondary windows (e.g. multi-screen POS, pop-up chat window, or floating payment dialog), all views MAY connect to a common SharedWorker to maintain consistent in-memory state; (3) When all connected mini-app views close, the super-app runtime enforces worker disposal and memory reclamation within 30 seconds.

title: MessagePort Connection Handshake: Explicit Port Management & Structured Cloning
category: Cross-Context Isolation, Bridge Security & Concurrency Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§ 10.2.4 The SharedWorker Object & MessagePort)
summary: Defines point-to-point MessageChannel connection handshakes between browsing views and the shared worker global scope.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Communication with a SharedWorker is mediated exclusively through the 'MessagePort' interface exposed via 'worker.port'. Inside the SharedWorkerGlobalScope, connection attempts trigger the 'connect' event ('self.onconnect = (e) => { const port = e.ports[0]; port.start(); ... }'). Crucially, because ports communicate asynchronously, developers must invoke 'port.start()' (or set 'port.onmessage') to begin dispatching queued messages. Data transferred across 'port.postMessage(data, transfer)' undergoes the HTML Structured Clone Algorithm, enabling safe passage of complex objects, ArrayBuffers, and MessagePorts without memory aliasing. If a connected window crashes or terminates, the port remains dormant until collected by the runtime garbage collector. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app inter-view communication standards require: (1) Mini-apps connecting to SharedWorkers MUST implement heartbeat polling or explicit disconnect messages ('port.postMessage({ type: 'DISCONNECT' })') before window unload; (2) The SharedWorker MUST validate all incoming message payloads against strict schema contracts before processing state mutations; (3) Store review linters flag unhandled 'connect' events or failure to invoke 'port.start()' which causes frozen messaging pipes.

title: Centralized Network Hub: Singleton WebSocket / SSE Multiplexing & Connection Consolidation
category: Cross-Context Isolation, Bridge Security & Concurrency Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard & W3C WebSocket API Integration Standards
summary: Consolidates real-time network connections across multiple mini-app tabs into a single background WebSocket or SSE connection.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When users open multiple instances or sub-views of a mini-app (e.g. browsing different chat channels or tracking stock tickers in multiple windows), establishing duplicate WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) connections wastes mobile battery, network sockets, and server concurrency capacity. A SharedWorker acts as an origin-level singleton network broker: a single persistent WebSocket connection is opened inside 'SharedWorkerGlobalScope', and incoming messages are demultiplexed and dispatched to subscribed client ports. Conversely, outbound actions from any connected tab are serialized and sent over the shared socket. This architecture reduces backend server load by N-fold and prevents state desynchronization between tabs. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app network efficiency and battery governance guidelines mandate: (1) Mini-apps supporting multi-window or multi-tab usage with real-time streaming MUST multiplex persistent network connections through a SharedWorker; (2) The SharedWorker MUST implement exponential backoff reconnection strategies and handle offline/online network transition events; (3) The super-app host container enforces a maximum limit of 2 concurrent WebSocket connections per mini-app origin inside the SharedWorker context.

title: In-Memory State Arbitration: Cross-View Cache Synchronization & Web Locks Integration
category: Cross-Context Isolation, Bridge Security & Concurrency Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard & W3C Web Locks API (§ 4 Execution Environment)
summary: Coordinates in-memory state, prevents race conditions, and synchronizes client-side caching across concurrent mini-app views.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Because SharedWorkerGlobalScope provides a shared JavaScript memory heap accessible to all connected tabs of an origin, it acts as an authoritative in-memory state manager. In e-commerce and retail mini-apps, shopping cart quantities, user session tokens, and local cache entries can be held centrally within worker variables, ensuring instantaneous consistency across all open views without requiring constant disk reads from IndexedDB or localStorage. When combined with the W3C Web Locks API ('navigator.locks.request()'), the SharedWorker can orchestrate mutually exclusive mutations, guaranteeing that concurrent user interactions in separate tabs cannot produce race conditions, negative inventory selections, or duplicate checkout submissions. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app data integrity standards mandate: (1) Mini-apps with multi-tab shopping carts or financial ledger states MUST coordinate mutations through a SharedWorker or W3C Web Locks to prevent conflicting double-spends; (2) Sensitive tokens stored in worker memory MUST be flushed immediately upon user sign-out or session revocation signals; (3) Store QA automated tests execute concurrent simulated clicks across dual tabs to verify that state synchronization remains deterministic and race-condition free.

title: Shared Worker Resource Governance: CPU Quotas, Memory Caps & Watchdog Eviction
category: Cross-Context Isolation, Bridge Security & Concurrency Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard & Super-App Container Resource Policy
summary: Establishes container-level resource quotas, idle shutdown policies, and memory leak defenses for shared worker processes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Because SharedWorkers operate independently of visible windows, they pose potential risks of runaway background resource consumption, crypto-mining, and uncollected memory leaks if developer scripts retain references indefinitely. Browser engines enforce strict lifecycle constraints: when the last MessagePort connection is closed (e.g. all tabs navigated away or closed), the worker becomes eligible for termination. Furthermore, mobile container hosts implement process watchdog monitors that observe worker CPU usage and memory footprints. If a worker continuously consumes high CPU without active UI connections, or exceeds the container heap threshold, the host terminates the worker process. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platform host controls for SharedWorkers enforce: (1) Maximum heap memory for a SharedWorker is clamped to 64 MB on mobile hardware profiles; (2) The container watchdog terminates any SharedWorker that remains active for > 60 seconds after all client ports have disconnected; (3) Background CPU consumption by a SharedWorker when the host super-app is minimized is restricted to 0% (threads are frozen via OS cgroups/QoS policies); (4) Store review automated static analyzers audit worker scripts to detect infinite loops and unbounded array caches.

title: WHATWG FileSystemObserver: Asynchronous Filesystem Change Notification & Change Records
category: Data Governance, Offline Persistence & Client Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard (FileSystemObserver Interface & FileSystemChangeRecord)
summary: Establishes asynchronous, non-polling notification of file and directory mutations within sandboxed storage contexts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG File System specification introduces 'FileSystemObserver', an observer interface designed to detect file and directory hierarchy changes asynchronously without polling. Instantiated via 'const observer = new FileSystemObserver(callback)', the observer monitors target 'FileSystemHandle' instances (both files and directories). The callback receives a list of 'FileSystemChangeRecord' objects and the observer instance. Each change record details: 'root' (the watched FileSystemHandle), 'changedHandle' (the modified file or directory handle), 'type' (mutation category: 'appeared', 'disappeared', 'modified', 'moved', or 'unknown'), and 'relativePathComponents' (an array of path components tracing from root to the modified entity). This eliminates high-overhead periodic directory stat traversals and battery-draining polling loops. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app sandbox storage guidelines mandate: (1) Mini-apps observing local cache directories, offline documents, or asset repositories MUST utilize FileSystemObserver rather than setInterval polling; (2) The container webview MUST implement strict backpressure buffers, batching high-frequency change records (e.g. during bulk database sync) into single macro-task dispatches; (3) Store review linters flag recursive polling loops over FileSystemDirectoryHandle, requiring migration to FileSystemObserver.

title: FileSystemObserver.observe(): Observation Scoping, Recursive Directory Trees & Permission Binding
category: Data Governance, Offline Persistence & Client Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard (§ FileSystemObserver.observe method & options)
summary: Defines target handle attachment, recursive directory subtree monitoring, and origin sandbox validation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Observation begins via 'observer.observe(handle, options)'. The 'options' dictionary supports 'recursive: true|false' (defaulting to false). When 'recursive' is true on a FileSystemDirectoryHandle, the underlying operating system file watcher (such as inotify on Linux/Android, FSEvents on macOS/iOS, or ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) monitors all descendant subdirectories and nested files. Calling observe() on a handle outside the mini-app's permitted origin sandbox or without valid read permissions immediately throws a SecurityError or NotAllowedError. Multiple handles can be observed by a single FileSystemObserver instance, with records aggregated into a single callback batch. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host container policy dictates: (1) Recursive observation MUST be restricted to depths <= 5 subdirectories within the mini-app Origin Private File System (OPFS) or user-picked project trees to prevent native OS file-descriptor exhaustion; (2) Mini-apps observing user-selected external directory trees MUST handle permission revocations gracefully without crashing the UI thread; (3) Automated store review audits verify that mini-apps do not register redundant duplicate observers on overlapping directory paths.

title: FileSystemObserver Lifecycle: Explicit Disconnection, Garbage Collection & OS Watcher Reclamation
category: Data Governance, Offline Persistence & Client Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard (§ FileSystemObserver.disconnect & unobserve)
summary: Governs observer teardown, unregistering native OS kernel watchers to eliminate kernel handle leakage and memory pinning.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Active filesystem observers hold references to operating system file event hooks. The 'disconnect()' method on FileSystemObserver stops the observer from observing any handles and clears all queued change records pending dispatch. Calling 'unobserve(handle)' specifically removes observation for a designated FileSystemHandle while keeping other observed targets active. If a window navigates, crashes, or is discarded by the host memory manager, the browser engine automatically tears down the associated kernel inotify/FSEvents handles. However, within long-running Single Page Applications, failure to invoke disconnect() retains DOM closures and prevents garbage collection of associated FileSystemHandles. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer standards mandate: (1) Mini-apps MUST call 'observer.disconnect()' during component unmount, page freeze ('freeze' Page Lifecycle event), or window unload; (2) The container watchdog actively monitors active inotify handles per webview, killing webview processes that leak > 32 active OS filesystem watch descriptors; (3) Store static code analysis scans verify deterministic observer cleanup patterns in mini-app lifecycle hooks.

title: OPFS & SQLite WAL File Synchronization: Coordinated Multi-Worker & Multi-View Persistence
category: Data Governance, Offline Persistence & Client Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard & SQLite Wasm with OPFS Coordinated Architecture
summary: Coordinates SQLite Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and local state invalidation across concurrent mini-app worker contexts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When mini-apps utilize high-performance SQLite WebAssembly backed by the Origin Private File System (OPFS), writes mutate the main database file and companion Write-Ahead Log ('-wal') and shared memory ('-shm') files. Because FileSystemSyncAccessHandle locks files exclusively in worker contexts, other auxiliary threads or secondary browsing contexts cannot continuously read the active database without causing lock contention. By placing a FileSystemObserver on the OPFS root directory, secondary workers and UI windows receive push notifications of '-wal' modifications, allowing them to invalidate in-memory query caches or trigger non-blocking checkpoint reads without executing active lock polling. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Multi-threaded mini-app architecture criteria enforce: (1) Mini-apps utilizing SQLite Wasm with OPFS MUST use FileSystemObserver or BroadcastChannel to signal database mutation events across views; (2) Auxiliary reporting threads MUST NOT acquire exclusive write locks during active UI user interaction tasks; (3) Store QA tests verify that multi-tab POS or inventory updates reflect across concurrent views within <= 100 ms of transaction commit.

title: Storage Observer Privacy Sandboxing: Covert Timing Side-Channel Defense & Path Sanitization
category: Data Governance, Offline Persistence & Client Storage Isolation
standard_reference: WHATWG File System Living Standard (§ Security & Privacy Considerations)
summary: Prevents covert channel metadata leakage, path traversal attacks, and cross-origin file system finger-printing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] FileSystemChangeRecord structures sanitize path information to prevent host filesystem reconnaissance. In 'relativePathComponents', paths are reported relative only to the explicitly granted root handle; absolute operating system paths (e.g. '/data/user/0/com.superapp/...') are never exposed to the web runtime. Furthermore, to mitigate covert timing side-channels (where malicious scripts deduce background user activity or disk encryption status through microsecond file event timing), browser implementations apply temporal quantization to change notifications, coalescing rapid successive writes into singular 'modified' events. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app security and privacy rules mandate: (1) Mini-apps are strictly prohibited from parsing relativePathComponents to infer host platform directory structures or OS versions; (2) The container webview MUST enforce strict origin-private path clamping, ensuring no symlinks or external mount references can leak into FileSystemObserver notifications; (3) Automated store review security probes attempt directory traversal exploits and verify that change events remain strictly contained within the mini-app's isolated storage quota.

title: WebAuthn largeBlob Extension: Authenticator-Bound Cryptographic Storage for Decentralized State
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (§ 10.4 Large blob storage extension 'largeBlob')
summary: Enables reading and writing opaque encrypted payloads directly onto FIDO2 authenticators bound to discoverable passkeys.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WebAuthn Level 3 'largeBlob' registration and authentication extension permits Relying Parties (RPs) to store and retrieve opaque binary data directly on a FIDO2 authenticator or passkey keychain. During 'navigator.credentials.create()', the RP declares 'extensions: { largeBlob: { support: 'required' | 'preferred' } }'. Upon credential generation, the authenticator returns 'largeBlob: { supported: true }'. During subsequent 'navigator.credentials.get()' invocations, the client can either read the stored blob via 'extensions: { largeBlob: { read: true } }' (retrieving the decrypted ArrayBuffer in 'authResults.getClientExtensionResults().largeBlob.blob') or write a replacement payload via 'extensions: { largeBlob: { write: dataArrayBuffer } }' (returning 'written: true'). The payload is cryptographically encrypted using symmetric keys derived within the authenticator hardware, making it unreadable without biometric user presence verification. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app zero-trust and decentralized identity standards mandate: (1) Mini-apps implementing decentralized identity, end-to-end encrypted messaging, or client-side wallet seeds MAY request 'largeBlob' storage to hold offline root keys without relying on cloud keychains; (2) The super-app host container MUST verify authenticator 'largeBlob' capability before exposing client write operations; (3) Store review security audits verify that stored blobs do not exceed authenticator capacity (typically 1 KB to 4 KB) and handle authenticator full errors gracefully.

title: WebAuthn Device Public Key (devicePubKey) Extension: Hardware Binding & Passkey Sync Verification
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (§ 10.5 Device Public Key Extension 'devicePubKey')
summary: Cryptographically distinguishes between synchronized cloud passkeys and physical device hardware trust anchors.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Multi-device passkeys (synced via Apple iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager) provide seamless consumer recovery, but financial-grade enterprise applications require proof that a specific physical mobile device executed the assertion. The WebAuthn 'devicePubKey' extension solves this: during registration and authentication, the RP requests 'extensions: { devicePubKey: { attestation: 'direct' | 'none' } }'. The authenticator generates or accesses a device-bound asymmetric key pair resident in the device's hardware enclave (e.g. Android Keystore StrongBox or Apple Secure Enclave). The assertion includes a signature over the authentication response signed by the device private key, alongside an attestation statement proving physical hardware residency. This allows the RP to verify whether an assertion came from a newly synced untrusted device or a recognized, enrolled corporate device. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app high-security and financial mini-app standards mandate: (1) Banking, securities trading, and enterprise administration mini-apps MUST request the 'devicePubKey' extension during high-value transaction authorization; (2) The super-app identity gateway validates the device signature against enrolled device fingerprints before clearing transactions > 50,000,000 VND; (3) Store review compliance checks verify that financial mini-apps trigger step-up multi-factor SMS or out-of-band biometric verification when an unrecognized 'devicePubKey' is observed.

title: WebAuthn Conditional Mediation API: Frictionless Form Autofill & Passkey Discovery
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (§ 5.1.4 Conditional UI Mediation & PublicKeyCredential)
summary: Integrates passkey authentication directly into HTML username/password autofill suggestions without modal popups.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Before the advent of Conditional UI, WebAuthn required modal browser dialogs that interrupted user workflow. The static method 'PublicKeyCredential.isConditionalMediationAvailable()' returns a Promise resolving to true if the client webview supports conditional mediation. When available, the application initiates an asynchronous passkey discovery request on page load: 'navigator.credentials.get({ mediation: 'conditional', publicKey: { ... } })'. HTML input fields configured with 'autocomplete='username webauthn'' display available passkeys in the native autofill dropdown. Selecting an identity instantly prompts biometric verification and completes authentication without requiring navigation to a dedicated sign-in view. If the user chooses to type credentials manually, the pending conditional request can be aborted cleanly via an AbortController signal. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app mini-app authentication UX guidelines require: (1) Mini-apps featuring user sign-in MUST query 'PublicKeyCredential.isConditionalMediationAvailable()' and implement conditional passkey autofill where supported; (2) Mini-apps MUST provide fallback username/password or phone OTP input paths when conditional mediation is unavailable or rejected; (3) Store UX review criteria reject mini-apps that display blocking modal passkey prompts immediately on launch without user intent.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Hybrid Protocol: QR-Code Cross-Device Authentication & BLE Presence Proximity
standard_reference: FIDO Alliance Client to Authenticator Protocol (CTAP) v2.1 (§ 9 Hybrid Transport caBLE)
summary: Enables cross-device authentication pairing desktop/kiosk mini-apps with mobile phone authenticators via QR codes and BLE.
detail: [SPEC FACT] FIDO CTAP 2.1 specifies the 'hybrid' transport (formerly known as caBLE - cloud-assisted BLE). When an untrusted browser context (such as a desktop web browser, POS terminal, or smart kiosk) requests WebAuthn credentials from a user whose passkey is stored on their mobile smartphone, the client initiates a hybrid handshake. The client generates an ephemeral QR code encoding an encrypted tunneling session URL and cryptographic nonce. Scanning the QR code with the smartphone's super-app or native camera establishes a secure WebSocket relay. Proximity is cryptographically enforced via ephemeral Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) advertisement beacons: the smartphone and client verify physical co-location within <= 10 meters, preventing remote relay and man-in-the-middle phishing attacks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Omni-channel super-app and desktop mini-app standards mandate: (1) Desktop and smart TV mini-apps MUST support the CTAP 2.1 hybrid transport to allow seamless login using the user's mobile super-app wallet; (2) The QR-code pairing handshake MUST enforce a maximum TTL of 60 seconds before session invalidation; (3) Store security review validates that proximity verification prevents cross-site session hijacking across network subnets.

title: WebAuthn Relying Party ID Scoping & Web App Origin Association: Cross-Origin Passkey Federation
standard_reference: W3C Web Authentication Level 3 (§ 5.1.2 Relying Party Parameters & RP ID validation)
summary: Governs RP ID domain boundary enforcement, suffix matching, and multi-tenant mini-app passkey federation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In WebAuthn, 'rp.id' defines the cryptographic namespace of the credential. By specification, an origin may only create or assert credentials for an RP ID that is a registrable domain suffix of the calling origin's effective domain (e.g. 'checkout.superapp.vn' can claim 'rp.id: superapp.vn', but cannot claim 'bank.com'). If a third-party mini-app hosted at 'merchant.miniapp.superapp.vn' attempts to invoke WebAuthn, it is bound to its origin domain hierarchy. To allow shared passkeys across multiple related domains or between native apps and mini-app webviews, modern operating systems support Digital Asset Links (assetlinks.json on Android) and Apple App Site Association (apple-app-site-association on iOS), which cryptographically verify bidirectional domain linkages before permitting cross-origin RP ID assertions. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app identity architecture standards mandate: (1) First-party ecosystem mini-apps MAY share the super-app root RP ID ('superapp.vn') only if their domains are explicitly enrolled in the super-app's verified origin manifest; (2) Third-party merchant mini-apps MUST register their own independent RP ID to prevent cross-tenant credential theft; (3) The super-app host webview enforces strict clientDataJSON origin validation, rejecting any attempt by a sandboxed mini-app to impersonate the host super-app identity.

title: IETF RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs - Standardized Error Semantics & Media Type
category: Operational Reliability, Change Governance & Distributed Tracing
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs, obsoleting RFC 7807)
summary: Establishes modern machine-readable HTTP error representation using 'application/problem+json' and 'application/problem+xml'.
detail: [SPEC FACT] IETF RFC 9457 standardizes error responses for HTTP APIs, officially obsoleting RFC 7807. RFC 9457 defines the 'application/problem+json' media type containing standard top-level JSON members: 'type' (a URI reference that identifies the problem type, defaulting to 'about:blank'), 'status' (the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence), 'title' (a short, human-readable summary of the problem type that SHOULD NOT change between occurrences), 'detail' (a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence), and 'instance' (a URI reference identifying the specific occurrence of the problem). RFC 9457 clarifies extension member handling, explicitly forbids changing error semantics based on HTTP status text, and introduces strict rules for parsing custom extension members while preserving forward compatibility. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app gateway API standards mandate: (1) All super-app backend APIs and mini-app partner gateway endpoints MUST return RFC 9457 compliant 'application/problem+json' payloads for 4xx and 5xx HTTP responses; (2) Error responses MUST NOT expose internal stack traces, database schema names, or private server IP addresses in the 'detail' field; (3) Store automated API conformance suites test partner mini-app endpoints against RFC 9457 schemas, flagging non-compliant unstructured JSON error bodies.

title: IETF RFC 9440: Client-Cert HTTP Header Field - Transporting Client Mutual TLS Certificates to Gateways
category: Operational Reliability, Change Governance & Distributed Tracing
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9440 (Client-Cert HTTP Header Field)
summary: Standardizes forwarding client mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates from reverse proxies and edge load balancers to origin services.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In modern cloud infrastructure, TLS termination occurs at edge ingress proxies (such as Envoy, NGINX, or Cloudflare) rather than at origin application servers. Prior to RFC 9440, proprietary and insecure HTTP headers (such as 'X-Client-Cert', 'SSL-Client-Cert') were used to convey client certificates to backend services. IETF RFC 9440 standardizes the 'Client-Cert' header field using RFC 8941 Structured Field Values (specifically a Byte Sequence denoted by ':base64:'). The header contains the exact DER-encoded client X.509 certificate received during the mTLS handshake. An optional companion header 'Client-Cert-Chain' conveys intermediate certificate authorities. Because this header grants authentication rights, edge proxies MUST sanitize, overwrite, or strip any client-supplied 'Client-Cert' headers received from untrusted external networks. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app zero-trust edge architecture mandates: (1) Reverse proxies terminating B2B partner mTLS connections MUST populate the RFC 9440 'Client-Cert' header before forwarding requests to internal store services; (2) Edge gateways MUST unconditionally strip incoming 'Client-Cert' headers from external mobile clients to prevent certificate spoofing; (3) Store internal microservices validating FAPI mTLS tokens MUST parse client certificates from RFC 9440 structured fields.

title: RFC 9457 Problem Extensions: Distributed Trace Correlation & Error Categorization Codes
category: Operational Reliability, Change Governance & Distributed Tracing
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9457 (§ 3.2 Extension Members & § 4 Security Considerations)
summary: Defines domain-specific extension members within Problem Details for end-to-end trace correlation and error categorization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 9457 Section 3.2 allows problem details documents to be extended with additional domain-specific members. In enterprise distributed systems, standard members are augmented with: 'code' (an immutable machine-readable error classification string, e.g. 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS' or 'QUOTA_EXCEEDED'), 'trace_id' (correlating to the W3C Trace Context 'traceparent' trace-id), 'retry_after' (suggested cooldown in seconds matching the Retry-After header), and 'invalid_params' (an array detailing field-level JSON validation failures). These extensions allow client libraries to make programmatic retry or remediation decisions without parsing localized prose text. RFC 9457 cautions that extension member names must not collide with standard members or future RFC revisions. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app platform client SDK guidelines require: (1) Mini-app client network interceptors MUST extract 'trace_id' and 'code' from RFC 9457 responses to correlate frontend error logs with backend distributed traces; (2) Form validation error responses MUST return an 'invalid_params' array containing 'name', 'reason', and 'rule' attributes; (3) Store telemetry pipelines ingest Problem Details extensions to aggregate real-time error heatmaps per mini-app.

title: Mutual TLS Certificate-Bound Access Tokens: RFC 9440 Gateway Integration with RFC 8705
category: Operational Reliability, Change Governance & Distributed Tracing
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9440 & RFC 8705 (OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication and Certificate-Bound Access Tokens)
summary: Integrates edge-forwarded client certificates with OAuth 2.0 certificate-bound token verification at internal API gateways.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In Financial-Grade API (FAPI 2.0) deployments, access tokens are cryptographically bound to the client's mTLS certificate via the 'cnf.x5t#S256' confirmation claim in the JWT. When the reverse proxy terminates mTLS and forwards the certificate via the RFC 9440 'Client-Cert' header, the downstream API gateway extracts the DER certificate, computes its SHA-256 fingerprint, and compares it directly with the 'cnf.x5t#S256' claim in the Bearer token. If the fingerprints do not match exactly, the gateway rejects the request with HTTP 401 Unauthorized and an RFC 9457 problem detail of type 'https://api.superapp.vn/errors/invalid-token-binding'. This ensures sender-constrained token security even when microservices run behind TLS-terminating load balancers. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app financial settlement and B2B merchant API standards mandate: (1) Gateways validating certificate-bound access tokens MUST compute SHA-256 digests over the RFC 9440 Client-Cert header payload; (2) Rejection of mismatched tokens MUST return an RFC 9457 response with code 'TOKEN_BINDING_MISMATCH'; (3) Store security compliance audits test gateway defenses against certificate substitution and token replay attacks.

title: Client-Side Problem Handling: Structured Error Parsing, Offline Fallback & Sentry Telemetry
category: Operational Reliability, Change Governance & Distributed Tracing
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9457 (§ 3 Problem Details JSON Object & Client Handling Guidelines)
summary: Establishes standardized client-side response interceptors, mapping Problem Details into user-friendly UI degradation states.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Client applications encountering HTTP 4xx or 5xx responses inspect the 'Content-Type' response header. When 'application/problem+json' is detected, the mini-app runtime parses the payload into a typed ProblemDocument. Rather than displaying generic 'Network Error' alerts, client UI components use the 'type' URI and 'code' to trigger contextual fallbacks: for instance, an 'OUT_OF_STOCK' problem updates inventory buttons to disabled state; a 'RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED' problem initiates an exponential backoff countdown based on the 'retry_after' member. Furthermore, unhandled Problem Details are automatically dispatched to the super-app crash and telemetry reporting pipeline via the W3C Reporting API. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app developer SDK requirements dictate: (1) The official super-app HTTP client library MUST automatically parse RFC 9457 problem documents and expose them as typed JavaScript Error instances; (2) Mini-apps MUST NOT present raw technical error codes or untranslated backend detail strings directly to end-users in consumer checkout flows; (3) Store quality assurance reviews run chaos testing, injecting RFC 9457 429 and 503 problem responses to verify graceful UI degradation without application crashing.

title: W3C Web App Manifest: 'shortcuts' Member & ShortcutInfo Dictionary Structure
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Manifest Working Draft (§ shortcuts member & ShortcutInfo dictionary)
summary: Standardizes declarative shortcuts in the web app manifest, defining key tasks and destinations exposed to host launchers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Web App Manifest specification defines the 'shortcuts' member as an array of ShortcutInfo dictionaries. Each ShortcutInfo object represents a link to a key task or destination within the web application. The dictionary supports the following normative members: 'name' (USVString, mandatory, human-readable label presented to users in context menus), 'short_name' (USVString, optional, truncated label used when space is constrained), 'description' (USVString, optional, contextual purpose of the shortcut for accessibility), 'url' (USVString, mandatory, the target URL resolved against the manifest URL; MUST be within the manifest's 'scope'), and 'icons' (sequence of ManifestImageResource dictionaries providing platform-tailored graphical assets). When the user invokes a shortcut from the host launcher, the user agent opens the application window navigated directly to the specified shortcut URL. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app catalog and package validation rules mandate: (1) Every mini-app manifest 'shortcuts' array MUST contain between 1 and 4 entries; additional entries beyond 4 are pruned by store ingestion pipelines to match OS launcher display limits; (2) The 'url' member of each shortcut MUST resolve strictly within the declared mini-app 'scope' and MUST use HTTPS or the super-app custom mini-app URI scheme; any cross-origin URL triggers immediate package rejection; (3) Each shortcut MUST define both 'name' (<= 20 characters) and 'short_name' (<= 12 characters) to guarantee clean, non-truncated rendering across Android App Shortcuts and iOS Quick Action action sheets.

title: Shortcut Icons Asset Specifications: Sizing, MIME-Types & Launcher Theming Adaptation
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Manifest (§ ManifestImageResource & icon purpose rules)
summary: Establishes resolution, format, and masking requirements for mini-app shortcut graphical resources.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Web App Manifest (§ Image resource processing), the 'icons' member inside a ShortcutInfo dictionary specifies an array of image resources. Each image object defines 'src' (relative or absolute URL), 'sizes' (space-separated list of dimensions, e.g. '96x96 192x192'), 'type' (MIME type such as 'image/png' or 'image/svg+xml'), and 'purpose' ('any', 'maskable', or 'monochrome'). On modern mobile operating systems (Android 8+ Adaptive Icons and Material You / iOS 18 Tinted Home Screen), launcher quick action menus require specialized graphical assets: square raster images (recommended 96x96 px or 192x192 px) or vector SVGs, with 'monochrome' purpose assets utilized for OS dark mode, dynamic system accent theming, or accessibility high-contrast displays. Missing or corrupted icon assets cause host launchers to fall back to a generic default mini-app glyph. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app asset compliance checks require: (1) Mini-app developers MUST provide at least one PNG icon with dimensions 96x96 or 192x192 pixels or a scalable SVG for each shortcut item; (2) Total combined payload for all shortcut icons MUST NOT exceed 256 KB per mini-app package; (3) Store CI/CD automated review linters verify that all icon URLs resolve to local package files rather than external CDN URLs, preventing remote tampering, network latency during launcher long-press, or unauthorized tracking via icon request referrers.

title: Host OS Launcher Quick Actions: Android ShortcutManager & iOS UIApplicationShortcutItem Bridge
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: WICG App Shortcuts Explainer & Mobile OS Launcher Integration Guidelines
summary: Maps declarative manifest shortcuts into native OS launcher menus via platform shortcut managers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Host super-app containers project manifest shortcuts into the mobile operating system's native quick action interfaces. On Android, the super-app container invokes 'ShortcutManager.setDynamicShortcuts()' or publishes pinned shortcuts, wrapping each manifest ShortcutInfo into a native 'ShortcutInfo.Builder' with an Intent targeted at the mini-app runtime activity containing the serialized target mini-app app_id and deep-link route. On iOS, the container dynamically populates 'UIApplication.shared.shortcutItems' with 'UIApplicationShortcutItem' instances when a mini-app is installed or added to the user's favorites. When a user long-presses the super-app icon on their home screen or launcher, the OS displays the registered quick actions without launching the parent super-app home UI first. [STORE REQUIREMENT] The super-app host container architecture specifies: (1) When a mini-app is pinned to the host OS home screen or added to 'My Mini Apps' shelf, the host container bridge MUST register up to 3 priority shortcuts into the OS shortcut manager; (2) Shortcut intent dispatching MUST route directly through the host security gateway, validating that the calling process matches the OS launcher before initiating the cold-start of the isolated mini-app sandbox; (3) Host bridge APIs (e.g. 'my.setShortcuts' or 'wx.setShortcuts') MUST permit dynamic runtime shortcut updates (e.g. recent orders, favorite transfer recipient) subject to a rate-limiting throttle of at most 5 updates per hour to prevent OS IPC exhaustion.

title: Shortcut Deep-Linking: Query Parameter Routing, Session Rehydration & Sandbox Isolation
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Manifest (§ Navigation scope and URL handling)
summary: Governs deep-link parameter passing, security validation, and session preservation during shortcut launches.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'url' member of a ShortcutInfo dictionary frequently carries query string parameters or hash fragments (e.g. '/orders?tab=recent', '/pay?scan=true', '/chat/support') to direct the mini-app runtime to a specific nested view. When launched from an OS launcher shortcut, the container webview processes the target URL according to the W3C Web App Manifest launch rules. If an instance of the mini-app is already active in background memory, the container must reconcile the new launch via the Web App Launch API ('launch_handler') or host lifecycle events (e.g. 'onShow({ path, query, scene: 1014 })'), delivering the shortcut parameters without discarding uncommitted form state or triggering unnecessary full-page reloads. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store review criteria and container runtime security mandate: (1) Mini-app shortcuts MUST NOT embed sensitive tokens, session credentials, or unencrypted PII directly in the shortcut query parameters; (2) The super-app host container MUST sanitize all incoming shortcut query parameters against script injection, path traversal ('../'), and protocol smuggling before passing them into the mini-app runtime environment; (3) In multi-instance or single-instance container architectures, shortcut launches MUST trigger the standardized lifecycle event ('onAppRoute' / 'onShow') with a dedicated referrer identifier ('source: os_launcher_shortcut') allowing mini-apps to track acquisition channel conversion safely.

title: Shortcuts Governance: Multi-Locale Localization, Screen Reader Semantics & Store Review Linters
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C Web App Manifest (§ Localization of manifest members & accessibility considerations)
summary: Enforces internationalization, descriptive accessibility labels, and automated store linter rules for shortcuts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C manifest internationalization rules and accessibility guidelines (WCAG 2.2), shortcut items exposed to system context menus must be accessible to assistive technologies (TalkBack, VoiceOver) and adapt dynamically to system locale changes. The 'description' property in ShortcutInfo provides assistive screen readers with an extended accessible description of the shortcut action (e.g. 'View and track your active food delivery orders' for a shortcut labeled 'Track Order'). When a super-app supports multi-locale packages, manifest shortcuts must leverage localized manifest resource bundles or locale-specific manifest files corresponding to the user's active BCP 47 language preference, ensuring that launcher action labels render in the correct system language. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store automated compliance pipelines enforce the following quality gates: (1) Developers deploying mini-apps across multi-lingual regions (e.g. VN, EN, TH, LA) MUST provide localized shortcut names in their app manifest localization tables; (2) Every shortcut MUST define a non-empty 'description' attribute containing between 10 and 100 characters, failing automated submission checks if descriptions are identical to 'name' or left blank; (3) Store review linters verify that shortcut destinations are functional routes that do not return 404/500 HTTP errors or render empty white screens when launched directly without prior warm-up.

title: WHATWG HTML Popover API: Declarative Top-Layer Overlays & 'popover' Global Attribute
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§ The popover attribute & Top Layer rendering)
summary: Establishes native browser top-layer overlay rendering without z-index conflicts using declarative HTML attributes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML specification standardizes the 'popover' global attribute, enabling any HTML element to be rendered in the browser's browser-managed 'top layer'. When set to 'auto' or 'manual' (e.g. '<div popover="auto">'), the element is hidden by default ('display: none') until invoked. Trigger elements (e.g. '<button popovertarget="my-popover" popovertargetaction="toggle|show|hide">') declaratively control the popover's visibility without requiring custom JavaScript click handlers. Crucially, elements in the top layer exist outside standard stacking contexts, completely eliminating legacy CSS 'z-index: 99999' wars, overflow clipping from parent 'overflow: hidden' containers, and complex fixed-positioning hacks. The pseudo-element '::backdrop' allows customizable scrim styling behind the active popover. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app UI component standards mandate: (1) Mini-app modal dropdowns, tooltips, action menus, and contextual sheets SHOULD migrate from legacy z-index wrapper divs to the native HTML Popover API to eliminate DOM clipping and layout recalculation overhead; (2) Mini-app packages submitting custom modal components with z-index values exceeding 10,000 are flagged by store static analyzers, recommending standard popover attributes; (3) The host container runtime MUST support the standard Popover API polyfill for legacy webview instances while enforcing native top-layer acceleration on modern engines.

title: Popover Light Dismiss & Focus Management: Keyboard Accessibility & Nested Menu Trees
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§ Popover light dismiss algorithms & focus navigation)
summary: Governs automatic dismissal heuristics, 'Escape' key traps, and accessible focus management in popover hierarchies.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Popover API defines distinct behavioral semantics for 'popover="auto"' versus 'popover="manual"'. Popovers with 'auto' implement native 'light dismiss': clicking anywhere outside the popover element, pressing the 'Escape' key, or opening another unrelated 'auto' popover immediately dismisses the active popover and fires the 'beforetoggle' and 'toggle' (with 'newState: closed') events. In contrast, 'manual' popovers do not auto-dismiss and must be closed programmatically or via explicit target action buttons. Furthermore, the Popover API maintains an ancestor tree of nested popovers (such as sub-menus and cascading dropdowns), ensuring that clicking an item within a child popover does not dismiss its ancestor popover chain. Focus is handled cleanly: opening an 'auto' popover can focus the first autofocusable child, and upon closing, focus returns deterministically to the invoking button element. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Mini-app accessibility and UX review requirements specify: (1) Ephemeral UI elements (tooltips, dropdowns, combo-boxes) MUST use 'popover="auto"' to guarantee standard mobile light dismiss and hardware 'Back' / 'Escape' button handling; (2) Mini-apps MUST NOT intercept 'beforetoggle' to prevent dismissal of 'auto' popovers, as trap-dismissal violates WCAG 2.2 non-interference guidelines and super-app UX rules; (3) Store QA testing verifies that closing a mini-app popover restores focus to the trigger element without resetting scroll position or dropping virtual keyboard accessibility focus.

title: W3C CSS Anchor Positioning Level 1: Declarative Overlay Tethering & Zero-JS Layout Alignment
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C CSS Anchor Positioning Module Level 1 (Working Draft)
summary: Enables anchoring top-layer popovers and tooltips to arbitrary reference elements purely via declarative CSS.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C CSS Anchor Positioning specification introduces native browser capabilities to anchor fixed or absolute elements (including top-layer popovers) to specific target elements in the DOM without JavaScript computation. An anchor element is designated using 'anchor-name: --my-anchor-id'. The positioned element associates with it via 'position-anchor: --my-anchor-id' and positions itself using the 'anchor()' function (e.g. 'top: anchor(bottom); left: anchor(center)') or the high-level 'position-area' property (e.g. 'position-area: bottom span-right'). Crucially, the browser's compositor recalculates anchor geometry directly during scrolling and resizing on the render thread, completely eliminating jank, scroll lag, and the performance penalties of third-party JavaScript positioning libraries (such as Popper.js or Floating UI) that rely on 'requestAnimationFrame' or 'getBoundingClientRect' polling. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app rendering and performance criteria mandate: (1) Mini-apps deploying floating menus, item callouts, or anchored badges SHOULD adopt CSS Anchor Positioning to minimize main-thread execution time and bundle size; (2) Store automated performance audits verify that mini-apps do not attach continuous scroll or resize event listeners solely to reposition tooltips, as main-thread scroll listener thrashing degrades super-app frame rate (FPS < 55 on mid-tier mobile hardware); (3) Container runtime stylesheets provide fallback positioning tokens for older webview engines lacking full anchor positioning support.

title: CSS @position-try & Fallback Schemes: Viewport Collision Avoidance & Screen Edge Flipping
category: Interoperable Discovery, Launch Contracts & Protocol Handlers
standard_reference: W3C CSS Anchor Positioning (§ position-try-fallbacks & @position-try rule)
summary: Provides automated, declarative repositioning of anchored popovers when colliding with viewport boundaries or mobile keyboards.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A fundamental challenge of mobile overlay layout is viewport clipping when the anchor element sits near the edge of the screen or when the software keyboard emerges. CSS Anchor Positioning solves this natively via '@position-try' rules and the 'position-try-fallbacks' property. Developers can define custom fallback positions or use pre-defined flipping keywords: 'position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, --custom-fallback'. If the primary anchored position overflows the visible viewport, the browser automatically evaluates the fallback candidates in order, selecting the first position that fits entirely within the available screen real estate without overflowing. This process occurs in the browser layout pipeline before painting, preventing layout shifting, flickering, or partial occlusion of critical interactive elements. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app UX quality standards dictate: (1) All mini-app anchored popovers and menus MUST declare 'position-try-fallbacks' (at minimum 'flip-block') to ensure complete visibility when invoked near the top navigation bar or bottom screen bezel; (2) In mobile form entry views, popover menus attached to input fields MUST handle on-screen keyboard emergence without being pushed offscreen or obscured by system input method editors (IME); (3) Store review linters verify that popovers do not cause horizontal scrolling ('overflow-x: auto') on 360px mobile viewports during fallback recalculations.

title: Super-App Host UI Sandboxing: Top-Layer Containment & Anti-Capsule Hijacking Policies
category: Security Architecture, Boundary Hardening & Client Isolation
standard_reference: Super-App Container Security Architecture & Top-Layer Containment Standards
summary: Prevents mini-app popovers from obscuring host navigation capsule buttons, permission dialogs, or security indicators.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Because the HTML Popover API and 'dialog' elements render into the browser top layer, untrusted or malicious mini-app code could theoretically create a full-screen, transparent, or visually deceptive top-layer popover that intercepts touches or disguises itself as the host super-app chrome. In particular, super-app platforms (such as WeChat, Alipay, and Grab) maintain a persistent native host 'capsule button' (containing 'Close', 'More Options', and official verified domain badges) positioned at the top-right corner of the mobile viewport. If a mini-app's webview top layer were unconstrained, a mini-app could spoof host dialogs or prevent the user from exiting the mini-app by placing an invisible or misleading popover directly over the host close button. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app container security rules strictly enforce top-layer containment: (1) The host container native chrome (capsule button, URL bar, SSL security badges, system permission prompts) MUST be rendered in a separate native OS view layer stacked strictly ABOVE the Webview container, ensuring that no webview top layer element can ever occlude or capture touch events meant for host navigation controls; (2) Mini-app stylesheets MUST NOT use negative margins, CSS transforms, or fixed coordinates that attempt to position popovers into the designated host safe-area exclusion zones ('env(safe-area-inset-top)'); (3) Automated store review dynamic analysis tests mini-app popovers against anti-clickjacking criteria, automatically rejecting any mini-app that attempts to block the host exit gesture or simulate super-app system authorization dialogs.

title: W3C Audio Output Devices API: HTMLMediaElement.setSinkId() & Speaker Routing Governance
category: Security Architecture, Boundary Hardening & Client Isolation
standard_reference: W3C Audio Output Devices API (Candidate Recommendation)
summary: Governs programmatic routing of audio streams to specific physical output devices and hardware sink sandboxing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Audio Output Devices API standardizes the mechanism by which web applications route audio playback from HTMLMediaElement ('<audio>' or '<video>') to a specific physical output transducer (such as built-in earpiece, external loudspeaker, Bluetooth headset, or USB audio interface). The method 'element.setSinkId(sinkId)' accepts a valid 'deviceId' obtained from 'MediaDevices.enumerateDevices()' or 'MediaDevices.selectAudioOutput()'. Passing an empty string '""' resets audio playback to the operating system's default output device. If the target 'sinkId' does not exist or access has been restricted by permissions, 'setSinkId()' rejects with a NotFoundError or NotAllowedError. Access to non-default audio sinks is gated by the Permissions Policy directive 'speaker-selection'. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host container audio governance mandates: (1) Mini-apps invoking 'element.setSinkId()' MUST declare the 'speaker-selection' capability in their mini-app manifest; unauthorized invocations are blocked by the host webview sandbox, returning an empty sink list; (2) In multi-tenant mini-app containers, backgrounded or non-active mini-apps are stripped of speaker routing permissions, preventing audio playback redirection from disrupting concurrent host VoIP calls or active foreground mini-apps; (3) Store privacy linters verify that mini-apps do not attempt to probe or fingerprint users through persistent audio sink device IDs across container sessions.

title: MediaDevices.selectAudioOutput(): User-Mediated Audio Sink Consent & Anti-Fingerprinting
category: Privacy Architecture, Consent Propagation & Data Lifecycle
standard_reference: W3C Audio Output Devices API (§ MediaDevices.selectAudioOutput)
summary: Provides user-mediated device selection dialogs for audio output without exposing persistent hardware identifiers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To prevent passive browser fingerprinting via device enumeration, the Audio Output Devices API introduces 'navigator.mediaDevices.selectAudioOutput(options)'. Instead of allowing a script to silently inspect all connected physical speakers and Bluetooth peripherals, this method displays a native, browser-mediated device picker prompt to the end-user. Calling 'selectAudioOutput()' strictly requires transient user activation (a prior user gesture such as a click or tap). Upon the user selecting a specific speaker or headset, the promise resolves with a 'MediaDeviceInfo' object containing a session-scoped, origin-partitioned 'deviceId'. If the user dismisses the prompt, the promise rejects with an AbortError or NotAllowedError. The Permissions Policy feature identifier 'speaker-selection' controls whether an embedded iframe or mini-app origin can display this dialog. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app privacy architecture specifies: (1) Mini-apps requiring audio redirection (e.g. telemedicine, voice messaging, meeting rooms) MUST invoke 'selectAudioOutput()' rather than requesting broad microphone permissions solely to inspect speaker device lists; (2) The host container UI MUST display a clear native system sheet indicating which mini-app is requesting speaker redirection; (3) The generated 'deviceId' MUST be salted and partitioned per mini-app origin to prevent cross-app device correlation across the super-app ecosystem.

title: W3C Media Capture Region: Region Capture & CropTarget DOM Stream Sandboxing
category: Security Architecture, Boundary Hardening & Client Isolation
standard_reference: W3C Region Capture Specification (Candidate Recommendation)
summary: Enables precise bounding-box cropping of tab video capture tracks to specific DOM elements, preventing screen data leaks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a web application captures a browser tab using 'getDisplayMedia()', the resulting video track traditionally includes the entire document viewport—exposing navigation bars, adjacent unshared panels, and private notifications. The W3C Region Capture specification solves this through the 'CropTarget' interface. A mini-app generates a crop target token via 'const cropTarget = await CropTarget.fromElement(targetElement)'. The application then mutates the active screen-capture video track via 'await videoTrack.cropTo(cropTarget)'. The browser's media pipeline immediately crops the video frame stream strictly to the bounding box of the target DOM element in the compositor thread. If the element moves, resizes, or animates, the crop region tracks it synchronously. Passing 'null' to 'cropTo()' restores uncropped tab capture. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app screen-sharing and collaboration guidelines dictate: (1) Mini-apps offering document sharing, interactive presentation, or customer support screen casting MUST utilize Region Capture to isolate the target content container from surrounding super-app navigation chrome; (2) The host container MUST enforce that 'CropTarget.fromElement()' can only target elements within the mini-app's own DOM tree, throwing a NotAllowedError if a script attempts to crop to the host super-app top bar, bottom dock, or system floating capsules; (3) Store review linters verify that screen-sharing mini-apps handle 'cropTo()' promise rejections gracefully when elements are removed from the DOM.

title: WICG Element Capture: RestrictionTarget & Occlusion-Free Sub-Capture Isolation
category: Security Architecture, Boundary Hardening & Client Isolation
standard_reference: WICG Element Capture Specification (Draft Community Group Report)
summary: Isolates and records specific DOM subtrees while entirely eliminating occluding overlapping elements and dialogs.
