detail: [SPEC FACT] While Region Capture (CropTarget) crops the video stream to a 2D bounding box, any overlapping elements (such as incoming chat notifications, drop-down menus, floating popovers, or host security alerts) that enter that bounding box are still captured in the recorded stream, presenting severe privacy risks. WICG Element Capture addresses this by isolating the DOM subtree itself using the 'RestrictionTarget' interface. Developers produce a target via 'const target = await RestrictionTarget.fromElement(element)' and bind it to a display track via 'await track.restrictTo(target)'. Unlike simple cropping, Element Capture renders ONLY the target element and its DOM descendants into the video stream: any overlapping siblings, parent dialogs, or top-layer popovers floating over the element are completely omitted from the captured video frames. Passing 'null' removes the restriction. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Store privacy and customer data protection requirements mandate: (1) Mini-apps recording or streaming user workspace content (e.g. financial spreadsheet mini-apps, contract signing tools) MUST use Element Capture ('restrictTo') whenever supported to prevent customer chat bubbles, biometric prompts, or push notifications from inadvertently leaking into recorded video streams; (2) Host container security policy prevents mini-apps from calling 'RestrictionTarget.fromElement()' on any host-injected security overlay; (3) Store QA suites verify that financial and enterprise mini-apps implement Element Capture fallbacks to protect sensitive consumer data during screen sharing.

title: Media Capture Sandboxing: Container Privacy Badges, Track Mutexes & Permission Revocation
category: Privacy Architecture, Consent Propagation & Data Lifecycle
standard_reference: Super-App Container Media Governance & Hardware Capture Security Policy
summary: Establishes container-level indicator badges, background muting, and strict permissions policy gating for media capture.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Real-time audio routing and screen sub-capture represent high-privilege device interfaces. Under W3C Permissions Policy, access to display capture and audio output is controlled via the 'display-capture' and 'speaker-selection' directives. When an application initiates screen or audio capture, the operating system and container must display prominent, persistent visual privacy indicators (e.g. orange microphone dot, green camera indicator, or red recording icon in the system status bar). If the user navigates away from the capturing tab or switches to another mini-app, the container media session must enforce deterministic lifecycle state transitions, including automatically pausing or blacking out screen capture frames and muting audio capture tracks to prevent background surveillance. [STORE REQUIREMENT] Super-app host container policy enforces the following media boundaries: (1) Whenever a mini-app possesses an active screen capture track (cropped via CropTarget or restricted via RestrictionTarget) or audio output sink, the host container MUST render a persistent, tamper-proof privacy banner across the top of the viewport displaying the mini-app's verified name and a 1-tap 'Stop Sharing' kill-switch; (2) Navigating away, minimizing the mini-app, or receiving a higher-priority phone call MUST immediately invoke 'track.stop()' or mute media tracks, revoking capture until the user explicitly regains focus and grants re-activation; (3) Store automated review gates reject any mini-app that attempts to bypass display-capture user prompts or conceal media recording indicators.

[SPEC FACT] The NavigationPreloadManager interface provides methods for managing the preloading of resources in parallel with service worker startup. When a mini-app navigation request is dispatched, browser engines traditionally boot the service worker process before initiating the network request, causing a startup delay of 50ms-250ms on mobile devices. Navigation Preload allows the browser engine to start downloading the HTML response concurrently while the worker thread initializes, eliminating cold-start latency bottlenecks for super-app micro-frontends.

[SPEC FACT] The NavigationPreloadManager.enable() method enables the preloading of navigation requests, returning a Promise that resolves to undefined once enabled. In super-app container architectures, mini-app Service Workers must invoke 'await registration.navigationPreload.enable()' inside their 'activate' event handler. If called before activation settles or on an inactive registration, the promise rejects with an InvalidStateError, ensuring navigation preload is only active for fully installed, authenticated container partitions.

[SPEC FACT] The NavigationPreloadManager.setHeaderValue() method configures the value of the 'Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload' HTTP request header sent with navigation preload requests, defaulting to 'true'. Super-app edge gateways and origin servers can inspect this header to return an optimized, stripped HTML shell or serialized bootstrap payload instead of the full redundant client bundle, cutting initial payload transfer sizes and expediting sub-second Time-to-Interactive (TTI).

[SPEC FACT] FetchEvent.preloadResponse returns a Promise that resolves to the preloaded Response, or undefined if navigation preload is disabled or not applicable (e.g. for non-navigation subresource fetches). In resilient super-app service worker architectures, the fetch handler awaits 'event.preloadResponse' inside 'event.respondWith()'; if the network preload fails or resolves with a 5xx gateway error, the handler deterministically falls back to the local CacheStorage shell or IndexedDB offline snapshot.

[SPEC FACT] The W3C Service Worker specification defines NavigationPreloadManager as a property of ServiceWorkerRegistration with state attributes { enabled: boolean, headerValue: ByteString }. Navigation preloads are initiated strictly for top-level frame and sub-frame navigation requests (request mode 'navigate'). Mini-app stores mandate that mini-apps serving dynamic authenticated user dashboards implement Navigation Preload to prevent perceived UI freezes during WebView process recycling.

[SPEC FACT] WebGL2RenderingContext provides an interface to the OpenGL ES 3.0 graphics rendering context for HTML <canvas> elements, exposed via canvas.getContext('webgl2'). It introduces native 3D textures, uniform buffer objects (UBOs), multiple render targets (MRT), transform feedback, and full floating-point texture support. In super-app graphic and gaming mini-apps, WebGL 2.0 provides standardized GPU acceleration across modern mobile devices without requiring native SDK compilation, executing inside the sandboxed WebView DOM.

[SPEC FACT] The 'webglcontextlost' event is fired on an HTMLCanvasElement when the GPU driver or browser compositor resets or forcibly reclaims the WebGL context (e.g. during mobile GPU driver crashes, device lock/sleep, or OS memory pressure). If the mini-app listens for 'webglcontextlost' and invokes 'event.preventDefault()', it signals to the browser engine that it intends to recover state when resources become available; without calling preventDefault(), the WebGL context is permanently dead and cannot be restored.

[SPEC FACT] The 'webglcontextrestored' event is fired on an HTMLCanvasElement after the context was lost and the system successfully re-initializes the GPU context. All previously allocated WebGL resources (shaders, programs, textures, framebuffers, vertex buffer objects) are completely invalidated. Super-app store technical quality standards mandate that WebGL mini-apps implement an idempotent state restoration pipeline upon 'webglcontextrestored', re-compiling shaders and re-uploading cached asset textures without crashing or displaying a blank canvas.

[SPEC FACT] The WEBGL_lose_context extension exposes methods 'loseContext()' and 'restoreContext()' to simulate GPU context loss and restoration programmatically. Super-app automated app store review pipelines utilize this extension inside headless test runners (e.g. WebDriver BiDi / Puppeteer) to simulate memory pressure context evictions, verifying that submitted 3D/graphics mini-apps cleanly handle context reclamation and recover within 1,500ms without unhandled JavaScript exceptions.

[SPEC FACT] WebGLRenderingContext.isContextLost() and WebGL2RenderingContext.isContextLost() return a boolean indicating whether the rendering context has been lost. Mini-app render loops driven by requestAnimationFrame() must poll gl.isContextLost() prior to issuing expensive draw calls (e.g. gl.drawElements, gl.drawArrays); if true, the loop must suspend shader dispatch and asset streaming, preventing mobile GPU bus saturation and battery drain while waiting for context restoration.

[SPEC FACT] The WebAssembly Component Model extends core Wasm modules with typed interfaces, component composition, and language-independent interoperability via the WebAssembly Interface Type (WIT) IDL. Unlike traditional raw linear-memory Wasm modules that require unsafe pointer arithmetic across language barriers, components encapsulate their own isolated linear memories and exchange high-level structured values (records, variants, lists, strings, resources) across strictly typed canonical ABI boundaries. In super-app modular mini-app runtimes, components enable third-party plugins (e.g. cryptography, image processing, business rule engines) to be securely executed without risking host memory corruption.

[SPEC FACT] The Bytecode Alliance defines standards and open-source runtimes (such as Wasmtime and JCO) enforcing capability-based security for WebAssembly components. Under this paradigm, guest Wasm components possess zero ambient authority: they cannot access the local filesystem, network sockets, environment variables, or host system clocks unless the super-app host container explicitly links and injects capability handles at instantiation time. This eliminates supply-chain dependency vulnerabilities where compromised third-party npm/crate dependencies silently exfiltrate credentials.

[SPEC FACT] WASI 0.2 (WASI Preview 2) formalizes modular, capability-safe system interfaces built on the Component Model, deprecating the monolithic POSIX-like WASI Preview 1. WASI 0.2 standardizes fine-grained interfaces including wasi:cli, wasi:clocks (monotonic and wall clocks), wasi:filesystem (pre-opened directory descriptors with restricted path operations), wasi:io (streams and pollables), and wasi:http (outgoing HTTP client requests). Super-app mini-app containers implement host-side WASI 0.2 providers that clamp outbound HTTP requests strictly to the developer console domain allowlist and sandboxed OPFS directories.

[SPEC FACT] The Component Model specification defines the Canonical ABI ('canon lift' and 'canon lower' operations) for transferring structured data between components. The Canonical ABI enforces strict allocation contracts: memory allocations occur dynamically within the receiving component's address space via host-provided realloc functions, and string transfers validate UTF-8 encoding. Any attempt by a rogue mini-app component to trigger an out-of-bounds memory read or write causes an immediate Wasm trap, terminating the faulted component without destabilizing the super-app host application.

[SPEC FACT] The W3C WebAssembly Core Specification establishes formal validation rules ensuring type safety, structured control flow, and deterministic execution of WebAssembly bytecode before execution begins. In super-app app store submission and continuous delivery pipelines, binary validation statically verifies that Wasm binaries adhere to the module format, declare valid type signatures, restrict table index ranges, and operate within declared maximum linear memory limits (e.g. max memory clamped to 64MB-128MB per mini-app instance), guaranteeing runtime stability across multi-tenant mobile clients.

title: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy restrict-properties: Fine-Grained Window Proxy Property Filtering
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §7.2 Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy & WICG COOP restrict-properties
summary: COOP restrict-properties allows cross-origin popup interactions while strictly restricting window access to postMessage, closed, and blur/focus, mitigating Spectre without breaking partner OAuth or checkout flows.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The standard 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin' strictly severs all JavaScript references between opening and opened browsing contexts by setting window.opener to null, preventing legitimate multi-window interactions such as federated identity logins, external payment approvals, and merchant popup callbacks. 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: restrict-properties' provides an intermediate isolation tier that maintains window references across origins but restricts accessible WindowProxy properties exclusively to postMessage(), window.closed, window.focus(), and window.blur(). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app host environments mandate that external partner mini-apps and auxiliary authentication/settlement popups set 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: restrict-properties'. This ensures that malicious third-party code cannot inspect window.location.href, access DOM nodes, or probe sensitive navigation timings of the super-app or sibling mini-apps, while simultaneously retaining deterministic cross-window messaging capability. Container runtime enforcement verifies that when a mini-app launches a top-level auxiliary browsing context, cross-origin communication is confined strictly to authenticated structured cloning channels.

title: Window.postMessage TargetOrigin Clamping & Structured Serialization Hardening
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §9.4 Cross-document messaging
summary: Mandatory targetOrigin enforcement and structured clone transfer verification in window.postMessage eliminate wildcard destination leaks and prototype pollution attacks across mini-app boundaries.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Invoking window.postMessage(message, targetOrigin, [transfer]) without specifying an exact targetOrigin (such as using the wildcard '*') exposes the serialized message payload to any arbitrary domain that currently occupies or navigates the target window context. The HTML specification mandates that user agents only dispatch the 'message' event to the target window if the target window's active document origin matches targetOrigin. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Automated store linter gates and static analysis AST scanners reject any mini-app bundle containing window.postMessage calls with '*' as targetOrigin. Mini-apps communicating with host containers or auxiliary popups must specify the explicit canonical HTTPS origin of the receiver. Furthermore, all transmitted payload schemas must validate through the Structured Clone Algorithm without cyclic or prototype-polluting payloads, and sensitive high-bandwidth byte buffers (such as camera frames or crypto keys) must utilize Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer/ImageBitmap) with explicit zero-copy ownership transfer.

title: Window.opener Disownment & Reverse Tabnabbing Mitigation in Mini-App Navigation
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §7.1.3 Browsing context names & window.opener
summary: Automatic window.opener disownment (rel='noopener noreferrer') prevents untrusted external links opened by mini-apps from hijacking the parent window via location.replace().
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a web browsing context opens a new window via window.open() or an anchor element with target='_blank', the opened target receives a reference to the initiator via window.opener. In the absence of 'noopener', the untrusted target document can manipulate window.opener.location to navigate the caller to a spoofed phishing page (reverse tabnabbing), even if the two contexts are completely cross-origin. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app WebView and WebKit container hooks intercept all window.open and anchor navigation dispatches initiated within mini-app sandboxes. The container automatically injects 'rel=noopener noreferrer' and sets window.opener = null for any outbound URL resolving outside the mini-app's verified domain scope. If an authenticated multi-step workflow requires reciprocal messaging, the host establishes a mediated MessageChannel or transient Web Locks lease rather than permitting direct window.opener DOM pointers.

title: MessageChannel & MessagePort Transferability for Isolated Two-Way Mini-App Communication
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §9.5 Channel messaging
summary: Transferring MessagePort instances via initial postMessage handshakes establishes private, point-to-point, bidirectional RPC conduits between host and mini-apps that bypass window global event listeners.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Channel messaging creates two interconnected MessagePort endpoints (port1 and port2). Passing port2 as a Transferable object in an initial postMessage handshake allows two browsing contexts or workers to communicate exclusively over a private asynchronous channel, isolating subsequent traffic from global 'message' event listeners and third-party script eavesdropping. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app host architectures utilize MessageChannel pairing as the default IPC bridge for mini-app extensions and embedded widgets. Upon initializing an iframe or sub-window, the host transfers a dedicated MessagePort to the child context. All subsequent native bridge calls (payment requests, biometric auth, camera streaming) execute across this dedicated port with strict request-response UUID tagging, automatic 5,000 ms timeouts, and queue-draining lifecycle hooks (port.start() / port.close()) to avoid memory leaks.

title: Window.closed Polling & Auxiliary Window Crash Detection in Host Runtimes
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §7.3.3 The Window object — closed property
summary: Even under strict COOP restrict-properties isolation, window.closed remains readable to enable parent containers to detect popup dismissal, user cancellation, and unhandled child crashes.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The boolean property window.closed indicates whether the referenced browsing context has been closed. Crucially, under WICG COOP restrict-properties and HTML Living Standard WindowProxy invariants, 'closed' is one of the few properties that remains accessible across origins. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] When a mini-app delegates user verification, KYC document upload, or merchant checkout to a sandboxed popup window, the host runtime establishes a high-efficiency background watchdog interval (polling window.closed at 250 ms intervals or utilizing Page Visibility / Lifecycle hooks). If the user dismisses the popup window or if the child process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) termination, the parent immediately detects window.closed === true, tears down pending promise queues, cancels held transactional locks, and presents an actionable recovery UI without leaving the user stranded in an indefinite loading state.

title: Custom Elements formAssociated & attachInternals: Standardized Form Participation
category: Component Architecture, DOM Encapsulation & UX Standards
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13.5 Element internals and form-associated custom elements
summary: Declaring 'static formAssociated = true' and calling attachInternals() enables custom Web Components in mini-apps to seamlessly participate in native HTML forms and lifecycle events.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Historically, custom Web Components could not participate directly in native HTML <form> submission, validation, or reset pipelines without brittle hidden <input> hacks. The WHATWG HTML standard formalizes Form-Associated Custom Elements (FACE): by setting 'static formAssociated = true' on the component class and invoking 'this.attachInternals()' in its constructor, an autonomous custom element receives an ElementInternals instance that grants access to form control state, validation flags, and form submission lifecycle hooks. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app design system UI libraries (e.g., custom currency inputs, telecom phone number selectors, loyalty coupon pickers) must declare formAssociated = true. This architectural requirement ensures that mini-app developers constructing e-commerce checkout forms or KYC submission flows interact with design system components using standard HTML form APIs, completely eliminating synthetic form-serialization libraries and reducing client JavaScript footprint by up to 35%.

title: ElementInternals.setFormValue: Multipart Submission, State Restoration & BFCache Resilience
category: Component Architecture, DOM Encapsulation & UX Standards
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13.5.1 The ElementInternals interface — setFormValue()
summary: setFormValue() allows custom elements to pass structured string or FormData values to native form submissions while managing serialized state for automatic browser navigation restore.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The ElementInternals.setFormValue(value, state) method sets the element's submission value. The value parameter can be a string, a File, or a FormData instance containing multiple named entries. Furthermore, the optional state parameter enables the component to serialize internal transient state (such as caret position or uncommitted draft tokens) that the browser automatically restores via formStateRestoreCallback() when users navigate back via Back-Forward Cache (bfcache). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Store review criteria mandate that complex multi-field custom components (such as address pickers containing province, district, and street inputs) expose their internal fields via FormData payloads in setFormValue(). When a user navigates away from a mini-app to inspect terms and returns, the container invokes formStateRestoreCallback, ensuring zero data loss and flawless UX continuity across mobile lifecycle transitions.

title: ElementInternals.setValidity: Standardized Constraint Validation & Accessible Error Messages
category: Component Architecture, DOM Encapsulation & UX Standards
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13.5.1 The ElementInternals interface — setValidity()
summary: Custom elements set native ValidityState flags (valueMissing, patternMismatch, customError) via setValidity(), integrating directly into form.checkValidity() and CSS pseudo-classes (:valid/:invalid).
detail: [SPEC FACT] Calling internals.setValidity(flags, message, anchor) informs the host user agent of the component's validation status. The flags parameter takes a ValidityStateFlags dictionary (e.g., { valueMissing: true, patternMismatch: false }), the message parameter sets the localized validationMessage string, and the anchor element determines where the native validation message bubble points. This automatically syncs with the element's :valid and :invalid CSS pseudo-classes and makes form.checkValidity() and form.reportValidity() work seamlessly. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Mini-app compliance rules require all custom inputs in financial and transactional flows to enforce constraint validation through setValidity(). Rather than rendering non-standard inline error divs that screen readers ignore, components must supply localized error messages to setValidity(). This ensures that the super-app accessibility layer announces form errors consistently to VoiceOver and TalkBack users, complying with WCAG 2.2 AA Form Validation standards.

title: ElementInternals ARIA Property Reflection: Shadow DOM Accessible Roles & States
category: Component Architecture, DOM Encapsulation & UX Standards
standard_reference: W3C Accessibility Object Model & WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13.5 ElementInternals ARIA mixin
summary: ElementInternals reflects native ARIA roles, states, and form label associations without polluting outer DOM attributes or breaking Shadow DOM encapsulation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Custom elements encapsulating an internal Shadow DOM traditionally suffered from accessibility leakage: assigning role or aria-* attributes directly to the host element polluted developer-facing HTML attributes and risked external style collisions. ElementInternals implements the ARIAMixin interface (e.g., internals.role = 'combobox', internals.ariaExpanded = 'true'), exposing accessible semantics directly to the platform accessibility tree while keeping host attributes pristine. Additionally, internals.labels returns a NodeList of associated native <label> elements. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app component guidelines require all UI design system components to configure semantic roles and dynamic states exclusively via internals.role and internals.aria* properties. Clicking an external <label for='my-custom-input'> automatically focuses the internal shadow input via internals, ensuring 100% feature parity with platform form controls across iOS and Android assistive technologies.

title: CustomElementRegistry.define & Scoped Element Registries: Collision-Free Host Integration
category: Component Architecture, DOM Encapsulation & UX Standards
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §4.13.1 The CustomElementRegistry interface & W3C Scoped Custom Element Registries
summary: Mandating hyphenated naming conventions, prototype validation, and scoped registries prevents global namespace collisions between mini-app plugins and host design systems.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The customElements.define(name, constructor, [options]) method registers a custom element. The specification requires that 'name' must be a valid custom element name containing a hyphen (e.g., 'superapp-button') and throws a NotSupportedError if the name is already registered. To resolve cross-plugin tag collisions, W3C Scoped Custom Element Registries allow creating isolated CustomElementRegistry instances per ShadowRoot (new ShadowRoot({ registry })). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] To prevent mini-apps or embedded third-party SDKs from overwriting container-level custom elements (such as <superapp-header> or <superapp-bottom-sheet>), the store review gate enforces strict vendor prefixing (e.g., 'ma-<appid>-<component>') in all customElements.define calls. Furthermore, super-app host shells running modern engines sandbox sub-components using scoped custom element registries, ensuring that multiple micro-frontends can load differing versions of the same UI library without encountering fatal name collision exceptions.

title: CSS @font-face size-adjust: Fallback Font Normalization & CLS Mitigation
standard_reference: W3C CSS Fonts Module Level 4 §5.1 Font property descriptors: the size-adjust descriptor
summary: size-adjust normalizes the glyph dimensions of system fallback fonts to match web fonts, eliminating Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) during asynchronous typography loading.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a web font loads asynchronously over a mobile network, the browser swaps from a local fallback font (e.g., Roboto, San Francisco, or Arial) to the target web font. Differences in glyph advance widths and bounding boxes cause text reflow, resulting in sudden layout shifts measured by Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). The CSS @font-face 'size-adjust' descriptor defines a scaling percentage applied to glyph outlines and metrics for a specific font face, allowing developers to match the optical width of the fallback font exactly to the incoming web font. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app performance budgets require mini-apps utilizing custom brand typography to declare calibrated fallback @font-face rules with 'size-adjust'. By scaling fallback fonts (e.g., 'size-adjust: 92%'), the text line length and wrap points remain identical before and after the font loads. In automated CI/CD performance test suites, this practice reduces font-induced layout shifts to 0, ensuring strict compliance with the super-app Core Web Vitals target of CLS <= 0.05.

title: CSS Metric Overrides (ascent-override, descent-override, line-gap-override): Vertical Jitter Elimination
standard_reference: W3C CSS Fonts Module Level 4 §5.2 Font metric override descriptors
summary: Overriding ascent, descent, and line-gap metrics aligns fallback font vertical baselines perfectly with web fonts, preventing catastrophic vertical page jumps during hydration.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Even when horizontal glyph widths match, font baseline differences cause vertical layout shifts: if the fallback font has an ascent of 80% and descent of 20% while the custom web font has an ascent of 95% and descent of 25%, line heights shift abruptly upon font swap, causing whole paragraphs and interactive CTA buttons to jump vertically. The 'ascent-override', 'descent-override', and 'line-gap-override' descriptors define the baseline distance, descent distance, and line-to-line spacing explicitly, overriding the OpenType/TrueType OS/2 table metrics of the underlying font. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Automated store linters inspect mini-app CSS stylesheets to verify that every @font-face declaration for web fonts is accompanied by a metric-matched local fallback declaration containing 'ascent-override' and 'descent-override'. This architectural standard eliminates the notorious 'button hop' issue where mobile users tap a payment or confirmation button just as the font swaps, accidentally hitting an adjacent element.

title: CSS font-display: swap vs optional: Adaptive Bandwidth & Network-Aware Typography
standard_reference: W3C CSS Fonts Module Level 4 §5.3 The font-display descriptor
summary: Configuring font-display: optional or swap combined with metric overrides prevents the Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) and eliminates layout shifts on congested cellular networks.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'font-display' descriptor determines how a font face is displayed based on whether and when it is downloaded. 'font-display: block' gives a 3-second invisible block period causing severe FOIT. 'font-display: swap' gives a 0ms block period and an infinite swap period, ensuring text is immediately readable using fallback fonts but causing layout shift if metrics are uncalibrated. 'font-display: optional' gives an extremely brief block period (~100ms) and zero swap period: if the font is in memory cache, it renders immediately; if not, the fallback font is used for the entire session and the web font is cached in the background for subsequent visits. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app network governance policies mandate 'font-display: optional' for body copy and content-heavy mini-apps on 2G/3G connections (or when Save-Data: on is active). On high-speed 4G/5G connections, mini-apps may use 'font-display: swap' provided that size-adjust and ascent-override descriptors are configured on fallback font declarations, guaranteeing both instant text availability and zero cumulative layout shift.

title: Document.fonts (FontFaceSet.load) & Programmatic Preloading: Splash Screen Typography Warmup
standard_reference: W3C CSS Font Loading Module Level 3 §4 The FontFaceSet interface — load()
summary: Programmatically preloading critical typography strings via document.fonts.load() during super-app splash screen transitions eliminates font swapping after main view hydration.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The CSS Font Loading API exposes 'document.fonts' (an instance of FontFaceSet). The method 'document.fonts.load(font, [text])' returns a Promise that resolves when all font faces matching the specified font description are fetched and loaded into memory. Specifying the optional 'text' parameter triggers subset-aware font loading, fetching only the unicode-range subsets required for initial view rendering. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] When a user launches a mini-app, the super-app host container displays a native skeleton splash screen for 150-300ms. During this interval, the host runtime invokes document.fonts.load('16px CustomBrandFont') concurrently with service worker navigation preloading. By the time the mini-app UI dismisses the skeleton loader and renders its DOM, document.fonts.status is already 'loaded'. This guarantees that the first contentful paint (FCP) renders immediately with production typography, completely avoiding the fallback-to-webfont layout transition.

title: PerformanceObserver LayoutShift Telemetry: Automated CLS Gating for Mini-App Releases
standard_reference: W3C Layout Instability API §2 The LayoutShift interface
summary: Observing 'layout-shift' performance entries via PerformanceObserver enables automated CI and real-user monitoring to de-list mini-apps violating CLS <= 0.1 thresholds.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Layout Instability API exposes the 'layout-shift' entry type to PerformanceObserver. Each LayoutShift entry reports a 'value' calculated as (impact fraction * distance fraction), along with 'sources' indicating which DOM elements moved, 'hadRecentInput' indicating whether the shift occurred within 500ms of user interaction (which excludes intentional shifts), and 'lastInputTime'. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) sums the highest score window of unprompted layout shifts across the page lifecycle. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app client observability SDKs register a buffered PerformanceObserver for 'layout-shift'. If a mini-app registers unprompted layout shifts (hadRecentInput === false) exceeding a score of 0.1 during automated review or in p95 real-user telemetry (RUM), the store governance pipeline flags the app for layout instability. The automated diagnostics report highlights the exact DOM elements and CSS font loading events responsible, enforcing font metric override adoption before production clearance is granted.

title: WHATWG CloseWatcher API & Hardware/Gesture Back Navigation Mediation
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §6.10 Close requests and close watchers
summary: CloseWatcher standardizes multi-level UI dismissals (modals, sheets, drawers) in response to Android back gestures, Esc keys, and host close actions without dirtying browser history.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The CloseWatcher interface in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§6.10) provides a dedicated, platform-agnostic mechanism to intercept close requests—such as the hardware/gesture Back button on Android or the Esc key on desktop—without hacking window.history with synthetic hash changes. Instantiating 'new CloseWatcher({ signal })' registers an active close watcher on the window's close watcher stack. When a close request is issued, the user agent dispatches a 'cancel' event (which can be prevented via event.preventDefault() only if the window has history-action activation) followed by a 'close' event. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Traditional mini-apps attempted to handle custom bottom sheets and nested drawers by pushing fake history states via history.pushState(), leading to corrupted back-stack navigation when the user tried to exit the mini-app. By adopting CloseWatcher, mini-app UI components (e.g., custom pickers, action sheets, side drawers) push a CloseWatcher instance onto the host stack. When the user initiates a back swipe or the super-app top navigation 'Back' button is tapped, the host delegates the close request to the top-most CloseWatcher. The component handles its own teardown cleanly while preserving the super-app host container's outer routing state.

title: CloseWatcher 'cancel' Event & History-Action Activation: Unsaved Changes Guardrails
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §6.10.1 Close requests — Abuse Prevention
summary: CloseWatcher's cancelable 'cancel' event requires history-action user activation to prevent modal trapping while enabling legitimate confirmation prompts for dirty forms.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WHATWG HTML §6.10.1, the 'cancel' event on a CloseWatcher is cancelable via event.preventDefault() if and only if the window currently possesses history-action user activation. Once a cancel event is canceled or a close request is processed, that user activation is consumed. If the user immediately submits a second close request (such as pressing the Back button twice in succession without intervening interaction), the user agent bypasses any preventDefault() call in the cancel listener and immediately dispatches the 'close' event, destroying the watcher. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Rogue or poorly implemented mini-apps could otherwise hijack user back navigation by indefinitely preventing close actions, trapping the user inside an unwanted promotional view or checkout funnel. The super-app host container enforces this standard behavior across both native back buttons and gesture navigation: if a mini-app form with unsaved changes cancels a close request, the super-app allows a confirmation modal ('Discard changes?'); but if the user persists with a secondary back gesture, the host terminates the watcher stack and allows container navigation, eliminating back-button trapping attacks.

title: CloseWatcher Instance Grouping & Unactivated Close Watcher Coalescing
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §6.10.2 The CloseWatcher interface — construction algorithms
summary: Constructing multiple CloseWatcher instances without user activation automatically coalesces them into a single close group, preventing Denial of Service through stacked watchers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The CloseWatcher construction algorithm enforces strict activation gating. If a script instantiates a second (or subsequent) CloseWatcher without user activation having occurred since the previous construction, the new watcher is grouped together with the existing unactivated close watcher. Consequently, a single close request triggers the simultaneous closure and destruction of all coalesced watchers in that group, rather than requiring the user to tap Back repeatedly. A web developer only gains a separate, independent close watcher slot if construction is triggered by a discrete user activation or if previous watchers are explicitly destroyed via watcher.destroy(). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Automated store review scanning statically and dynamically audits mini-app scripts for CloseWatcher construction loops. If an ad script or background timer spawns recursive CloseWatcher instances to simulate multiple modal layers, the browser engine's grouping algorithm prevents user fatigue. Furthermore, super-app quality gates enforce that every constructed CloseWatcher binds an AbortSignal tied to component unmount: 'new CloseWatcher({ signal: componentAbortSignal })', ensuring zero memory leaks when mini-app views unmount.

title: CloseWatcher.destroy() & Programmatic Close Reconciliation
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §6.10.2 CloseWatcher destroy() algorithm
summary: Explicit invocation of CloseWatcher.destroy() deactivates the watcher from the window stack without firing 'close' events, maintaining synchronization during programmatic UI dismissals.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'destroy()' method of the CloseWatcher interface immediately deactivates the watcher, removing it from the window's close watcher stack so that it will no longer receive 'cancel' or 'close' events. Crucially, calling destroy() does not fire the 'close' event handlers, allowing developers to distinguish between user-initiated close requests (handled via requestClose() or hardware gestures) and programmatic teardowns (such as a successful form submission or parent component unmounting). Deactivating an active watcher frees up the user activation slot for subsequent watcher construction. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In super-app component frameworks (such as WindVane or WeChat Mini Programs), UI components frequently close programmatically when an asynchronous network call completes (e.g., loading spinner dismiss or OTP verification success). Mini-app SDK guidelines mandate calling 'watcher.destroy()' when an overlay is dismissed programmatically. Failing to destroy the watcher leaves stale listeners on the stack, causing subsequent legitimate user Back taps to close unintended background layers or trigger orphaned callbacks.

title: CloseWatcher Integration with HTML Popover API and Modal Dialog Elements
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §6.10 Close requests — interaction with modal dialogs and popovers
summary: CloseWatcher forms the shared underlying primitive for <dialog showModal()> and [popover], guaranteeing a unified Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) dismissal stack across native and custom widgets.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML specification harmonizes modal HTML elements—specifically '<dialog>.showModal()' and elements with the 'popover' attribute—with the CloseWatcher infrastructure. When a modal dialog or popover element is presented, the user agent internally attaches a close watcher to the document's top-level close watcher stack. Custom CloseWatcher instances created by application JavaScript participate in the exact same stack. As a result, close requests follow strict Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) resolution order regardless of whether the topmost overlay is an HTML dialog, a native popover, or a custom Canvas/WebGL UI sheet managed via JavaScript. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Complex super-app mini-apps (such as multi-vendor food delivery or ride-hailing checkout) regularly combine HTML popovers (e.g., address selector dropdowns) with custom Canvas graphics (e.g., interactive seat selection maps). By adhering to the shared CloseWatcher LIFO stack, the user's back gesture predictably dismisses the seat map first, then the address dropdown, before finally navigating away from the order screen. The super-app store review checklist verifies that third-party frameworks do not implement isolated keydown listeners that conflict with the browser's native LIFO close watcher resolution.

title: W3C Compute Pressure API Level 1 & PressureObserver System Workload Telemetry
standard_reference: W3C Candidate Recommendation: Compute Pressure Level 1 §4 The PressureObserver interface
summary: PressureObserver provides hardware-isolated telemetry on system CPU and thermal load states (nominal, fair, serious, critical), enabling dynamic algorithmic degradation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Compute Pressure Level 1 specification standardizes the 'PressureObserver' interface, allowing web applications to observe pressure states from underlying system resources (specifically 'cpu'). Calling 'observer.observe(source, options)' starts asynchronous telemetry delivery. The callback receives an array of 'PressureRecord' objects whenever the system pressure state transitions between four normalized states: 'nominal' (minimal workload), 'fair' (moderate workload with ample headroom), 'serious' (high workload approaching thermal throttling), and 'critical' (severe pressure requiring immediate load shedding). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] High-compute mini-apps (such as WebAssembly photo filters, on-device OCR, WebGL mini-games, and WebCodecs real-time communications) can easily overwhelm mobile processors, triggering severe UI jank, frame drops, and battery drain. The super-app host container exposes the Compute Pressure API, allowing mini-apps to register an observer with a coarse sampleInterval (e.g., 1000-2000ms). When pressure transitions to 'serious' or 'critical', the mini-app runtime dynamically scales back background rendering loops, lowers video resolution, or defers non-critical indexing tasks, maintaining system-wide super-app UI responsiveness.

title: Compute Pressure Permissions Policy Gating & Cross-Origin Privacy Defense
standard_reference: W3C Compute Pressure Level 1 §9 Permissions Policy & Privacy Considerations
summary: Compute Pressure observation is strictly gated by the 'compute-pressure' Permissions Policy and requires top-level browsing context focus to prevent cross-app timing side-channels.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Compute Pressure §9, calling 'observe()' in an execution context where the 'compute-pressure' feature is disallowed by Permissions Policy throws a 'NotAllowedError' DOMException. Furthermore, user agents restrict pressure updates to top-level browsing contexts or active, focused execution contexts. If an iframe or embedded view loses focus, pressure record delivery is suspended until the context becomes active again. This restriction prevents malicious embedded scripts from correlating system-wide CPU spikes with user keystrokes, password hashing, or cryptographic operations in neighboring processes (mitigating CPU acoustic and timing side-channels). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] The super-app WebView container configures strict Permissions Policy headers ('Permissions-Policy: compute-pressure=(self)'). Embedded third-party iframes (such as merchant ad banners or external payment widgets) are denied 'compute-pressure' access by default. Only verified top-level mini-app modules running in verified origins can observe system pressure. The store compliance audit scans mini-app manifests to ensure pressure data is not transmitted off-device for device fingerprinting or cross-session user profiling.

title: PressureRecord State Taxonomy & Rate-Limited Sampling Quantization
standard_reference: W3C Compute Pressure Level 1 §5 The PressureRecord interface
summary: PressureRecord reports coarse, quantized states and relative timestamps rather than raw CPU clock frequencies or core temperatures, eliminating hardware fingerprinting vectors.
detail: [SPEC FACT] A 'PressureRecord' exposes three read-only attributes: 'source' (e.g., 'cpu'), 'state' ('nominal' | 'fair' | 'serious' | 'critical'), and 'time' (a high-resolution DOMHighResTimeStamp relative to the time origin). To eliminate side-channel fingerprinting and prevent microarchitectural timing attacks, the specification explicitly forbids exposing raw clock frequencies, exact CPU utilization percentages, core temperature Celsius values, or fan speeds. Furthermore, the user agent clamps the 'sampleInterval' parameter to a platform-defined minimum threshold (typically >= 1000ms), discarding sub-second sampling requests. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In mobile super-app runtimes, exposing detailed SoC thermal sensors would allow malicious developers to fingerprint specific device batches, battery health degradation curves, and chip stepping revisions. By standardizing on coarse 4-state PressureRecord taxonomies, the super-app guarantees developer utility (knowing when to shed compute load) while completely insulating user devices from invasive hardware fingerprinting. Store telemetry verifies that mini-apps handle all four enum values cleanly without unhandled exceptions.

title: PressureObserver.takeRecords(), unobserve() & Lifecycle Teardown
standard_reference: W3C Compute Pressure Level 1 §4.4 The takeRecords() method & cleanup algorithms
summary: PressureObserver.takeRecords() empties the queued record buffer prior to disconnect(), ensuring deterministic state recovery without memory leaks or lingering OS sensor subscriptions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Compute Pressure §4.4, 'takeRecords()' synchronously returns any queued 'PressureRecord' objects that have not yet been dispatched to the observer's callback, immediately emptying the internal record queue. Calling 'unobserve(source)' stops monitoring the specified resource, while 'disconnect()' deactivates all source subscriptions on that observer instance. When all active observers for a given source disconnect, the browser engine releases the underlying OS-level thermal and CPU performance monitoring handles (such as Android Thermal HAL or Linux thermal sysfs watchers), eliminating background polling overhead. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] When a mini-app page transitions to background, freezes, or is unmounted, lingering observer subscriptions can cause CPU wakeups and prevent the JavaScript VM heap from being collected. Super-app lifecycle guidelines mandate that mini-apps invoke 'observer.disconnect()' inside their 'pagehide' or custom lifecycle 'onHide' handlers. In automated performance regression testing, the store sandbox checks that mini-app processes have 0 active PressureObserver instances remaining 5 seconds after navigation away from the compute-intensive view.

title: PressureObserver.knownSources & Feature Detection for Progressive Enhancement
standard_reference: W3C Compute Pressure Level 1 §4.1 The knownSources attribute
summary: Static PressureObserver.knownSources inspects browser and OS platform capability support, enabling graceful fallbacks on legacy mobile chipsets without throwing NotSupportedError.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The static, read-only property 'PressureObserver.knownSources' returns a frozen array of strings indicating which pressure sources are recognized by the user agent (currently ['cpu']). If a web application passes an unsupported source to 'observe()', or if the underlying platform kernel does not implement compute pressure drivers, 'observe()' rejects with a 'NotSupportedError' DOMException. Checking 'PressureObserver.knownSources.includes('cpu')' alongside standard 'if ('PressureObserver' in window)' feature checks ensures safe progressive enhancement across heterogeneous device fleets. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-apps serve hundreds of millions of users spanning premium flagship smartphones to low-cost budget devices where Android Thermal HAL support may be disabled or fragmented. Mini-app developer SDKs wrap PressureObserver in a resilient telemetry adapter: if knownSources is empty or observe() throws NotSupportedError, the adapter seamlessly falls back to frame-budget heuristic monitoring (e.g., measuring requestAnimationFrame delta spikes over 16.6ms). This guarantees consistent runtime degradation behavior across all devices without risking unhandled promise rejections during startup.

title: W3C Async Clipboard API Web Custom Formats ('web ') & Arbitrary Payload Interop
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: W3C Clipboard API and events §7.2 ClipboardItem Interface — Web Custom Formats
summary: Web custom formats prefix arbitrary MIME types with 'web ' in ClipboardItem, allowing rich mini-app payloads to pass through the OS clipboard without destructive sanitization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Clipboard API and events specification standardizes web custom formats (formerly known as clipboard pickling). Web authors can read and write arbitrary, non-standardized data payloads (such as custom CAD models, spreadsheet formula ASTs, or rich graphics structures) by prefixing the MIME type string with 'web ' (e.g., 'web application/vnd.miniapp.payload' or 'web text/html'). When written via navigator.clipboard.write([new ClipboardItem({ 'web application/json': blob })]), the browser engine maps the payload to an OS-specific pickled format representation (e.g., 'org.w3.web-custom-format.type-0' on macOS/iOS, 'Web Custom Format0' on Windows, 'application/web;type=...' on Linux/Android) alongside a JSON-formatted format map. This prevents the OS or browser from executing destructive HTML tag stripping or re-encoding on proprietary data structures. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Cross-mini-app collaboration (e.g., copying a complex table from an accounting mini-app and pasting it into an invoicing or messaging mini-app) historically suffered from severe data loss because default 'text/html' clipboard operations strip data-attributes and custom schemas. By establishing standard 'web application/vnd.superapp-table+json' custom formats, the super-app ecosystem allows mini-apps and native host modules to transfer lossless domain models across sandboxes without relying on server-side staging databases.

title: ClipboardItem.supports() Feature Negotiation for Standard and Custom MIME Types
standard_reference: W3C Clipboard API and events §7.2.1 The supports() method
summary: The static ClipboardItem.supports(type) method validates format support for both standard and 'web '-prefixed formats before write operations, preventing runtime TypeError exceptions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The static method 'ClipboardItem.supports(type)' evaluates whether the user agent supports reading and writing the given MIME type on the underlying platform clipboard. It accepts standard well-known types (e.g., 'text/plain', 'text/html', 'image/png') as well as web custom format types prefixed with 'web ' (e.g., 'web image/avif' or 'web text/csv'). Calling supports() returns a synchronous boolean. If an unsupported format is passed directly to the ClipboardItem constructor without checking supports(), subsequent clipboard operations throw a TypeError or DOMException upon write(). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app client platforms vary dramatically in clipboard capabilities: modern desktop engines support SVG, AVIF, and custom pickled formats, whereas legacy mobile WebViews may restrict clipboard writing strictly to plain text and PNG. Mini-app developer SDKs mandate checking 'ClipboardItem.supports('web ' + format)' during copy-paste feature initialization. If unsupported, the SDK automatically provides a fallback multi-representation ClipboardItem (combining the raw custom format with a sanitized 'text/plain' or 'text/html' fallback), ensuring clipboard actions never throw uncaught exceptions.

title: Clipboard API Write Permissions & Transient User Activation Gating
standard_reference: W3C Clipboard API and events §8 Permissions & User Activation Requirements
summary: Writing to navigator.clipboard requires a secure HTTPS context and transient user activation, mitigating covert clipboard poisoning and background payload replacement.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Clipboard API §8, invoking 'navigator.clipboard.write()' or 'navigator.clipboard.writeText()' requires two fundamental security prerequisites: the execution context must be a Secure Context (HTTPS or localhost), and the document must have transient user activation (such as a direct click, tap, or keypress event within the activation lifetime window). Furthermore, the document must be the active, focused top-level browsing context. Attempting to write to the clipboard in a background tab, from an unactivated timer callback, or inside an unfocused iframe rejects the returned Promise with a 'NotAllowedError' DOMException. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Covert clipboard poisoning is a critical attack vector in super-app environments, where a rogue mini-app could attempt to overwrite a user's copied cryptocurrency wallet address, banking OTP, or confidential discount code with an attacker-controlled value. Super-app container security policies strictly enforce transient activation checks on all clipboard APIs. Background workers and non-interactive scripts are prohibited from accessing the clipboard. Store security screening inspects minified JavaScript for 'navigator.clipboard.write' invocations outside of user-gesture event handlers, rejecting non-compliant builds.

title: Clipboard Reading & Web Custom Format Deserialization Sanitization
standard_reference: W3C Clipboard API and events §10 Security and Privacy — Unsanitized payload processing
summary: Because web custom formats bypass native OS HTML sanitization, receiving applications must strictly validate and sanitize deserialized custom payloads prior to DOM insertion.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Standard clipboard types like 'text/html' are sanitized by the browser engine (stripping <script> tags, inline javascript: URLs, and dangerous SVG attributes) before paste. In contrast, web custom formats prefixed with 'web ' preserve the raw, unsanitized byte representation exactly as written by the origin application. When a web application invokes 'clipboardItem.getType("web text/html")' or a custom JSON type, the returned Blob represents raw user input. Deserializing this blob without strict input validation, JSON schema validation, or HTML sanitization introduces severe DOM-based XSS and remote code execution vulnerabilities in receiving contexts. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] The super-app SDK provides a hardened 'SuperAppClipboard.readCustom(format, schema)' bridge wrapper. When a mini-app consumes a web custom format, the SDK automatically runs the incoming payload through a zero-trust schema validator and a DOMPurify/Sanitizer API filter before returning typed data to the application. If the pasted content contains unrecognized properties or script sinks, the SDK rejects the payload and alerts the user, guaranteeing that cross-app copy-paste cannot become a vector for cross-origin exploit propagation.

title: OS Clipboard Atom Pool Quota Management & Resource Exhaustion Defense
standard_reference: W3C Clipboard Pickling Explainer & Architecture Constraints §3 Atom Pool Limits
summary: Limiting web custom formats to <= 100 registrations per session prevents exhaustion of host OS global clipboard atom tables (Windows atom space and macOS UTType registrations).
detail: [SPEC FACT] On underlying desktop and mobile operating systems, registering dynamic clipboard formats consumes entries in shared operating system atom pools (such as the global atom table on Windows accessed via RegisterClipboardFormat, or system-wide UTType registries on Darwin). To prevent malicious scripts from flooding and exhausting the OS global atom pool—which would cause system-wide stability failures and prevent all other desktop/native applications from copying or pasting—browser implementations cap each user session to a maximum of 100 unique web custom formats. The browser maintains a format map mapping MIME types to reusable platform format slots, deduplicating repetitive format declarations. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] A poorly architected super-app host running dozens of mini-apps concurrently could risk atom exhaustion if mini-apps dynamically generated random MIME types (e.g., 'web text/app-' + Math.random()). Super-app developer specifications mandate that mini-apps declare their custom clipboard formats statically in their mini-app manifest ('clipboard_custom_formats: ["web application/vnd.mybrand.order"]'). The super-app host pre-registers and validates these types at launch, rejecting dynamically generated, randomized MIME types to protect host operating system stability.

title: W3C ManagedMediaSource API & Power-Efficient Adaptive Video Streaming
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions v2 §4 ManagedMediaSource Interface
summary: ManagedMediaSource transfers buffer lifecycle and network pacing control back to the user agent, optimizing streaming efficiency, battery life, and high-speed radio usage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Media Source Extensions v2 specification introduces the 'ManagedMediaSource' interface (inheriting from MediaSource) to address critical performance and battery drain inefficiencies in client-driven adaptive streaming. While traditional MSE granted JavaScript applications complete, unconstrained control over segment appending, it lacked visibility into system memory pressure, modem power states, and hardware decoders. ManagedMediaSource empowers the user agent to actively signal optimal fetching windows and autonomously evict inactive buffer ranges when physical memory is constrained. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps frequently embed rich video experiences (e.g., short-video feeds, live shopping streams, educational webinars). On resource-constrained mobile devices running multiple backgrounded mini-apps, legacy MSE video players cause aggressive battery depletion and Out-Of-Memory (OOM) OS process termination by over-buffering ahead of the playhead. By enforcing ManagedMediaSource in the super-app media player component, the container coordinates with underlying mobile power governors to conserve CPU cycles and battery without degrading playback continuity.

title: ManagedMediaSource 'streaming' Property and startstreaming/endstreaming Events
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions v2 §4.1 streaming attribute & streaming events
summary: The 'streaming' boolean property and paired 'startstreaming' and 'endstreaming' events signal to web applications exactly when to fetch segments or allow modems to enter low-power sleep states.
detail: [SPEC FACT] ManagedMediaSource exposes a read-only boolean attribute 'streaming' and dispatches two core lifecycle events: 'startstreaming' and 'endstreaming'. When 'streaming' is true, the user agent indicates that buffer levels are low, a user-initiated seek has occurred into an unbuffered region, or network conditions are optimal for burst downloading, prompting the application to fetch segments via fetch(). When 'streaming' transitions to false, the user agent indicates that sufficient forward buffer has been accumulated. The application must suspend outbound segment requests, allowing cellular and Wi-Fi modems to power down into low-power sleep states. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Continuous background segment polling by mini-app media players is a leading contributor to device thermal throttling and cellular radio battery drain. The super-app SDK abstracts player engines (e.g., HLS.js or Shaka Player) to subscribe to 'startstreaming' and 'endstreaming'. The engine suspends chunk fetching immediately upon 'endstreaming' and resumes upon 'startstreaming'. Automated store performance testing verifies that mini-app video players do not emit network requests while streaming is false, preventing store rejection for battery inefficiency.

title: ManagedSourceBuffer & Autonomous 'bufferedchange' Coded Frame Eviction
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions v2 §5 ManagedSourceBuffer & BufferedChangeEvent
summary: ManagedSourceBuffer allows the user agent to run coded frame eviction algorithms at any time under memory pressure, dispatching 'bufferedchange' events to notify the application.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When 'addSourceBuffer(type)' is invoked on a ManagedMediaSource instance, it creates a 'ManagedSourceBuffer' rather than a standard SourceBuffer. Unlike standard SourceBuffers, which only evict frames during an active appendBuffer() call, a ManagedSourceBuffer permits the user agent's media engine to execute the 'Coded Frame Eviction' algorithm asynchronously at any time in response to system memory pressure. Upon purging unplayed or distant past buffer ranges, the user agent fires a 'bufferedchange' event containing 'addedRanges' and 'removedRanges' TimeRanges, notifying JavaScript that previously loaded ranges must be re-requested if the playhead seeks back. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] When a user switches between mini-apps in a super-app (e.g., pausing an e-learning video to approve a payment in a banking mini-app), the host container faces aggressive RAM pressure from the newly active webview. ManagedSourceBuffer allows the browser engine to silently purge cached 4K/1080p video frames from the paused mini-app without crashing the process. The mini-app's bufferedchange listener updates its internal index, seamlessly fetching evicted segments only if the user resumes playback.

title: 5G High-Speed Radio Coalescing & Modem Power State Synchronization
standard_reference: Apple WebKit / W3C MSE v2 Hardware Architecture Guidelines for ManagedMediaSource
summary: ManagedMediaSource enables mobile operating systems to burst video data over high-power 5G modems and return radios to low-power RRC idle states, reducing cellular power drain.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Cellular radios operating on 5G New Radio (NR) networks consume substantially higher instantaneous power when the radio frequency (RF) transceiver is active in Radio Resource Control (RRC) Connected mode compared to RRC Idle/Inactive mode. Traditional MSE fetches small 2-to-4-second video chunks at frequent intervals, keeping the cellular modem continuously active and generating severe battery drain. ManagedMediaSource allows the browser to calculate optimal burst transfer windows, downloading larger segment batches at gigabit 5G speeds during 'startstreaming' and quickly allowing the modem to power down into sleep states. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mobile frameworks implement network intelligence telemetry that monitors active connection types (via Network Information API) and aligns mini-app streaming policies. In 5G cellular environments, the container configures ManagedMediaSource buffering thresholds to maximize burst efficiency, preventing micro-buffering requests from sustaining high-power modem states. Store certification audits verify that streaming video mini-apps comply with burst-and-sleep radio profiles.

title: Off-Thread ManagedMediaSource Construction in Dedicated Web Workers
standard_reference: W3C Media Source Extensions v2 §4.2 DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope Integration
summary: Constructing ManagedMediaSource inside Dedicated Web Workers offloads segment fetching, demuxing, and buffer appending from the main UI thread, preserving Core Web Vitals INP.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C MSE v2 formalizes the construction of ManagedMediaSource instances inside 'DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope'. By checking 'ManagedMediaSource.canConstructInDedicatedWorker' or passing the MediaSource handle via 'MediaProvider' / 'createObjectURL' back to the main thread HTMLMediaElement, web applications can execute data fetching (fetch/ReadableStream), cryptographic decryption, and SourceBuffer appending entirely off the main thread. This completely decouples heavy ArrayBuffer manipulation and WebM/ISOBMFF demuxing from the UI rendering thread. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In interactive mini-apps (such as live commerce where video plays alongside real-time chat, product carousels, and checkout sheets), executing appendBuffer() on the main thread causes significant jank and degrades Interaction to Next Paint (INP > 200ms). The super-app standard mandates that third-party streaming mini-apps execute media buffering inside a Dedicated Web Worker when ManagedMediaSource worker support is available. This guarantees 60fps UI responsiveness during intense video segment processing.

title: WHATWG Invoker Commands API (commandfor & command) Declarative UI Control
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Open UI Invoker Commands Specification §2 command & commandfor attributes
summary: Invoker Commands allow <button> elements to declaratively control popovers, dialogs, and custom targets via 'commandfor' and 'command' attributes without JavaScript event boilerplate.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Invoker Commands API adds 'commandfor' (an IDREF pointing to a target element in the document) and 'command' (a built-in or custom action identifier) attributes to HTMLButtonElement. When the button is activated via any Human Input Device (click, touch, Space, or Enter key), the browser natively dispatches a 'CommandEvent' on the target element and executes default platform behaviors without requiring userland 'addEventListener('click')' scripting. If 'command' is missing or unrecognized without custom prefixing, it defaults to an invalid state where no action occurs, preventing accidental triggers. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Lightweight mini-app architectures require high performance and minimal initial JavaScript bundle sizes. By leveraging declarative 'commandfor' and 'command', mini-app UI templates can wire up interactive dialogs, menus, and bottom sheets directly in parsed HTML markup before client-side hydration or framework bundles finish executing. This delivers immediate interactive responsiveness on low-end devices and cuts hundreds of lines of fragile event-binding boilerplate across mini-app components.

title: Standard Built-in Commands for Popovers and Modal Dialogs
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Open UI Invoker Commands §3 Built-in Command Types
summary: Invoker Commands define standardized built-in actions ('show-modal', 'close', 'request-close', 'toggle-popover', 'show-popover', 'hide-popover') with automatic accessible state reflection.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The specification codifies normative built-in commands mapped to specific interactive HTML elements: for '<dialog>', commands include 'show-modal' (invoking showModal()), 'close' (invoking close(button.value)), and 'request-close' (invoking requestClose(button.value)); for elements with the 'popover' attribute, commands include 'toggle-popover', 'show-popover', and 'hide-popover'. When built-in commands target their respective elements, the user agent automatically synchronizes accessibility tree properties (such as 'aria-expanded') and ensures focus transitions follow established platform accessibility standards. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Fragmented UI implementations in third-party mini-apps frequently fail accessibility audits (WCAG 2.2 AA) by neglecting keyboard focus traps or omitting aria-expanded state attributes on custom modal triggers. Standardizing on built-in invoker commands ensures that mini-app confirmation prompts, date pickers, and filter sheets are natively accessible across screen readers (VoiceOver, TalkBack) without manual developer intervention. Super-app automated quality gates recommend built-in invoker commands for all modal interactions.

title: Custom Invoker Commands with Dashed-Ident Syntax ('--custom-action')
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Open UI Invoker Commands §4 Custom Command Extensibility
summary: Custom invoker commands must use the '--' dashed-ident namespace, guaranteeing that custom application actions will never conflict with future standardized platform commands.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Web authors can define custom actions on any DOM element by assigning a command value starting with a double dash ('--'), adopting the CSS dashed-ident convention (e.g., command="--add-to-cart" or command="--rotate-card"). Browsers normatively guarantee that native built-in commands will never begin with '--'. When a button with a custom command is invoked, the user agent dispatches a CommandEvent on the target element with 'event.command' reflecting the dashed string and 'event.source' referencing the invoking button element, allowing component logic to handle the interaction cleanly. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Mini-app design systems and Web Components (e.g., custom tabs, carousels, or audio players) use custom invoker commands to decouple triggers from target components. An add-to-cart button can declare 'commandfor="cart-drawer" command="--add-item" value="item-12345"', firing a typed CommandEvent directly on the cart component. This eliminates spaghetti querySelector code and event bus subscriptions, creating clean, testable component boundaries within mini-app runtimes.

title: CommandEvent Interface, Event Lifecycle, and Cancelable Side-Effect Control
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Open UI Invoker Commands §5 CommandEvent Interface & Dispatch
summary: CommandEvent is a non-bubbling, composed, trusted, and cancelable event fired on the target element, allowing script handlers to intercept or prevent default browser actions.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'CommandEvent' interface extends the base DOM Event. Crucially, CommandEvents are non-bubbling (bubbles: false), composed (composed: true, crossing Shadow DOM boundaries), trusted (isTrusted: true when initiated by real user input), and cancelable (cancelable: true). If a web author attaches an 'addEventListener("command", (e) => ...)' listener to the target element and calls 'event.preventDefault()', the browser skips the default built-in action (such as opening the dialog or hiding the popover). Event handlers can read 'event.source' to inspect the button that initiated the command and 'event.command' to identify the requested action. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app security frameworks leverage CommandEvent's cancelable lifecycle to enforce security and business integrity checks before modals open. For example, before a sensitive financial transfer confirmation dialog is displayed, the mini-app's command listener verifies transaction preconditions or rate limits; if validation fails, 'event.preventDefault()' cancels dialog rendering. Furthermore, because CommandEvent has 'isTrusted: true', host security bridges can verify that actions originated from physical user clicks rather than synthetic click() injection.

title: Form Participation Disambiguation and button[type=button] Enactment Rules
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Open UI Invoker Commands §6 Button Activation Steps & Form Owner Interaction
summary: Buttons with command/commandfor inside forms must declare type='button' to prevent accidental form submission; command attributes override popovertarget when both are declared.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To prevent unexpected side effects and form validation loops, the WHATWG specification mandates that if a '<button>' has a form owner (i.e. is nested in or references a '<form>') and has 'type="submit"' (or lacks an explicit type attribute, defaulting to submit in standard forms), any 'command' and 'commandfor' attributes are ignored during button activation, preserving normal form submission. Consequently, form-participating invoker buttons must explicitly declare 'type="button"' to invoke target commands. Additionally, if an element declares both 'popovertarget' and 'commandfor', 'commandfor' takes precedence and 'popovertarget' is ignored. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Form-heavy mini-apps (such as loan applications, tax declarations, or multi-step checkout funnels) frequently experience state corruption when developers inadvertently create buttons that submit the form while attempting to toggle a terms-and-conditions modal. Super-app linter rules and store verification pipelines validate that any button declaring 'commandfor' inside a form explicitly includes 'type="button"', eliminating accidental double-submissions and form validation blocking.

title: IETF RFC 9605 Secure Frame (SFrame) & Zero-Trust Media Conferencing Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9605 Secure Frame (SFrame) §1 Introduction & §3 Architecture
summary: RFC 9605 standardizes SFrame, providing lightweight authenticated end-to-end encryption for media frames so central media servers (SFUs) route streams without access to plaintext audio/video.
detail: [SPEC FACT] IETF RFC 9605 defines Secure Frame (SFrame), an end-to-end encryption (E2EE) and authentication format for multi-party audio and video media. Unlike traditional WebRTC hop-by-hop SRTP encryption—where the central Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) decrypts all media to inspect RTP headers and re-encrypts toward recipients—SFrame encrypts media at the frame level before packetization. The central media routing server (SFU) can inspect unencrypted RTP transport metadata and SFrame headers to make dynamic switching, bitrate adaptation, and forwarding decisions, but remains mathematically barred from accessing plaintext audio or video data. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps increasingly embed real-time collaboration, telemedicine consultations, enterprise board meetings, and private social video calling. Entrusting cloud SFU media servers with unencrypted corporate or health conversations exposes the super-app ecosystem to massive data breach and wiretapping liabilities. By standardizing on RFC 9605 SFrame, mini-apps achieve zero-trust real-time communications: media payloads are encrypted with client keys inside the mini-app sandbox, ensuring that intermediate super-app routing servers and cloud SFUs never possess plaintext audio or video data.

title: SFrame Frame Format: Key ID, Counter (CTR), and AEAD Encapsulation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9605 §4 SFrame Frame Format & §4.1 Header
summary: SFrame header specifies a compact 1-to-8 byte Key ID (KID), a monotonically increasing Counter (CTR) for nonce generation, and an AEAD authentication tag, minimizing packet overhead.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under RFC 9605 §4, an SFrame-protected payload consists of an SFrame Header followed by the AEAD ciphertext and authentication tag. The header contains a flexible Key ID (KID) identifying the sender's active cryptographic key, encoded as a compact variable-length integer (1 to 8 octets), and a Counter (CTR) field representing a monotonically increasing frame counter. SFrame derives a unique initialization vector (IV/nonce) for each frame by XORing the frame counter with a salt derived from the sender key, completely eliminating nonce-reuse vulnerabilities across high-framerate video streams while maintaining minimal byte overhead. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Mobile bandwidth in emerging markets is constrained and sensitive to protocol bloat. Legacy application-layer wrapper protocols introduced 40-80 bytes of overhead per packet, degrading mobile radio performance and causing fragmentation. SFrame's compact header structure introduces as little as 4-6 bytes of overhead per media frame, enabling multi-party 60fps video calling and spatial audio in mini-apps without incurring packet MTU fragmentation or radio bandwidth penalties.

title: SFrame Standardized Cipher Suites: AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9605 §5 Cipher Suites & §5.1 Mandatory and Recommended Suites
summary: RFC 9605 standardizes high-performance AEAD cipher suites (AES_128_GCM, AES_256_GCM, and CHACHA20_POLY1305) with 80-bit and 128-bit authentication tags tailored for low-latency media.
detail: [SPEC FACT] RFC 9605 §5 defines standardized SFrame cipher suites utilizing Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD). The suite catalog includes 'AES_128_GCM_128' (mandatory to implement), 'AES_128_GCM_80' (truncated 80-bit tag for bandwidth-constrained audio), 'AES_256_GCM_128', and 'CHACHA20_POLY1305_128'. By using standard AEAD primitives, SFrame guarantees both confidentiality and strong cryptographic integrity for every transmitted media frame. The authenticated associated data (AAD) binds the SFrame header itself to the payload, preventing adversaries or malicious SFUs from modifying the KID or Counter fields without detection. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mobile runtimes execute on a vast spectrum of hardware, from low-end ARM Cortex devices without hardware AES acceleration to flagship smartphones with dedicated cryptographic coprocessors. Super-app WebRTC engines negotiate CHACHA20_POLY1305 on budget devices to achieve maximum CPU efficiency and low thermal output, while activating AES_128_GCM on hardware-accelerated chips. Store security baseline standards mandate that all E2EE conference mini-apps implement RFC 9605 cipher suites.

title: Anti-Replay Verification and Cryptographic Sliding Window Governance
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9605 §6 Cryptographic Processing & Anti-Replay
summary: Receiving endpoints maintain an anti-replay sliding window tracking the SFrame Counter (CTR), rejecting replayed frames and out-of-order packets falling outside the window.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under RFC 9605 §6, SFrame decapsulation enforces an anti-replay mechanism based on a sliding bitmask window. Because real-time UDP network delivery often results in packet reordering, the receiver maintains the highest observed counter (CTR_max) and a sliding window of recent counters (typically 64 to 128 frames). If an incoming frame has a CTR that has already been observed within the window or falls behind the trailing edge of the sliding window, the frame is immediately discarded without AEAD decryption. This prevents an active network adversary or compromised SFU from replaying recorded audio or video sequences (such as a replayed 'Yes, I authorize' voice snippet).
