[SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Financial authorization, digital identity verification, and telemedicine mini-apps are vulnerable to video/audio replay spoofing if transport streams can be captured and reinjected. Super-app WebRTC transform pipelines implement RFC 9605 anti-replay verification at the receiver boundary. Mini-apps handling high-assurance video interactions must verify that the anti-replay window is active, rejecting packets failing replay checks and logging security violation telemetry to the super-app auditing service.

title: WebRTC Encoded Transform (Insertable Streams) SFrame Pipeline Integration
category: Host Bridge, Protocol Handlers, Navigation & Lifecycle
standard_reference: W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform & RFC 9605 Integration Architecture
summary: SFrame executes inside Web Workers via WebRTC Encoded Transform (RTCRtpScriptTransform), encrypting RTCEncodedVideoFrame/RTCEncodedAudioFrame chunks before transmission.
detail: [SPEC FACT] On the web platform, RFC 9605 SFrame is implemented using the W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform specification ('RTCRtpScriptTransform' / Insertable Streams). In the transform worker, outgoing 'RTCEncodedVideoFrame' and 'RTCEncodedAudioFrame' chunks pass through a TransformStream where SFrame encapsulation prepends the SFrame header, encrypts the media payload using WebCrypto or optimized WebAssembly, and attaches the AEAD tag. On the receiving end, the reverse TransformStream decapsulates the SFrame header, verifies the anti-replay window, decrypts the payload, and forwards the clean frame to the browser's hardware video decoder. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Implementing SFrame via RTCRtpScriptTransform in Dedicated Web Workers ensures zero frame drops and maintains flawless UI thread responsiveness during high-definition 60fps video streams. Mini-app developer SDKs provide pre-compiled, audited SFrame Web Worker modules, allowing third-party developers to enable zero-trust end-to-end encryption with a single configuration flag ('e2ee: { mode: "sframe", keyRotationInterval: 300 }') without writing low-level cryptographic code.

title: W3C Resource Timing Level 2 & Detailed Subresource Waterfall Telemetry
standard_reference: W3C Resource Timing Level 2 §4 PerformanceResourceTiming Interface
summary: Resource Timing Level 2 exposes high-precision phase breakdowns of subresource network requests, establishing granular observability for mini-app packaging, bundle loading, and API latency.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Resource Timing Level 2 specification extends PerformanceEntry to define 'PerformanceResourceTiming', capturing microsecond-resolution DOMHighResTimeStamp milestones for every resource fetched by the user agent. The metric pipeline decomposes network requests into deterministic lifecycle phases: redirectStart/redirectEnd, workerStart (Service Worker boot latency), domainLookupStart/domainLookupEnd (DNS resolution), connectStart/connectEnd (TCP three-way handshake), secureConnectionStart (TLS cryptographic negotiation), requestStart, responseStart (Time To First Byte / TTFB), and responseEnd (body download completion). Additionally, transferSize, encodedBodySize, and decodedBodySize quantify HTTP compression ratios and network cache hits (transferSize == 0). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps pull heterogeneous assets across CDNs, host gateways, and partner microservices. By attaching a PerformanceObserver with type 'resource' and buffered=true, the host container captures network waterfall diagnostics across all child mini-app frames. Slow network phases (such as excessive DNS lookups or bloated TLS handshakes across unbundled third-party origins) are flagged during store review and runtime telemetry, enforcing strict subresource budget limits (total mini-app payload transferSize <= 4MB, responseStart <= 600ms on 4G networks).

title: W3C Server-Timing API & Full-Stack Infrastructure Tracing Correlation
standard_reference: W3C Server-Timing §3 The Server-Timing Header Field
summary: The Server-Timing HTTP header transmits backend processing metrics and distributed trace IDs to the mini-app runtime without exposing sensitive internal topology.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Server-Timing specification establishes an HTTP response header mechanism allowing upstream web servers and API gateways to communicate performance metrics to the user agent. Encoded as 'Server-Timing: metric_name;dur=123.4;desc="Description"', the user agent parses the metrics and exposes them programmatically via 'performance.getEntriesByType("resource")[n].serverTiming'. Each PerformanceServerTiming entry provides name, duration, and description attributes. When combined with W3C Trace Context (traceparent), Server-Timing correlates client-side TTFB latency with specific microservice spans (e.g., db_query;dur=45.2, cache_lookup;dur=1.1, auth_verify;dur=12.0). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app architectures, mini-app API calls route through a multi-tenant API gateway before reaching backend banking, telco, or merchant backends. The gateway injects standardized Server-Timing metrics into upstream API responses. The super-app client SDK aggregates serverTiming arrays and bundles them with client-side PerformanceResourceTiming metrics into telemetry payloads. This bridges frontend latency regressions directly to backend database deadlocks or microservice cold-starts without requiring intrusive server log correlation.

title: PerformanceResourceTiming Interface & Service Worker workerStart Disambiguation
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Resource Timing §4.1 PerformanceResourceTiming Attributes
summary: PerformanceResourceTiming provides programmatic access to resource fetching diagnostics, specifically isolating Service Worker startup overhead via workerStart.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The PerformanceResourceTiming interface provides read-only properties describing the network timeline of resources. A crucial attribute is 'workerStart': if a Service Worker is registered and handles the fetch event, workerStart records the timestamp immediately before dispatching FetchEvent to the worker thread. If the Service Worker process is cold, workerStart precedes fetchStart by several hundred milliseconds, quantifying worker boot penalty. When a request is fulfilled directly from CacheStorage within the Service Worker, transferSize evaluates to 0 while decodedBodySize reflects the uncompressed asset size, providing programmatic verification of offline-first caching strategies. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-app containers deploy dedicated Service Workers to handle offline caching, package bundle extraction, and dynamic request routing. PerformanceResourceTiming enables automated container diagnostics to measure workerStart latency across different mobile CPU chipsets. If worker startup exceeds 250ms on low-end devices, the container dynamically pivots to native navigation preloads or inline package streaming, preventing cold-start delays from degrading the mini-app launch experience.

title: Timing-Allow-Origin (TAO) Header & Cross-Origin Side-Channel Protection
standard_reference: W3C Resource Timing Level 2 §5 Cross-origin data protection & Timing-Allow-Origin
summary: Timing-Allow-Origin controls cross-origin exposure of detailed network timing attributes, preventing XS-Leaks and timing side-channel attacks against third-party endpoints.
detail: [SPEC FACT] To protect user privacy and prevent timing side-channel attacks (Cross-Site Search / XS-Leaks), user agents zero out detailed timing attributes (redirectStart/End, domainLookupStart/End, connectStart/End, secureConnectionStart, requestStart, responseStart) for cross-origin resources, setting them identical to startTime/responseEnd unless the server explicitly grants access via the 'Timing-Allow-Origin' (TAO) HTTP header. The header accepts a wildcard ('Timing-Allow-Origin: *') or specific origins ('Timing-Allow-Origin: https://miniapp.superapp.vn'). Without a valid TAO header, cross-origin subresources only reveal overall duration and transferSize=0, preventing malicious scripts from probing intranet resources or inferring user authentication state via network latency variations. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps frequently consume resources hosted across partner CDNs, analytics providers, and third-party payment gateways. The super-app standard mandates that partner CDNs serving mini-app subresources must explicitly supply 'Timing-Allow-Origin: https://<superapp-domain>' or wildcard '*' for public immutable assets. Simultaneously, sensitive authenticated APIs (such as payment authorization endpoints) must strictly omit TAO or restrict it to authenticated host origins, ensuring timing side-channel safety while preserving full performance observability for core mini-app infrastructure.

title: Server-Timing HTTP Header Syntax & Cross-Origin Privacy Gating
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Server-Timing §3.1 Syntax and Processing
summary: Server-Timing mandates strict header parsing syntax and ties its programmatic DOM availability to Timing-Allow-Origin verification to prevent server architecture leakage.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The Server-Timing header format conforms to RFC 8941 Structured Fields or comma-delimited tokens: 'Server-Timing: miss, db;dur=53, app;dur=47.2;desc="Transaction Engine"'. In browsers implementing the W3C Server-Timing specification, 'performance.getEntriesByType("resource")[n].serverTiming' is completely suppressed (empty array) for cross-origin resources unless the response also includes a valid 'Timing-Allow-Origin' header matching the requesting origin. This prevents third-party attackers from discovering backend topology, caching hit/miss status, or internal database response times of embedded resources. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In a super-app ecosystem, mini-app developers require diagnostic visibility into their own dedicated backend services without exposing internal system details to competing mini-apps. The super-app API gateway automatically attaches Server-Timing headers to mini-app API traffic while injecting strict Timing-Allow-Origin headers pinned strictly to the verified mini-app origin. Furthermore, the gateway strips sensitive server internals (such as database query text or internal IP addresses) from the description parameter, enforcing clean enterprise telemetry hygiene.

title: W3C Pointer Events Level 3 & Unified Multi-Modal Hardware Input Abstraction
standard_reference: W3C Pointer Events - Level 3 §5 PointerEvent Interface
summary: Pointer Events Level 3 unifies mouse, pen/stylus, and multi-touch hardware inputs into a single event model with rich physical device telemetry.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Pointer Events Level 3 specification establishes a hardware-agnostic input abstraction superseding fragmented MouseEvent and TouchEvent architectures. A PointerEvent provides unified lifecycle events (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel, pointerover, pointerout, pointerenter, pointerleave) accompanied by hardware telemetry: pointerId (unique hardware identifier), pointerType ('mouse', 'pen', 'touch'), isPrimary (identifying the active contact in multi-touch gestures), pressure (normalized [0.0, 1.0]), tangentialPressure, width/height (contact geometry in CSS pixels), tiltX/tiltY (degrees [-90, 90]), and altitudeAngle/azimuthAngle (spherical stylus orientation). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps span diverse interactive modalities, including biometric signature capture in financial contracts, canvas sketching in creative tools, and complex pan/zoom controls in mapping mini-apps. Developing separate handlers for touch and mouse causes event-order race conditions (such as 300ms click delays and double-firing). The super-app standard mandates Pointer Events Level 3 as the sole normative input model. The host container polyfills or normalizes native touch gestures into standard PointerEvents, enforcing predictable input handling across Android, iOS, and desktop webviews.

title: PointerEvent Interface & Advanced Stylus/Pen Telemetry Attributes
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Pointer Events §5.1 PointerEvent Attributes
summary: PointerEvent exposes high-fidelity stylus attributes (pressure, tilt, twist, azimuth/altitude), enabling enterprise-grade digital signature and drawing precision.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The PointerEvent interface introduces specialized attributes essential for high-precision pen input. 'pressure' provides a float between 0.0 and 1.0 (with 0.5 representing nominal pressure for devices lacking pressure sensors). 'tiltX' and 'tiltY' measure the angle between the stylus axis and the screen normal, while 'altitudeAngle' and 'azimuthAngle' provide a spherical coordinate alternative matching standard 3D rendering and digital art tablet hardware. 'twist' records the clockwise rotation of the stylus barrel in degrees [0, 359]. When a user hovers a stylus above the display, 'pointermove' events fire with pressure=0, allowing rich hover preview states without triggering selection. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Financial leasing, banking, and insurance mini-apps in a super-app ecosystem require legally binding biometric electronic signatures (e-Signatures compliant with Decree 130/2018/ND-CP / Law on Electronic Transactions). By utilizing PointerEvent stylus telemetry, mini-app signature components capture continuous pressure, velocity, and tilt vectors alongside coordinate timestamps. The super-app cryptographic bridge signs this multi-dimensional biometric telemetry with the device's hardware key, providing non-repudiation and forensic auditability for high-value contracts.

title: getCoalescedEvents() & Sub-Frame High-Fidelity Stroke Reconstruction
standard_reference: W3C Pointer Events Level 3 §5.2 getCoalescedEvents method
summary: getCoalescedEvents() grants access to all intermediate hardware touch/pen coordinate points merged by the browser event loop during a single animation frame.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern touchscreens and digitizers sample input at 120Hz to 240Hz, whereas the browser main thread and screen compositor typically render at 60Hz or 120Hz. To avoid event loop congestion, user agents coalesce multiple intermediate hardware touch samples into a single dispatch of 'pointermove'. The 'getCoalescedEvents()' method returns a sequence of PointerEvent objects representing all un-coalesced raw hardware events that occurred since the previous dispatch. Each coalesced event retains its unique high-precision timestamp, precise fractional coordinates, and instantaneous pressure values. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] When mini-app users draw rapid curves or write signatures on a canvas, drawing solely from the dispatched pointermove event produces jagged, polygonal strokes due to missed intermediate points. By invoking e.getCoalescedEvents(), mini-app drawing engines reconstruct the full 240Hz trajectory, delivering silky-smooth stroke interpolation and accurate velocity curves. Store quality gates verify that e-signature and drawing mini-apps consume getCoalescedEvents() to prevent broken or degraded signature capture on high-refresh-rate mobile devices.

title: getPredictedEvents() & Algorithmic Low-Latency Stroke Prediction
standard_reference: W3C Pointer Events Level 3 §5.3 getPredictedEvents method
summary: getPredictedEvents() provides speculative future pointer positions calculated by the browser's hardware Kalman filter, eliminating visible stylus tracking latency.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Due to display scanout time and hardware processing pipelines, drawing on a digital touchscreen exhibits physical latency (typically 15ms to 35ms between the physical pen tip and the drawn ink line). The 'getPredictedEvents()' method returns a sequence of synthetic PointerEvent objects generated by the user agent's predictive motion algorithms (such as Kalman filters or polynomial regression based on recent velocity and acceleration). These predicted points indicate where the pointer is expected to be by the time the next display frame finishes scanning out. Applications draw speculative ink to predicted coordinates, discarding and replacing them once authoritative hardware events arrive in subsequent frames. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps competing with native mobile apps often suffer from perception of 'web lag' during stylus annotation or document markup. The super-app standard provides a hardware-accelerated canvas utility component that automatically leverages getPredictedEvents(). By speculatively extending ink trails to the pen tip, perceived drawing latency is reduced from ~30ms to under 8ms, matching native iOS PencilKit and Android S-Pen responsiveness.

title: setPointerCapture() & Robust Cross-Boundary Touch Interaction Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Pointer Events Level 3 §6 Setting and releasing pointer capture
summary: setPointerCapture redirects all subsequent pointer events to a target element even if the contact moves outside its visual boundaries, preventing lost touch gestures.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Pointer capture re-targets all future events for a specific pointerId to a target Element until released via 'releasePointerCapture(pointerId)' or when the pointer is lifted (pointerup/pointercancel). While capture is active, the capturing element continuously receives pointermove and pointerup events even if the pointer drifts outside the browser viewport, over child iframes, or across competing DOM nodes. Crucially, the specification defines 'gotpointercapture' and 'lostpointercapture' lifecycle events, ensuring deterministic cleanup if the user agent forcibly revokes capture (e.g., when an OS-level incoming call dialog or notification shade intercepts touch). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Mini-app UI components (such as custom sliders, range pickers, audio scrubbers, and bottom sheet drag handles) frequently fail or glitch when a fast touch drag strays beyond the component's bounding box. Without pointer capture, events leak to parent scroll containers or host navigation bars. The super-app UI component framework mandates setPointerCapture() on pointerdown for all drag-and-drop and scrubbing controls. Furthermore, listeners on 'lostpointercapture' guarantee state reconciliation and prevent stuck drag states if the host super-app displays a security modal.

title: WHATWG MIME Sniffing Standard & Content-Type Ambiguity Defense
standard_reference: WHATWG MIME Sniffing Standard §4 Matching a MIME type pattern
summary: The WHATWG MIME Sniffing Standard specifies deterministic byte pattern matching algorithms to eliminate legacy browser heuristics that cause cross-site script execution.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Legacy web browsers historically examined resource byte prefixes (magic numbers) to guess MIME types when the HTTP 'Content-Type' header was missing, generic (application/octet-stream), or incorrect. The WHATWG MIME Sniffing standard formalizes precise algorithms for image, audio/video, font, and text sniffing, defining exact byte masks for formats like GIF87a/89a, PNG, JPEG, and WebP. Importantly, section 6 dictates that when an HTTP response contains an invalid or text/plain header, browsers must not sniff HTML tags (<html, <script) if the context requires safety. Exploiting loose sniffing, attackers upload malicious polyglot images containing embedded HTML/JavaScript to image hosting endpoints, tricking browsers into executing them as script. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps allow user-generated content (UGC), avatar uploads, and dynamic document downloads. If the super-app container or mini-app asset CDN relies on ambient MIME sniffing, polyglot files can execute within the mini-app origin, compromising authentication tokens and private storage. The super-app standard mandates that all container asset loaders, local package proxies, and CDN edge endpoints implement WHATWG MIME sniffing validation and strip ambiguous Content-Type declarations before asset injection.

title: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff & Strict Execution MIME Gating
standard_reference: WHATWG Fetch Standard §3.2.1 Corb & X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
summary: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff instructs the user agent to strictly enforce declared MIME types, aborting execution of mislabeled scripts and stylesheets.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' HTTP response header disables the browser's MIME type sniffing algorithms. Under 'nosniff', the browser enforces two strict security barriers: (1) Scripts (<script src>) are rejected and will not execute unless their declared Content-Type header matches a valid JavaScript MIME type ('application/javascript', 'text/javascript', 'application/ecmascript', etc.); (2) Stylesheets (<link rel="stylesheet">) are rejected unless served with 'text/css'. If an attacker uploads a JavaScript payload masquerading as an image (image/png) or plain text (text/plain), 'nosniff' causes the fetch to fail with a network error, completely neutralizing MIME-confusion XSS attacks. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-app packages consist of HTML, JS bundles, CSS stylesheets, and static media served via internal package protocols (e.g., miniapp-package:// or localhost webview proxies). The super-app host container mandates that internal protocol handlers and edge CDN servers append 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' to every single response. Store review automated scanners inspect packaged headers and fail any mini-app that attempts to bypass nosniff, ensuring robust defense against script smuggling.

title: WHATWG Fetch Standard & Destination-Specific MIME Type Gating
standard_reference: WHATWG Fetch Standard §4.3 Fetch response processing & MIME types
summary: WHATWG Fetch mandates destination-aware MIME validation across request contexts (script, style, worker, audio, video), preventing cross-origin data theft.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG Fetch Standard defines strict response validation based on 'request.destination'. When destination is 'script' or 'worker', the response's extract-a-MIME-type algorithm must yield a JavaScript MIME type if nosniff is set, and must not match audio/video/image types. Furthermore, Fetch specifies Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) and Opaque Response Blocking (ORB), which inspect initial response bytes even in 'no-cors' mode: if a cross-origin resource fetched as script actually begins with JSON, HTML, or XML patterns, ORB blocks the response body to prevent side-channel memory leaks (Spectre) and XSSI vulnerabilities. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps operate in a sandboxed webview where third-party libraries might attempt unauthorized cross-origin requests. The super-app runtime intercepts fetch() calls at the bridge layer, enforcing destination-specific MIME validation and validating that API responses returning sensitive customer JSON data are never fetchable via <script src> tags. This guarantees that multi-tenant mini-apps cannot exploit cross-origin read leaks against banking or telco backend APIs.

title: JavaScript Modules (ESM) & Mandatory JavaScript MIME Type Enforcement
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / ECMAScript & WHATWG HTML §8.1.3 Module Scripts
summary: ECMAScript Modules (type='module') unconditionally require a valid JavaScript MIME type, bypassing legacy compatibility quirks and enforcing strict CORS.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Unlike legacy classic scripts (<script>) which historically permitted relaxed MIME sniffing on same-origin endpoints, the HTML and ECMAScript specifications mandate that module scripts (<script type="module">) and dynamic imports ('import()') must always be served with a valid JavaScript MIME type ('text/javascript', 'application/javascript'). Any response with an incorrect MIME type (e.g., text/plain, application/octet-stream, text/html) results in an immediate load failure, regardless of whether 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' is present. Furthermore, module scripts are unconditionally subject to CORS rules, requiring valid Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers for cross-origin module trees. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Enterprise super-app mini-app frameworks use modern ES Module packaging for tree-shaking, lazy-loading, and micro-frontend federation. The super-app package builder and local webview cache interceptor enforce valid 'text/javascript' MIME mapping for all virtual .js and .mjs bundle chunks. Store submission pipelines verify that mini-app code relies on strict ES Module loading, eliminating obsolete classic script behaviors and closing legacy CORS-bypass vectors.

title: WebAssembly Streaming Compilation & Mandatory 'application/wasm' Validation
standard_reference: W3C WebAssembly Web API §3 Streaming Compilation & application/wasm
summary: WebAssembly.compileStreaming and instantiateStreaming require the HTTP Content-Type to be explicitly 'application/wasm', rejecting mislabeled binary payloads.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C WebAssembly Web API defines high-performance streaming compilation interfaces: 'WebAssembly.compileStreaming' and 'WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming'. To enable JIT compilation concurrent with network download, the specification strictly mandates that the Response object must evaluate to a MIME type of 'application/wasm'. If the Content-Type header is missing, incorrect, or accompanied by an incompatible charset parameter, the promise rejects immediately with a TypeError before compiling any bytecode. This strict MIME requirement prevents binary confusion attacks and guarantees that non-Wasm binary assets (such as corrupted archives or obfuscated media) are never fed into the browser's high-privilege native compiler. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In super-app applications, compute-intensive tasks (such as eKYC face biometric liveness detection, QR barcode scanning, and cryptographic token verification) are executed via WebAssembly modules. The super-app package distribution service signs and serves Wasm binaries with explicit 'Content-Type: application/wasm' and 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff'. Mini-app developers must use compileStreaming for optimal launch performance, with automated store compliance tools verifying that Wasm assets adhere strictly to W3C MIME standards.

title: W3C Beacon API & Asynchronous Out-of-Band Analytics Delivery
standard_reference: W3C Beacon API Candidate Recommendation §4 The Beacon Interface
summary: The W3C Beacon API defines an asynchronous out-of-band transport mechanism to transmit analytics and telemetry to web servers without delaying unload or impacting page performance.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Beacon API introduces the 'navigator.sendBeacon(url, data)' method, specifically engineered to schedule asynchronous HTTP POST requests handled out-of-process by the user agent. Historically, developers attempted to send telemetry during page dismissal using synchronous XMLHttpRequest or by dynamically injecting images in unload handlers, which caused severe browser UI jank, delayed tab closing, or suffered silent packet dropping when the rendering process was torn down. In contrast, navigator.sendBeacon guarantees that data is queued and reliably transmitted even after the originating document has completely unloaded. The browser manages the HTTP request life cycle autonomously, avoiding blocking the main execution thread or delaying navigation to the next document. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In high-volume super-app environments hosting financial, e-commerce, and telco mini-apps, tracking user drop-off, checkout funnel exit, and crash breadcrumbs during container destruction is vital for operational visibility. Mini-apps that execute heavy network requests inside 'pagehide' or 'beforeunload' degrade navigation fluidity and trigger ANR watchdogs. The super-app SDK mandates the use of navigator.sendBeacon (or its container bridge equivalent) for closing-telemetry packets, providing a standardized telemetry gateway that enforces payload size limits and queues outgoing pings into background network workers.

title: navigator.sendBeacon Interface Semantics & Quota Constraints
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Beacon API §4.1 sendBeacon Method & Queue Limits
summary: navigator.sendBeacon returns a boolean status indicating whether the user agent successfully scheduled the transmission within internal buffer limits.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'navigator.sendBeacon(url, data)' method accepts an endpoint URL and an optional payload, which can be an ArrayBuffer, Blob, DOMString, or FormData. The method returns 'true' if the user agent successfully queued the payload for transmission, and 'false' if the browser was unable to queue the request (typically because pending payload size exceeds the user agent's internal beacon queue limit, commonly 64KB across concurrent unloads). Unlike fetch(), sendBeacon does not return a Promise; the calling script cannot observe HTTP status codes, response headers, or response bodies. This one-way fire-and-forget semantic ensures that the browser can immediately release document JavaScript context resources without waiting for server ACKs. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-app telemetry clients must check the boolean return value of sendBeacon. If false is returned, the client SDK must discard low-priority metrics or compress breadcrumbs into emergency storage (such as IndexedDB or native bridge crash buffers) rather than attempting synchronous retries. The super-app platform standard requires that mini-app analytics payloads be capped at <= 16KB per beacon call, preventing buffer exhaustion and ensuring 100% telemetry capture reliability across budget mobile devices.

title: Beacon API Architecture & Integration with Modern Page Lifecycle
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Beacon API §2 Overview & Lifecycle Integration
summary: The Beacon API coordinates with modern visibility state transitions to reliably offload session telemetry prior to process suspension.
detail: [SPEC FACT] As modern mobile browsers transitioned away from legacy 'unload' events—which are completely unreliable on modern mobile operating systems and prevent Back/Forward Cache (bfcache) optimizations—the W3C Beacon API became the standard mechanism for session flush operations. The recommended design pattern triggers sendBeacon() within the 'visibilitychange' event when document.visibilityState changes to 'hidden'. This guarantees that data is dispatched whether the user switches tabs, backgrounds the host application, or navigates away. Network transmission is executed with low priority and background scheduling, preventing contention with critical rendering resources on subsequent pages. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app ecosystems where mini-apps are loaded in embedded webviews or sub-activities, relying on legacy window.onunload is strictly prohibited by store review rules because mobile OS window managers (Android Activity onDestroy, iOS viewDidDisappear) terminate processes abruptly. The super-app standard dictates that mini-apps hook visibilitychange listeners to flush pending analytics via sendBeacon. Automated review linters flag any use of synchronous XHR or blocking loops in termination handlers.

title: WHATWG Fetch 'keepalive' Flag & Beacon Transport Convergence
standard_reference: WHATWG Fetch Standard §5.4 Fetch with keepalive
summary: WHATWG Fetch specifies the 'keepalive: true' flag, unifying beacon-style out-of-band requests with modern Promise-based fetch semantics.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG Fetch Standard defines the 'keepalive' boolean flag on RequestInit. When set to true, 'fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body, keepalive: true })' instructs the browser to allow the HTTP request to outlive the document execution context, sharing the same underlying browser network buffer pool as navigator.sendBeacon. However, fetch with keepalive provides significant advantages over sendBeacon: it supports custom HTTP headers (such as Authorization Bearer tokens, API keys, and custom X-Trace-Id correlation headers), allows diverse HTTP methods (PUT, POST, DELETE), and enables credentials modes (same-origin, include). Total pending keepalive bytes are constrained by the browser (typically 64KB across all concurrent requests per client) to protect device memory. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] While navigator.sendBeacon is optimal for simple telemetry, super-app enterprise mini-apps often require authenticated telemetry and signed audit events when closing a session. The super-app runtime bridge polyfills and optimizes fetch({ keepalive: true }) by attaching host authentication tokens and trace headers at the native network stack, enabling mini-apps to report audit and transaction closure events securely without getting killed by webview destruction.

title: Beacon API Privacy Sandboxing, CORS Enforcement & Header Restrictions
standard_reference: W3C Beacon API §5 Privacy and Security Considerations
summary: The Beacon specification mandates strict CORS compliance and restricts request headers to prevent unauthorized cross-origin data exfiltration.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Beacon specifications, cross-origin beacon requests must comply with the CORS protocol. When sendBeacon transmits a payload with a non-simple MIME type (such as application/json), the browser must trigger a preflight OPTIONS request before transmitting the payload; however, because the originating document may unload before the preflight completes, the beacon payload may be dropped if CORS preflights fail or are not pre-cached. To guarantee reliable transmission without preflight delays, beacon data is traditionally transmitted as text/plain, multipart/form-data, or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Furthermore, user agents restrict beacon requests to secure contexts (HTTPS) and enforce user privacy controls (such as Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control, and Private Browsing restrictions). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app security gateways must prevent rogue mini-apps from abusing sendBeacon to exfiltrate cached sensitive banking data to unauthorized third-party endpoints. The super-app host container enforces strict domain allowlisting on all beacon endpoints: URLs passed to sendBeacon must resolve to approved domains declared in the mini-app manifest's 'network_egress' rules. Calls to unlisted origins are intercepted and blocked by the webview native bridge.

title: Back/Forward Cache (bfcache) Architecture & Instant Navigation Restoration
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Living Standard §7.4 Browsing the Web & Session History Traversal
summary: The Back/Forward Cache (bfcache) freezes an entire document's live DOM and JavaScript execution heap in memory, enabling instantaneous back and forward navigations.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The WHATWG HTML specification standardizes session history traversal, defining how user agents preserve browsing context states. The Back/Forward Cache (bfcache) is an in-memory optimization that stores a complete snapshot of a web page—including its DOM tree, JavaScript object heap, active worker threads, and layout state—when the user navigates away. When the user navigates back, the browser restores the page instantly without parsing HTML, evaluating JavaScript, or re-executing subresource network requests. This reduces page load time from seconds to milliseconds (0ms TTFB/FCP), completely eliminating blank screens. However, during bfcache residence, all JavaScript timers (setTimeout, setInterval), microtasks, and network connections (WebSocket, WebRTC) are completely paused. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps frequently employ multi-page navigation flows (e.g., product catalog -> product detail -> checkout -> payment status). If mini-app pages are forced to perform full cold reloads when users press the container back button, battery consumption spikes and transaction drop-off rates increase. The super-app standard requires container webviews (Android WebView and iOS WKWebView) to enable bfcache capabilities, ensuring that returning to a previous mini-app view is instantaneous while memory-capped background tabs are safely discarded if memory pressure occurs.

title: PageTransitionEvent & event.persisted State Reconciliation
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / WHATWG HTML §7.4.5 PageTransitionEvent.persisted
summary: The 'pageshow' event and its 'persisted' boolean property allow scripts to distinguish between fresh document loads and restorations from bfcache.
detail: [SPEC FACT] When a page is loaded or restored, the browser fires the 'pageshow' event on the window object, providing a 'PageTransitionEvent' parameter. The 'persisted' read-only property returns a boolean: 'false' indicates an initial page load (or full navigation reload), while 'true' indicates that the page was restored directly from the bfcache without re-executing initialization scripts. Because JavaScript execution was paused rather than restarted, scripts do not re-run DOMContentLoaded or window.onload. Therefore, applications must use the 'pageshow' event checking 'event.persisted === true' to re-validate cached user authentication, refresh stale UI data (such as account balance, shopping cart item counts, or inventory status), and re-subscribe to real-time notification streams. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In fintech and e-commerce mini-apps, displaying stale financial balances or expired discount coupons after a back navigation can lead to severe business disputes and regulatory non-compliance. The super-app SDK mandates that mini-app state managers register 'pageshow' handlers. When 'event.persisted' is true, the mini-app must perform lightweight background data re-validation against the host bridge without tearing down the existing DOM, achieving instant render speed with guaranteed data consistency.

title: Window 'pagehide' Event & Clean Transition to Suspended State
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / WHATWG HTML §7.4.4 The Window pagehide Event
summary: The 'pagehide' event signals document dismissal, allowing applications to clean up transient resources while preserving bfcache eligibility.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'pagehide' event fires on the Window object when the user navigates away from the page. Like 'pageshow', it receives a PageTransitionEvent whose 'persisted' property indicates whether the user agent intends to preserve the document in bfcache ('true') or discard and destroy it ('false'). Applications use pagehide to pause ongoing animations, stop video playback, save unsaved form drafts to IndexedDB, and close ephemeral communication channels. Crucially, the presence of a 'pagehide' listener does NOT prevent the page from entering bfcache, unlike legacy 'unload' event listeners which disqualify pages from bfcache in major rendering engines. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-app developers frequently leave open IndexedDB transaction locks, audio players, or hardware sensor streams when navigating to external views. The super-app host container standard requires developers to use 'pagehide' (instead of unload) to release shared hardware locks (such as W3C Web Locks, camera tracks, or BLE connections). Store review automated testing harnesses verify that mini-app codebases contain zero 'unload' listeners, preserving 100% bfcache compatibility.

title: PerformanceNavigationTiming & Back/Forward Navigation Telemetry
standard_reference: W3C Navigation Timing Level 2 §4.2 PerformanceNavigationTiming.type
summary: PerformanceNavigationTiming.type exposes navigation entry types, allowing real-user monitoring (RUM) pipelines to isolate back_forward traversals.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Navigation Timing Level 2, the 'PerformanceNavigationTiming.type' attribute returns one of four strings: 'navigate' (standard navigation), 'reload' (page refresh), 'back_forward' (session history traversal), or 'prerender' (speculative pre-rendering). When a navigation is served from bfcache, a new PerformanceNavigationTiming entry is not created by default in classical browsers, but modern RUM frameworks utilize PerformanceObserver tracking soft navigation and pageshow persisted timings to categorize history traversals. Measuring the ratio of 'back_forward' navigations that successfully utilize bfcache versus those that fall back to full network reloads provides a critical metric for client-side operational efficiency. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app performance telemetry modules collect PerformanceNavigationTiming metrics across all hosted mini-apps. The platform operations dashboard aggregates bfcache hit ratios as a core Quality of Service (QoS) key performance indicator. Mini-apps that demonstrate high back/forward navigation volume but suffer from 0% bfcache hits (due to legacy blocking scripts or improper cache-control headers) are flagged during automated store reviews with actionable optimization reports.

title: bfcache Blocking Anti-Patterns, Cache-Control & Store Gating
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / Browser Engine Architecture: bfcache Invalidation Rules
summary: Platform policies and automated store gates identify and eliminate common architectural anti-patterns that prevent bfcache activation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Browsers will disqualify a page from entering the bfcache if it violates specific runtime constraints: (1) Registration of legacy 'unload' event listeners; (2) Serving pages with 'Cache-Control: no-store' HTTP headers (historically treated by WebKit and Chromium as an explicit directive not to cache live page state, though modern browsers are refining this); (3) Active open connections that cannot be gracefully paused, such as active WebRTC peer connections, unfinished IndexedDB transactions, or open Web Locks; (4) Retaining cross-origin window.opener references without 'noopener' or COOP isolation. When these conditions are present, the browser is forced to discard the page and perform a costly cold reload upon traversal. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] To guarantee standard-grade instant navigation across the entire ecosystem, the super-app store review pipeline implements automated static and dynamic bfcache audits. The store test harness executes a synthetic launch-navigate-back sequence against submitted mini-apps, inspecting devtools/CDP 'BackForwardCache.canStorePage' and 'notRestoredReasons' telemetry. Mini-apps that fail bfcache restoration due to preventable code defects (such as dangling unload listeners or unclosed locks) receive automated remediation notices prior to release approval.

title: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 & Container Directive Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 §3 Policy Delivery & Directive Hierarchy
summary: W3C CSP Level 3 establishes a declarative defense-in-depth policy framework that restricts resource fetching, script execution, and frame nesting in user agents.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The W3C Content Security Policy Level 3 specification defines the 'Content-Security-Policy' HTTP response header and meta tag delivery mechanism. CSP allows site administrators to declare an authoritative whitelist of origins, cryptographic nonces, and hashes for executable code and subresources. By restricting the origins from which scripts, images, media, and stylesheets can be loaded, CSP mitigates Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), data injection, and clickjacking attacks. In CSP Level 3, fallback directives are structured hierarchically: 'default-src' serves as the fallback for fetch directives like 'script-src', 'style-src', 'img-src', and 'connect-src', while navigation and framing directives ('base-uri', 'form-action', 'frame-ancestors') operate independently and cannot be defaulted to default-src. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps run within shared webview containers where an XSS vulnerability could allow an attacker to invoke privileged host bridge APIs (e.g., camera, location, payments, contact list). The super-app standard mandates that all mini-app HTML shells and dynamic webviews enforce a strict CSP Level 3 policy injected by the host container proxy. This ensures that third-party scripts cannot establish unauthorized outbound sockets or execute arbitrary eval() strings, establishing a mathematically verifiable execution perimeter.

title: CSP 'default-src' Fallbacks & 'connect-src' Egress Boundaries
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C CSP Level 3 §4.2 default-src & §4.4 connect-src
summary: The 'default-src' directive provides a defensive baseline while 'connect-src' strictly confines asynchronous network interfaces (fetch, XHR, WebSocket, EventSource).
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'default-src' directive defines the default policy for fetching resources when specific fetch directives are absent. For maximum security, a strict policy sets 'default-src 'none'', requiring developers to explicitly opt-in each resource type. The 'connect-src' directive specifically restricts the URLs which can be loaded using script interfaces, including 'fetch()', 'XMLHttpRequest', 'WebSocket', 'EventSource', and 'navigator.sendBeacon()'. If a script attempts to initiate a network request to an origin not explicitly permitted by connect-src (or default-src if connect-src is omitted), the browser immediately blocks the request and dispatches a SecurityPolicyViolationEvent. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] To prevent unauthorized data exfiltration and covert command-and-control communication, the super-app platform compiler synthesizes 'connect-src' rules directly from the mini-app's manifest permissions. If a mini-app declares domain permissions for 'api.merchant.com', the generated CSP specifies 'connect-src 'self' https://api.merchant.com wss://api.merchant.com'. Any attempt by compromised npm dependencies to contact rogue telemetry or mining servers is instantly blocked at the browser engine level.

title: CSP 'base-uri' Directive & Relative Path Injection Defense
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C CSP Level 3 §5.1 base-uri Directive
summary: The 'base-uri' directive restricts the URLs that can be used in a document's <base> element, preventing attackers from hijacking relative resource URLs.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In HTML, the '<base href="...">' element specifies the base URL for all relative URLs in a document (such as relative script tags, image sources, and stylesheet links). In HTML injection vulnerabilities that fall short of full script execution, an attacker can inject a malicious '<base href="https://attacker.com/">' tag into the head of a document. Consequently, subsequent scripts loaded via relative paths (e.g., '<script src="app.js">') are resolved to 'https://attacker.com/app.js', achieving arbitrary code execution despite strict origin white-listing on scripts. The CSP 'base-uri' directive restricts which URLs can appear in a <base> element; setting 'base-uri 'none'' or 'base-uri 'self'' completely immunizes the application against base-tag hijacking. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-app packages package internal assets using relative paths (e.g., './assets/vendor.js'). If a mini-app renders unsanitized user content into its DOM header, base-tag hijacking could redirect internal mini-app asset loads to an attacker-controlled remote server. The super-app host container mandates 'base-uri 'none'' (or 'base-uri 'self'') on all mini-app documents, neutralizing base-tag manipulation and safeguarding the local package resolution boundary.

title: CSP 'frame-ancestors' & Container Clickjacking Sandboxing
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C CSP Level 3 §5.3 frame-ancestors Directive
summary: The 'frame-ancestors' directive specifies valid parents that may embed a page in an iframe, replacing the deprecated X-Frame-Options header.
detail: [SPEC FACT] The 'frame-ancestors' directive restricts which origins can embed the current document using '<frame>', '<iframe>', '<object>', '<embed>', or '<applet>'. Setting 'frame-ancestors 'none'' prevents any framing, while 'frame-ancestors 'self'' permits only same-origin framing. Crucially, frame-ancestors supersedes the legacy 'X-Frame-Options: DENY|SAMEORIGIN' header, offering granular multi-origin declarations and full enforcement across modern browser engines. If a document with 'frame-ancestors 'none'' is embedded by an external site, the user agent immediately blocks rendering of the inner frame, preventing UI redressing and clickjacking attacks where transparent overlays trick users into clicking high-privilege buttons. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-apps, mini-apps frequently display sensitive payment confirmation dialogs, identity approval screens, and credential prompts. If a mini-app page could be embedded by rogue third-party websites or malicious secondary webviews, attackers could perform clickjacking to authorize financial transfers. The super-app gateway injects 'frame-ancestors 'none'' on all checkout and authentication endpoints, or restricts framing exclusively to the verified internal super-app host origin ('frame-ancestors superapp://*').

title: CSP 'upgrade-insecure-requests' & Mixed-Content Elimination
standard_reference: MDN Web Docs / W3C Upgrade Insecure Requests §3 The Directive
summary: The 'upgrade-insecure-requests' directive instructs user agents to treat all insecure HTTP resource URLs as though they were HTTPS before fetching.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Modern web applications migrating legacy subresources or importing third-party content may accidentally reference insecure HTTP URLs. Under the W3C Upgrade Insecure Requests specification, delivering 'Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests' instructs the browser to automatically rewrite all HTTP request URLs to HTTPS prior to initiating the network fetch. This eliminates mixed-content warnings, prevents active network adversaries (man-in-the-middle attackers) from intercepting or modifying unencrypted subresources, and preserves confidentiality. If the target server does not support HTTPS on port 443, the request fails securely rather than falling back to plaintext HTTP. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Telco and banking super-apps operate across untrusted public Wi-Fi and mobile networks. If a mini-app fetches subresources (such as images, icons, or fonts) over plaintext HTTP, network attackers can alter the appearance of transactions or inject malicious payloads into legacy proxies. The super-app host platform strictly enforces 'upgrade-insecure-requests' on all mini-app webviews, automatically encrypting all outbound subresource traffic and rejecting insecure cleartext connections.

title: W3C Permissions API & navigator.permissions.query() Programmatic Status Inspection
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Permissions §5.1 navigator.permissions & §5.2 query() method
summary: The W3C Permissions API defines 'navigator.permissions.query()' taking a PermissionDescriptor dictionary to asynchronously inspect permission states prior to invoking intrusive native prompts.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Permissions §5.1 and §5.2, user agents expose the 'navigator.permissions' interface providing the 'query(permissionDesc)' method. This method accepts a 'PermissionDescriptor' dictionary containing a mandatory 'name' DOMString (e.g., 'geolocation', 'camera', 'microphone', 'notifications', 'persistent-storage', 'push', 'midi', 'screen-wake-lock') along with feature-specific parameters (such as 'userVisibleOnly' for push or 'panTiltZoom' for camera). The method returns a Promise resolving to a 'PermissionStatus' object reflecting the current authorization state without triggering interactive dialogs or prompting the user. If an unsupported or invalid permission name is queried, the user agent rejects the Promise with a 'TypeError'. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps operate within a zero-surprise permission architecture where cold-calling invasive hardware APIs (like camera, precise location, or microphone) degrades user trust and risks store rejection. The super-app host container standardizes 'navigator.permissions.query()' as the mandatory pre-flight gate. Mini-apps must inspect the permission state before rendering feature buttons. If the state is 'prompt', the mini-app UI displays an informative pre-permission primer modal explaining the business necessity. The host bridge transparently intercepts 'navigator.permissions.query()', translating it into native OS permission checks (Android ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission / iOS CLLocationManager.authorizationStatus) merged with super-app tenant policy matrices.

title: PermissionStatus Interface: 'granted', 'prompt', and 'denied' Tri-State Lifecycle
standard_reference: W3C Permissions §6 PermissionStatus interface & PermissionState enum
summary: The PermissionStatus interface exposes the 'state' property reflecting an authoritative tri-state enum ('granted', 'prompt', 'denied') governing hardware API accessibility.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Permissions §6 defines the 'PermissionStatus' interface inheriting from EventTarget. Its primary attribute is readonly attribute PermissionState state, which evaluates to exactly one of three string tokens: 'granted' (the origin is authorized to execute the powerful feature without further user interaction), 'denied' (the origin is strictly prohibited from executing the feature, and invocation will immediately fail without prompting the user), or 'prompt' (invoking the feature will require explicit user consent via an interactive platform prompt). User agents enforce that once state is 'denied', subsequent calls to the underlying API fail fast with a DOMException ('NotAllowedError'), preserving user privacy and preventing prompt fatigue. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app governance, the tri-state model is augmented with host container lifecycle states. If 'state' is 'denied' due to an explicit user refusal at the OS level or a super-app system settings revocation, the mini-app must not re-prompt repeatedly. The super-app SDK standardizes fallback UX flows: when 'state === "denied"', the mini-app renders a deep-link button routing the user directly to the native Super-App Container Settings screen via 'superapp.openSettings({ section: "permissions" })'. Store review policies penalize mini-apps that enter infinite prompt loops or fail to gracefully degrade when permissions evaluate to 'denied'.

title: PermissionStatus 'onchange' Event & Dynamic OS-Level Revocation Synchronization
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Permissions §6.1 The change event & EventHandler onchange
summary: The 'change' event on PermissionStatus allows mini-apps to listen for asynchronous permission state transitions caused by external OS settings modifications or host revoking grants.
detail: [SPEC FACT] According to W3C Permissions §6.1, a user agent must queue a task to fire an event named 'change' at the 'PermissionStatus' instance whenever the permission state for that feature changes. This typically occurs when a user navigates to the browser's origin settings, toggles global hardware switches (e.g., system-wide location toggle, microphone privacy mute), or when automated enterprise policies revoke access. The 'change' event inherits from Event, allowing mini-apps to bind listeners via 'status.addEventListener("change", ...)' or 'status.onchange = ...'. This guarantees that web applications maintain real-time reactive state synchronization rather than relying on stale cached permission flags. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps frequently run concurrently with native host features or survive in the Back/Forward Cache (bfcache) while users switch to native Android/iOS Settings. If a user revokes camera or location access in the OS settings while a ride-hailing or eKYC mini-app is suspended, returning to the webview without permission change synchronization leads to unhandled exceptions or broken camera feeds. The super-app host container registers native lifecycle broadcast receivers (e.g., Android OnRequestPermissionsResultCallback and iOS UIApplicationDidBecomeActiveNotification) and immediately fires synthetic 'change' events across all active PermissionStatus handles inside embedded webviews, enabling instantaneous UI re-rendering and resource teardown.

title: W3C Permissions Policy Cohesion & Cross-Origin Iframe Permission Attenuation
standard_reference: W3C Permissions §4 Permissions and Policy Controlled Features & W3C Permissions Policy §4
summary: Permissions API state queries strictly respect W3C Permissions Policy HTTP headers and iframe 'allow' attributes; features disabled by policy evaluate immediately to 'denied'.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Permissions §4 formalizes the integration between the Permissions API and the W3C Permissions Policy specification. When a document's execution environment is constrained by a Permissions Policy directive (delivered via the 'Permissions-Policy' HTTP header or an iframe's 'allow' attribute), the Permissions API query algorithm executes a policy check prior to evaluating user consent. If the policy denies the feature for the requesting origin (e.g., 'geolocation=()' or an embedded iframe missing the 'allow="camera"' token), 'navigator.permissions.query()' MUST return a PermissionStatus with 'state: "denied"', regardless of whether the end-user has previously granted permission to that origin. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app platforms utilize multi-tiered sandboxing where third-party mini-apps may embed secondary partner widgets or payment iframes. The super-app gateway injects a strict Permissions Policy header at the outer webview layer based on the mini-app's static manifest declaration. If a mini-app did not declare 'camera' in its 'manifest.json' capabilities, the container sets 'Permissions-Policy: camera=()'. When any internal script calls 'navigator.permissions.query({ name: "camera" })', the engine instantly returns 'denied' without dispatching native IPC bridges or prompting the OS, completely eliminating cross-origin permission escalation.

title: Super-App Container Multi-Tenant Permission Mediation & Store Compliance Gating
category: Host Bridge, Device Capabilities & Cross-Platform Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Permissions §8 Security and Privacy Considerations & Super-App Container Native Bridge Architecture
summary: Super-app container architectures mediate Permissions API queries through a 4-tier authorization pipeline: Manifest Declaration, Enterprise Admin Policy, Host Privacy Guard, and OS Authorization.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Permissions §8, permission delegation and querying must prevent fingerprinting and cross-origin tracking vectors. The specification allows user agents to implement custom authorization algorithms, rate-limiting, and ephemeral temporary grants (e.g., 'one-time grant' or 'session-only grant') that automatically reset when the browsing context navigates or terminates. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app runtimes (e.g., Viettel SuperApp, WeChat, Alipay), permission mediation cannot rely solely on raw webview defaults. The host container implements an authoritative 4-tier permission evaluation pipeline: (1) Manifest Scope Verification (the requested capability must be explicitly declared in the signed mini-app manifest approved during store review); (2) Enterprise Tenant Policy (corporate or telco MDM policies can globally blacklist capabilities such as Bluetooth or Screen Recording for regulated enterprise profiles); (3) Container Trust & Anti-Abuse (the container checks for transient user activation via UserActivation.isActive to prevent automated bot queries); and (4) Native OS Permission State (mapping to Android Keystore / iOS TCC databases). Store automated review pipelines audit mini-app source code using static analysis to ensure that every privileged API call is preceded by a verified 'navigator.permissions.query()' check and paired with descriptive rationale copy.

title: WHATWG Streams API: ReadableStream Architecture, Controller States, and Backpressure Flow Control
standard_reference: WHATWG Streams Standard §3.2 ReadableStream class & §3.3 ReadableStreamDefaultController
summary: The WHATWG Streams specification defines 'ReadableStream' for chunk-by-chunk asynchronous sequential data consumption, providing built-in backpressure signaling to prevent consumer buffer saturation.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WHATWG Streams §3.2, a 'ReadableStream' represents a source of sequential data chunks that can be asynchronously read over time. A ReadableStream encapsulates an underlying source and is driven by a 'ReadableStreamDefaultController'. The stream exposes the 'locked' boolean attribute and the 'getReader()' method, which locks the stream to a reader instance (such as 'ReadableStreamDefaultReader'), ensuring that only one consumer can access the stream at a time. The controller manages internal queuing through the 'desiredSize' property. If the consumer processes chunks slower than the producer enqueues them, 'desiredSize' drops to zero or below, mathematically signaling negative backpressure. Producers observing backpressure pause upstream chunk acquisition, preventing unbounded heap allocation and main-thread execution stalls. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Mobile super-apps routinely transfer large multi-megabyte payloads, such as offline map tiles, product catalogs, financial statement PDFs, and dynamic mini-app subpackages. If these payloads are ingested as monolithic ArrayBuffer or string objects, memory allocation spikes frequently trigger mobile OS low-memory termination (Android LMK / iOS Jetsam). The super-app runtime standardizes ReadableStream pipelines for all container network downloads and local storage reads. The container bridge monitors 'desiredSize' during chunk piping, pausing native socket buffers whenever the webview's JavaScript consumer indicates high downstream pressure.

title: WritableStream & UnderlyingSink Lifecycle: Asynchronous Write Pacing and Error Propagation
standard_reference: WHATWG Streams Standard §4.2 WritableStream class & §4.3 WritableStreamDefaultWriter
summary: The 'WritableStream' interface provides a standardized abstraction for writing streaming data to a sink, coordinating write promises, backpressure queues, and abort lifecycle signals.
detail: [SPEC FACT] In WHATWG Streams §4.2, 'WritableStream' represents a destination for data chunks, wrapping an underlying sink that implements optional lifecycle hooks: 'start(controller)', 'write(chunk, controller)', 'close()', and 'abort(reason)'. When a consumer writes data using 'writer.write(chunk)', the method returns a Promise that fulfills only when the underlying sink has accepted and processed the chunk. The writer's 'ready' property returns a Promise that fulfills when the stream's internal queue falls below its high-water mark, enabling the writer to pause chunk emission until capacity is available. If an error occurs during write operations or if 'writer.abort(reason)' is invoked, the error propagates immediately across the entire pipeline, rejecting outstanding write promises and triggering cleanup in the underlying sink. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps frequently upload telemetry batches, crash breadcrumbs, large media files, and offline transaction ledgers to container gateways. By encapsulating outgoing HTTP POST requests and local IndexedDB transaction logs behind WritableStream instances, the super-app container enforces strict write pacing. The container's host bridge implements an underlying sink that regulates native disk writes and socket transmissions, guaranteeing that unhandled network drops cleanly abort the stream and free held native buffers.

title: TransformStream & pipeThrough/pipeTo Composition: Composable In-Flight Processing
standard_reference: WHATWG Streams Standard §5.2 TransformStream class & §3.2.5.2 pipeThrough/pipeTo methods
summary: TransformStream pairs a ReadableStream and WritableStream into a single duplex transformation pipeline, enabling in-flight decompression, cryptography, and parsing via pipeThrough().
detail: [SPEC FACT] WHATWG Streams §5.2 defines 'TransformStream', an interface consisting of a pair of streams: a writable stream (the writable side) that accepts raw input chunks, and a readable stream (the readable side) that emits transformed output chunks. The underlying transformer specifies a 'transform(chunk, controller)' method that processes chunks in-flight and calls 'controller.enqueue(transformedChunk)'. ReadableStream exposes the chaining methods 'pipeThrough({ writable, readable })' and 'pipeTo(destination, options)'. The pipeTo algorithm automatically connects backpressure signals between source and destination: if the destination sink's buffer fills up, backpressure flows upstream through the TransformStream directly to the original ReadableStream producer. Furthermore, pipeTo provides deterministic error propagation and cancellation signals ('preventAbort', 'preventCancel', 'preventClose', 'signal'). [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app runtimes, mini-app packages are encrypted and compressed at the edge. The super-app client implements modular streaming pipelines using 'response.body.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream("gzip")).pipeThrough(new DecryptionTransformStream(sessionKey)).pipeThrough(new JsonLinesParserStream())'. This enables the mini-app to parse and render critical configuration records immediately as the first network packets arrive, drastically lowering Time to Interactive (TTI) without allocating intermediate in-memory files.

title: ReadableStreamBYOBReader & Byte Streams: Zero-Copy ArrayBuffer Transfer & Memory Optimization
standard_reference: WHATWG Streams Standard §3.7 ReadableStreamBYOBReader class & §3.5 ReadableByteStreamController
summary: ReadableStreamBYOBReader ('Bring Your Own Buffer') enables zero-copy streaming I/O by allowing consumers to pass pre-allocated ArrayBuffer views, eliminating garbage collection churn.
detail: [SPEC FACT] For high-throughput binary I/O, WHATWG Streams specifies byte streams constructed with '{ type: "bytes" }' and managed by a 'ReadableByteStreamController'. To read from a byte stream without incurring memory allocations for every incoming chunk, consumers instantiate a 'ReadableStreamBYOBReader' via 'stream.getReader({ mode: "byob" })'. The reader exposes the method 'read(view)', which accepts a typed ArrayBufferView (such as a Uint8Array) provided by the caller. During execution, the browser engine transfers the memory backing the view directly into the underlying native I/O buffer and returns a resolved promise containing the mutated view along with 'bytesRead'. Because the caller reuses the same allocated ArrayBuffer across successive read loops, zero temporary JavaScript heap objects are created, completely eliminating V8/JavaScriptCore Garbage Collection (GC) pauses during intensive streaming. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-apps executing high-frequency data streaming—such as live stock tickers, real-time gaming state synchronization, WebGPU texture streaming, and high-resolution camera barcode scanning—suffer severe frame drops if garbage collection interrupts the 60fps/120fps render loop. The super-app host container standardizes BYOB byte streams across all high-throughput native-to-webview bridges. Mini-apps pre-allocate a reusable 64KB Uint8Array ring buffer passed to 'byobReader.read(buffer)', ensuring zero GC jitter and maintaining smooth UI responsiveness under heavy network saturation.

title: Stream Teeing (ReadableStream.tee()), Locking Invariants & Memory Leak Prevention
standard_reference: WHATWG Streams Standard §3.2.5.4 tee() method & §3.2.2 Locked Streams
summary: The 'tee()' method branches a ReadableStream into two independent branches, requiring careful lifecycle governance to avoid buffer bloat when branches are consumed at asymmetric rates.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under WHATWG Streams §3.2.5.4, invoking 'readableStream.tee()' locks the original stream and returns a two-element array containing two new, independent ReadableStream instances: '[branch1, branch2]'. Each branch receives identical copies of all chunks emitted by the original underlying source. However, because both branches draw from the same upstream source, if one branch is actively consumed while the other branch remains unread or paused, the underlying tee engine must internally buffer all unconsumed chunks in memory to ensure the stalled branch eventually receives them. If an unread branch is abandoned without being canceled, the internal queue grows unbounded, causing catastrophic memory leaks. To reclaim memory, consumers must explicitly cancel unused branches via 'branch.cancel()', which allows the user agent to discard the queue and propagate cancellation upstream once both branches are closed. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise super-app telemetry and audit architectures, mini-app network responses are frequently split: one branch feeds the UI rendering component while the second branch feeds an audit logging and local caching pipeline. The super-app container SDK provides a safe wrapper around 'tee()': if the secondary analytics branch fails to consume chunks within an aggressive 5-second timeout window or encounters an error, the container automatically executes 'branch2.cancel("analytics_timeout")'. This defensive cancellation invariant preserves the primary UI stream, prevents mobile RAM exhaustion, and enforces robust multi-tenant runtime isolation.

title: W3C DOMMatrix Interface: 2D & 3D Affine Transformations, Matrix Math, and Hardware Composition
standard_reference: W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §3 The DOMMatrix and DOMMatrixReadOnly interfaces
summary: The W3C DOMMatrix interface provides a standardized, hardware-accelerated 4x4 mathematical matrix representation for 2D and 3D affine coordinate transformations in web rendering engines.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §3 defines the 'DOMMatrixReadOnly' and mutable 'DOMMatrix' interfaces. Representing a 4x4 transformation matrix, DOMMatrix supports both 2D transformations (using components a, b, c, d, e, f) and full 3D projective transformations (m11 through m44). The interface exposes high-performance transformation primitives including 'translate(tx, ty, tz)', 'scale(scaleX, scaleY, scaleZ)', 'rotate(rotX, rotY, rotZ)', 'multiply(otherMatrix)', 'inverse()', and 'transformPoint(point)'. The 'is2D' boolean attribute indicates whether the matrix represents a purely 2D affine transformation, enabling rendering engines to optimize matrix multiplications by bypassing 3D perspective computations. The 'fromMatrix()' and 'fromFloat32Array()' static factory methods allow zero-overhead serialization and ingestion of matrix data directly from WebGL/WebGPU vertex buffers. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app mini-apps incorporate rich dynamic UIs, custom data visualization charts, interactive maps, and cross-platform canvas animations. Manually calculating transformation matrices in pure JavaScript generates heavy CPU overhead and GC churn. By standardizing on native DOMMatrix instances, mini-apps delegate complex matrix inversions and multi-layer affine transforms directly to native browser engine C++ implementations and hardware GPUs. The super-app host container leverages DOMMatrix to synchronize smooth gesture-driven zooming and panning across embedded webview boundaries without dropping below 60fps.

title: DOMPoint & Coordinate Projection: 2D/3D Point Arithmetic and Matrix Multiplication
standard_reference: W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §1 The DOMPoint and DOMPointReadOnly interfaces
summary: The DOMPoint interface represents 2D and 3D geometric coordinates (x, y, z, w), supporting native matrix transformation via matrixTransform() for point-in-polygon and touch hit-testing.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C Geometry Interfaces §1, 'DOMPoint' and 'DOMPointReadOnly' represent a point in a 2D or 3D coordinate space with coordinates 'x', 'y', 'z', and the perspective division component 'w' (defaulting to 1.0). The primary computational method on DOMPointReadOnly is 'matrixTransform(matrix)', which accepts a DOMMatrixInit dictionary or DOMMatrix instance. The method multiplies the point's 4D homogeneous vector [x, y, z, w] by the 4x4 matrix and returns a new DOMPoint instance containing the transformed coordinates. This provides mathematically rigorous, constant-time coordinate space projection between local element coordinates, viewport coordinates, and rotated 3D canvas planes. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In super-app e-commerce and retail kiosks, mini-apps render interactive floor plans, seat-selection layouts, and augmented-reality product previews. When users tap on a rotated or scaled visual element, translating the physical screen touch coordinates (from PointerEvent clientX/clientY) into the internal canvas element's coordinate space traditionally required fragile trigonometry. The super-app SDK standardizes 'DOMPoint.fromPoint({x, y}).matrixTransform(elementMatrix.inverse())', allowing mini-apps to execute sub-millisecond hit-testing directly against native GPU compositing layers.

title: DOMRect & Bounding Geometry: Axis-Aligned Box Mathematics and Viewport Collision Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §2 The DOMRect and DOMRectReadOnly interfaces
summary: DOMRect defines a rectangle parameterized by origin coordinates (x, y) and dimensions (width, height), standardizing boundary calculations and collision detection.
detail: [SPEC FACT] W3C Geometry Interfaces §2 defines 'DOMRectReadOnly' and 'DOMRect', characterizing a rectangle through its origin attributes 'x' and 'y', dimensions 'width' and 'height', and derived boundary attributes 'top', 'right', 'bottom', and 'left'. The specification standardizes directional dimension handling: 'width' and 'height' can be negative numbers, in which case 'left' evaluates to 'x + width' and 'right' evaluates to 'x' (with corresponding logic for 'top' and 'bottom'). The static factory method 'DOMRect.fromRect({ x, y, width, height })' allows instantaneous instantiation of standardized rect objects. DOMRect is the foundational return type for modern DOM layout introspection APIs, including 'Element.getBoundingClientRect()' and 'Range.getClientRects()'. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] Super-app host platforms enforce strict UI layout sandboxing to protect host chrome controls (such as the persistent navigation header, safety capsule button, and bottom tab bar) from being obscured or hijacked by mini-app content. The super-app security monitor inspects mini-app modal overlays and floating action buttons by computing their DOMRect boundaries via getBoundingClientRect(). If a mini-app renders an element whose DOMRect overlaps the reserved native capsule area (wx.getMenuButtonBoundingClientRect parity), the container layout manager automatically offsets or clips the offending element, neutralizing UI redressing and clickjacking vulnerabilities.

title: DOMQuad Interface: Non-Axis-Aligned Quadrilateral Sandboxing and Bounds Calculation
standard_reference: W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §4 The DOMQuad interface
summary: The DOMQuad interface represents an arbitrary quadrilateral defined by four corner DOMPoint objects, enabling precise geometric modeling of CSS-transformed and rotated elements.
detail: [SPEC FACT] While DOMRect is restricted to axis-aligned bounding boxes, modern CSS transformations (skew, rotate, 3D perspective) warp rectangular elements into non-axis-aligned convex quadrilaterals. W3C Geometry Interfaces §4 defines 'DOMQuad', an object consisting of four corner points: 'p1', 'p2', 'p3', and 'p4' (each a DOMPoint). A DOMQuad can be instantiated directly via 'new DOMQuad(p1, p2, p3, p4)' or synthesized from an axis-aligned rect using 'DOMQuad.fromRect(rect)'. Crucially, DOMQuad provides the 'getBounds()' method, which calculates and returns a tight axis-aligned 'DOMRectReadOnly' enclosing the entire transformed quadrilateral, taking into account any skew or 3D rotation applied to its vertices. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] In enterprise document scanning, OCR receipt capture, and contract digital signatures inside mini-apps, optical camera feeds capture skewed documents at arbitrary angles. The super-app vision SDK utilizes DOMQuad to encapsulate detected quadrilateral document boundaries extracted from native machine learning engines. Passing DOMQuad objects across the JavaScript bridge allows mini-apps to render real-time boundary overlays and perspective-corrected cropping grids with zero serialization overhead.

title: Geometry Interfaces Serialization, Structured Clone Compatibility, and Worker Offloading
standard_reference: W3C Geometry Interfaces Module Level 1 §5 Algorithms and Structured Clone Support
summary: All W3C Geometry interfaces support the HTML Structured Clone algorithm and JSON serialization, allowing offloading of heavy computational geometry to Web Workers.
detail: [SPEC FACT] According to W3C Geometry Interfaces §5 and the WHATWG HTML standard, instances of DOMPoint, DOMPointReadOnly, DOMRect, DOMRectReadOnly, DOMQuad, DOMMatrix, and DOMMatrixReadOnly are serializable objects fully compatible with the Structured Clone Algorithm. Furthermore, each interface implements a 'toJSON()' method returning an idiomatic JavaScript object literal containing all public numeric coordinates. Because geometry interfaces are structured-cloneable, they can be seamlessly passed between Window contexts, Dedicated Web Workers, and Shared Workers via 'postMessage()', or stored in IndexedDB and CacheStorage without manual serialization boilerplate. [SUPERAPP ARCHITECTURE] High-performance mini-apps (such as CAD architectural plan viewers, 3D product customizers, and gaming engines) perform thousands of matrix multiplications and bounding-box recalculations per second. Executing these geometric calculations on the main UI thread degrades the Interaction to Next Paint (INP) metric and introduces frame stutters. The super-app architecture offloads all spatial indexing, collision detection trees (BVH), and affine transformation computations to Dedicated Web Workers by dispatching structured DOMMatrix and DOMQuad objects via postMessage(). The main UI thread receives pre-computed bounds ready for immediate canvas hardware rendering, ensuring consistent 120fps performance on modern mobile displays.

title: W3C CSS Typed Object Model API: Typed Representation & Elimination of CSSOM Parsing Overhead
standard_reference: W3C CSS Typed OM Level 1 §1 Overview & §2 Architecture
summary: The CSS Typed OM API exposes CSS values as typed JavaScript objects rather than raw strings, eliminating repetitive string serialization and CSS parser roundtrips in rendering engines.
detail: [SPEC FACT] Under W3C CSS Typed OM Level 1 §1-§2, the traditional CSS Object Model (CSSOM) requires developers to manipulate styles as concatenated strings (e.g., element.style.opacity = '0.5' or style.transform = 'translate3d(' + x + 'px, ' + y + 'px, 0)'). Every string assignment forces the browser engine's C++ style engine to tokenize, parse, and validate the string into internal CSS representations, creating significant CPU overhead, string garbage collection (GC) pressure, and silent parse failures on typo errors. The CSS Typed OM introduces typed JavaScript objects implementing 'CSSStyleValue' and 'StylePropertyMap', allowing direct manipulation of the engine's internal typed representation. Numerical values are stored as 'CSSNumericValue' subclasses with explicit unit types, bypassing the CSS parser completely during programmatic mutations.
