Super-app store submission checks verify that mini-apps declare standardized fontStretch values ('condensed', 'expanded', 'semi-condensed', etc.) rather than unsupported browser-proprietary properties.

title: MDN CanvasRenderingContext2D.fontVariantCaps: Capitalization Styling & Small-Caps Sandboxing
description: Reviews the fontVariantCaps property on 2D canvas contexts, covering small-caps, petite-caps, and titling capitalization rendering in mini-app graphics.
detail: The CanvasRenderingContext2D.fontVariantCaps property controls the use of alternate glyphs for capital letters (such as small-caps, all-small-caps, petite-caps, and unicase). This provides canvas-based mini-app games, certificates, and branding headers with advanced OpenType typographic capabilities without loading bulky secondary font binaries. The super-app host container ensures that canvas font variant changes trigger synchronous font metrics invalidation, preventing glyph collision during rapid UI redraws.

title: W3C Web Neural Network API (WebNN): Hardware Acceleration & Graph Compilation Sandboxing
description: Analyzes the W3C WebNN specification for direct hardware acceleration (GPU, NPU, CPU) of ML inference graphs, resource isolation, and container security controls.
detail: The W3C Web Neural Network API (WebNN) defines a dedicated web standard for executing deep learning models with direct hardware acceleration across heterogeneous silicon (DirectML on Windows, Core ML on macOS/iOS, NNAPI/Vulkan on Android). Super-app runtimes leverage WebNN to run computer vision, natural language processing, and generative AI features inside client-side mini-apps without incurring round-trip server latency or egress bandwidth costs. Store security governance mandates that WebNN compilation pipelines validate compute graphs against operator injection, restrict maximum tensor buffer allocations, and enforce process isolation to prevent side-channel timing attacks on shared hardware accelerators.

title: WebNN Architecture Explainer: MLContext Creation, Asynchronous Compute, and Origin Isolation
description: Examines the WebNN architectural explainer, covering navigator.ml.createContext() permission prompts, device selection, and user privacy guarantees.
detail: The WebNN architectural explainer details how navigator.ml initializes MLContext instances tailored to specific power preferences ('default', 'high-performance', or 'low-power'). Because direct NPU/GPU execution can leak cryptographic keys or user behavioral traces via cache-timing attacks, WebNN restricts execution to secure contexts (HTTPS) and integrates with Permissions Policy ('compute-pressure' and device access gates). Super-app containers sandbox WebNN instances so that untrusted third-party mini-apps cannot enumerate underlying chipset serials or run unattended background inference without explicit user consent.

title: W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group: Cross-Platform Interoperability & Conformance Testing
description: Reviews the W3C Web Machine Learning Working Group and Community Group ecosystem, test suites, and cross-vendor conformance standards.
detail: The W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group coordinates cross-browser and cross-vendor implementation testing for WebNN across Chromium, Gecko, and WebKit engines. Super-app platform operators deploy automated Web Platform Tests (WPT) derived from the Community Group test suite into their mini-app compliance runners. This ensures that custom vision and speech models embedded in mini-app store submissions produce bit-exact or numerically consistent outputs across Android and iOS execution runtimes without crashing the host container.

title: WebNN Polyfill Architecture: Pure WebAssembly/Wasm SIMD Fallback Engine & Conformance Harness
description: Analyzes the official WebNN polyfill architecture, providing predictable CPU fallback execution via Wasm SIMD when native NPU/GPU drivers are unavailable.
detail: The official WebNN Polyfill repository provides a standardized JavaScript and WebAssembly fallback layer that implements the complete WebNN API specification on platforms lacking native browser WebNN drivers. Built upon optimized Wasm SIMD kernel operations, the polyfill guarantees functional equivalence across legacy devices. Super-app store compliance pipelines provide this polyfill in the container core so mini-app developers can build against the future-proof WebNN API without fragmenting their codebase across device generations.

title: WebNN Canonical Samples: Real-Time Mobile Vision, Face Detection, and Execution Profiling
description: Examines the official WebNN sample implementation repository, evaluating reference pipelines for MobileNet, SqueezeNet, and semantic segmentation in web containers.
detail: The WebNN Samples repository establishes reference implementation patterns for on-device computer vision, face detection, background blur, and audio noise suppression running inside sandboxed web runtimes. In a super-app mini-app store, these benchmarks serve as standard qualification fixtures. Store audit pipelines measure tensor execution latency, peak memory allocation, and power draw against WebNN reference fixtures to certify that third-party AI mini-apps maintain consistent 60 FPS UI interaction during active model inference.

title: MDN Web Docs OTPCredential Interface: navigator.credentials.get() Integration & User Consent
description: Reviews the OTPCredential interface, user permission prompts, and lifecycle management within the Credential Management API framework.
detail: The OTPCredential interface extends the Credential Management API, allowing web applications to request SMS OTPs via navigator.credentials.get({otp: {transport: ['sms']}}). When invoked, the platform displays an operating system-level permission sheet asking the user to confirm sharing the received code with the application. In super-app architectures, the host container can proxy the Web OTP lifecycle, providing seamless 1-tap OTP autofill in checkout, onboarding, and high-value transaction flows while preserving strict user consent.

title: MDN OTPCredential.code Property: Code Sanitization, AbortSignal Timeouts, and Error Handling
description: Examines OTPCredential.code extraction, timeout management with AbortController, and exception handling during SMS reception.
detail: The OTPCredential.code property returns the sanitized string containing the received verification code. Store standards mandate that mini-apps pair navigator.credentials.get() calls with an AbortSignal from an AbortController configured with a timeout (typically 60-120 seconds). If an SMS fails to arrive, the request aborts cleanly, allowing the UI to offer fallback authentication mechanisms (e.g. voice call, manual input, or authenticator app) without locking the main thread or leaving pending listeners in the runtime.

title: web.dev: Web OTP API Architectural Guide, Cross-Origin Iframe Delegation, and Permissions Policy
description: Analyzes the web.dev Web OTP architectural guide, focusing on iframe delegation via otp-credentials feature policy and UX best practices.
detail: The web.dev architectural guide details advanced deployment patterns for the Web OTP API, including delegating OTP retrieval to cross-origin iframes using the 'allow="otp-credentials"' attribute on the iframe element. In a super-app ecosystem hosting federated payment gateways or third-party banking widgets inside mini-apps, explicit Permissions Policy delegation ensures that embedded checkout frames can securely receive domain-bound SMS codes without exposing user communications to unintended origins.

title: WICG Web OTP Explainer: SMS Privacy, Anti-Interception Guarantees, and Store Compliance
description: Reviews the Web OTP explainer regarding SMS privacy isolation, prevention of full SMS inbox reading, and super-app store review requirements.
detail: The Web OTP explainer highlights that unlike legacy native permissions (such as Android READ_SMS or RECEIVE_SMS which grant blanket access to all personal messages), Web OTP only grants the app access to the single verification code specifically formatted for its verified origin. Super-app store compliance policies prohibit mini-apps from requesting native SMS permissions and mandate adoption of the Web OTP standard, ensuring user privacy and regulatory compliance under international personal data protection frameworks (such as GDPR and Decree 13/2023/ND-CP).

title: MDN CredentialsContainer.preventSilentAccess(): Session Termination & Explicit Re-Authentication
description: Analyzes CredentialsContainer.preventSilentAccess() in credential lifecycle governance, preventing automatic credential leakage after user logout.
detail: The CredentialsContainer.preventSilentAccess() method disables automatic credential presentation during subsequent calls to navigator.credentials.get(). In super-app mini-app environments hosting fintech and banking micro-services, calling preventSilentAccess() upon user logout or session timeout is mandatory. This ensures that a subsequent user or session cannot silently acquire active identity credentials or OTP authentications without triggering explicit interactive user confirmation, closing session hijacking attack vectors on shared mobile devices.

title: MDN WebSocketStream API: ReadableStream/WritableStream Integration & Backpressure Sandboxing
description: Analyzes the WebSocketStream API integrating WHATWG Streams with WebSockets to provide ergonomic backpressure management and memory leak defense.
detail: The WebSocketStream API replaces the legacy event-based WebSocket interface by integrating WHATWG ReadableStream and WritableStream. In high-frequency super-app trading, gaming, and real-time chat mini-apps, legacy WebSockets frequently caused memory exhaustion (OOM) because incoming messages accumulated faster than the JavaScript event loop could process them, while outbound messages backed up in client buffers without native throttling. WebSocketStream enforces native backpressure: when the consumer is busy, TCP window scaling automatically throttles incoming network packets, preventing unbounded memory growth.

title: web.dev: WebSocketStream Practical Guide, Flow Control & Memory Safety in Web Apps
description: Reviews web.dev recommendations for adopting WebSocketStream for continuous streaming, bidirectional piping, and memory safety.
detail: The web.dev architectural guide details how WebSocketStream combines the low latency of WebSockets with the ergonomic flow control of Streams. By allowing mini-app developers to directly pipe streams (e.g. ReadableStream.pipeTo(wss.writable)), data transfers can be chained with TransformStreams (such as TextDecoderStream or CompressionStream) without manual chunking. For super-app host containers, this deterministic stream lifecycle prevents runaway memory allocations and simplifies sandboxed resource accounting.

title: Chrome for Developers: WebSocketStream Capabilities, DedicatedWorker Offloading & Store Certification
description: Evaluates Chrome's implementation of WebSocketStream, off-main-thread streaming, and store review conformance requirements.
detail: Chrome documentation specifies that WebSocketStream is accessible within both Window contexts and DedicatedWebWorkers. In super-app container runtimes, delegating high-throughput WebSocketStream connections to dedicated Web Workers prevents main-thread jank and keeps UI rendering at 60/120fps. Store review guidelines require mini-apps handling binary streaming protocols (e.g., telemetry feeds, audio packets, real-time gaming state) to utilize WebSocketStream over legacy WebSockets to comply with Interaction to Next Paint (INP) benchmarks.

title: MDN WebSocketStream.opened: Asynchronous Handshake Resolution & Protocol Negotiation
description: Examines the WebSocketStream.opened promise interface for deterministic handshake completion, extensions, and selected subprotocols.
detail: The WebSocketStream.opened property returns a Promise that resolves to a WebSocketOpenInfo dictionary containing readable (ReadableStream), writable (WritableStream), extensions, and protocol once the WebSocket connection is established. Unlike legacy onopen callbacks which could fire during unhandled microtask queues, the opened promise guarantees that stream consumers only attach after cryptographic TLS and HTTP upgrade negotiations succeed, preventing race conditions during mini-app initialization.

title: MDN WebSocketStream.closed: Graceful Teardown, Clean Closure Codes & Abnormal Disconnect Forensics
description: Analyzes WebSocketStream.closed promise semantics for deterministic resource cleanup and network error forensics in sandboxed containers.
detail: The WebSocketStream.closed property returns a Promise that resolves to a WebSocketCloseInfo dictionary (code and reason) upon clean socket closure, or rejects when an abnormal transport termination occurs (e.g., TCP reset, TLS failure). Super-app container watchdogs monitor the closed promise to release allocated buffer handles, revoke transient network grants, and distinguish normal mini-app exit from network anomalies without risking memory leaks from hanging event listeners.

title: IETF RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1 Specification, Strict Message Framing & Request Smuggling Defense
description: Analyzes RFC 9112 standards governing HTTP/1.1 request syntax, message framing, and boundary disambiguation between proxies and servers.
detail: RFC 9112 (obsoleting RFC 7230) establishes normative rules for HTTP/1.1 message parsing. Section 6 explicitly defines handling of Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding header combinations: if a message is received with both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length, the Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length, and intermediaries must reject or sanitize ambiguous messages. For super-app edge API gateways proxying mini-app backend requests, strict adherence to RFC 9112 message framing is required to prevent HTTP request smuggling, cache poisoning, and credential cross-contamination across multi-tenant workloads.

title: IETF RFC 9112 (Datatracker): Chunked Transfer Coding, Trailer Fields & Edge Smuggling Mitigations
description: Reviews RFC 9112 provisions on chunk-size parsing, trailer field limitations, and strict whitespace normalization at reverse proxies.
detail: Section 7.1 of RFC 9112 mandates that recipient parsers reject chunk extensions with invalid characters and treat any whitespace between header field names and colons as a protocol error (Section 5.1). In super-app infrastructure, frontend reverse proxies and backend mini-app microservices must enforce identical RFC 9112 chunk parsing logic. Discrepancies in whitespace handling or chunk-size integer overflow parsing are prime vectors for HTTP desynchronization attacks, where malicious mini-apps could smuggle unauthorized requests into shared backend HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection pools.

title: MITRE CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')
description: Analyzes the Common Weakness Enumeration entry for HTTP request smuggling and automated static/dynamic gateway verification criteria.
detail: CWE-444 defines vulnerabilities occurring when an intermediary (such as an edge load balancer or super-app API gateway) and a target upstream server interpret ambiguous HTTP request boundaries differently (e.g. CL.TE, TE.CL, and TE.TE discrepancies). In super-app ecosystems hosting untrusted third-party mini-apps, CWE-444 flaws enable malicious mini-apps to hijack requests of other users, bypass edge security controls, and exfiltrate sensitive session tokens. Store security vetting mandates that host gateways either normalize all inbound HTTP/1.1 traffic or downgrade/upgrade to end-to-end HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to inherently eliminate delimiter ambiguity.

title: PortSwigger Web Security: Advanced HTTP Request Smuggling & Frontend-Backend Desync Defenses
description: Evaluates practical HTTP request smuggling attack vectors (CL.TE, TE.CL, obfuscated TE headers) and defensive gateway configurations.
detail: PortSwigger research catalogs practical exploitation techniques where malformed headers (such as 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' with leading spaces, multiple Content-Length headers, or line wrapping) exploit discrepancies between frontend CDN edge layers and backend services. To harden super-app mini-app hosting perimeters, architecture guidelines enforce HTTP/2 from edge to upstream servers, configure reverse proxies to strictly reject any request containing ambiguous length indicators, and isolate backend connection pools per mini-app tenant ID.

title: OWASP WSTG-INPV-15: Testing for HTTP Splitting and Request Smuggling in Enterprise Gateways
description: Details OWASP Web Security Testing Guide procedures for identifying and mitigating HTTP splitting and desync vulnerabilities in web gateways.
detail: The OWASP Testing Guide outlines methodology for auditing edge proxies and web application firewalls (WAFs) against CRLF injection, response splitting, and request smuggling. In super-app platforms, mini-app network gateways must undergo automated dynamic vulnerability scans verifying that CR (0x0D) and LF (0x0A) characters in header values are rejected outright with HTTP 400 Bad Request, preventing mini-apps from injecting forged HTTP headers or splitting responses to poison downstream mobile client webview caches.

title: IETF RFC 8879: TLS Certificate Compression (Brotli, Zstandard, Zlib) for Handshake Latency Optimization
description: Analyzes RFC 8879 defining certificate compression algorithms to shrink TLS 1.3 handshake packet sizes and prevent TCP round-trip amplification.
detail: RFC 8879 specifies the CertificateCompressionAlgorithm extension (extension type 27) for TLS 1.3, standardizing Brotli (1), Zlib (2), and Zstandard (3) algorithms to compress X.509 certificate chains. Standard enterprise X.509 chains frequently exceed 3-5KB, exceeding the initial TCP congestion window (initcwnd of ~10 MSS) and triggering extra round-trips over cellular networks. Compressing certificate chains down to ~1KB allows TLS 1.3 handshakes to complete within a single round-trip (1-RTT), significantly accelerating cold-start connection latency for super-app mini-apps on mobile 4G/5G connections.

title: IETF RFC 8879 (Datatracker): TLS Certificate Decompression Memory Limits & DoS Defense
description: Reviews security considerations in RFC 8879 regarding decompression bombs, memory ceilings, and mobile client resource exhaustion defenses.
detail: Section 7 of RFC 8879 addresses decompression bomb risks, requiring implementations to bound the maximum uncompressed certificate size (typically capping uncompressed buffers at 64KB-128KB) and limit decompression CPU time. In super-app client networking engines (e.g. Cronet, OkHttp, or custom TLS stacks), enforcing strict decompression limits prevents malicious or compromised partner domains from exhausting mobile device RAM and freezing the host application process during mini-app TLS handshakes.

title: IANA TLS ExtensionType Values Registry: compress_certificate (27) Specification & Standards Tracking
description: Examines the official IANA registry entry for TLS extension compress_certificate (27) and registered compression algorithm IDs.
detail: The IANA TLS ExtensionType registry formally tracks compress_certificate as extension value 27, defined in RFC 8879, alongside TLS Certificate Compression Algorithm IDs (zlib=1, brotli=2, zstd=3). Conformance auditing for super-app edge load balancers and container network stacks mandates support for modern algorithm ID 2 (Brotli) and ID 3 (Zstandard) to ensure maximum compression efficiency and interoperability with major mobile OS TLS providers (BoringSSL and Apple Secure Transport).

title: IETF RFC 9460: Service Binding (SVCB) and HTTPS Resource Records in DNS for Seamless Protocol Upgrade
description: Analyzes RFC 9460 defining HTTPS DNS resource records to deliver ALPN parameters, port numbers, and Encrypted ClientHello configurations.
detail: RFC 9460 standardizes the SVCB and HTTPS DNS resource record (RR) types, enabling recursive resolvers and clients to learn service capabilities (such as supported ALPN protocols h2/h3, port redirection, and Encrypted ClientHello 'ech' parameter keys) in a single initial DNS lookup. For super-app mini-app network gateways, publishing HTTPS RR records eliminates redundant HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect round-trips and enables zero-RTT protocol upgrades to HTTP/3 and ECH encryption directly from DNS resolution.

title: Cloudflare Engineering: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) Deployment, SNI Privacy & Edge Security
description: Reviews Cloudflare's deployment guide for ECH (RFC draft-ietf-tls-esni), encrypting the Server Name Indication (SNI) against network surveillance.
detail: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH, the evolution of ESNI) encrypts the entire ClientHello message—including the sensitive Server Name Indication (SNI)—under a public key published via DNS HTTPS records (RFC 9460). In super-app multi-tenant ecosystems hosting healthcare, finance, or government service mini-apps, ECH prevents network operators, public Wi-Fi sniffers, and intermediate middleboxes from eavesdropping on which specific mini-app domain a user is accessing, closing the last unencrypted metadata leak in the TLS handshake.

title: IETF RFC 9420: Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol Core Architecture & TreeKEM Asynchronous Group Key Agreement
description: Examines RFC 9420 establishing MLS as an Internet Standards Track protocol for efficient, scalable end-to-end encrypted group messaging with continuous forward secrecy and post-compromise security.
detail: RFC 9420 defines the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol, operating at the application layer to provide end-to-end encryption, message authentication, and membership integrity for groups ranging from two to tens of thousands of participants. MLS employs TreeKEM, a tree-based cryptographic key agreement algorithm where group members occupy the leaves of a binary ratchet tree, reducing the computational and message complexity of adding or removing members and updating keys from O(N) to O(log N). In super-app platforms hosting collaborative multi-tenant mini-apps (such as corporate chat, multi-party fintech approvals, healthcare consultations, and merchant negotiations), TreeKEM allows the host messaging fabric to arbitrate zero-trust message routing between client runtimes and backend services without having access to cleartext payloads or long-term cryptographic keys.

title: IETF RFC 9420 (Datatracker): Forward Secrecy, Post-Compromise Security & Epoch Key Evolution in Ratchet Trees
description: Analyzes the cryptographic ratchet mechanisms in RFC 9420 guaranteeing Forward Secrecy (FS) and Post-Compromise Security (PCS) across state transitions.
detail: Under RFC 9420, every group modification—such as adding a member, removing an evicted member, or periodically refreshing a leaf node's key material via an Update proposal—creates a Commit message that advances the group to a new sequential epoch. The TreeKEM update operation derives a new group encryption secret while deterministically erasing previous node secrets, establishing Forward Secrecy (FS) against past message decryption if a device is subsequently compromised. Furthermore, because uncompromised members inject fresh cryptographic entropy during Commit processing, MLS guarantees Post-Compromise Security (PCS), enabling a compromised mini-app client session to autonomously heal and restore cryptographic confidentiality in subsequent epochs once malware or unauthorized memory inspection is terminated.

title: MLS Architecture & Threat Model: Zero-Trust Delivery Service Isolation & Metadata Minimization
description: Reviews the MLS protocol threat model and Delivery Service (DS) isolation principles published by the MLS working group community.
detail: The MLS architecture strictly separates the untrusted Delivery Service (DS)—responsible for ordering and distributing group packets—from the cryptographic Authentication Service (AS) and group endpoints. The DS cannot inspect encrypted application data, manipulate group membership undetected, or selectively drop commit messages without triggering verifiable epoch state mismatches on recipient clients. For enterprise super-app host architectures, this architecture provides a standardized blueprint: the super-app cloud acts purely as an untrusted DS routing MLS-encrypted frames across isolated mini-app sandbox instances, third-party enterprise backends, and user mobile devices. Even in the event of an infrastructure-level cloud breach or database dump at the super-app gateway, sensitive financial, enterprise, or medical mini-app communications remain cryptographically unreadable.

title: IETF MLS Working Group: Cross-Platform Interoperability, Key Packages & Extension Governance
description: Evaluates the IETF MLS charter and standardization milestones governing asynchronous client onboarding via KeyPackages and verifiable credentials.
detail: The IETF MLS Working Group standardized KeyPackages—self-contained, cryptographically signed bundles containing a client's public keys, supported ciphersuites, extensions, and identity credentials (such as X.509 certificates or Verifiable Credentials). KeyPackages are uploaded to a public repository, allowing existing group members to add new mini-app instances or user participants asynchronously without requiring the target client to be online. In super-app mini-app store governance, the store catalog registry serves as an authoritative KeyPackage distribution and attestation hub: when a user launches a B2B or multi-user mini-app, the container fetches verified KeyPackages signed by the mini-app developer's root identity, ensuring cryptographically verifiable multi-party channels without out-of-band key exchanges.

title: IETF RFC 9420: Group Lifecycle State Machine (Welcome, Commit, Proposal) & Mobile Container Memory Governance
description: Specifies the processing rules for Welcome, Commit, and Proposal messages within resource-constrained mobile container environments.
detail: Section 12 of RFC 9420 outlines the operational lifecycle of MLS groups: a creator generates an initial ratchet tree, joins members via Proposals, and commits changes by transmitting a Welcome message encrypted under the joiner's KeyPackage secrets alongside a Commit message to existing members. When adapted to super-app hybrid WebView/native runtimes, MLS state objects (consisting of the ratchet tree and epoch secrets) must be isolated within secure native container memory (e.g. Android Keystore / Apple Keychain backed SQLite or OPFS) rather than exposed directly to untrusted JavaScript execution contexts. The host bridge provides high-level APIs (`superapp.crypto.mls.joinGroup`, `superapp.crypto.mls.sendMessage`) while enforcing strict epoch state garbage collection to prevent mobile memory leakage during long-running group sessions.

title: IETF RFC 9525: Service Identity in TLS & Public Key Infrastructure / Modern X.509 Certificate Matching
description: Analyzes RFC 9525 establishing updated Internet Standards Track rules for verifying service identities in TLS certificates, formally obsoleting RFC 6125.
detail: RFC 9525 defines normative requirements for matching reference domain identifiers against presented identifiers in X.509v3 certificates during TLS session establishment. It mandates that clients check the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension—specifically dNSName, uniformResourceIdentifier (URI), and iPAddress entries—and formally deprecates fallback to the Subject Common Name (CN) field. For super-app edge gateways and container TLS trust stacks, RFC 9525 requires rejecting any server certificate where identity relies solely on CN without a valid SAN dNSName entry, mitigating historical certificate spoofing vectors and enforcing modern PKI hygiene across all registered mini-app backend endpoints.

title: IETF RFC 9525 (Datatracker): Wildcard Domain Restrictions, IDNA Internationalization & Subdomain Boundary Auditing
description: Reviews Section 6 of RFC 9525 governing wildcard certificates, internationalized domain name (IDNA) processing, and subdomain matching restrictions.
detail: Section 6 of RFC 9525 establishes strict limits on wildcard domain matching: the wildcard character (*) MUST appear only as the entire first (leftmost) label of a presented dNSName (e.g. `*.example.com` is valid, but `*foo.example.com` or `baz.*.example.com` are invalid), and wildcards MUST NOT match across multiple label boundaries (e.g. `*.example.com` matches `a.example.com` but never `b.a.example.com`). Furthermore, wildcards are prohibited for public suffix registries or top-level domains. For internationalized domain names (IDNA), comparison MUST be performed in A-label (punycode) format. Super-app store review pipelines must enforce RFC 9525 wildcard restrictions when verifying mini-app declared domain allowlists in manifests, preventing partner apps from using overbroad wildcards that inadvertently encompass unauthorized host or third-party subdomains.

title: IETF RFC 6125 (Historical Evolution): Representation & Verification of Domain-Based Application Service Identity
description: Examines the historical lineage of RFC 6125 and the architectural transitions required by its replacement with RFC 9525 in modern secure application architectures.
detail: RFC 6125 was published in 2011 to consolidate domain matching rules across application protocols (HTTPS, SIP, XMPP, LDAP, SMTP). While RFC 6125 permitted legacy clients to fall back to the Common Name if no SAN was present, RFC 9525 completely eliminates this fallback and tightens wildcard rules. In super-app platform governance, tracking this transition is essential for backward compatibility: legacy enterprise internal CA certificates that still rely on CN must be flagged in automated mini-app store validation tools, prompting publishers to re-issue certificates with explicit SAN dNSName attributes before production onboarding.

title: CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements: SAN Mandatory Inclusion, Certificate Profile & Revocation Standards
description: Reviews CA/B Forum Baseline Requirements aligning public CA issuance practices with RFC 9525 TLS certificate verification standards.
detail: The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements for the Issuance and Management of Publicly-Trusted Certificates mandate that Certificate Authorities populate the Subject Alternative Name extension for all server certificates and strictly validate domain control according to standardized DCV (Domain Control Validation) methods. In super-app multi-tenant ecosystems, the store verification backend utilizes CA/B Forum compliance checks alongside RFC 9525 parsing to verify that mini-app API domains are issued by CAs adhering to Baseline Requirements, check OCSP / CRL revocation statuses, and reject private self-signed certificates unless the mini-app is specifically configured for an enterprise intranet profile.

title: IETF RFC 9525: Multi-Tenant Host Bridge Network Egress & Subdomain Takeover Defense
description: Details the application of RFC 9525 reference identifier matching within super-app container network stacks and host bridge egress firewalls.
detail: When a mini-app issues network requests via `fetch()`, `XMLHttpRequest`, or native container bridge proxies (`superapp.request`), the host container must perform RFC 9525 compliant identity verification. The container matches the requested URI against the developer's declared manifest domain allowlist (reference identifier) and verifies that the TLS certificate presented by the destination server matches according to RFC 9525 rules. This eliminates subdomain takeover vulnerabilities where an attacker points an expired cloud CNAME to their own server and presents a valid certificate for a different domain or an invalid wildcard, ensuring that mini-app network traffic is strictly confined to cryptographically authenticated partner endpoints.

title: WHATWG DOM Standard: EventTarget Interface Architecture, Event Phases & Dispatch Algorithm
description: Examines the WHATWG DOM Living Standard specifications for EventTarget, detailing capturing, target, and bubbling phases in component trees.
detail: The WHATWG DOM Standard defines the `EventTarget` interface, implemented by Node, Element, Document, Window, and various worker contexts. The event dispatch algorithm processes events across three distinct phases: (1) Capturing phase, propagating down from Window through ancestor nodes to the target's parent; (2) Target phase, evaluating listeners registered directly on the EventTarget; (3) Bubbling phase, propagating back upward toward the root document unless bubbling is disabled. In super-app modular component architectures, understanding this dispatch tree is fundamental: host container shells register capturing listeners on root containers to intercept unhandled gesture or navigation events, while sandboxed mini-app components execute within scoped subtrees, preventing rogue child components from canceling host-level back gestures or security audits.

title: WHATWG EventTarget.addEventListener: Passive Listeners, Once Execution & Signal Lifecycle Binding
description: Reviews the AddEventListenerOptions dictionary (capture, once, passive, signal) and its performance and memory leak mitigation impacts.
detail: The `addEventListener(type, listener, options)` method accepts an `AddEventListenerOptions` dictionary containing boolean flags `capture`, `once`, `passive`, and an `AbortSignal signal`. Marking scroll and touch event listeners (`touchstart`, `touchmove`, `wheel`) as `passive: true` guarantees to the browser engine that the listener will not call `preventDefault()`, enabling the compositor thread to scroll immediately without blocking on JavaScript execution, directly improving Core Web Vitals (INP and FID). Furthermore, passing a component-scoped `AbortSignal` allows the mini-app runtime to automatically clean up all associated listeners when a page or view is unmounted, completely eliminating cross-page memory leaks in persistent super-app single-process WebViews.

title: WHATWG Event.isTrusted: Synthetic Event Discrimination & Anti-Clickjacking Financial Gatekeeping
description: Analyzes the Event.isTrusted read-only boolean property separating genuine hardware user actions from script-generated synthetic events.
detail: The `Event.isTrusted` property is a read-only boolean that returns `true` when the event was generated by a genuine user interaction (such as a physical screen tap, mouse click, or hardware key press) and `false` when the event was synthesized or dispatched via script (`element.dispatchEvent()`, `element.click()`). In super-app client container security architectures, `isTrusted` acts as a mandatory verification gate for high-risk operations: financial checkout buttons, permission consent dialogs, biometric auth triggers, and OAuth authorization grants MUST verify `event.isTrusted === true`. Synthetic events dispatched by third-party mini-app scripts or malicious embedded iframes are rejected, mitigating automated clickjacking and bot-driven credential theft.

title: WHATWG DOM Event Propagation Controls: stopPropagation, stopImmediatePropagation & preventDefault Hygiene
description: Specifies event propagation control methods and default action suppression across multi-tenant container component trees.
detail: WHATWG DOM provides `stopPropagation()` to halt event propagation past the current target during capture or bubbling, and `stopImmediatePropagation()` to additionally prevent subsequent listeners on the same element from executing. `preventDefault()` signals that the default platform action (e.g. form submission, link navigation, text selection) should not execute. Super-app store review rules mandate propagation hygiene: mini-apps must not call `stopPropagation()` on root document events or host container boundary nodes, as this breaks super-app host telemetry, global analytics, pull-to-refresh gestures, and platform keyboard management. Conversely, mini-app component libraries must isolate internal widget interactions to prevent synthetic bubbling conflicts.

title: WHATWG CustomEvent Interface: Structured Detail Payload Serialization & Composed Boundary Traversal
description: Evaluates the CustomEvent constructor, detail dictionary payload validation, and composed flag traversal across Shadow DOM boundaries.
detail: The `CustomEvent` interface enables application components to dispatch domain-specific synthetic events carrying custom data via the `detail` property (`new CustomEvent(type, { detail: {...}, bubbles: true, composed: true })`). When `composed: true` is set, the custom event can traverse out of Shadow DOM trees into the light DOM. In super-app modular mini-app frameworks, `CustomEvent` is utilized to implement an asynchronous in-page event bus: the super-app container dispatches standardized lifecycle events (`miniAppResume`, `miniAppPause`, `networkStateChange`, `themeChange`), while mini-app components subscribe via standard `window.addEventListener`. The container sanitizes and structured-clones the `detail` payload to prevent prototype pollution or cross-context script injection.

title: IETF RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Cryptographic Handshake & Forward Secrecy Sandboxing
description: Standardizes the TLS 1.3 protocol architecture eliminating legacy vulnerable cipher suites, reducing handshake latency to 1-RTT, and enforcing mandatory ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange for Forward Secrecy across mini-app container network egress.
detail: IETF RFC 8446 defines the TLS 1.3 cryptographic protocol. Key requirements for mini-app architectures: (1) Deprecation of insecure algorithms: completely eliminates static RSA key exchange, CBC-mode ciphers, SHA-1, and RC4, mandating Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES-CCM); (2) 1-RTT Handshake: client sends KeyShare in ClientHello alongside supported cipher suites, eliminating one full round trip compared to TLS 1.2; (3) Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE) key exchange ensures perfect forward secrecy (PFS), preventing retrospective decryption of historical mini-app traffic even if private keys are subsequently compromised; (4) Encrypted Handshake: certificates and extension payloads are encrypted after ServerHello, masking server identity and client certificates from passive eavesdroppers.

title: MDN Transport Layer Security (TLS) Web Security & Container Configuration Standard
description: Establishes runtime operational controls for Transport Layer Security in modern web runtimes, mandating minimum TLS version enforcement (TLS 1.2/1.3) and secure cipher configurations within WebView containers.
detail: MDN TLS documentation establishes modern baseline criteria for secure transport in web execution contexts: (1) Container network configuration must explicitly disable SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 at the native engine layer (e.g., Android NetworkSecurityConfig and iOS App Transport Security NSAppTransportSecurity); (2) Modern ciphersuite selection must prioritize TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256; (3) Elimination of Renegotiation Vulnerabilities: TLS 1.3 replaces insecure renegotiation with Post-Handshake Authentication and NewSessionTicket mechanisms; (4) Certificate validation in super-app WebViews must enforce strict X.509 path building, expiration checks, and reject cleartext HTTP traffic across all mini-app execution contexts.

title: HTTP Early-Data Header & 0-RTT Anti-Replay Mitigation Standard
description: Specifies the Early-Data request header and gateway-level replay protections for 0-RTT TLS handshakes, restricting zero-RTT early data strictly to safe idempotent HTTP methods.
detail: The Early-Data HTTP header (defined in RFC 8470 and documented by MDN) mitigates replay attacks inherent to 0-RTT resumption: (1) 0-RTT Early Data allows clients to transmit request payloads in the first packet before the TLS handshake finishes, but is fundamentally susceptible to replay attacks by network observers; (2) Intermediaries and mini-app API gateways must mark forwarded 0-RTT requests with 'Early-Data: 1'; (3) Security policy mandates that mini-app servers must reject or defer non-idempotent HTTP methods (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, financial transactions) received in early data by responding with HTTP 425 (Too Early); (4) Super-app API gateways must maintain a sliding-window replay cache or disable 0-RTT entirely for sensitive financial microservices and wallet endpoints.

title: IETF Datatracker RFC 8446 Lifecycle & Cryptographic Extension Governance
description: Tracks the normative lifecycle, errata, and operational requirements of RFC 8446, including supported_versions extension negotiation and downgrade attack mitigations.
detail: The normative specification tracked on IETF Datatracker establishes strict handshake state machines and downgrade protection: (1) The 'supported_versions' extension in ClientHello must specify TLS 1.3 (0x0304) and is the sole authoritative mechanism for version negotiation; (2) Anti-Downgrade Sentinel: if a server is forced by an active attacker to negotiate TLS 1.2 or below, it embeds specific 8-byte magic values in ServerHello.random ('DOWNGRD\x01' or 'DOWNGRD\x00') that modern clients detect to abort the connection with an illegal_parameter alert; (3) Key derivation architecture based on HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function, RFC 5869) establishes strict cryptographic separation between client_handshake_traffic_secret, server_handshake_traffic_secret, and application_traffic_secrets.

title: IETF RFC 8470 Using Early Data in HTTP & 425 Too Early Response Code
description: Standardizes HTTP semantics over TLS early data, establishing the HTTP 425 (Too Early) status code and defining safe retry semantics for idempotent request delivery in mini-app networks.
detail: IETF RFC 8470 defines standard HTTP behavior when traversing 0-RTT early data: (1) Safe request classification: servers and proxies may process early data only if the request is known to be safe and idempotent (RFC 7231 / RFC 9110 safe methods like GET/HEAD without side-effects); (2) If a server receives a request in early data that could alter persistent state or trigger financial mutation, it MUST respond with status code 425 (Too Early); (3) Client retry behavior: when a client receives a 425 response, it must re-transmit the request only after the TLS handshake has successfully completed (1-RTT), guaranteeing no-replay semantics; (4) Super-app runtime networking engines must intercept 425 responses automatically and transparently retry them on the established 1-RTT connection without bubbling errors to mini-app business logic.

title: IETF RFC 9000 QUIC A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport Standard
description: Establishes the core QUIC transport protocol architecture eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking, providing independent multi-stream multiplexing, and enabling seamless connection migration across mobile network handoffs.
detail: IETF RFC 9000 standardizes QUIC as an encrypted UDP-based transport: (1) Head-of-line blocking elimination: unlike TCP where packet loss halts all streams on a connection, QUIC streams are independently flow-controlled and delivered, ensuring packet loss in one mini-app asset (e.g. image texture) does not delay critical RPC or UI payloads; (2) Connection Migration: QUIC endpoints identify connections using 64-bit to 160-bit Connection IDs (CIDs) rather than IP 4-tuples; when a mobile user switches between Wi-Fi and 4G/5G, connection state persists seamlessly without re-handshaking; (3) Native Encryption: all QUIC packets except initial negotiation are fully encrypted, protecting transport metadata and packet headers from middlebox tampering; (4) Monotonically increasing packet numbers prevent ambiguity in round-trip time (RTT) calculation.

title: IETF Datatracker RFC 9000 QUIC Specification & Protocol Governance
description: Governs the normative lifecycle, transport parameters, flow-control ceilings, and stream limit negotiation of the RFC 9000 QUIC transport protocol for mobile execution environments.
detail: Tracked on IETF Datatracker, RFC 9000 mandates explicit transport parameter exchange during the TLS handshake: (1) max_idle_timeout dictates container connection reclamation to preserve mobile device battery; (2) initial_max_data and initial_max_stream_data limits enforce strict memory budgets on buffers allocated per mini-app connection, preventing memory exhaustion under high-throughput streaming; (3) initial_max_streams_bidi and initial_max_streams_uni control peer concurrency limits; (4) Stateless Reset tokens allow servers to cleanly terminate stale connections after container crashes or load-balancer restarts without leaking state.

title: IETF RFC 9001 Using TLS to Secure QUIC & Crypto Stream Key Phase Rotation
description: Standardizes the integration of TLS 1.3 cryptographic key exchange into QUIC packet headers, establishing epoch key isolation, key update phase rotation, and header protection against packet tampering.
detail: IETF RFC 9001 defines the cryptographic framing for QUIC transport: (1) Packet Protection: TLS 1.3 key derivation generates specific keys and IVs for Initial, Handshake, and 1-RTT Application data packets, ensuring distinct security epochs; (2) Header Protection: encrypts packet numbers and key phase bits using a dedicated header protection cipher mask, preventing passive observers from tracking packet flow or predicting sequence numbers; (3) Key Phase Updates: allows peers to roll cryptographic keys periodically during long-running sessions (e.g., live streaming or real-time game state) without tearing down the underlying QUIC connection; (4) Anti-Amplification Limits: limits unvalidated client address amplification to 3x bytes received until address validation is completed via PATH_CHALLENGE / PATH_RESPONSE or Retry tokens.

title: IETF RFC 9002 QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control Architecture
description: Defines loss detection algorithms, probe timeout (PTO) mechanics, and modular congestion control algorithms (NewReno/CUBIC/BBR) optimized for volatile mobile wireless links in mini-app super-apps.
detail: IETF RFC 9002 specifies loss detection and congestion management for QUIC: (1) RTT Estimation: calculates smoothed_rtt, rttvar, and min_rtt using precise packet acknowledgment timestamps, eliminating TCP retransmission ambiguity; (2) Probe Timeout (PTO): replaces classic TCP Retransmission Timeouts (RTO) with dynamic PTO calculations, sending opportunistic probe packets to rapidly detect tail drops on cellular networks; (3) Persistent Congestion: detects multi-packet loss spanning longer than persistent congestion duration and resets congestion window to the minimum allowed ceiling (kMinimumWindow = 2 * max_datagram_size); (4) Pacing: enforces packet pacing at the container transport layer to avoid queue burstiness at cellular basestations.

title: MDN TLS Practical Implementation Guide & Modern Super-App Cipher Governance
description: Provides authoritative implementation guidelines for modern TLS deployments, specifying configuration requirements for forward secrecy, cipher ordering, and certificate chain verification in client-server container ecosystems.
detail: The MDN Practical TLS Implementation Guide details operational deployment configurations: (1) Mozilla Modern Configuration profile enforces TLS 1.3 exclusively (or TLS 1.2 with AEAD ciphers as fallback), banning CBC ciphers, 3DES, and RC4; (2) Certificate Chain Validation: container trust managers must ensure intermediate CA certificates are delivered properly and OCSP Stapling (RFC 6066 / RFC 6960) is implemented to prevent blocking network lookups during TLS handshakes; (3) Session Resumption: mandates session tickets (RFC 5077 / RFC 8446) with frequent key rotation to preserve forward secrecy across resumed sessions; (4) Strict Transport Security (HSTS, RFC 6797) with includeSubDomains and preload flags must be enforced across all mini-app API domains.

title: W3C Web App Manifest - App Information & Marketplace Discovery Metadata Standard
description: Defines normative Web App Manifest extensions for application discovery, detailed descriptions, category taxonomy, screenshot layout metadata, and content rating integrations.
detail: The W3C Manifest App Information specification defines standardized metadata keys for mini-app catalog discovery and store presentation: (1) 'description' member provides plain-text localized summaries explaining purpose and capabilities; (2) 'categories' member defines an array of standard taxonomic tags (e.g., 'business', 'finance', 'utilities', 'shopping') used for marketplace indexing, filtering, and search engine optimization; (3) 'screenshots' member specifies visual promotional assets with mandatory form_factor ('wide' or 'narrow'), label accessibility descriptions, and dimensions; (4) 'iarc_rating_id' provides seamless integration with the International Age Rating Coalition global content rating system.

title: MDN Web App Manifest categories Member & Marketplace Taxonomy Governance
description: Documents the categories member syntax, allowable taxonomy list, and automated store categorization requirements for mini-app packaging manifests.
detail: MDN documentation specifies the structure and handling of the 'categories' manifest member: (1) Manifest authoring rules define 'categories' as an array of lowercase strings conforming to the W3C standard taxonomy (e.g., ['finance', 'utilities']); (2) Mini-app store intake automation parses these strings against approved platform taxonomies, rejecting custom or non-standard entries during static manifest linting; (3) Automated categorization feeds directly into super-app store recommendation graphs, browse-by-category UI tabs, and safety policy filters (e.g., filtering out 'gambling' or 'social' in enterprise or child profiles); (4) Enforces a maximum limit of 5 categories per mini-app to prevent keyword spamming and catalog degradation.

title: MDN Web App Manifest description Member & Localized Storefront Information
description: Standardizes the description manifest member for application purpose clarification, assistive technology screen reading, and store preview generation.
detail: MDN documentation for the 'description' manifest member defines requirements for store rendering and accessibility: (1) Provides a human-readable string summarizing the primary functionality and user proposition of the mini-app; (2) Assistive technology integration: screen readers and accessibility agents use this field to announce mini-app capabilities to visually impaired users before container launch; (3) Store validation gates enforce minimum (e.g., 20 characters) and maximum (e.g., 1024 characters) length constraints, stripping harmful HTML/script tags to prevent stored XSS in store discovery interfaces; (4) Multi-lingual support: combines with manifest localization extensions to dynamically present localized descriptions matching user device locale.

title: MDN Web App Manifest screenshots Member & Responsive Visual Asset Verification
description: Specifies the screenshots array dictionary for rich store installation previews, responsive aspect ratio qualification, and automated visual asset verification.
detail: MDN Web App Manifest 'screenshots' documentation specifies visual asset delivery: (1) Array of image objects containing 'src', 'sizes', 'type', and optional 'form_factor' ('wide' for desktop/tablets, 'narrow' for mobile phones); (2) 'label' attribute provides mandatory accessible text alternative for screen readers; (3) Store ingestion pipelines automatically verify screenshot assets for resolution compliance, aspect ratio uniformity, valid MIME types (image/png, image/webp, image/jpeg), and file size boundaries (e.g., max 2MB per image) to guarantee fast catalog rendering; (4) Dynamic presentation: super-app store client selects appropriate screenshot sets matching the host device form factor.

title: MDN Web App Manifest iarc_rating_id & Global Content Age Rating Federation
description: Specifies the iarc_rating_id manifest member binding mini-apps to official International Age Rating Coalition certificates for parental controls and jurisdictional distribution compliance.
detail: MDN documentation defines the 'iarc_rating_id' member for age-rating verification: (1) Contains the alphanumeric certificate ID issued by the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) questionnaire system; (2) Store review automation queries the central IARC API using this ID to verify the declared age rating and content descriptors (violence, bad language, simulated gambling, user interaction); (3) Enables automated parental control enforcement: super-apps running in supervised or child accounts automatically block mini-apps whose IARC rating exceeds the configured age threshold; (4) Jurisdictional compliance: automatically maps IARC certifications to regional rating bodies (ESRB in North America, PEGI in Europe, USK in Germany, ClassInd in Brazil, ACB in Australia).

title: W3C Identifiers for WebRTC's Statistics API: Real-Time Telemetry & Quality Architecture
description: Establishes the normative framework for WebRTC statistics collection, defining standardized metrics objects, hierarchical stats types, and deterministic telemetry dictionary schemas for real-time media streams.
detail: The W3C WebRTC Statistics specification defines standardized statistical objects for monitoring RTC connections: (1) Standardizes the RTCStats dictionary baseline (timestamp, type, id) representing instantaneous network and codec performance snapshots; (2) Classifies telemetry hierarchies across transport, candidate-pair, inbound-rtp, outbound-rtp, and remote-inbound-rtp objects; (3) Mandates privacy protections preventing cross-session tracking via normalized monotonic timestamps and isolated statistical contexts; (4) Provides super-app runtimes with uniform QoS telemetry hooks to monitor packet loss, jitter, and frame rendering quality in live streaming and voice mini-apps.

title: MDN RTCStatsReport Interface: Read-Only Map-Like Telemetry Introspection
description: Standardizes RTCStatsReport as an asynchronous read-only map of RTCStats objects, enabling programmatic query, iteration, and aggregation of real-time peer connection telemetry.
detail: MDN RTCStatsReport documentation establishes the programmatic API for inspecting WebRTC metrics: (1) RTCStatsReport implements read-only Map-like semantics (forEach, entries, keys, values, get, has, size), mapping report IDs directly to typed statistics dictionaries; (2) Decouples statistics gathering from media pipeline execution, preventing UI thread stalls during intensive media sessions; (3) Facilitates automated health checks in mini-app store sandboxes by providing structured diagnostic metrics without requiring raw media buffer access; (4) Enforces strict immutability, ensuring that captured telemetry snapshots cannot be tampered with by untrusted third-party guest scripts.

title: MDN RTCPeerConnection.getStats(): Asynchronous Telemetry Extraction & Track Filtering
description: Specifies the RTCPeerConnection.getStats() promise-based method for retrieving comprehensive or track-filtered statistics reports, governing sampling cadence and sandbox overhead.
detail: MDN RTCPeerConnection.getStats() defines the interface for collecting diagnostic telemetry: (1) Returns a Promise resolving to an RTCStatsReport covering the entire peer connection or a specific MediaStreamTrack target; (2) Enables granular diagnostic filtering, allowing developers to isolate audio vs video packet metrics without invoking full-connection parsing; (3) Super-app runtime sandboxes must govern getStats() polling frequency (recommended minimum 1000ms interval) to mitigate CPU consumption and battery drain; (4) Serves as the authoritative data source for automated connection diagnostics and network degradation adaptation in interactive mini-apps.

title: MDN RTCInboundRtpStreamStats: Inbound Media Quality & Packet Degradation Telemetry
description: Standardizes RTCInboundRtpStreamStats for measuring inbound RTP stream quality, tracking packet loss, jitter buffer delays, and decoded frame performance in mini-app communication sessions.
detail: MDN documentation for RTCInboundRtpStreamStats details the metrics payload for receiving media streams: (1) Exposes critical receiver attributes including packetsReceived, packetsLost, jitter, bytesReceived, and headerBytesReceived; (2) Provides jitter buffer telemetry (jitterBufferDelay, jitterBufferEmittedCount) enabling adaptive media playout optimization; (3) Measures video decoding performance via framesDecoded, keyFramesDecoded, and framesDropped, directly informing container QoS regulators; (4) Allows super-app platforms to establish minimum network performance SLAs and automatically trigger adaptive resolution downscaling when packet loss thresholds are breached.

title: MDN RTCOutboundRtpStreamStats: Outbound Transmission & Encoder Performance Sandboxing
description: Specifies the RTCOutboundRtpStreamStats interface for measuring egress RTP transmission, hardware encoder utilization, and quality limitation attribution in mini-app broadcast pipelines.
detail: MDN RTCOutboundRtpStreamStats defines egress media metrics for WebRTC senders: (1) Details transmission volume and pacing via packetsSent, bytesSent, and retransmittedPacketsSent; (2) Introduces qualityLimitationReason ('none', 'cpu', 'bandwidth', 'other') and qualityLimitationDurations to attribute transmission throttling deterministically; (3) Exposes frame encoding telemetry (framesEncoded, totalEncodeTime) to monitor client-side hardware encoder saturation; (4) Enables super-app store review engines to verify that mini-apps respect system thermal and bandwidth constraints, preventing battery depletion and device overheating during prolonged live sessions.

title: W3C Service Workers: Navigation Preload & Parallel Boot Network Pipeline
description: Normatively defines Navigation Preload within the Service Workers standard, enabling contemporaneous network request dispatching during service worker boot to eliminate boot-time latency penalties.
detail: The W3C Service Workers specification standardizes Navigation Preload to resolve worker startup delays: (1) Eliminates the critical path bottleneck where navigation requests are delayed while the service worker thread spins up from cold storage; (2) Enables the browser engine to initiate navigation HTTP fetch concurrently with worker lifecycle activation; (3) Defines the ServiceWorkerRegistration.navigationPreload attribute exposing the NavigationPreloadManager interface; (4) Super-app mini-app containers leverage navigation preload to achieve sub-100ms cold-start navigation parity with native mobile applications.

title: MDN NavigationPreloadManager Interface: Cold-Start Preload State & Configuration
description: Documents the NavigationPreloadManager interface for inspecting and controlling navigation preload behavior, enabling service workers to dynamically manage early network fetches.
detail: MDN NavigationPreloadManager documentation specifies programmatic preload orchestration: (1) Provides methods getState(), enable(), disable(), and setHeaderValue() accessed via registration.navigationPreload; (2) getState() returns a Promise resolving to a NavigationPreloadState object containing 'enabled' boolean and 'headerValue' string; (3) Isolates preload lifecycle to active service worker registrations, preventing unauthorized cross-origin request manipulation; (4) Super-app core runtimes utilize NavigationPreloadManager to warm up dynamic mini-app subresources during container initialization.

title: MDN NavigationPreloadManager.enable(): Declarative Boot-Phase Network Concurrency
description: Specifies NavigationPreloadManager.enable() to activate parallel network dispatch during service worker awakening, mitigating cold-start startup overhead.
detail: MDN NavigationPreloadManager.enable() establishes the activation mechanics for navigation preloading: (1) Returns a Promise resolving upon successful persistence of the preload configuration across worker restarts; (2) Once enabled, any navigation request immediately fires an HTTP GET in parallel with worker thread bootstrapping; (3) Prevents blank-screen delays during heavy JavaScript bundle loading or native runtime initialization; (4) Recommended as a mandatory best practice in super-app mini-app store certification checklists for network-dependent transactional mini-apps.

title: MDN NavigationPreloadManager.setHeaderValue(): Upstream Server Differentiation Telemetry
description: Standardizes NavigationPreloadManager.setHeaderValue() for configuring custom Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload HTTP header values, enabling backend route optimization.
detail: MDN documentation defines custom header configuration via setHeaderValue(): (1) Allows the service worker to set a custom string value for the 'Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload' HTTP header (defaulting to 'true'); (2) Enables upstream API gateways and origin servers to distinguish preload requests from standard browser navigations; (3) Allows backend servers to return lightweight partial responses or tailored payloads optimized for client-side cache reconciliation; (4) Super-app API gateways inspect this header to bypass unnecessary edge rendering and deliver raw JSON state for fast client hydration.

title: MDN FetchEvent.preloadResponse: Promise-Based Early Response Arbitration
description: Specifies FetchEvent.preloadResponse within the service worker fetch handler, providing seamless promise resolution to consume parallel preloaded network responses.
detail: MDN FetchEvent.preloadResponse specifies response reconciliation in service worker event handling: (1) Exposes event.preloadResponse returning a Promise resolving to the preloaded Response, or undefined if preload is disabled; (2) Enables race conditions between cache lookup and preloaded network delivery via event.respondWith(async () => { ... }); (3) Ensures graceful fallback: if the network preload fails or 404s, the worker can fall back to IndexedDB/CacheStorage without bubbling an unhandled network error; (4) Super-app container caching frameworks mandate preloadResponse integration to achieve zero-latency offline-first UX while preserving immediate freshness.

title: W3C Page Visibility Level 2: Execution State & Power Governance Standard
description: Defines the normative Page Visibility Level 2 specification, establishing programmatic interfaces to determine Document visibility and govern background CPU/timer throttling.
detail: The W3C Page Visibility Level 2 specification standardizes execution state observation: (1) Defines document.hidden (boolean) and document.visibilityState ('visible', 'hidden') reflecting top-level and iframe render visibility; (2) Mandates the 'visibilitychange' event dispatched synchronously when visibility state transitions occur; (3) Directs user agents to throttle timers, animations, and non-essential background tasks when documents transition to 'hidden'; (4) Super-app container sandboxes leverage Page Visibility to pause video playback, halt WebGL render loops, and freeze background audio when mini-apps are backgrounded or tab-switched.

title: MDN Document.visibilityState: Viewport Inspection & Resource Throttling
description: Documents Document.visibilityState property semantics ('visible', 'hidden'), providing deterministic visibility detection to prevent background battery and network waste.
detail: MDN Document.visibilityState documentation establishes developer semantics for visibility governance: (1) Returns an enumerated string: 'visible' (page is at least partially visible on screen) or 'hidden' (page is minimized, backgrounded, or OS lock screen active); (2) Serves as the primary heuristic for pausing telemetry beacons, stopping polling intervals, and suspending audio context processing; (3) In super-app multi-window or tabbed architectures, accurately tracks whether a mini-app pane is actively viewed or stacked in background memory; (4) Eliminates resource contention by preventing background mini-apps from monopolizing main-thread CPU and GPU resources.

title: MDN Document visibilitychange Event: Reactive Lifecycle Transition Arbitration
description: Specifies the Document 'visibilitychange' event interface, enabling event-driven state transitions, persistent state serialization, and session teardown handling.
detail: MDN visibilitychange event documentation defines lifecycle transition event handling: (1) Fired on the Document whenever visibilityState changes, serving as the most reliable indicator of user departure compared to unreliable unload/beforeunload events; (2) Mandated as the standard trigger for committing pending transactional data to IndexedDB or transmitting analytic pings via navigator.sendBeacon(); (3) Enables mini-apps to cleanly mute media, release camera/microphone hardware locks, and suspend WebSocket heartbeats; (4) Super-app review guidelines require mini-apps to bind visibilitychange listeners to ensure graceful state restoration upon re-entry.

title: W3C Screen Orientation API: Display Geometry & Orientation Lock Standard
description: Establishes the W3C Screen Orientation standard, defining screen geometry types, dynamic rotation events, and programmatic orientation locking for mobile runtimes.
detail: The W3C Screen Orientation specification defines the programmatic control of screen orientation: (1) Standardizes the ScreenOrientation interface accessed via screen.orientation; (2) Classifies screen orientations into OrientationType ('portrait-primary', 'portrait-secondary', 'landscape-primary', 'landscape-secondary'); (3) Specifies screen.orientation.angle representing rotational angle relative to the device's natural orientation; (4) Provides orientation 'change' events to trigger dynamic UI layout re-computation and viewport recalculations in adaptive mobile mini-apps.

title: MDN ScreenOrientation.lock(): Programmatic Viewport Locking & Permission Sandboxing
description: Documents ScreenOrientation.lock() and unlock() methods, governing programmatic orientation locking, user activation constraints, and manifest display prerequisites.
detail: MDN ScreenOrientation.lock() specifies orientation locking semantics: (1) Syntax: screen.orientation.lock(orientation) returns a Promise resolving when screen lock is applied; (2) Requires fullscreen context or standalone/fullscreen web app manifest display mode in most browser implementations; (3) Throws 'NotSupportedError' if the host platform or windowing manager does not allow locking; (4) Super-app container security policy must govern orientation locking to prevent malicious mini-apps from trapping users in inverted orientations or breaking host super-app navigation controls.

title: W3C Permissions Policy Level 1: Declarative Host-Mediated Feature Delegation
description: Establishes the normative W3C Permissions Policy Level 1 standard, enabling super-app hosts to selectively enable, disable, and delegate hardware APIs and powerful platform capabilities across browsing contexts and embedded frames.
detail: W3C Permissions Policy Level 1 standardizes declarative control over powerful browser features: (1) Defines structured HTTP header syntax 'Permissions-Policy' utilizing RFC 8941 Structured Field Values for dictionary and list serialization; (2) Replaces legacy Feature-Policy, providing fine-grained origin allowlists ('self', specific origins, '*', or '()'); (3) Mandates that features not explicitly delegated to cross-origin mini-app frames inherit a default allowlist of '()', preventing unauthorized access to camera, microphone, geolocation, and payment instruments; (4) Standardizes container-level capability isolation, ensuring third-party mini-app dependencies cannot access privileged device sensors without explicit super-app delegation.

title: MDN Permissions-Policy HTTP Header: Gateway-Level Capability Sandboxing
description: Documents the syntax, directives, and enforcement semantics of the Permissions-Policy HTTP header for server and API gateway runtime enforcement across mini-app distributions.
detail: MDN Permissions-Policy header documentation defines web platform capability restrictions: (1) Standardizes directive declaration syntax (e.g., 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(self "https://miniapp.superapp.vn")'); (2) Restricts access to sensitive client-side APIs across documents and nested execution contexts; (3) Enforces default restrictive postures where unlisted cross-origin frames are automatically denied access to sensitive hardware; (4) Super-app distribution servers and reverse proxies must inject hardened Permissions-Policy headers on all mini-app package responses to eliminate capability escalation risks.

title: MDN Permissions-Policy camera Directive: Optical Sensor Access Sandboxing
description: Specifies the 'camera' policy-controlled feature directive, governing video capture hardware access and preventing unauthorized eKYC or background video surveillance in mini-apps.
detail: MDN camera directive documentation governs optical capture hardware isolation: (1) Controls whether the current document or child iframes can use video input devices via MediaDevices.getUserMedia() or ImageCapture; (2) Default allowlist is 'self', restricting camera activation strictly to top-level origins unless explicitly delegated; (3) When denied, navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia() immediately rejects with NotAllowedError without showing runtime permission prompts; (4) Super-app store review requirements mandate that mini-apps declare camera intent in manifests, and host containers clamp camera permissions to verified eKYC and optical scanning workflows.

title: MDN Permissions-Policy geolocation Directive: Physical Location Privacy Isolation
description: Governs the 'geolocation' feature directive, isolating GNSS and cellular trilateration data access to prevent covert physical location harvesting by embedded mini-apps.
detail: MDN geolocation directive documentation defines location hardware sandboxing: (1) Controls access to Geolocation.getCurrentPosition() and Geolocation.watchPosition(); (2) Default allowlist is 'self', blocking third-party embedded tracking scripts from acquiring physical GPS/Wi-Fi positioning data; (3) When blocked by policy, calls immediately return GeolocationPositionError.PERMISSION_DENIED without user prompting; (4) Store governance requires ride-hailing and logistics mini-apps to bind geolocation requests to active UI interactions, with super-app runtime enforcing background location revocation.

title: MDN HTMLIFrameElement.allow Attribute: Granular Frame Capability Delegation
description: Documents the 'allow' attribute on iframe elements, standardizing declarative capability delegation and permission containment for nested mini-app container runtimes.
detail: MDN HTMLIFrameElement.allow specifies programmatic and declarative feature delegation to child browsing contexts: (1) Syntax matches Permissions Policy feature directives, allowing per-frame capability grants (e.g., allow="payment; usb 'none'"); (2) Inherits parent document restrictions; an iframe cannot be granted capabilities that the parent container document was denied by HTTP headers; (3) Interoperates with the 'sandbox' attribute to establish multi-layered defense-in-depth isolation; (4) Super-app web runtime shells use the allow attribute to enforce least-privilege sandboxing, preventing unverified mini-app child frames from executing unauthorized native bridge calls.

title: WICG Speculation Rules Specification: Declarative Prefetch & Prerender Architecture
description: Establishes the normative WICG Speculation Rules specification, enabling declarative JSON-driven rules for prefetching and prerendering navigation targets to achieve instantaneous mini-app screen transitions.
detail: WICG Speculation Rules standardizes declarative speculative loading: (1) Defines structured JSON format embedded in <script type="speculationrules"> for configuring prefetch and prerender actions; (2) Supports URL-based patterns and document-based selector rules (e.g., 'where': {'and': [{'href_matches': '/*'}, {'not': {'selector_matches': '.no-prerender'}}]}}); (3) Establishes resource and privacy boundaries: prerendered pages execute in an invisible background browsing context with restricted network and hardware access until activation; (4) Super-app navigation shells utilize speculation rules to pre-warm next-likely mini-app views based on user scroll velocity and viewport proximity.

title: MDN <script type="speculationrules">: Declarative Navigation Acceleration
description: Documents the syntax, JSON structure, and browser integration of the <script type="speculationrules"> element for configuring client-side speculative preloading in web applications.
detail: MDN documentation specifies the structure of speculationrules script blocks: (1) Syntax requires type="speculationrules" containing a valid JSON object with 'prefetch' and/or 'prerender' keys; (2) Specifies 'source' ('list' or 'document') and 'urls' array or 'where' predicates; (3) Incorporates 'eagerness' levels ('immediate', 'eager', 'moderate', 'conservative') to dynamically match user intent cues (hover, mousedown, or programmatic trigger); (4) Provides super-app developer SDKs with a standard declarative interface to eliminate transition blank screens without custom native preload hacks.

title: MDN Speculation Rules API: Dynamic Runtime Speculation Management
description: Details the Speculation Rules API architecture, runtime compatibility, and programmatic insertion of speculative prefetching and prerendering rules into live DOM contexts.
detail: MDN Speculation Rules API documentation outlines runtime behavior: (1) Enables dynamic script injection via document.createElement('script') to add speculation rules dynamically in single-page mini-apps; (2) Prevents resource contention by automatically throttling speculative fetches under low-memory or Data Saver conditions; (3) Eliminates the cross-origin privacy leaks of legacy <link rel="prerender"> by enforcing strict credential and cookie partitioning; (4) Super-app catalog stores leverage the API to preload featured mini-app entrypoints during idle cycles, achieving sub-50ms Time-to-Interactive (TTI).

title: MDN PerformanceNavigationTiming.activationStart: Prerender Activation Telemetry
description: Documents the activationStart property of PerformanceNavigationTiming, measuring the exact duration between navigation start and prerendered document activation to quantify user-perceived latency.
detail: MDN PerformanceNavigationTiming.activationStart specifies prerender timing telemetry: (1) Returns a DOMHighResTimeStamp representing when a prerendered document is activated and brought to the foreground; (2) For non-prerendered navigations, activationStart is identically 0; (3) Critical for accurate Core Web Vitals (FCP, LCP) calculation, ensuring that metrics measure duration from user activation rather than background initialization; (4) Super-app store analytics pipelines consume activationStart to benchmark the real performance uplift of prerendered mini-app launches.

title: MDN Document.prerendering Property: Background Pre-Activation Execution State
description: Documents the Document.prerendering boolean attribute and prerenderingchange event, governing execution state detection and deferral of side-effect operations during prerender cycles.
detail: MDN Document.prerendering documentation defines execution isolation during background prerendering: (1) document.prerendering returns true while the page is being prerendered prior to user navigation, switching to false upon activation; (2) Dispatches the 'prerenderingchange' event on the Document when activation occurs; (3) Mandates that disruptive actions (audio playback, intrusive analytics logging, payment popups, biometric prompts) MUST be gated while document.prerendering is true; (4) Mini-app quality review guidelines require developers to defer heavy background work and analytics beacons until prerendering completes.

title: W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform: Off-Thread Media Frame Sandboxing & E2EE Standard
description: Establishes the normative W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform standard, enabling Dedicated Workers to inspect, modify, and cryptographically encrypt/decrypt encoded audio and video frames before network transmission.
detail: W3C WebRTC Encoded Transform standardizes direct programmatic access to media pipelines: (1) Defines RTCRtpScriptTransform to route encoded media frames directly into Dedicated Web Workers via TransformStreams; (2) Operates on compressed video/audio bits before packetization, enabling client-side End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) using SFrame or custom cryptographic protocols; (3) Guarantees main-thread UI responsiveness by offloading heavy cryptographic transformations and ML frame analysis to background threads; (4) Standardizes security controls ensuring that third-party mini-app workers cannot leak raw frame buffers across origin boundaries.

title: MDN RTCRtpScriptTransform Interface: Worker Media Stream Pipeline Orchestration
description: Documents the RTCRtpScriptTransform interface for instantiating and binding DedicatedWorker-based transformation streams to RTCRtpSender and RTCRtpReceiver pipelines.
detail: MDN RTCRtpScriptTransform documentation specifies worker pipeline configuration: (1) Constructor syntax: new RTCRtpScriptTransform(worker, options, transferList) passes custom configuration and Transferable objects into the worker scope; (2) Attaches to sender.transform or receiver.transform to intercept outbound and inbound RTP frame streams; (3) Encapsulates frame handling within dedicated worker scopes, preventing unprivileged guest scripts from tampering with encrypted streams; (4) Super-app telehealth and secure communication mini-apps utilize RTCRtpScriptTransform to enforce zero-trust E2EE compliance.

title: MDN RTCRtpScriptTransformer Interface: Dedicated Worker Frame Processing Context
description: Documents the RTCRtpScriptTransformer interface available in DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope, managing the readable and writable streams of encoded media chunks.
detail: MDN RTCRtpScriptTransformer documentation defines the worker-side transform interface: (1) Exposed via the rtctransform event in DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope (e.g., self.onrtctransform = (event) => ...); (2) Exposes transformer.readable (ReadableStream) and transformer.writable (WritableStream) transporting RTCEncodedAudioFrame or RTCEncodedVideoFrame objects; (3) Facilitates pipeline piping via readable.pipeThrough(transformStream).pipeTo(writable) with native backpressure flow control; (4) Ensures crash isolation: any unhandled exception in worker frame processing drops frames gracefully without terminating the super-app host container.

title: MDN RTCEncodedAudioFrame Interface: Sandboxed Encoded Audio Payload Inspection
