description: Documents the RTCEncodedAudioFrame interface representing encoded audio chunks, detailing metadata inspection, timestamp alignment, and binary buffer modification.
detail: MDN RTCEncodedAudioFrame specifies encoded audio chunk manipulation: (1) Provides 'data' attribute (ArrayBuffer) containing compressed audio bitstream (e.g., Opus); (2) Exposes 'timestamp' (RTP timestamp) and getMetadata() returning sequence number, synchronization source (SSRC), and payload type; (3) Enables developers to insert cryptographic authentication tags or proprietary voice watermarks into audio packets; (4) Super-app audio governance requires strict size and format validation on modified data buffers to prevent audio decoder exploitation on receiving clients.

title: MDN RTCEncodedVideoFrame Interface: Compressed Video Chunk Inspection & E2EE
description: Documents the RTCEncodedVideoFrame interface representing encoded video slices (H.264, VP8/VP9, AV1), enabling frame type classification, metadata introspection, and payload encryption.
detail: MDN RTCEncodedVideoFrame documentation defines encoded video frame control: (1) Exposes 'type' ('key' vs 'delta'), allowing selective cryptographic header protection without encrypting codec-critical NAL unit headers; (2) getMetadata() provides width, height, spatialIndex, temporalIndex, frameId, and dependency structure; (3) Exposes 'data' (ArrayBuffer) representing the raw compressed bitstream; (4) Super-app security controls mandate that mini-app video calling engines sanitize metadata and preserve RTP frame sequencing to maintain video synchronization under poor network conditions.

title: MDN Crypto.getRandomValues(): Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generation
description: Standardizes the generation of cryptographically strong pseudorandom values into typed arrays via Crypto.getRandomValues(), eliminating insecure PRNGs in mini-apps.
detail: MDN Crypto.getRandomValues() documentation specifies cryptographically secure randomness: (1) Operates synchronously over integer-based TypedArray instances (Int8Array, Uint8Array, Uint16Array, Int32Array, Uint32Array, BigInt64Array, BigUint64Array); (2) Enforces a strict byte length quota of 65,536 bytes (64 KiB) per invocation, throwing a QuotaExceededError if requested byte length exceeds this ceiling; (3) Uses an underlying OS-level entropy pool (e.g., /dev/urandom or OS CSPRNG), preventing predictable session tokens or session nonces; (4) Super-app security guardrails prohibit Math.random() in authentication, signing, or CSRF token generation, enforcing Crypto.getRandomValues() across all sandbox contexts.

title: MDN Crypto.randomUUID(): Cryptographically Secure RFC 4122 Version 4 UUID Generation
description: Standardizes native generation of RFC 4122 version 4 UUIDs via crypto.randomUUID(), providing collision-resistant identifiers for client requests and analytics events.
detail: MDN Crypto.randomUUID() specification defines native UUID generation: (1) Returns a canonical 36-character string representation of an RFC 4122 Version 4 UUID (e.g., '36b8f84d-df4e-4d49-b662-bcde71a8764f'); (2) Only available in Secure Contexts (HTTPS/localhost), preventing unauthenticated or degraded environments from generating untrusted identifiers; (3) Eliminates third-party JavaScript UUID polyfills (e.g., uuid npm package), reducing bundle footprint and avoiding compromised supply chain dependencies; (4) Super-app tracing architecture leverages crypto.randomUUID() for client-side transaction correlation IDs and idempotent checkout idempotency tokens.

title: MDN SubtleCrypto.digest(): Asynchronous Cryptographic Hash Generation & Subresource Integrity
description: Standardizes non-blocking cryptographic message digests via subtle.digest() across SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 for data integrity and artifact verification.
detail: MDN SubtleCrypto.digest() specifies asynchronous hashing algorithms: (1) Takes an algorithm identifier ('SHA-256', 'SHA-384', 'SHA-512') and an ArrayBuffer/TypedArray, returning a Promise resolving to an ArrayBuffer containing the raw binary digest; (2) Operates asynchronously off the main thread, preventing UI freezing when computing hashes of large data payloads, offline assets, or transaction receipts; (3) Legacy insecure algorithms like SHA-1 or MD5 are deprecated or restricted from high-assurance validation flows; (4) Super-app container verification pipelines utilize crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', data) to verify package chunk hashes and validate local database checksums before executing updates.

title: MDN SubtleCrypto.encrypt(): Authenticated Symmetric & Asymmetric Encryption Sandboxing
description: Documents authenticated payload encryption using AES-GCM and RSA-OAEP via SubtleCrypto.encrypt(), ensuring data confidentiality and integrity in local storage.
detail: MDN SubtleCrypto.encrypt() documentation governs hardware-accelerated encryption: (1) Supports modern authenticated symmetric ciphers (AES-GCM, AES-CBC, AES-CTR) and asymmetric schemes (RSA-OAEP); (2) AES-GCM requires explicit initialization vector (IV) parameters and supports additional authenticated data (AAD) alongside customizable authentication tag lengths (up to 128 bits); (3) Prevents key material extraction when paired with non-extractable CryptoKey handles; (4) Super-app storage standards require mini-apps handling sensitive PII, cached credentials, or offline health records to encrypt SQLite/IndexedDB records using crypto.subtle.encrypt with AES-GCM.

title: MDN SubtleCrypto.sign(): Cryptographic Digital Signatures & Non-Repudiation Sandboxing
description: Standardizes cryptographic digital signing via subtle.sign() across ECDSA, Ed25519, HMAC, and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, ensuring request integrity and non-repudiation.
detail: MDN SubtleCrypto.sign() specifies digital signature generation: (1) Supports asymmetric signature algorithms (ECDSA with P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, RSA-PSS, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) and symmetric HMAC; (2) Accepts a private CryptoKey or secret key and data buffer, resolving to an ArrayBuffer containing the signature bytes; (3) Enforces strict algorithm binding preventing key substitution attacks across different signing schemes; (4) Super-app financial APIs mandate subtle.sign for client-side transaction authorizations, creating tamper-evident cryptographic tokens signed by hardware-bound keys before transmission to host gateway endpoints.

title: MDN Element.replaceChildren(): Atomic DOM Replacement & XSS/Mutation Mitigation
description: Standardizes atomic replacement of an element's child nodes via replaceChildren(), preventing intermediate detached DOM states and optimizing memory churn.
detail: MDN Element.replaceChildren() specification defines high-performance DOM replacement: (1) Atomically replaces all existing child nodes of an Element with a new set of Node or string arguments in a single operation; (2) Calling replaceChildren() without arguments provides a standardized, memory-safe mechanism to completely empty an element, eliminating legacy innerHTML = '' patterns; (3) Avoids parser invocation and bypasses HTML deserialization risks, mitigating parser-mutation XSS vectors; (4) Emits a unified batch of MutationObserver records, preventing excessive layout recalculations during dynamic mini-app page re-rendering.

title: MDN Node.cloneNode(): Deep Template Subtree Cloning & Inert Prototype Sandboxing
description: Documents Node.cloneNode() deep and shallow DOM cloning algorithms, detailing event listener isolation, custom element lifecycle, and template instantiation.
detail: MDN Node.cloneNode() documentation specifies subtree replication: (1) Takes an optional boolean parameter 'deep' (defaulting to false); when true, recursively clones the entire descendant subtree, including attributes and text nodes; (2) Crucially does NOT copy event listeners attached via addEventListener() or assigned via JavaScript properties (e.g., node.onclick), establishing an isolated clean event boundary; (3) When cloning <template> contents (template.content.cloneNode(true)), instantiates inert DocumentFragment nodes without executing embedded scripts until attached to live document; (4) Super-app component engines use cloneNode for high-throughput list virtualizer rendering.

title: MDN Node.contains(): Inclusive Subtree Hierarchy Verification & Boundary Sandboxing
description: Documents Node.contains() boundary checking to verify whether a target node is a descendant or self, preventing out-of-bounds DOM manipulations.
detail: MDN Node.contains() specification defines DOM tree membership testing: (1) Returns a boolean indicating whether a node is a descendant of a given node, or is the node itself (inclusive container check); (2) Returns false if the target node is null, detached, or belongs to a different document/ShadowRoot without open encapsulation; (3) Essential for click-outside dismissal algorithms in dropdowns, modal sheets, and context menus to ensure click events originated outside container boundaries; (4) Super-app security middleware utilizes Node.contains to verify that third-party UI widgets do not escape their assigned iframe or custom element mount point.

title: MDN Element.closest(): Upward DOM Traversal & Scoped Boundary Containment
description: Standardizes traversing up the DOM tree from the current element to find the closest ancestor matching CSS selectors, enforcing component containment.
detail: MDN Element.closest() documentation specifies upward traversal: (1) Traverses the Element and its parents towards the document root until it finds a node that matches the specified CSS selector string; (2) Returns null if no ancestor matches the selector or if traversal hits ShadowRoot boundary in closed mode; (3) Enables event delegation patterns: mini-apps listen on top-level root containers and resolve target widgets via event.target.closest('[data-action]'), drastically reducing event listener overhead; (4) Super-app host shells use element.closest to ensure interactive elements are contained within authorized viewport safe zones before triggering sensitive host actions.

title: MDN Node.compareDocumentPosition(): Bitmask Positional Auditing & Z-Order Validation
description: Documents Node.compareDocumentPosition() bitmask comparisons, providing topological auditing of node placement and preventing DOM hierarchy spoofing.
detail: MDN Node.compareDocumentPosition() specifies topological relationship auditing: (1) Returns a bitmask representing the relative position of two nodes in document order (DOCUMENT_POSITION_DISCONNECTED [1], PRECEDING [2], FOLLOWING [4], CONTAINS [8], CONTAINED_BY [16], IMPLEMENTATION_SPECIFIC [32]); (2) Facilitates strict validation of element ordering to detect clickjacking overlays or out-of-order injected DOM siblings; (3) Provides deterministic sorting criteria for virtualized accessibility tree nodes and custom focus rings; (4) Super-app review and runtime security monitors use compareDocumentPosition to verify that disclaimer text and payment confirmation summaries precede user submit buttons in the DOM order.

title: MDN CSS transition-property: Animatable Property Specification & Isolation
description: Standardizes the definition of CSS properties that participate in transitions via transition-property, isolating animated styling to compositor-safe attributes.
detail: MDN CSS transition-property specification defines property transition scoping: (1) Accepts comma-separated CSS property names or the keyword 'none' or 'all'; (2) Prohibits the use of 'all' in performance-critical super-app stylesheets to prevent unintentional layout thrashing on expensive properties like width, height, or margin; (3) Restricts transitions to GPU-accelerated compositing properties (transform, opacity, filter) where hardware layers bypass reflow/repaint pipelines; (4) Super-app automated CSS linters enforce explicit property declarations in transition-property to prevent animation jank across low-tier mobile chipsets.

title: MDN CSS transition-duration: Temporal Interpolation Ceilings & Battery Optimization
description: Standardizes the temporal length of transitions via transition-duration, bounding execution times to prevent lingering GPU wakeups and mobile battery drain.
detail: MDN CSS transition-duration specification governs transition timing bounds: (1) Specifies the time an animation takes to complete, expressed in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms); (2) Default value is 0s, resulting in instantaneous property changes; (3) Super-app UX quality standards enforce duration caps (typically <= 400ms for modal entrances and <= 250ms for micro-interactions) to maintain snappy mobile responsiveness; (4) Setting duration to 0s upon prefers-reduced-motion: reduce media query ensures compliance with WCAG 2.2 accessibility requirements for users with vestibular motion disorders.

title: MDN CSS transition-timing-function: Physics Interpolation Curves & Ergonomics
description: Documents mathematical easing functions via cubic-bezier, steps, and keyword functions in transition-timing-function, providing ergonomic mobile physics.
detail: MDN CSS transition-timing-function specification defines interpolation physics: (1) Defines the rate of change of property values over time using mathematical curves (ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2), steps(n, jump-term)); (2) Custom cubic-bezier parameters allow developers to craft platform-native deceleration curves (e.g., cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1.0)) matching iOS UIKit and Android Material motion tokens; (3) Guarantees deterministic value calculation at every frame interval; (4) Super-app design systems mandate standard easing tokens across all mini-app components to ensure a cohesive native look and feel.

title: MDN Element transitionend Event: Lifecycle Completion Synchronization & Teardown
description: Documents the transitionend DOM event dispatched when a CSS transition completes, enabling asynchronous UI state synchronization and DOM cleanup.
detail: MDN Element transitionend event specification defines completion callbacks: (1) Dispatched when a CSS transition has finished playing; (2) Event object inherits from TransitionEvent, exposing propertyName (name of property that transitioned), elapsedTime (time in seconds), and pseudoElement; (3) Enables mini-apps to synchronize DOM removal or class toggles after an outbound animation completes (e.g., removing a modal dialog after fade-out); (4) Super-app animation orchestrators attach one-time transitionend listeners with fallback safety timers to prevent hanging async promises if the element is removed from the DOM before completion.

title: MDN Element transitioncancel Event: Interrupted Transition Handling & Resource Cleanup
description: Documents the transitioncancel DOM event fired when an ongoing transition is aborted, preventing stranded locks and resource leaks during rapid user input.
detail: MDN Element transitioncancel event specification defines interruption handling: (1) Fired when a CSS transition is canceled before completion—such as when transition-property changes, display is set to 'none', or property value is altered mid-flight; (2) Provides propertyName and elapsedTime at the exact moment of cancellation; (3) Critical for mobile touch interactions where rapid tap-and-drag gestures interrupt ongoing transitions; (4) Super-app component frameworks listen for transitioncancel to reset state flags, unblock gesture arbitration locks, and de-allocate hardware GPU layers immediately without waiting for a transitionend that will never fire.

title: MDN History API: SPA Navigation Lifecycle & Session History Sandboxing
description: Standardizes browser session history manipulation via the History interface, enabling single-page mini-app routing without full page reloads.
detail: MDN History API specification defines session history manipulation: (1) Exposes window.history interface allowing web applications to navigate backward and forward through user session history; (2) Enables programmatic modification of the URL and session state without causing document reloads or destroying in-memory state; (3) Mandates same-origin security boundaries: attempts to push or replace URLs belonging to a different origin throw a SecurityError DOMException; (4) Super-app runtime architectures sandbox window.history within the mini-app root path, intercepting cross-subpath mutations to ensure navigation remains strictly constrained within registered manifest scope.

title: MDN history.pushState(): Client-Side Route State Ingestion & History Stack Sandboxing
description: Documents history.pushState() for adding new state entries to browser history, detailing serializable state object boundaries and URL origin restrictions.
detail: MDN history.pushState() specification defines history entry creation: (1) Takes state, unused (title), and optional url parameters, pushing a new entry into the session history stack; (2) State parameter must be serializable via the Structured Clone Algorithm; browsers enforce size limits (typically 2 MiB in Chromium and 640 KiB in Firefox), throwing DataCloneError if serialization fails or size ceiling is breached; (3) Passing cross-origin URLs throws SecurityError; (4) Super-app containers wrap pushState to enforce synthetic history depth caps (e.g., maximum 50 entries) and synchronize route changes with native host navigation headers and custom back-button bars.

title: MDN history.replaceState(): In-Place History Modification & Clean Route Sandboxing
description: Standardizes in-place modification of current history entry via replaceState(), preventing redundant history stack bloat during transient query/filter mutations.
detail: MDN history.replaceState() documentation defines in-place history mutation: (1) Replaces the current session history entry with updated state object and URL without altering stack length; (2) Useful for non-reversible state transitions—such as filtering product catalogs, updating search query parameters, or updating checkout step state; (3) Mitigates 'back-button traps' where excessive pushState calls prevent users from returning to the host super-app shell via hardware or gesture back navigation; (4) Super-app store review criteria flag excessive pushState spam in mini-apps and recommend replaceState for ephemeral state updates to preserve clean back navigation.

title: MDN Window popstate Event: Session History Traversal & State Restoration
description: Documents the popstate DOM event dispatched on active window when active history entry changes between entries for the same document.
detail: MDN Window popstate event specification defines history traversal: (1) Dispatched when user navigates session history (e.g., via browser Back/Forward buttons, history.back(), history.go()); (2) Event object exposes state property containing a copy of the structured clone state passed to pushState or replaceState; (3) Does not fire upon pushState() or replaceState() invocations, only upon actual history traversal; (4) Super-app host bridges listen to popstate to harmonize native host gestures with mini-app route unstacking, ensuring smooth page transitions and avoiding orphaned sub-view memory leaks.

title: MDN Window hashchange Event: Fragment Identifier Mutation & Anchor Sandboxing
description: Standardizes the hashchange event fired when URL fragment identifier (#) changes, providing lightweight routing and deep anchor link navigation.
detail: MDN Window hashchange event documentation specifies fragment tracking: (1) Fired synchronously when the URL fragment identifier changes (either programmatically or via anchor link clicks); (2) Exposes oldURL and newURL read-only properties containing complete URL strings before and after the transition; (3) Operates without server network requests or document teardowns; (4) Super-app security layers inspect hashchange events to sanitize target fragment IDs against DOM XSS vectors (e.g., location.hash sink vulnerabilities) and prevent clickjacking via unexpected internal anchor scrolling.

title: MDN HTMLDetailsElement toggle Event: Collapsible Content State Mutation Sandboxing
description: Standardizes the toggle event dispatched on <details> elements upon expanding or collapsing, synchronizing disclosure widgets and layout reflows.
detail: MDN HTMLDetailsElement toggle event documentation specifies disclosure lifecycle: (1) Dispatched on <details> element whenever its open attribute changes state (either via user click on <summary> or programmatic mutation); (2) Fires asynchronously after the state mutation has settled in the DOM; (3) Exposes oldState ('open' or 'closed') and newState ('open' or 'closed') via the inheriting ToggleEvent interface; (4) Super-app responsive layouts monitor details toggle events to trigger dynamic virtual list height recalculations and lazy-load nested catalog assets only when sections expand.

title: MDN HTMLDetailsElement.name: Exclusive Accordion Grouping & Native Disclosure Sandboxing
description: Documents HTMLDetailsElement.name property for exclusive accordion behavior, natively grouping multiple <details> elements without JavaScript orchestration.
detail: MDN HTMLDetailsElement.name documentation specifies native accordion grouping: (1) Reflects the HTML name attribute of the <details> element; (2) Multiple <details> elements sharing the same name string form an exclusive accordion group where opening one automatically closes any previously open sibling; (3) Operates entirely in browser native C++ layout code, eliminating complex custom JavaScript state synchronization logic; (4) Super-app design guidelines mandate using native details[name] for mobile FAQ sheets and settings accordions, reducing main-thread CPU overhead on budget mobile devices.

title: MDN ToggleEvent Interface: Unified Declarative State Mutation Event Architecture
description: Standardizes the ToggleEvent interface dispatched by collapsible and popover elements, exposing structured oldState and newState transition telemetry.
detail: MDN ToggleEvent interface specification defines state transition data: (1) Represents events that notify when an element toggles between open/closed states (e.g., <details> elements, popovers, and dialogs); (2) Inherits from standard Event interface, carrying read-only oldState and newState string properties; (3) Guaranteed to dispatch consistently regardless of whether the toggle was initiated via declarative HTML attributes, CSS invokers, or imperative script calls; (4) Super-app analytics pipelines hook into ToggleEvent to capture standardized telemetry on user interaction flows and expandable UI section dwell times.

title: MDN ToggleEvent.oldState: Prior Lifecycle State Introspection & Reversibility Auditing
description: Documents ToggleEvent.oldState property indicating the prior state of a toggling UI element ('open' or 'closed'), supporting state rollbacks.
detail: MDN ToggleEvent.oldState documentation specifies antecedent state introspection: (1) Read-only string property returning 'open' or 'closed' indicating the state before the toggle event occurred; (2) Enables deterministic state rollback routines if a subsequent async condition (e.g., authentication check, network confirmation) fails after user toggles an accordion or popover; (3) Facilitates accurate directional animations (expanding vs collapsing transitions) in hybrid animation controllers; (4) Super-app UI frameworks inspect oldState to ensure state transitions follow valid lifecycle paths and prevent corrupted double-open states.

title: MDN ToggleEvent.newState: Target Lifecycle State Verification & Lazy-Loading Triggers
description: Documents ToggleEvent.newState property indicating target state of a toggling UI element ('open' or 'closed'), gating deferred asset loading.
detail: MDN ToggleEvent.newState specification defines succeeding state introspection: (1) Read-only string property returning 'open' or 'closed' indicating the state the element is transitioning into; (2) When newState === 'open', mini-app components trigger lazy-loading of embedded images, iframes, or heavy WebGL canvases; (3) When newState === 'closed', components pause background timers, pause embedded video streams, and de-allocate expensive visual resources; (4) Super-app resource governance frameworks mandate listening to newState to ensure memory-intensive resources are discarded when collapsible containers close.

title: MDN HTMLDialogElement cancel Event: Native Escape Interception & State Teardown Sandboxing
description: Standardizes the cancel event fired when user attempts to close a native modal <dialog> via the Escape key, allowing graceful validation or cancellation veto.
detail: MDN HTMLDialogElement cancel event documentation defines dismissal interception: (1) Dispatched directly to an open <dialog> element when user triggers a native dismiss gesture (such as pressing the Escape key on hardware keyboards or sending back key events); (2) Event is cancelable: calling event.preventDefault() suppresses dialog dismissal, allowing mini-apps to prompt 'Discard unsaved changes?' confirmations before closing; (3) Followed by the close event if not canceled; (4) Super-app host review policies require mini-apps to handle cancel events gracefully rather than unconditionally trapping users within non-dismissable full-screen modal overlays.

title: MDN HTMLDialogElement close Event: Modal Lifecycle Termination & Result Synchronization
description: Documents the close event fired when a native <dialog> element closes, providing deterministic synchronization of return values and DOM focus cleanup.
detail: MDN HTMLDialogElement close event specification defines modal termination callbacks: (1) Dispatched when a dialog closes—whether via dialog.close(), form submission with method='dialog', or keyboard escape; (2) Non-cancelable event dispatched after dialog has been removed from the top layer and its open attribute removed; (3) Enables mini-apps to read dialog.returnValue and process user selection or form input; (4) Automatically restores keyboard focus to previously focused element outside the dialog, maintaining compliance with WCAG 2.2 focus management accessibility standards across super-app mini-apps.

title: MDN HTMLDialogElement.returnValue: Typed Modal Result Passing & Form Sandboxing
description: Documents HTMLDialogElement.returnValue property storing return value of a closed dialog, enabling clean data passing between modal and caller contexts.
detail: MDN HTMLDialogElement.returnValue specification defines modal output propagation: (1) String property reflecting the value passed to dialog.close(returnValue) or the value of the submitting button in a <form method='dialog'>; (2) Persists after dialog closure, allowing parent view controllers to retrieve user choice synchronously during or after the close event; (3) Eliminates hacky global variable leakage or detached promise-based monkey-patching; (4) Super-app UI component libraries standardize on dialog.returnValue to cleanly pass selected payment methods, address tokens, or consent choices back to host orchestrators.

title: MDN Element scrollend Event: Compositor Scroll Termination & Inertia Settlement Sandboxing
description: Standardizes the scrollend event fired on Elements when a scroll operation has completed, eliminating error-prone debounce timers for scroll settlement.
detail: MDN Element scrollend event specification defines scroll completion telemetry: (1) Dispatched on an Element when scrolling has completed—including programmatic scrolls, user touch flings, mousewheel inertia, and keyboard navigation; (2) Fires precisely when visual scroll offset has fully settled and all momentum has ceased; (3) Eliminates legacy patterns relying on setTimeout(..., 150) scroll listener debouncing which caused false-positive triggers and excessive CPU wakeups; (4) Super-app virtualized lists and carousel banners use element scrollend to safely initiate heavy DOM hydration and lazy image decodes only after kinetic movement stops.

title: MDN Document scrollend Event: Viewport Scroll Cessation & Dynamic Chrome Synchronization
description: Documents the scrollend event fired on Document when document-level viewport scrolling ceases, coordinating host header collapse and pull-to-refresh resets.
detail: MDN Document scrollend event specification defines viewport-level scroll cessation: (1) Dispatched to Document when the scrolling of the main document root has concluded; (2) Bubbles up from scrolling containers to Document, allowing centralized observation of viewport motion across all nested sub-views; (3) Enables super-app host shells to synchronize native top bar collapse/expand animations without stuttering during active user gestures; (4) Integrates with analytics engines to measure true user read/dwell time across long-form catalog pages by tracking the delta between scroll start and document scrollend events.

title: IETF RFC 7519: JSON Web Token (JWT) Core Claims Architecture & Temporal Boundary Validation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7519 Sections 4.1 (Registered Claim Names) & 7.2 (Validating a JWT)
key_takeaways: RFC 7519 standardizes a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties across distributed environments.

Defines seven core registered claim names: 'iss' (issuer identifier URL/string), 'sub' (subject principal identifier), 'aud' (audience array or principal identifier), 'exp' (expiration time in seconds since Unix epoch), 'nbf' (not-before time), 'iat' (issued-at time), and 'jti' (unique JWT identifier for replay mitigation).

Establishes strict validation rules requiring processing parties to reject tokens where the current time is greater than or equal to 'exp' or strictly before 'nbf', while allowing a small bounded clock skew (recommended <= 60 seconds).

Requires that super-app authorization gateways verify that the 'aud' claim strictly contains the identifying URI of the target resource server or mini-app domain before granting execution context access.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that all identity assertions and cross-context delegation tokens exchanged between the super-app host container and third-party mini-apps conform to RFC 7519.
Enforce presence and strict verification of 'iss', 'sub', 'aud', 'exp', and 'jti' claims on every mini-app session token, rejecting tokens missing lifetime bounds.
Implement a maximum expiration lifetime ('exp' - 'iat') of 300 seconds for client-issued tokens, paired with sender-constrained proof-of-possession or host session refresh tokens.

title: IETF RFC 7515: JSON Web Signature (JWS) Compact Serialization & Cryptographic Integrity Protection
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7515 Section 3 (Cryptographic Computation) & Section 7 (Compact Serialization)
key_takeaways: RFC 7515 defines JSON Web Signature (JWS), representing digitally signed or MACed content using JSON data structures.

Defines JWS Compact Serialization as three Base64URL-encoded octet sequences separated by period ('.') characters: BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWS Payload) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWS Signature).

Specifies standard protected header parameters: 'alg' (cryptographic algorithm identifier), 'jku' (JWK Set URL), 'jwk' (JSON Web Key), 'kid' (Key ID hint), 'x5u' (X.509 URL), and 'crit' (critical header parameters).
Requires cryptographic signature calculation over the exact ASCII representation of the JWS Signing Input (header . payload), guaranteeing tamper-proof transit over unsecure transport channels.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require all manifest signatures, client attestation tokens, and bridge IPC transaction receipts to use RFC 7515 JWS Compact Serialization.
Enforce strict validation of the 'alg' header parameter against an approved cryptographic whitelist (ES256, ES384, EdDSA/Ed25519) established during mini-app registration.
Prohibit the acceptance of unauthenticated or detached signatures in client-side bridge APIs, binding the complete payload to the signature input.

title: IETF RFC 7517: JSON Web Key (JWK) & JWK Set (JWKS) Cryptographic Key Federation Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7517 Section 4 (JWK Parameters) & Section 5 (JWK Set Format)
key_takeaways: RFC 7517 represents cryptographic keys as JSON data structures, standardizing parameters including 'kty' (key type, e.g. EC, RSA, OKP), 'use' (public key use: 'sig' or 'enc'), 'key_ops' (key operations array), 'alg' (intended algorithm), and 'kid' (unique key identifier).
Standardizes the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) structure containing a top-level 'keys' array of JWK objects, enabling automated public key discovery and rolling key rotation without coordination overhead.
Defines cryptographic key parameters for elliptic curves ('crv', 'x', 'y') and RSA ('n', 'e'), avoiding proprietary binary ASN.1/DER encoding formats in web architectures.
Specifies security considerations regarding private and symmetric key confidentiality, mandating that private key material must never appear in public JWKS documents.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that super-app identity providers and verified enterprise mini-app backends publish public keys via HTTPS JWKS endpoints discoverable via standard metadata.
Require all JWK keys to include unique 'kid' values and explicit 'use': 'sig' parameters, enabling seamless zero-downtime key rotation cycles across the ecosystem.
Implement gateway-level caching of JWKS endpoints with HTTP Cache-Control max-age compliance and asynchronous background refresh to prevent key-fetching bottlenecks.

title: IETF RFC 7638: JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint Canonicalization & Key Identification
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7638 Section 3 (JSON Web Key Thumbprint Specification)
key_takeaways: RFC 7638 defines a standardized, deterministic method for computing a cryptographic hash digest (thumbprint) over the required members of a JSON Web Key (JWK).

Specifies strict canonicalization rules: construct a normalized JSON object containing only the required public key members (e.g. 'crv', 'kty', 'x', 'y' for EC keys), sort keys lexicographically, eliminate whitespace, and serialize to UTF-8 before applying SHA-256 hashing.
Enables unambiguous, deterministic derivation of key identifiers ('kid') and subject public key fingerprints without relying on arbitrary developer-supplied strings.
Eliminates key collision risks and enables mutual-TLS and DPoP sender-constrained token bindings to cryptographically reference public keys via their canonical JWK thumbprint ('jkt').
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt RFC 7638 SHA-256 JWK Thumbprints ('jkt') as the mandatory standard for auto-generating 'kid' headers and client certificate confirmation claims across all mini-app services.
Use JWK thumbprint canonicalization when verifying public keys registered by third-party mini-app developers in the developer console to prevent duplicate key injection.
Enforce strict JSON normalization and lexicographical key sorting in security gateway validation pipelines before evaluating cryptographic thumbprint equality.

title: IETF RFC 7523: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication & Authorization Grants
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7523 Section 2.2 (Client Authentication) & Section 3 (JWT Validation)
key_takeaways: RFC 7523 standardizes the use of a signed JWT assertion as an OAuth 2.0 client authentication credential (`client_assertion_type = urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`) and authorization grant.

Replaces shared static client secrets with asymmetric cryptographic authentication: the mini-app client signs an assertion using its private key, which the super-app authorization server validates against registered public keys.

Requires that the JWT assertion contain 'iss' (client ID), 'sub' (client ID), 'aud' (token endpoint URI), 'exp' (short expiration window, e.g. <= 5 minutes), and a unique 'jti' nonce to guarantee single-use replay protection.
Eliminates credential interception vulnerabilities inherent in static passwords or client secrets stored in mobile apps or third-party web configurations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 7523 `private_key_jwt` client authentication for all enterprise and regulated financial mini-app backend integrations, deprecating static client secrets (`client_secret_post` and `client_secret_basic`).
Require the super-app token endpoint to cache and reject previously seen 'jti' identifiers within the assertion validity window ('iat' to 'exp') to provide absolute anti-replay guarantees.
Enforce that the 'aud' claim in client assertions matches the exact token endpoint URL of the super-app authorization server, preventing token cross-substitutions.

title: IETF RFC 8725: JWT BCP Algorithm Verification & Mandatory 'none' Algorithm Rejection
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.1 (Perform Algorithm Verification) & Section 3.1 (Algorithm Confusion)
key_takeaways: RFC 8725 specifies Best Current Practices (BCP) for JSON Web Tokens, codifying critical security countermeasures against widespread implementation vulnerabilities.

Mandates that JWT libraries and verifiers perform strict cryptographic algorithm verification: the receiver MUST explicitly verify that the 'alg' header matches an expected algorithm configured for that specific issuer and context.

Requires that verifiers MUST NOT rely on the 'alg' parameter in the token header to determine the cryptographic verification key, preventing algorithm confusion attacks (such as treating an RSA public key as an HMAC secret key).
Explicitly mandates that tokens using the 'none' algorithm ('alg': 'none') MUST be rejected unless explicitly expected in a specific non-security context, preventing trivial signature bypass.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure all super-app gateway token decoders and client-side bridge validators to reject any JWT containing 'alg': 'none' with an unhandled security violation event.
Enforce strict issuer-to-algorithm mapping tables at the API gateway: do not allow incoming JWT headers to dynamically specify symmetric vs asymmetric verification schemes.
Implement automated store review static analysis scanning third-party mini-app dependencies to verify that bundled JWT parsers adhere to RFC 8725 algorithm pinning.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Explicit Token Typing ('typ') & Cross-JWT Substitution Mitigation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.8 (Use Explicit Typing) & Section 3.11 (Cross-JWT Substitution)
key_takeaways: Cross-JWT substitution occurs when a valid token issued for one purpose (e.g. an ID token or access token) is accepted by a vulnerable endpoint designed for a different purpose (e.g. an authorization grant or logout token).

RFC 8725 recommends explicit token typing using the 'typ' header parameter with explicit media types or registered type names (e.g., 'at+jwt' for access tokens, 'dpop+jwt' for DPoP proofs, 'secevent+jwt' for security events).

The recipient MUST check that the 'typ' header contains the expected value before validating claims, ensuring that semantic boundaries between different token classes are enforced at the transport layer.
Eliminates subtle privilege escalation and state confusion bugs where mini-apps re-use user profile ID tokens as administrative bridge execution tokens.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce explicit 'typ' header values across all super-app token variants: use 'miniapp-session+jwt' for container sessions, 'miniapp-authz+jwt' for bridge permissions, and 'at+jwt' for resource access.
Mandate that all verification handlers at super-app gateways and bridge endpoints validate the exact 'typ' header before processing any claims.
Include explicit token type rejection in the developer SDK test suite, verifying that mini-app backends properly reject tokens with mismatched 'typ' headers.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Bounded Clock Skew, Short Token Lifetimes & 'jti' Anti-Replay Cache Governance
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.2 (Validate Expiration Time) & Section 2.5 (Use and Validate 'jti')
key_takeaways: RFC 8725 provides normative operational guidance for temporal claim validation: clock skew allowances between distributed systems should be bounded to a few seconds (never more than a minute).
Recommends minimizing token lifetimes ('exp' - 'iat') to reduce the window of opportunity for stolen token exploitation, especially in mobile or untrusted client runtimes.
Specifies that whenever anti-replay protection is required, tokens MUST include a cryptographically random, collision-resistant JWT ID ('jti') claim.

Directs relying parties to maintain a high-performance in-memory cache (e.g. distributed Redis or memory grid) of processed 'jti' identifiers, retaining each entry until the token's 'exp' timestamp plus clock skew has elapsed.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Set the maximum clock skew tolerance in super-app verification gateways to exactly 30 seconds, rejecting any tokens with wider temporal drift.
Require all high-privilege bridge invocations (such as biometric auth or fund transfers) to carry single-use JWTs with unique 'jti' nonces and a maximum validity window of 60 seconds.
Deploy an edge-level distributed anti-replay bloom filter and TTL cache indexed by 'jti' to prevent replay attacks across multiple gateway instances.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Critical Header ('crit') Enforcement & Extension Parameter Integrity
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.7 (Process the 'crit' Header Field) & Section 3.10 (Missing Header Parameters)
key_takeaways: The 'crit' (critical) header parameter indicates that extensions to the JOSE specifications are being used that MUST be understood and processed by the recipient.

RFC 8725 mandates that if the recipient encounters a JWS/JWT containing a 'crit' list that includes header parameter names not recognized or supported by the recipient, the token MUST be rejected immediately.

Ensures forward and backward protocol compatibility while preventing security-critical extensions (such as hardware binding, geographic fences, or regulatory constraints) from being silently ignored by naive parsers.
Requires that the 'crit' parameter itself must only reside within the protected header, ensuring that critical directives cannot be stripped or altered during transit.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Utilize the 'crit' header parameter whenever super-app security policies inject custom claims (such as container isolation tier 'x-miniapp-tier' or hardware attestation references) into JWT assertions.
Configure all mini-app framework SDKs to strictly fail closed if an unknown parameter is listed in the 'crit' header, preventing security downgrade attacks.
Prohibit the use of unauthenticated unprotected headers in all mini-app cryptographic transactions, requiring 100% of headers to reside in the protected signature envelope.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Header Injection Defense & Embedded Public Key ('jwk'/'jku') Restrictions
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 3.12 (Embedded Keys in Header) & Section 3.9 (JWK Set URL Injection)
key_takeaways: Attackers can forge JWT signatures by injecting self-signed keys into embedded 'jwk' header fields or directing verifiers to malicious servers via the 'jku' (JWK Set URL) parameter.
RFC 8725 warns that implementations MUST NOT trust embedded keys ('jwk') or fetch keys from unvalidated URLs ('jku') without an established, pre-existing out-of-band trust mechanism.
Recommends rejecting embedded 'jwk' parameters in incoming client-supplied tokens unless the embedded key itself has been signed by a trusted Certificate Authority or verified out-of-band.
Requires strict domain allowlisting and TLS certificate validation if resolving dynamic 'jku' URLs, preventing Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and key substitution attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Explicitly disable support for embedded 'jwk' header parameters in all super-app gateway token verification middleware, requiring key lookup solely by pre-registered 'kid'.
Restrict 'jku' resolution strictly to the verified HTTPS origin of registered enterprise mini-app developers, rejecting any non-allowlisted key fetch attempts.
Implement gateway SSRF firewalls blocking key fetch requests to internal loopback (127.0.0.1/8), link-local, or private RFC 1918 subnet IP spaces.

title: IETF RFC 9101: JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR) & Anti-Tampering Request Objects
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9101 Section 4 (Request Object) & Section 5 (Passing a Request Object by Value)
key_takeaways: RFC 9101 defines JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR), standardizing the encapsulation of OAuth 2.0 authorization request parameters inside a cryptographically signed (and optionally encrypted) JWT request object.

Solves fundamental browser/bridge request tampering risks: query parameters passed in plain URL redirects or WebView bridge invocations can be intercepted, stripped, or manipulated by malicious on-device code.

Specifies that parameters passed inside the signed request object override any duplicate query string parameters, guaranteeing the non-repudiation and integrity of requested scopes, redirect URIs, and transaction parameters.
Requires that the JWT request object contain 'iss' (client ID), 'aud' (authorization server URL), 'iat', 'exp', and 'response_type', preventing injection or cross-app relay attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require all high-value mini-app authorization and consent requests to be encapsulated as RFC 9101 JAR request objects signed by the mini-app developer's registered private key.
Instruct the super-app authorization server to ignore unauthenticated plaintext query parameters when a valid JAR request object is provided.
Integrate JAR verification into the super-app bridge layer, verifying that permission escalation requests are cryptographically bound to the registered mini-app manifest.

title: IETF RFC 9101: Request Object by Reference ('request_uri') & Retrieval Security Controls
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9101 Section 6 (Passing a Request Object by Reference) & Section 10.3 (Server-Side Request Forgery)
key_takeaways: RFC 9101 standardizes passing request objects by reference via the 'request_uri' parameter, avoiding mobile URL length limitations and reducing network overhead.

Establishes critical security rules for authorization servers fetching 'request_uri': must enforce HTTPS, validate server certificates, and verify that the URI matches a pre-registered allowlist or is an opaque URI created via Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR, RFC 9126).

Mandates robust defenses against Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): authorization servers MUST NOT fetch arbitrary URIs provided by untrusted clients, and MUST enforce strict network timeouts and response size limits (e.g. <= 100KB).

Recommends combining JAR with PAR (RFC 9126) so that the mini-app pushes the request object directly over an authenticated backchannel, completely eliminating external server GET requests during user authorization.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Combine RFC 9101 and RFC 9126 by requiring mini-app backends to push JAR request objects directly to the super-app PAR endpoint, obtaining an ephemeral single-use 'request_uri'.
Disallow external unauthenticated 'request_uri' HTTP dereferencing by the super-app authorization server, closing all potential SSRF vectors.
Enforce a maximum 60-second TTL on all generated PAR 'request_uri' references, invalidating the handle immediately upon first redemption.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Symmetric Key Entropy, Key Derivation & HMAC Signing Boundaries
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.6 (Validate Symmetric Key Length) & Section 3.2 (Weak Symmetric Keys)
key_takeaways: A frequent failure mode in JWT implementations is the use of human-memorable passwords or low-entropy strings as symmetric HMAC keys ('HS256', 'HS384', 'HS512'), exposing tokens to offline dictionary and rainbow table cracking.

RFC 8725 strictly mandates that when symmetric algorithms are used, the key MUST have a cryptographic bit length at least as large as the output digest size of the hash function (e.g. >= 256 bits of cryptographically random entropy for HS256).

Recommends generating symmetric keys using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) or deriving them through standardized key derivation functions (HKDF / PBKDF2 with high iteration counts).
Advises against sharing symmetric keys across multiple services or mini-app tenants, since compromise of one service allows forgery of tokens across all other participating services.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce an architectural ban on symmetric HMAC signing ('HS256') for cross-tenant super-app-to-mini-app communications, requiring asymmetric public-key cryptography (ES256 / EdDSA).
In isolated internal microservices where symmetric tokens are utilized, enforce automated CI/CD entropy checks ensuring secret keys contain a minimum of 256 bits of high-entropy randomness.
Prohibit the derive-and-share pattern of secret keys across distinct mini-app developer accounts, strictly isolating cryptographic trust domains.

title: IETF RFC 8725: Payload Claim Sanitization, Privacy Minimization & Injection Defense
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8725 Section 2.10 (Avoid Sending PII Unencrypted) & Section 3.8 (SQL and Command Injection via Claims)
key_takeaways: Because standard JWS tokens are only signed (integrity-protected) and encoded with Base64URL, their claims payload is readable by any party possessing the token, including intermediate proxies, logs, and client scripts.

RFC 8725 mandates that personally identifiable information (PII) or sensitive operational secrets MUST NOT be transmitted in plain JWS payloads; implementations must use JSON Web Encryption (JWE) or pairwise pseudonymous identifiers (PPID).

Warns that claims extracted from JWTs MUST NOT be trusted for SQL queries, shell commands, or HTML rendering without rigorous sanitization and parameterized queries, as attackers can embed injection payloads within signed tokens.
Specifies that token payloads should adhere to the principle of data minimization, carrying only the minimum claims required for the immediate authorization decision.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that super-app user identity assertions passed to third-party mini-apps use pairwise pseudonymous identifiers ('sub' = PPID) instead of cleartext national IDs, phone numbers, or emails.
Require nested JSON Web Encryption (JWE inside JWS) for any token containing sensitive payment, health, or KYC verification data.
Implement automated store review checks ensuring that mini-app backend APIs treat all decoded JWT claims as untrusted input subject to strict typing and parameterization.

title: IETF RFC 9101 & JARM: JWT Secured Authorization Response Mode (JARM) Integration
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9101 Section 8 (Security Considerations) & Financial-grade API: JWT Secured Authorization Response Mode
key_takeaways: While RFC 9101 protects the authorization request from client to server, the response from the authorization server to the mini-app client remains vulnerable to redirection attacks, response parameter injection, and token leakage in URL referrers.

JWT Secured Authorization Response Mode (JARM) extends RFC 9101 by returning the entire authorization response (authorization code, state, error parameters) as a signed JWT assertion via the `response_mode = query.jwt` or `fragment.jwt` parameters.

Provides end-to-end cryptographic non-repudiation and response integrity: the client verifies the authorization server's digital signature and checks that 'iss', 'aud', and 'state' match the initial request.
Completely eliminates authorization code injection attacks and state manipulation in mobile super-app WebView containers and native deep-link callbacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate the implementation of JARM (`response_mode = query.jwt`) for all regulated fintech and e-government mini-apps operating on the super-app platform.
Ensure that the super-app authorization response JWT includes the original client 'state', a cryptographic 'code' hash, and a short 60-second expiration timestamp.
Provide pre-configured JARM response verification utilities within the super-app developer SDK to guarantee zero-defect response validation.

title: IETF RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) by OAuth Public Clients in Mini-App Runtimes
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7636 Section 4 (Protocol Flow) & Section 4.1 (Client Creates a Code Verifier)
key_takeaways: RFC 7636 specifies Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) to mitigate authorization code interception attacks on OAuth 2.0 public clients operating in native apps and embedded WebViews.
Client creates a cryptographically random high-entropy secret 'code_verifier' with minimum 43 and maximum 128 characters from unreserved characters [A-Z, a-z, 0-9, '-', '.', '_', '~'].
Client derives 'code_challenge' = BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))) when code_challenge_method is 'S256', transmitting code_challenge and code_challenge_method to authorization endpoint.
When exchanging the authorization code at the token endpoint, client presents the plaintext 'code_verifier'; authorization server computes SHA-256 and compares it with stored challenge.
Mandates that the 'plain' transformation method MUST NOT be used unless client cannot compute SHA-256 (which is prohibited in modern secure mini-app runtimes).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 7636 PKCE with code_challenge_method='S256' for all mini-app OAuth authorization code flows; fail-closed on any request omitting PKCE or using 'plain'.
Generate cryptographically random code_verifier using Web Cryptography API (crypto.getRandomValues) inside the mini-app isolated sandbox.
Ensure the super-app authorization bridge caches the code_challenge securely and validates the code_verifier before releasing delegated access tokens.

title: IETF RFC 7636: Authorization Code Interception Attack Model & Custom Scheme Binding Protections
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7636 Section 1 (Introduction & Attack Model) & Section 7.1 (Entropy of the Code Verifier)
key_takeaways: Identifies the threat wherein multiple apps register the same custom URI scheme on mobile operating systems, allowing a rogue app to intercept authorization codes returned via redirects.
In WebView-based mini-app architectures, malicious scripts or compromised iframe contexts might intercept redirected URI parameters containing authorization codes.
PKCE cryptographically binds the authorization code to the specific client instance that initiated the request, as only the genuine initiator possesses the ephemeral 'code_verifier'.
Requires at least 256 bits of entropy in the code_verifier to make brute-force preimage attacks computationally infeasible.
Specifies that authorization servers must enforce one-time use of authorization codes and invalidate any active authorization codes if an invalid code_verifier is presented.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement one-time use and strict client-instance binding for all authorization codes issued to mini-apps within the super-app environment.
Invalidate all pending tokens and raise security alerts if a mismatched code_verifier is presented during mini-app token exchange.
Enforce minimum 256-bit entropy generation for all PKCE verifiers within the mini-app container SDK.

title: IETF RFC 8414: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata Discovery Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8414 Section 2 (Authorization Server Metadata) & Section 3 (Obtaining Metadata)
key_takeaways: RFC 8414 defines a standardized metadata format and JSON document structure for OAuth 2.0 authorization servers.
Specifies discovery via well-known URI: '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server' affixed to the issuer URL.
Defines core metadata attributes: 'issuer', 'authorization_endpoint', 'token_endpoint', 'jwks_uri', 'registration_endpoint', 'scopes_supported', and 'response_types_supported'.
Enables dynamic client configuration and interoperable federation without hardcoded endpoint URLs across client applications.
Mandates that the 'issuer' parameter returned in the JSON metadata must exactly match the URI used to retrieve the configuration.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish super-app identity server metadata conforming to RFC 8414 at '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server'.
Enforce strict issuer matching in mini-app SDK discovery clients to prevent server impersonation and DNS spoofing.
Cache metadata documents respecting HTTP Cache-Control headers with automated background re-validation.

title: IETF RFC 8414: Server Metadata Security, PKCE & Algorithm Capability Advertisement
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8414 Section 2 (Metadata Parameters) & Section 7 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: RFC 8414 standardizes capability advertisement parameters: 'code_challenge_methods_supported', 'token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported', 'token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported'.
Allows authorization servers to declare support for 'S256' in 'code_challenge_methods_supported', signalling clients to enforce PKCE.
Requires transport layer security (TLS 1.2+ / TLS 1.3) for all metadata endpoints to prevent tampering and downgrade attacks.
Mitigates metadata spoofing by enforcing that clients verify the digital signature of signed metadata if 'signed_metadata' JWT is utilized.
Recommends validating that token and authorization endpoints belong to authorized enterprise host domains.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Include 'code_challenge_methods_supported': ['S256'] in the super-app OAuth metadata to enforce modern PKCE across all mini-apps.
Advertise supported JWS algorithms (e.g. ES256, EdDSA) in metadata and reject weak legacy ciphers (none, RS128).
Require TLS 1.3 certificate pinning or validation against the super-app trust store when mini-app SDKs fetch identity metadata.

title: IETF RFC 9207: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Issuer Identification in Authorization Responses
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9207 Section 2 (Authorization Response) & Section 3 (Client Processing Rules)
key_takeaways: RFC 9207 specifies a parameter 'iss' that is returned in the authorization response to prevent Mix-Up Attacks.

In environments where clients interact with multiple authorization servers (e.g. super-app marketplace with multi-tenant IdPs), an attacker can fool a client into sending an authorization code to a malicious server.
When receiving an authorization response containing 'code' and 'iss', the client MUST verify that the 'iss' value matches the issuer URI of the authorization server to which it directed the user.
If the 'iss' value does not match or is absent when expected, the client MUST abort the authorization flow and MUST NOT exchange the authorization code.
Authorization servers indicate support for RFC 9207 by including 'authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported': true in their RFC 8414 metadata.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 9207 'iss' parameter in all authorization responses returned to mini-apps from super-app identity providers.
Enforce client-side check in mini-app SDKs verifying response 'iss' against the target IdP issuer URI before making token requests.
Advertise 'authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported': true in the super-app OAuth 2.0 discovery metadata.

title: IETF RFC 7591: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Architecture for Mini-App Onboarding
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7591 Section 2 (Client Registration Request) & Section 3 (Client Information Response)
key_takeaways: RFC 7591 defines a standard RESTful protocol allowing OAuth 2.0 clients to register dynamically with an authorization server.
Client posts a JSON registration request to the 'registration_endpoint' advertised in RFC 8414 server metadata.
Specifies standard client metadata parameters: 'redirect_uris', 'client_name', 'client_uri', 'logo_uri', 'scope', 'grant_types', 'response_types', and 'token_endpoint_auth_method'.
The authorization server responds with HTTP 201 Created containing unique 'client_id', registration access credentials, and the effective registered metadata.
Eliminates manual developer console friction while establishing cryptographically verifiable client identities.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose an RFC 7591 compliant dynamic client registration endpoint on the super-app identity gateway for automated mini-app provisioning.
Mandate inclusion of 'client_name', 'redirect_uris', and 'token_endpoint_auth_method' in all registration requests.
Enforce that registered redirect_uris strictly conform to verified mini-app package origins or secure custom URL schemes.

title: IETF RFC 7591: Software Statement Assertions & Cryptographic Mini-App Supply Chain Attestation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7591 Section 2.3 (Software Statement) & Section 3.1.1 (Client Registration Error Response)
key_takeaways: RFC 7591 standardizes 'software_statement', a cryptographically signed JSON Web Signature (JWS) containing client metadata assertions issued by a trusted third party or app store authority.
When presented during dynamic client registration, the authorization server cryptographically validates the signature of the software statement using the issuer's public key.
Values asserted inside the software statement override developer-supplied parameters, preventing unauthorized alteration of security properties.
Mitigates impersonation attacks where a malicious client registers with misleading names, scopes, or redirection targets.
Returns 'invalid_software_statement' or 'unapproved_software_statement' if the attestation fails signature checks or comes from an untrusted issuer.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require third-party mini-apps to present an official 'software_statement' signed by the Super-App Marketplace Review Authority during client onboarding.
Bind permissions, granted scopes, and certified publisher attributes directly within the signed software statement.
Fail-closed and reject registration requests containing expired, invalid, or self-signed software statements.

title: IETF RFC 7591: Client Authentication Methods & Key Association in Registration
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7591 Section 2 (Client Metadata: jwks_uri, jwks, token_endpoint_auth_method)
key_takeaways: RFC 7591 specifies 'token_endpoint_auth_method' parameters: 'none' (public client), 'client_secret_post', 'client_secret_basic', 'client_secret_jwt', and 'private_key_jwt'.
Supports binding client public keys via 'jwks' (literal JWK Set) or 'jwks_uri' (HTTPS endpoint hosted by client developer).
For public clients operating purely on the client side (e.g. mini-apps running in sandboxed WebViews), 'token_endpoint_auth_method' MUST be 'none' combined with PKCE.
For confidential backend-driven mini-apps, 'private_key_jwt' is preferred over shared client secrets, eliminating static credential leakage.
Specifies error handling with 'invalid_client_metadata' when incompatible authentication methods or invalid JWK Sets are supplied.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce 'token_endpoint_auth_method': 'none' combined with RFC 7636 PKCE for frontend-only mini-apps.
Mandate 'private_key_jwt' with RFC 7517 JWKS key rotation for enterprise mini-apps possessing dedicated backend servers.
Reject legacy 'client_secret_basic' and static client secrets in all newly registered mini-apps.

title: IETF RFC 7592: OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Lifecycle (Read, Update, Delete)
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7592 Section 2 (Client Configuration Endpoint) & Section 3 (Operations)
key_takeaways: RFC 7592 defines management operations on dynamically registered OAuth clients via the Client Configuration Endpoint.
Specifies HTTP GET for reading current registration state, HTTP PUT for replacing/updating metadata, and HTTP DELETE for client de-provisioning.
Secures the Client Configuration Endpoint using a dedicated, high-privilege 'registration_access_token' issued during initial registration.
Mandates that the client configuration URI ('registration_client_uri') must be unique per registered client and guarded against unauthorized tampering.
Enables mini-app developers to update redirection URIs, application titles, and public keys without requiring complete re-registration.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement RFC 7592 Client Configuration Endpoints enabling automated mini-app lifecycle management during version upgrades and deprecations.
Protect management endpoints using scoped bearer tokens with short lifespans and audit logging on every update/delete operation.
Trigger automated security re-verification and marketplace compliance scans whenever 'redirect_uris' or 'jwks_uri' metadata is updated via PUT.

title: IETF RFC 7592: Registration Access Token Rotation & Granular Client Decommissioning
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7592 Section 2.1 (Client Configuration Response) & Section 3.3 (Delete Client Configuration)
key_takeaways: RFC 7592 provides for optional rotation of the 'registration_access_token' in responses to successful GET or PUT operations.
When rotated, the previous registration access token is immediately revoked, preventing token reuse across stale management scripts.
Executing HTTP DELETE immediately revokes the client's registration: client_id is deactivated, all outstanding access and refresh tokens are invalidated, and subsequent token requests fail.
Specifies error semantics returning HTTP 401 Unauthorized for expired/revoked registration tokens and HTTP 403 Forbidden for insufficient permissions.
Crucial for immediate kill-switch execution when a mini-app is delisted or found to be violating platform security policies.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce instant token revocation and client invalidation across all gateway nodes upon HTTP DELETE of a mini-app client configuration.
Rotate registration access tokens on every metadata modification to limit the attack window in case of developer CI/CD token leaks.
Integrate marketplace kill-switch triggers directly into the RFC 7592 client de-provisioning pipeline for emergency suspension.

title: IETF RFC 9449: Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) Architecture & Application-Layer Token Binding
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9449 Section 4 (DPoP Proof JWT) & Section 4.2 (DPoP Proof JWT Syntax)
key_takeaways: RFC 9449 standardizes Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) at the application layer, allowing clients to cryptographically bind OAuth access and refresh tokens to a public/private key pair.
DPoP proof is a signed JWT passed in the HTTP 'DPoP' request header with protected header parameters: 'typ': 'dpop+jwt', 'alg' (asymmetric signature algorithm, e.g. ES256), and 'jwk' (public key).

Payload contains mandatory claims: 'jti' (unique per-proof UUID), 'htm' (HTTP request method in uppercase, e.g. 'POST', 'GET'), 'htu' (HTTP request URI without query and fragment), and 'iat' (issued-at timestamp).
Eliminates the vulnerability of bearer tokens where any entity intercepting the token can impersonate the legitimate client.
Requires no mTLS infrastructure or client-side X.509 certificates, making it ideal for browser and mini-app WebView environments.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 9449 DPoP proof generation for all high-privilege and payment-related API calls made by mini-apps to super-app backend services.
Enforce strict validation of 'typ': 'dpop+jwt', 'htm', 'htu', and 'iat' on API gateways receiving DPoP proofs.
Implement in-memory ephemeral key pair generation via Web Cryptography API (crypto.subtle.generateKey) inside mini-app sandboxes.

title: IETF RFC 9449: Access Token Hash ('ath') Validation & JWK Thumbprint ('jkt') Confirmation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9449 Section 4.1 (DPoP Access Token) & Section 4.2 (Access Token Hash Claim)
key_takeaways: RFC 9449 defines the 'cnf' (confirmation) claim inside the access token containing a 'jkt' member, which holds the RFC 7638 SHA-256 thumbprint of the client's DPoP public key.
When presenting a DPoP-bound access token to a protected resource, the client's DPoP proof MUST include the 'ath' (access token hash) claim.
The 'ath' claim value is computed as BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(access_token))), binding the specific proof to the exact access token presented.
Resource servers verify that the SHA-256 thumbprint of the JWK in the DPoP proof header matches the 'jkt' value in the access token's 'cnf' claim.
Prevents token substitution and cross-token replay attacks across disparate resource servers and endpoints.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Issue sender-constrained access tokens containing 'cnf': {'jkt': '<thumbprint>'} to mini-apps upon successful DPoP token requests.
Verify that the 'ath' claim in the DPoP proof matches the presented access token hash prior to authorizing sensitive native bridge operations.
Reject requests with HTTP 401 and error='invalid_dpop_proof' if the public key thumbprint or token hash verification fails.

title: IETF RFC 9449: Server-Provided Nonce Handshake & Distributed Replay Mitigation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9449 Section 8 (Server-Provided Nonces) & Section 11.1 (Replay of DPoP Proofs)
key_takeaways: RFC 9449 specifies a server-provided nonce mechanism to prevent pre-computed or replayed DPoP proofs without maintaining large distributed cache state.
Authorization servers and resource servers supply a nonce via the 'DPoP-Nonce' HTTP response header.
If a client provides an absent or stale nonce, the server rejects the request with HTTP 400 or 401 and error='use_dpop_nonce', supplying a fresh 'DPoP-Nonce' header.
The client must immediately retry the request with a newly generated DPoP proof containing the provided 'nonce' claim.
Limits the validity window of DPoP proofs to milliseconds, effectively eliminating eavesdropping and replay vulnerabilities.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement 'DPoP-Nonce' response headers and challenge flows on super-app payment and identity authorization endpoints.
Configure mini-app network adapters to automatically detect 'use_dpop_nonce' errors, regenerate DPoP proofs with the new nonce, and transparently retry the request.
Enforce a strict maximum lifespan of 60 seconds on server-generated nonces to thwart replay attacks.

title: IETF RFC 9449: Token Endpoint Binding, Refresh Token Constraints & 'DPoP' Authentication Scheme
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9449 Section 5 (DPoP at the Token Endpoint) & Section 7 (The DPoP Authentication Scheme)
key_takeaways: To obtain a DPoP-bound access token, the client includes a valid DPoP proof in the HTTP request to the authorization server's token endpoint.
The token response contains 'token_type': 'DPoP' (instead of 'Bearer'), instructing the client to use the DPoP authentication scheme.
Protected resources are accessed by transmitting the HTTP authorization header formatted as: 'Authorization: DPoP <access_token>', accompanied by the 'DPoP: <dpop_proof>' header.
If a refresh token was issued with a DPoP proof, subsequent refresh requests MUST include a valid DPoP proof using the same cryptographic key.
Provides end-to-end sender-constraint throughout the entire token lifecycle from initial issuance through refresh.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure super-app token endpoints to return 'token_type': 'DPoP' for all registered mini-apps declaring DPoP support.
Mandate that mini-app bridge clients transmit 'Authorization: DPoP <token>' alongside the 'DPoP' proof header for protected bridge invocations.
Bind OAuth refresh tokens to the client's DPoP key pair, terminating the session immediately if refresh is attempted with an altered key.

title: IETF RFC 9449: Mini-App Security Considerations: Private Key Isolation & Web Crypto Integration
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9449 Section 11 (Security Considerations) & Section 11.2 (Key Storage & Exportability)
key_takeaways: RFC 9449 highlights that the security of DPoP relies fundamentally on the confidentiality and protection of the client's private signing key.
In browser/WebView environments, private keys MUST be marked non-extractable (extractable: false) when created via Web Cryptography API (SubtleCrypto.generateKey).
Non-extractable keys in IndexedDB or container secure storage prevent exfiltration via DOM XSS or cross-site scripting attacks.
Even if an attacker compromises the application DOM and exfiltrates an in-flight access token, the token is useless without the private key needed to sign valid DPoP proofs.
Warns against key sharing across distinct security origins, requiring strict origin isolation for DPoP key pairs.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that mini-app runtimes generate non-extractable CryptoKey pairs in hardware-backed keystores (Android Keystore / iOS Keychain) or secure WebCrypto storage.
Enforce strict per-mini-app origin sandboxing ensuring that DPoP private keys cannot be accessed by adjacent mini-apps or third-party web content.
Integrate DPoP proof generation into the core super-app bridge SDK to shield cryptographic signing operations from untrusted mini-app user code.

title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: ID Token Architecture, Core Claims & Temporal Boundaries
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 2 (ID Token Claims) & Section 3.1.3.6 (ID Token)
key_takeaways: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 specifies the ID Token as a cryptographically signed JSON Web Token (JWT) representing proof of authentication.

Mandatory claims include 'iss' (issuer HTTPS URL identical to OpenID Provider discovery endpoint), 'sub' (subject identifier unique to the user), 'aud' (audience containing client_id), 'exp' (expiration Unix epoch timestamp), and 'iat' (issued-at Unix epoch timestamp).

Contextual security claims include 'auth_time' (timestamp of actual user authentication ceremony), 'nonce' (client-generated challenge echoing the authorization request to thwart token replay), 'acr' (Authentication Context Class Reference for MFA/step-up levels), and 'amr' (Authentication Methods References array, e.g. ['pwd', 'fido', 'hwk']).
When the ID Token audience contains multiple values, an 'azp' (Authorized Party) claim MUST be present identifying the single OAuth 2.0 client that requested the token.
Enforces strict separation between authentication assertion (ID Token) and authorization credential (Access Token), preventing identity spoofing across distributed client runtimes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Issue signed ID Tokens from the super-app identity broker to requesting mini-apps upon explicit user consent and successful authentication.
Enforce strict validation of 'iss', 'aud', 'exp', 'iat', and 'nonce' claims within the mini-app SDK or backend gateway before establishing an authenticated user session.
Include 'auth_time' and 'acr' claims in all ID Tokens to enable mini-apps to assess authentication recency and enforce contextual step-up authentication for high-assurance operations.

title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: Normative ID Token Cryptographic Verification & Anti-Spoofing Rules
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 3.1.3.7 (ID Token Validation)
key_takeaways: Section 3.1.3.7 establishes normative verification algorithms that Relying Parties MUST execute prior to trusting an ID Token.
Signature validation MUST utilize the OpenID Provider's public keys fetched from its published JWKS URI and indexed by the JOSE header 'kid'.

Symmetric MAC signatures (HS256) require validating against the client_secret; asymmetric signatures (RS256, ES256) require verifying against published JWK keys, prohibiting the insecure 'none' algorithm.

The client MUST confirm that 'iss' matches the OpenID Provider's issuer identifier, 'aud' contains the client's registered client_id, and current time is strictly less than 'exp' (accounting for allowable clock skew <= 30 seconds).
If 'auth_time' is requested via max_age, the client MUST verify that elapsed time since 'auth_time' does not exceed the allowed threshold, rejecting stale authentication states.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate asymmetric digital signatures (ES256 or RS256) for all mini-app ID Tokens, completely prohibiting symmetric HS256 signatures on public mini-app clients.
Automate public key caching and dynamic rotation using the super-app's published '/.well-known/jwks.json' endpoint with strict HTTP Cache-Control headers.
Enforce a maximum allowable clock skew of 30 seconds and reject any ID Token with expired 'exp' or missing cryptographic signature during store review automated security scanning.

title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: Pairwise Pseudonymous Subject Identifiers (PPID) & Anti-Correlation Architecture
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 8 (Subject Identifier Types) & Section 8.1 (Pairwise Identifier Algorithm)
key_takeaways: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 defines two subject identifier types: 'public' (identical 'sub' value issued across all clients) and 'pairwise' (unique 'sub' value derived per client or sector).
Pairwise Pseudonymous Identifiers (PPID) prevent distinct third-party Relying Parties from correlating user activities, browsing habits, or behavioral data across unrelated mini-apps.
The OP derives the pairwise 'sub' using a cryptographically secure one-way hash: sub = SHA-256(Sector_Identifier + Internal_User_ID + OP_Salt).

The Sector_Identifier is derived from the host component of the client's registered redirect_uri, or explicitly defined via a 'sector_identifier_uri' referencing a JSON array of allowed redirect URIs.
Eliminates cross-app tracking without degrading single sign-on usability, fully satisfying GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design) and enterprise multi-tenant privacy mandates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate 'subject_type': 'pairwise' as the default subject identification scheme for all third-party mini-apps registered on the super-app store.
Generate pairwise 'sub' identifiers using SHA-256 with a hardware-protected master salt and the mini-app's registered developer organization sector ID.
Restrict 'public' subject identifiers exclusively to first-party super-app core system modules and certified enterprise corporate suites.

title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: UserInfo Endpoint Architecture, Scoped Claims & Bridge Sandboxing
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 5.3 (UserInfo Endpoint) & Section 5.4 (Requesting Claims using Scope Values)
key_takeaways: Section 5.3 defines the UserInfo Endpoint as an OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource that returns identity claims about the authenticated end-user.
Client accesses the endpoint by presenting an Access Token using Bearer authentication (RFC 6750) or sender-constrained DPoP (RFC 9449).

Claims are governed by standardized OAuth scopes: 'profile' (name, family_name, given_name, picture), 'email' (email, email_verified), 'phone' (phone_number, phone_number_verified), and 'address' (formatted postal address).
The UserInfo response MUST contain a 'sub' claim that matches exactly the 'sub' value in the ID Token issued to that client, preventing cross-user data splicing.
Response can be returned as application/json or optionally signed/encrypted as a JWT (Content-Type: application/jwt) for end-to-end non-repudiation.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose the super-app UserInfo endpoint through a rate-limited API gateway and internal native bridge with strict granular consent prompting.
