Verify that the 'sub' claim in the UserInfo response identically matches the ID Token 'sub' before hydrating mini-app user profiles.
Return signed JWT UserInfo responses (application/jwt) for sensitive financial and corporate enterprise mini-apps to guarantee non-repudiation.

title: OpenID Connect Core 1.0: Security Considerations, Nonce Verification & Bridge Token Isolation
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 Section 16 (Security Considerations) & Section 16.11 (Implicit Grant Threat)
key_takeaways: Section 16 details threats specific to federated identity: token substitution, cut-and-paste attacks, cross-site request forgery, and issuer/client confusion.
Mandates the use of the 'nonce' parameter to cryptographically bind authorization requests to the resulting ID Token, preventing replay attacks via captured responses.
Prohibits insecure storage of ID Tokens and Access Tokens in unpartitioned browser localStorage or non-secure cookies vulnerable to DOM XSS.
Requires that authorization responses delivered via URL hash fragments or redirects be immediately scrubbed from browser history using history.replaceState.
Stipulates that client redirection endpoints MUST be pre-registered using absolute HTTPS URIs with exact string matching to thwart open redirection exploits.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce cryptographically random, client-generated 'nonce' parameters (minimum 128 bits entropy) for all authentication requests initiated by mini-apps.
Store session tokens within isolated, host-managed native memory or encrypted Origin Private File System (OPFS), never exposing raw tokens to mini-app DOM JavaScript.
Implement automated URL fragment stripping via history.replaceState immediately following authorization code or token delivery across WebView navigation boundaries.

title: OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0: End-Session Endpoint, 'id_token_hint' & Post-Logout Redirection
standard_reference: OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 Section 2 (RP-Initiated Logout) & Section 3 (Redirection to RP After Logout)
key_takeaways: RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 standardizes client-driven session termination by directing the end-user's browser/WebView to the OP's 'end_session_endpoint'.

The logout request SHOULD include 'id_token_hint' containing the previously issued ID Token, which informs the OP about the user's identity and prevents logout denial-of-service across arbitrary sessions.
Optional parameter 'post_logout_redirect_uri' specifies where the OP redirects the client after completing logout; the URI MUST be pre-registered during client registration.
If 'post_logout_redirect_uri' is provided, 'id_token_hint' becomes MANDATORY to confirm authorization for the requested post-logout destination.
A client-generated 'state' parameter protects post-logout redirections against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and enables client state restoration.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement an 'end_session_endpoint' on the super-app identity broker conforming to RP-Initiated Logout 1.0.
Require mini-apps initiating logout via the native bridge to supply the valid 'id_token_hint' corresponding to their active session.
Enforce exact string matching on pre-registered 'post_logout_redirect_uris' and reject unregistered redirection attempts to prevent open redirect vulnerabilities.

title: OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0: Direct Server-to-Server 'logout_token' JWT & Session Termination
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0 Section 2.4 (Logout Token) & Section 2.5 (Back-Channel Logout Request)
key_takeaways: Back-Channel Logout 1.0 standardizes direct server-to-server HTTP POST communication from the OP to RP 'backchannel_logout_uri' endpoints, bypassing client browser/WebView limitations.

The payload consists of a signed 'logout_token' JWT containing 'iss', 'aud', 'iat', 'jti', 'events': {'http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout': {}}, and either 'sub' (subject ID) or 'sid' (session ID), or both.
The 'logout_token' MUST NOT contain a 'nonce' claim, explicitly preventing confusion attacks where a logout token is mistakenly processed as an ID Token.
The RP MUST validate the JWT signature, verify issuer and audience, confirm the presence of the logout event claim, and immediately revoke the indicated session state.
Provides reliable, deterministic logout synchronization even when mini-app WebViews are closed, frozen in background, or offline.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement Back-Channel Logout 1.0 webhooks on the super-app identity platform to notify third-party mini-app backend servers immediately upon global user sign-out.
Mandate that third-party mini-app backends register a verified 'backchannel_logout_uri' and validate the cryptographic signature and 'events' claim of received 'logout_token' JWTs.
Revoke server-side sessions and invalidate downstream refresh tokens upon receiving a verified 'logout_token' containing the user's 'sub' or 'sid'.

title: OpenID Connect Front-Channel Logout 1.0: Browser-Mediated Logout URIs & WebView Sandboxing
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Front-Channel Logout 1.0 Section 2 (Front-Channel Logout Operations) & Section 3 (Client Registration)
key_takeaways: Front-Channel Logout 1.0 defines browser-mediated logout where the OP renders hidden HTML iframes targeting registered 'frontchannel_logout_uri' endpoints of logged-in RPs.
If registered with 'frontchannel_logout_session_required': true, the OP appends 'iss' and 'sid' query parameters to the logout URI, identifying the specific session to terminate.
RPs process the request to clear browser-stored cookies, sessionStorage, and IndexedDB state associated with the specified session.

Third-party cookie blocking and partitioned storage (IETF CHIPS / Storage Access API) in modern WebViews can inhibit iframe session clearing, requiring fallback to postMessage or back-channel mechanisms.
Provides client-side UI cleanup and cache eviction across multiple simultaneously rendered mini-app contexts.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Support Front-Channel Logout 1.0 for embedded WebViews using host-mediated postMessage broadcasts across active mini-app container instances.
Provide native bridge event hooks ('onMiniAppLogoutRequested') enabling mini-apps to execute local storage clearing and UI teardown.
Combine front-channel notifications with Back-Channel Logout to guarantee session invalidation despite mobile WebView storage partitioning constraints.

title: OpenID Connect Session Management 1.0: Real-Time Session Status Polling & 'check_session_iframe'
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Session Management 1.0 Section 3 (Session Status Monitoring) & Section 4 (OP iframe)
key_takeaways: Session Management 1.0 enables Relying Parties to monitor the end-user's login status at the OP continuously without invoking server round-trips.
The OP hosts an invisible 'check_session_iframe' exposing a window.onmessage listener.
The RP hosts an iframe that transmits postMessage messages containing 'client_id + " " + session_state' to the OP iframe.
The OP iframe computes a cryptographic hash over client_id, origin, session_state, and current OP browser session cookie, responding with 'unchanged', 'changed', or 'error'.
Upon receiving 'changed', the RP executes step-up authentication, prompts the user, or terminates the local session immediately.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose real-time session status telemetry to mini-apps via the super-app native container bridge, replacing legacy polling iframes with native lifecycle callbacks.
Dispatch 'onSessionStateChanged' bridge events whenever the host user logs out, switches accounts, or completes a multi-factor step-up challenge.
Require mini-apps handling financial or confidential corporate data to subscribe to session state events and transition immediately to locked UI states on 'changed' signals.

title: OpenID Connect Logout Specifications: Security Considerations, DoS Defense & Session Hijacking Mitigation
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout Section 4 (Security Considerations) & RP-Initiated Logout Section 4
key_takeaways: Cross-client logout mechanisms are vulnerable to malicious logout injection and Denial-of-Service attacks if requests are not cryptographically authenticated.
RP-Initiated logout endpoints MUST require 'id_token_hint' or prompt explicit end-user confirmation before terminating sessions to prevent drive-by logout attacks via forged HTTP links.

Back-Channel 'logout_token' endpoints MUST verify the asymmetric JWT signature, ensure 'aud' strictly matches the receiving client_id, and enforce freshness checks via 'iat' (issued-at) to block replay attacks.
Session identifiers ('sid') MUST be cryptographically random and unguessable (minimum 128-bit entropy) to prevent session correlation and hijacking across distinct Relying Parties.
The OP and RP MUST implement rate limiting and timeout management (e.g. 5-second connection timeouts) on back-channel HTTP webhooks to prevent resource exhaustion during cascading logouts.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce strict cryptographic signature verification and 60-second freshness windows on all back-channel logout webhooks dispatched to mini-app backends.
Incorporate a host-level user confirmation prompt before executing global RP-initiated logout requests that lack a valid 'id_token_hint'.
Implement circuit breakers and bounded asynchronous webhook delivery queues (maximum 3 retries with exponential backoff) for mini-app logout notifications.

title: IETF RFC 8628: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant for Smart TV, POS & IoT Super-App Terminals
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8628 Section 3 (Protocol Flow) & Section 3.1 (Device Authorization Request)
key_takeaways: RFC 8628 standardizes the Device Authorization Grant, allowing Internet-connected devices with limited input capabilities (smart TVs, kiosk displays, retail POS terminals, IoT hardware) to obtain OAuth tokens via a secondary browser or mobile device.

The client initiates authorization by posting to '/device/code', receiving 'device_code' (secret polling identifier), 'user_code' (short, human-friendly code, e.g. 'WDJB-MJHT'), 'verification_uri' (URL for user entry), 'verification_uri_complete' (URL with pre-filled code, ideal for QR codes), 'expires_in', and polling 'interval' (default 5 seconds).
The device displays the user_code and QR code while polling the token endpoint using grant_type='urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code'.
The authorization server responds with error='authorization_pending' while awaiting user consent, or error='slow_down' if the client polls faster than the required interval (+5s backoff).
Upon user authorization on their mobile super-app, the polling request succeeds, returning access and refresh tokens without requiring textual credential entry on the constrained terminal.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement RFC 8628 Device Authorization Grant on the super-app platform to support cross-device mini-app authentication on smart TVs, POS terminals, and interactive retail kiosks.
Display 'verification_uri_complete' as a high-density QR code rendered directly by the terminal mini-app, enabling instant scanning and authorization via the mobile super-app wallet.
Enforce strict polling rate limits with mandatory 'slow_down' penalties (+5 seconds) and expire device codes after a maximum of 300 seconds.

title: IETF RFC 7662: OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection & Real-Time Authorization Querying
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7662 Section 2 (Introspection Endpoint) & Section 2.2 (Introspection Response)
key_takeaways: RFC 7662 defines a standardized HTTP POST introspection endpoint allowing protected resource servers to query the authorization server regarding the active state and metadata of an OAuth 2.0 token.
Resource server authenticates itself to the introspection endpoint and passes parameter 'token' (and optional 'token_type_hint').
Response is a JSON object with mandatory boolean 'active'. If false, no other state information is disclosed, preventing information leakage about invalid or revoked tokens.

If active is true, response provides authorized context: 'scope' (granted permission list), 'client_id' (client identifier), 'username' (resource owner), 'token_type' ('Bearer' or 'DPoP'), 'exp' (expiration timestamp), 'iat' (issued-at), 'nbf' (not-before), 'sub' (subject identifier), 'aud' (intended audience), and 'iss' (issuer).
Enables internal microservices and API gateways to validate opaque tokens, check dynamic revocation status, and enforce least-privilege without sharing symmetric decryption keys.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy an RFC 7662 compliant token introspection endpoint on the super-app identity cluster protected by mutual TLS (mTLS) or strong client credentials.
Mandate that internal super-app API gateways perform token introspection or cached introspection validation for all opaque tokens presented by mini-apps.
Enforce that introspection responses include 'client_id', 'scope', 'aud', and 'exp', rejecting requests where the token's audience does not match the target API microservice.

title: IETF RFC 7009: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation Protocol & Instant Client Kill-Switch Lifecycle
standard_reference: IETF RFC 7009 Section 2 (Token Revocation) & Section 2.1 (Revocation Request)
key_takeaways: RFC 7009 standardizes an HTTP POST revocation endpoint allowing clients to explicitly notify the authorization server that a previously issued token (access token or refresh token) is no longer needed.
Client submits 'token' and optional 'token_type_hint' ('access_token' or 'refresh_token') to the revocation endpoint.
If the revoked token is a refresh token and the authorization server invalidates the grant, all associated access tokens previously issued under that grant MUST also be invalidated.
The authorization server responds with HTTP 200 OK regardless of whether the token was active, expired, or already revoked, explicitly preventing token enumeration and scanning attacks.
Essential for clean user logout, credential rotation, mini-app uninstallation, and rapid revocation upon suspicious device activity.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose an RFC 7009 token revocation endpoint on the super-app platform integrated with the native mini-app container lifecycle.
Trigger automated token revocation immediately upon mini-app uninstallation, user permission withdrawal, or administrator marketplace takedown actions.
Configure cascading revocation such that revoking a mini-app's refresh token automatically invalidates all outstanding access tokens issued to that client across distributed gateways.

title: IETF RFC 8707: Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0 & Multi-Service Audience Downscoping
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8707 Section 2 (Resource Parameter) & Section 2.2 (Token Request)
key_takeaways: RFC 8707 introduces the 'resource' parameter into OAuth 2.0 authorization and token requests, enabling clients to specify the exact target resource server (API URI) where the requested token will be used.
The 'resource' value MUST be an absolute URI without a fragment identifier; multiple 'resource' parameters can be specified to request access to multiple services.

The authorization server downscopes issued access tokens such that the token's audience ('aud') is strictly restricted to the specified resource URI, preventing token reuse across unrelated resource servers.
If an authorization grant covers multiple resources, the client can use RFC 8707 at the token endpoint to request individual, downscoped access tokens for specific APIs as needed.
Mitigates the massive security risk where a compromised or malicious third-party resource server replays an access token against other internal resource servers within the super-app ecosystem.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require mini-apps requesting access tokens to specify target API microservices using RFC 8707 'resource' parameters (e.g. 'https://api.superapp.com/payments/v1').
Enforce strict single-audience ('aud') restriction on all issued JWT access tokens, ensuring tokens cannot be replayed against unindicated super-app microservices.
Enable progressive token downscoping at the token endpoint, allowing mini-apps to derive resource-specific access tokens from a broad user authorization grant.

title: OAuth 2.0 Security Architecture: Threat Modeling, Constrained Token Lifecycle & Revocation Federation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 8707 Section 5 (Security Considerations), RFC 7662 Section 4, RFC 7009 Section 3 & RFC 8628 Section 5
key_takeaways: Comprehensive token lifecycle governance requires synthesizing constrained device grants (RFC 8628), token introspection (RFC 7662), instant revocation (RFC 7009), and resource audience scoping (RFC 8707).
Cross-device authorization flows MUST enforce strict user verification and visual binding (e.g. code comparison) to defend against phishing and shoulder-surfing.
Introspection endpoints MUST authenticate callers and restrict responses based on caller identity, ensuring resource servers cannot snoop on tokens intended for external APIs.
Revocation endpoints MUST enforce idempotent status delivery (HTTP 200 OK) to eliminate side-channel timing leaks regarding token existence.
Combining audience-restricted tokens with sender-constrained DPoP proofs or mTLS guarantees defense-in-depth across multi-tenant super-app distributed infrastructure.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Establish a unified Token Lifecycle Governance policy across the super-app platform combining RFC 8707 resource targeting, RFC 7662 introspection, and RFC 7009 revocation.
Implement automated cross-service revocation propagation using distributed cache invalidation (Redis pub/sub or Apache Kafka) triggered whenever RFC 7009 revocation is invoked.
Mandate that all external and cross-device mini-app token requests undergo multi-factor authentication and explicit visual confirmation on the user's primary mobile device.

title: IETF RFC 9126: OAuth 2.0 Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR) Endpoint & Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9126 Section 2 (Pushed Authorization Request Endpoint)
key_takeaways: RFC 9126 introduces the Pushed Authorization Request (PAR) endpoint (`pushed_authorization_request_endpoint`), allowing OAuth 2.0 clients to initiate authorization directly via HTTP POST.
Client authenticates and pushes the authorization request payload directly to the authorization server, avoiding transmitting complex parameters through browser URL query strings.

The authorization server validates parameters immediately and responds with a short-lived, cryptographically random `request_uri` (URN starting with `urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:`) and an `expires_in` lifetime (default recommendation 60-90 seconds).
The client then directs the user's browser/WebView to the authorization endpoint passing only `client_id` and the opaque `request_uri`.
Completely eliminates URL parameter size limitations and prevents parameters from leaking into server access logs, browser history, or HTTP Referer headers.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate the PAR endpoint (`/as/par`) for all mini-app authorization requests across web-view and native bridge layers.
Configure a short `expires_in` lifetime of 60 seconds for generated `request_uri` tokens to prevent stale request execution.
Reject authorization requests at the super-app authorization endpoint if they contain parameters other than `client_id` and a valid, unexpired `request_uri`.

title: IETF RFC 9126: PAR Authorization Server Metadata & Client Enforcement Rules
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9126 Section 5 (Metadata Parameters) & Section 6 (Client Registration Metadata)
key_takeaways: RFC 9126 defines authorization server metadata `pushed_authorization_request_endpoint` (the URL of the PAR endpoint) and `require_pushed_authorization_requests` (boolean indicating if PAR is globally required).
Introduces client metadata `require_pushed_authorization_requests` to dynamically configure or enforce PAR compliance per registered OAuth client in DCR (RFC 7591).

When `require_pushed_authorization_requests` is set to `true`, the authorization server MUST reject any standard authorization request that does not present a valid `request_uri` produced by the PAR endpoint.
Client authentication rules identical to the Token Endpoint apply to the PAR endpoint, supporting mutual TLS, private_key_jwt, client_secret_jwt, or PKCE for public clients.
Standardizes error handling with codes such as `invalid_request_uri` and `invalid_client` conforming strictly to RFC 6749.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish `pushed_authorization_request_endpoint` and set `require_pushed_authorization_requests: true` in the super-app's `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` metadata.
Enforce `require_pushed_authorization_requests: true` in mini-app developer registration manifests and during automated marketplace review validation.
Return HTTP 400 with `invalid_request_uri` immediately if a mini-app attempts to execute an expired, replayed, or forged `request_uri`.

title: IETF RFC 9126: PAR Security Considerations, Request URI Entropy & Anti-Replay Defense
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9126 Section 7 (Security Considerations) & Section 4 (Authorization Request)
key_takeaways: The `request_uri` MUST be single-use and bound cryptographically or logically to the specific client that initiated the PAR request.
The authorization server MUST ensure that the `request_uri` contains at least 128 bits of cryptographic entropy to prevent brute-force guessing attacks.

If an authorization request presents a `request_uri` that was already used, or if the `client_id` in the authorization endpoint request does not match the client that authenticated at the PAR endpoint, the server MUST reject the request.
PAR completely neutralizes authorization request parameter injection and tampering across untrusted intermediary network devices, browser extensions, and operating system URL handlers.
PAR provides native compatibility with JWT-Secured Authorization Requests (JAR, RFC 9101), allowing clients to push signed `request` objects directly via POST without size limitations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce strict single-use semantics and client_id binding on all `request_uri` tokens in the super-app identity broker.
Implement high-entropy cryptographic generation (minimum 160 bits) for `request_uri` values using CSPRNG primitives.
Log and alert on any detected `request_uri` replay or cross-client substitution attempt as a critical security event in store threat telemetry.

title: OAuth 2.0 PAR: WebView & Native Bridge Sandboxed Invocation Pattern
standard_reference: RFC 9126 / OAuth for Native Apps Best Practice Bridge Architecture
key_takeaways: In super-app mini-app environments, delegating the PAR POST call to the host app container or backend gateway avoids exposing client credentials or complex claims inside the mini-app WebView.
Mini-app issues a declarative JS bridge call `superapp.auth.pushAuthorizationRequest(params)` which the host platform executes via a secure back-channel to the AS PAR endpoint.
The host container receives the `request_uri`, validates the requested scopes against mini-app manifest permissions, and opens the native authorization dialog or internal secure tab.
Prevents malicious script injection inside the mini-app from altering scope, redirect_uri, or PKCE code_challenge parameters in transit.
Drastically reduces HTTP traffic over the mini-app WebView interface and provides seamless UX without full browser navigation redirects.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement native container bridge method `superapp.auth.requestAuthorization()` wrapping RFC 9126 PAR back-channel communication.
Intercept and validate all pushed authorization scopes against the mini-app's verified store review permissions before forwarding to the AS PAR endpoint.
Provide developers with standard container SDK client wrappers that automate PAR invocation, PKCE generation, and error handling.

title: OAuth 2.0 PAR: Synergies with FAPI 2.0 & Rich Authorization Requests (RAR)
standard_reference: RFC 9126 & FAPI 2.0 Security Profile Section 5.3
key_takeaways: Financial-grade API (FAPI 2.0) mandates RFC 9126 PAR as a non-negotiable security requirement for high-value financial, banking, and payment transactions.
Rich Authorization Requests (RAR, RFC 9470) introduce fine-grained structured JSON authorization details (`authorization_details`) which frequently exceed HTTP GET URL length limits (2048 bytes).
PAR provides the necessary transport architecture for RAR, enabling structured payment details, transfer amounts, creditor accounts, and compliance metadata to be pushed cleanly via HTTP POST.
When combined with DPoP (RFC 9449) and PKCE (RFC 7636), PAR forms the gold-standard zero-trust mobile identity and authorization architecture.
Enables full auditing and tamper-proof verification of authorization requests before the resource owner is ever prompted for consent.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 9126 PAR for all mini-apps processing in-app purchases, financial transactions, or accessing sensitive banking APIs.
Pair PAR with RFC 9470 Rich Authorization Requests to pass structured transaction data directly to super-app payment authorization dialogs.
Require automated end-to-end integration tests verifying PAR, PKCE, and DPoP interoperability for all tier-1 financial mini-apps prior to store release.

title: OAuth 2.1: Specification Consolidation, Implicit Grant Deprecation & Bearer Query Prohibitions
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1 Section 1.3 (Major Differences from OAuth 2.0) & Section 4
key_takeaways: OAuth 2.1 consolidates and streamlines OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, RFC 6750) by incorporating Security BCP (RFC 9700), Native Apps (RFC 8252), and PKCE (RFC 7636) into a unified core standard.
Formally eliminates and removes the insecure Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) grant type, preventing credential harvesting and insecure legacy login architectures.
Formally eliminates and deprecates the Implicit Grant (`response_type=token`), removing access tokens returned in URL hash fragments vulnerable to history leakage and script interception.
Strictly prohibits passing Bearer Access Tokens in HTTP query strings (formerly permitted in RFC 6750 Section 2.3), eliminating token leakage into HTTP referrers, web logs, and browser bookmarks.
Enforces that the Authorization Code grant combined with PKCE is the single primary interactive authorization mechanism across all web, mobile, and mini-app clients.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt OAuth 2.1 as the foundational baseline specification for all mini-app store identity, authentication, and authorization protocols.
Completely block and reject any legacy Implicit Grant (`response_type=token`) or Resource Owner Password Credentials flow across the super-app identity broker.
Enforce that Bearer Access Tokens MUST only be transmitted via the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header or native bridge message bodies, never in URL query strings.

title: OAuth 2.1: Universal Mandatory PKCE Enforcement & S256 Transformation
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1 Section 4.1.1 (Authorization Request) & Section 4.1.3 (Access Token Request)
key_takeaways: Under OAuth 2.1, Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is no longer an optional extension; it is MANDATORY for ALL clients, including confidential backend clients as well as public mini-apps.
Prohibits the insecure `code_challenge_method=plain`; authorization servers MUST require `code_challenge_method=S256`.
The authorization request MUST include `code_challenge` derived via BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(code_verifier)), and the token request MUST include the original `code_verifier` with 43-128 characters.
Guarantees protection against authorization code interception attacks across inter-app custom URI schemes, intent filters, and shared OS process boundaries.
Provides symmetric cryptographic defense-in-depth even if an authorization code is intercepted or leaked from a redirection URI.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure the super-app identity server to unconditionally reject authorization requests lacking `code_challenge` or specifying `code_challenge_method=plain`.
Enforce `S256` transformation within the mini-app SDK core authentication libraries with zero developer configuration required.
Validate that `code_verifier` matching is performed in constant time on the authorization server to prevent timing side-channel attacks.

title: OAuth 2.1: Exact Redirect URI String Matching & Wildcard Path Prohibition
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1 Section 2.3.1 (Client Registration Redirection Endpoint)
key_takeaways: OAuth 2.1 requires clients to register full, exact redirect URIs and mandates exact string matching comparison by the authorization server.
Explicitly prohibits wildcard matching, regex matching, partial subdirectory matching, or path traversal expansion across registered redirection URIs.
For public clients, redirect URIs MUST either use HTTPS schemes or reverse-DNS private-use URI schemes (RFC 8252), prohibiting plain HTTP schemes except for loopback interfaces on native clients.
Prevents open redirector vulnerabilities where attackers append query parameters or path segments to redirect authorization codes to adversary servers.
Ensures complete determinism in authorization code delivery across super-app mini-app navigation frames.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce strict byte-for-byte exact redirect URI validation during both mini-app marketplace submission review and live authorization runtime checks.
Reject developer manifests containing wildcards (`*`), path traversals (`/../`), or unencrypted `http://` schemes in registered redirection endpoints.
Store registered redirect URIs in a tamper-proof metadata ledger and disallow dynamic URI modifications without full marketplace security re-review.

title: OAuth 2.1: Refresh Token Protection, Cryptographic Binding & Mandatory Rotation
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1 Section 4.3.3 (Refresh Token Usage) & Section 6
key_takeaways: OAuth 2.1 mandates that refresh tokens issued to public clients MUST either be sender-constrained (cryptographically bound via DPoP or mutual TLS) or utilize refresh token rotation with automatic reuse detection.
Under refresh token rotation, a new refresh token is issued with every token refresh response, and the previous refresh token is immediately invalidated.

If an invalidated refresh token is ever presented again, the authorization server MUST detect reuse, treat it as a token theft compromise, and immediately revoke all access and refresh tokens issued to that client authorization family.
Greatly mitigates the impact of refresh token exfiltration from client-side storage or mobile backups.
Ensures that compromised refresh tokens cannot be leveraged for prolonged unauthorized offline access.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement mandatory refresh token rotation with immediate invalidation and automated reuse detection across all super-app token endpoints.
Trigger automated session termination and invalidate all active user sessions for a mini-app if refresh token reuse is detected.
Pair refresh token rotation with DPoP sender-constraining (RFC 9449) for maximum defense-in-depth on public mini-app runtimes.

title: OAuth 2.1: Enterprise Migration Strategy, Workload Identity & Governance Architecture
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1 Section 7 (Security Considerations) & Architecture Guide
key_takeaways: Adopting OAuth 2.1 modernizes enterprise authorization architectures by enforcing least privilege, zero-trust primitives, and eliminating decade-old security anti-patterns.
For workload and machine-to-machine communications, OAuth 2.1 maintains client credentials grant but recommends pairing with short-lived tokens and cryptographic mTLS or DPoP proofs.
Establishes clear operational guardrails for super-app ecosystems: sandboxed token issuance, explicit consent boundaries, and automated audit logging of all token exchanges.
Provides an authoritative standard baseline that harmonizes mobile app security, web standards, and regulatory compliance frameworks (such as PSD2, Open Banking, and NIST SP 800-63).
Simplifies developer integration by presenting a clean, unambiguous specification without confusing deprecated flows.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish an OAuth 2.1 compliance checklist in the super-app developer portal and mandate adherence for all new mini-app submissions.
Establish an automated migration roadmap for legacy mini-apps to deprecate implicit flows, migrate to PKCE, and adopt strict redirect URI matching.
Conduct automated static analysis and dynamic API gateway scanning during CI/CD to detect non-compliant OAuth parameters before store deployment.

title: OpenID Federation 1.0: Entity Statements, Self-Signed Entity Configurations & Architecture
standard_reference: OpenID Federation 1.0 Section 2 (Overall Architecture) & Section 3 (Entity Statement)
key_takeaways: OpenID Federation 1.0 defines multilateral technical trust infrastructure enabling distributed entities to establish cryptographic trust without prior bilateral agreements.
The foundational building block is the Entity Statement: an explicitly typed JSON Web Token (`typ: entity-statement+jwt`, RFC 8725) containing metadata and signing keys (`jwks`).
Every entity in the federation publishes a self-signed Entity Statement about itself called an Entity Configuration at the well-known location `/.well-known/openid-federation`.
When `iss` equals `sub`, the statement is an Entity Configuration; when `iss` and `sub` differ, it is a Subordinate Statement issued by a superior entity about an immediate subordinate.
Federation Entity Keys (`jwks`) published in the Entity Configuration are used to verify digital signatures across the entire trust hierarchy.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish an official OpenID Federation Entity Configuration at `https://superapp.domain/.well-known/openid-federation` defining the super-app Trust Anchor or Intermediate Authority.
Require registered enterprise mini-apps and third-party developer organizations to host or provide verifiable Entity Configurations signed by their federation keys.
Enforce explicit typing `typ: entity-statement+jwt` and reject any malformed or untyped federation statements during store review and runtime resolution.

title: OpenID Federation 1.0: Hierarchical Trust Chains, Authority Hints & Discovery Resolution
standard_reference: OpenID Federation 1.0 Section 4 (Trust Chain) & Section 3.1.2 (authority_hints)
key_takeaways: A Trust Chain is an ordered sequence of Entity Statements proving trust between a Leaf Entity (such as a mini-app Relying Party or service) and a configured Trust Anchor.
The chain begins with the Leaf Entity's Entity Configuration (ES[0]) and traverses through zero or more Subordinate Statements issued by Intermediate Entities up to the Trust Anchor (ES[i]).
The `authority_hints` claim in an Entity Configuration contains an array of HTTPS Entity Identifiers pointing to immediate superiors that can issue subordinate statements for the entity.
Trust chain resolution algorithmically verifies that for each statement j, `ES[j].iss == ES[j+1].sub` and that ES[j] is cryptographically signed by a key in `ES[j+1].jwks`.
The Trust Chain culminates at a known, pre-configured Trust Anchor whose public keys are distributed out-of-band or embedded securely in host root certificates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Establish the super-app root security operator as the primary Trust Anchor for the internal mini-app ecosystem, anchoring all intermediate developer organizations.
Implement automated Trust Chain resolution within the super-app identity gateway to dynamically discover and verify mini-app metadata and signing keys.
Cache verified Trust Chains with strict adherence to the minimum expiration timestamp (`exp`) across all constituent Entity Statements, flushing upon revocation.

title: OpenID Federation 1.0: Subordinate Statements, Metadata Policies & Constraint Enforcement
standard_reference: OpenID Federation 1.0 Section 6 (Metadata Policy) & Section 3.1.3 (Subordinate Statements)
key_takeaways: Superior Entities (Trust Anchors and Intermediates) publish Subordinate Statements about their immediate subordinates via their `federation_fetch_endpoint`.
Subordinate Statements can define a `metadata_policy` containing JSON policy operators (`value`, `add`, `default`, `essential`, `one_of`, `subset_of`, `superset_of`) applied to subordinate metadata.
Metadata policies are applied hierarchically from top to bottom (Trust Anchor down to Leaf), restricting allowable scopes, grant types, token endpoint auth methods, or response types.
Section 6.2 defines `constraints` (such as `max_path_length` and `naming_constraints`) that restrict the depth and domain namespaces of subordinate trust paths.
Empowers federation operators to enforce strict security baselines across thousands of independent entities without requiring custom bilateral code or manual configuration.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Apply standardized `metadata_policy` rules in super-app Subordinate Statements to mandate `grant_types_supported: ["authorization_code"]` and enforce PKCE for all mini-apps.
Enforce `subset_of` constraints on requested OAuth scopes to prevent mini-apps from claiming unauthorized enterprise permissions.
Deploy `naming_constraints` in subordinate statements to restrict mini-app domain endpoints to verified developer web namespaces.

title: OpenID Federation 1.0: Trust Marks, Accreditation Architecture & Third-Party Auditing
standard_reference: OpenID Federation 1.0 Section 7 (Trust Marks) & Section 7.2 (Trust Mark Validation)
key_takeaways: A Trust Mark is a signed JWT representing a statement of conformance to a well-scoped set of trust, security, privacy, or interoperability requirements issued by an accreditation authority.
Trust Marks contain claims including `id` (trust mark identifier URI), `sub` (entity identifier of the accredited party), `iss` (accreditation authority URI), `iat`, and `exp`.
Entities display Trust Marks in their Entity Statements, allowing relying parties and end-users to verify official compliance certifications (e.g. ISO 27001, banking license, healthcare compliance).
Trust Marks can be verified either cryptographically using the issuer's published federation keys or dynamically via the Trust Mark issuer's `federation_status_endpoint`.
Provides a decentralized, cryptographically verifiable accreditation model that scales seamlessly across large multi-tenant application marketplaces.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Issue cryptographically signed Super-App Trust Marks (e.g., `verified_developer`, `financial_grade_certified`, `enterprise_audited`) during marketplace app approval.
Verify third-party regulatory Trust Marks presented by mini-apps using automated federation status endpoints before granting access to payment or personal data APIs.
Display visual trust badges in the mini-app store catalog backed directly by validated, unexpired OpenID Federation Trust Marks.

title: OpenID Federation 1.0: Multilateral Trust Architecture for Cross-Enterprise Super-Apps
standard_reference: OpenID Federation 1.0 Architecture & Multi-Tenant Deployment Profiles
key_takeaways: Super-apps operating across conglomerates, government portals, or cross-border telco alliances require decentralized trust management beyond monolithic identity silos.

OpenID Federation enables autonomous business units, external merchants, and partner telcos to manage their own intermediate authorities while maintaining a root trust relationship with the super-app platform.
Eliminates manual API key exchanges, static client secret provisioning, and brittle bilateral federation agreements across partner ecosystems.
Supports automated onboarding via dynamic client registration anchored in verified trust chains (`trust_chain` JWS header parameter).
Provides an authoritative, future-proof architectural blueprint for national-scale digital identity, e-government mini-apps, and open financial ecosystems.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Architect the super-app identity federation using a multilateral OpenID Federation hierarchy with distinct Intermediate Entities for telco, finance, retail, and government mini-apps.
Implement zero-touch mini-app onboarding via trust chain validation, replacing manual bilateral credential provisioning in enterprise tenant consoles.
Integrate federation historical event tracking (`federation_subordinate_events_endpoint`) to automatically synchronize mini-app suspension, key rotation, and status updates across the cluster.

title: IETF GNAP: Fine-Grained Grant Request Model, Client Key Presentation & Multi-Token Responses
standard_reference: draft-ietf-gnap-core-protocol Section 2 (Requesting Access) & Section 2.1 (Client Instance Identification and Key Presentation)
key_takeaways: GNAP (Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol) replaces OAuth 2.0's rigid redirect-and-scope model with direct, programmatic negotiation between a client instance and the Authorization Server (AS).

Clients initiate requests by posting a structured JSON document to the AS grant endpoint containing explicit resource access arrays (`access_token` with fine-grained types, actions, locations, and data types).

The client identifies its instance and presents its cryptographic public key (`client.key`) at initial negotiation, ensuring all subsequent requests and token usage are cryptographically bound to that key.
GNAP natively supports issuing multiple distinct access tokens within a single transaction response, each targeted with specific rights and audiences for different backend services.
Eliminates ambient authority and broad scope escalation by establishing exact, declaratively negotiated privileges before user interaction is initiated.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt GNAP request structures in the super-app JS bridge SDK (`superapp.auth.negotiateGrant`), allowing mini-apps to request specific API actions without requiring broad coarse-grained scopes.
Require mini-app WebViews to generate an ephemeral or device-bound WebCrypto public key passed in `client.key` during initial grant negotiation.
Issue distinct, segmented tokens when a mini-app requires access to separate backend domains (e.g., telco billing vs catalog metadata) in a single authorization turn.

title: IETF GNAP: Interaction Lifecycle, Interaction Handles & Non-Browser Multi-Channel Orchestration
standard_reference: draft-ietf-gnap-core-protocol Section 2.5 (User Interaction) & Section 4 (Interacting with the End User)
key_takeaways: GNAP decouples client initiation from user interaction, supporting diverse interaction modes including redirect, user code display, app launching, and out-of-band push notifications.
The client declares supported interaction modes (`start: ["redirect", "app", "user_code"]`) and completion mechanisms (`finish: {"method": "redirect", "uri": "...", "hash": "..."}`).
The AS returns interaction directives (`interact` object with `redirect` URI or `finish` handle) along with a continuation access token and continuation URI for the client.
Supports headless, voice-activated, smart TV, or in-store POS mini-apps where authentication occurs on a secondary trusted smartphone device while the client session remains active.
The `finish` hash parameter cryptographically binds the client's original interaction request with the callback, preventing authorization session injection and cross-site redirection attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize native super-app modal consent sheets as the primary GNAP interaction mode (`start: ["app"]`), bypassing WebView URL redirections entirely.
Implement out-of-band user approval for cross-device mini-app sessions (such as kiosk or TV apps) via push notifications delivered to the user's primary mobile super-app.
Enforce verification of the GNAP `finish` interaction hash inside the container bridge before resuming mini-app script execution.

title: IETF GNAP: Proof-of-Possession Token Binding & RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures
standard_reference: draft-ietf-gnap-core-protocol Section 7 (Key Proofing) & Section 7.3 (HTTP Message Signatures)
key_takeaways: GNAP enforces proof-of-possession (PoP) for all access tokens and continuation requests, strictly preventing bearer token replay if a token is intercepted.

Every access token issued by the AS is cryptographically associated with a client key; presentation of the token to a Resource Server (RS) requires signing the request with that corresponding private key.
Specifies RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures as the primary key-proofing mechanism, attaching `Signature` and `Signature-Input` headers covering method, target URI, timestamp, and body digest.
Eliminates shared client secrets and static credentials, utilizing asymmetric public keys (ECDSA P-256/Ed25519) registered or dynamically presented during negotiation.
Provides hardware-backed non-repudiation when keys are generated within mobile device secure enclaves or Keystore.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signing for all mini-app communications carrying GNAP access tokens across the super-app API gateway.
Provide automatic transparent signing in the native bridge layer using container-managed hardware keys so mini-app web code cannot leak the private key.
Reject unsigned or bearer-only access requests at all enterprise resource servers supporting the mini-app store.

title: IETF GNAP: Continuation API, Dynamic Privilege Step-Up & Grant Lifecycle Management
standard_reference: draft-ietf-gnap-core-protocol Section 5 (Continuing a Grant Request) & Section 5.3 (Modifying and Revoking Grants)
key_takeaways: GNAP introduces a stateful Grant Continuation API via a dedicated `continue` endpoint and continuation access token.
After user interaction finishes or when an app requires additional rights mid-session, the client submits a continuation request without restarting the entire authentication handshake.
Supports dynamic grant modification: clients can request incremental privileges (step-up authorization) or release unused capabilities during a running session.
The client can explicitly delete the grant via HTTP DELETE on the continuation URI, instantly revoking all associated access tokens and session handles across the ecosystem.
Enables just-in-time privilege escalation tailored for micro-transactions, high-value checkouts, or accessing sensitive biometric APIs.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Utilize GNAP continuation endpoints to implement progressive disclosure and incremental permission prompts as users navigate into deep mini-app features.
Trigger automated HTTP DELETE on the mini-app's continuation URI when the user closes the mini-app container or navigates back to the super-app home screen.
Log all continuation requests and grant modification events in the platform audit trail for security compliance and fraud detection.

title: IETF GNAP Resource Servers: RS-to-AS Decoupling, Capability Delegation & Token Introspection
standard_reference: draft-ietf-gnap-resource-servers Section 2 (Resource Server and AS Interaction) & Section 3 (Token Verification)
key_takeaways: The GNAP Resource Server (RS) specification formalizes the protocol interface between independent resource servers and the centralized GNAP Authorization Server.
Allows the RS to introspect incoming proof-of-possession tokens, verify client key bindings, and retrieve fine-grained capability metadata (authorized actions, data paths, user attributes).
Supports both reference tokens (resolved via real-time RS-to-AS backchannel queries) and structured cryptographic tokens (self-contained signed JWTs).
Defines standard RS error signaling (`GNAP-Error` header or JSON response) communicating insufficient privileges, expired keys, or required step-up authorization parameters.
Decouples microservices from identity logic, allowing third-party enterprise mini-app backends to integrate securely with the super-app authorization fabric.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy standard GNAP RS introspection endpoints on all super-app core service gateways (payments, user profile, messaging, device sensors).
Provide backend SDKs for third-party mini-app developers implementing GNAP RS token validation and client signature verification.
Standardize RS error codes to trigger automatic client-side continuation flows when step-up authentication is demanded by downstream APIs.

title: OpenID FAPI 2.0: Message Signing Architecture, End-to-End Non-Repudiation & RFC 9421 Profiles
standard_reference: FAPI 2.0 Message Signing Section 3 (Message Signing Profile) & Section 4 (Signature Verification)
key_takeaways: FAPI 2.0 Message Signing defines end-to-end cryptographic non-repudiation and payload integrity for high-value financial, banking, and e-commerce transactions.
Standardizes on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, attaching detached cryptographic signatures over both HTTP requests and HTTP responses.
Signatures cryptographically bind the sender identity, HTTP method, target URI, request headers, and content digest, preventing tampering by intermediary proxies or compromised network nodes.
Mandates deterministic canonicalization and strict verification of signature metadata parameters including `keyid`, `alg`, `created`, and `expires`.

Replaces deprecated custom JWT payload wrapping (e.g. JWS in HTTP body) with native, protocol-level HTTP header signatures that work transparently across diverse payload types (JSON, binary, streams).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce FAPI 2.0 Message Signing for all mini-app payment checkouts, fund transfers, and digital contract signing operations exceeding high-risk financial thresholds.
Implement native RFC 9421 signature generation within the super-app container core using the mobile device's Hardware Security Module (HSM) or Secure Enclave.
Require all partner banking and payment gateways to return FAPI 2.0 signed HTTP responses, verifying the server signature before displaying payment success screens in the mini-app.

title: OpenID FAPI 2.0: Mandatory Component Coverage, Content-Digest Integrity & Anti-Tampering
standard_reference: FAPI 2.0 Message Signing Section 3.2 (HTTP Request Signing) & Section 3.3 (HTTP Response Signing)
key_takeaways: Mandates that signed HTTP requests MUST cover at least `@method`, `@target-uri`, and `content-digest` (if a body is present), as well as authorization headers.
The `content-digest` component utilizes SHA-256 or SHA-512 hashing (per RFC 9530 / RFC 9421) to ensure the request/response body cannot be modified or truncated in transit.
For responses, the signature MUST cover `@status` and `content-digest`, linking the specific HTTP status code cryptographically to the returned data body.
Prohibits selective or partial field validation: if any covered component fails signature verification or hash matching, the entire transaction MUST fail immediately with an HTTP 401/400.
Protects against cross-endpoint replay attacks by binding the exact request target URI and path directly into the cryptographic signature envelope.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure the super-app API gateway to validate `@method`, `@target-uri`, `@status`, and `content-digest` on all signed API endpoints used by financial mini-apps.
Provide automated client-side hashing in the mini-app runtime bridge so web developers do not manually construct `content-digest` strings.
Log signature verification failures with component-level granularity in the security monitoring pipeline to detect network manipulation attempts.

title: OpenID FAPI 2.0: Algorithmic Rigor, Asymmetric Keys & Anti-Confusion Defenses
standard_reference: FAPI 2.0 Message Signing Section 5 (Cryptographic Considerations) & FAPI 2.0 Security Profile Section 5.2.2
key_takeaways: FAPI 2.0 Message Signing strictly restricts cryptographic algorithms to strong asymmetric ciphers: PS256 (RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256), ES256 (ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256), or Ed25519.
Explicitly forbids the use of RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (`RS256`), symmetric HMAC algorithms (`HS256`), and the `none` algorithm to eliminate signature forgery vulnerabilities.
Requires that signing keys are registered and verifiable via public JWKS endpoints or X.509 certificate chains bound to verified enterprise developer identities.
Mandates distinct key separation: signing keys used for FAPI message signing MUST NOT be reused for TLS client authentication (mTLS) or token encryption.
Enforces strict signature lifetime checks: signatures MUST include `created` and `expires` tags with maximum validity windows (typically <= 300 seconds) to prevent replay of captured signed messages.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce PS256 or ES256 exclusively for mini-app message signing across all super-app developer tiers, rejecting legacy RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 algorithms during app validation.
Implement automated cryptographic key rotation mechanisms in the developer portal, validating developer JWKS configurations against FAPI 2.0 strict requirements.
Enforce a maximum signature time-to-live of 60 seconds on all native bridge financial invocations to eliminate message replay windows.

title: OAuth 2.0 Grant Management: Grant Query, Consent Inspection & Enterprise Auditability
standard_reference: OAuth 2.0 Grant Management for OAuth 2.0 Section 3 (Grant Management Endpoint) & Section 4 (Query Grant)
key_takeaways: The OAuth 2.0 Grant Management specification introduces a dedicated Grant Management Endpoint and a persistent `grant_id` handle representing user consent.
Allows clients (or the super-app platform on behalf of users) to query active grants via `HTTP GET /grants/{grant_id}` to inspect currently authorized scopes, claims, and RAR authorization details.
Enables mini-apps to perform programmatic self-auditing before initiating workflows, confirming whether necessary permissions remain valid without triggering disruptive error handling.
Provides standardized JSON metadata detailing authorization status, resource boundaries, expiration timestamps, and delegating user identities.
Crucial for enterprise compliance (GDPR Article 15/17, PDP regulations) requiring transparent consent visualization and verification.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement the Grant Management API in the super-app consent subsystem, assigning a unique `grant_id` to each user/mini-app relationship.
Expose a client SDK method (`superapp.auth.getGrantStatus`) querying the grant endpoint to let mini-apps dynamically adapt UI states based on confirmed active permissions.
Integrate grant inspection into the super-app account dashboard, allowing users to view real-time granular privileges granted to each installed mini-app.

title: OAuth 2.0 Grant Management: Granular Consent Revocation, Action Lifecycle & User Privacy Centers
standard_reference: OAuth 2.0 Grant Management for OAuth 2.0 Section 5 (Revoke Grant) & Section 2 (Grant Management Actions)
key_takeaways: Specifies standardized grant management actions: `create`, `query`, `replace`, and `revoke` passed via the `grant_management_action` parameter.
Clients or users can revoke a specific grant by issuing an `HTTP DELETE /grants/{grant_id}` request to the grant management endpoint.
Revoking a grant immediately invalidates the grant handle, all associated access tokens, refresh tokens, and downscoped authorization artifacts across all resource servers.

Supports partial consent replacement: clients can update an existing grant (`grant_management_action=replace`) to drop unneeded scopes when a user disables specific features, minimizing data liability.
Harmonizes consent management across multiple devices, so revoking a grant on the user's phone immediately terminates authorization for corresponding sessions on tablets, smart TVs, or web instances.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide a one-click 'Revoke Permissions' button in the mini-app settings sheet that executes standard `HTTP DELETE` against the Grant Management endpoint.
Require mini-apps to execute `grant_management_action=replace` to shed sensitive privileges when users deactivate optional features within the mini-app.
Synchronize grant revocation events across the super-app event bus to notify resource servers and terminate active WebSocket connections instantaneously.

title: IETF RFC 8417: Security Event Token (SET) Architecture, JSON Profiling & Asynchronous Signaling
category: Security Events, Incident Response & Distributed Governance
standard_reference: RFC 8417 Section 2 (Security Event Token Format) & Section 3 (Security Event Claims)
key_takeaways: RFC 8417 defines the Security Event Token (SET), a standardized data structure based on JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for sharing asynchronous security event signals between administrative domains.
SETs use the mandatory explicit media type `typ: secevent+jwt` in the JWS header to eliminate cross-JWT token confusion and substitution attacks.
Introduces the `events` claim: a JSON object whose member keys are URIs identifying specific security event types (e.g. RISC or CAEP events) and whose values are event-specific metadata objects.
Mandates core tracking claims including `iss` (event transmitter), `iat` (issuance time), `jti` (unique event identifier for deduplication), and `sub` or `sub_id` (affected security subject).
Establishes a cryptographically signed, verifiable ledger of security incidents that can be exchanged between cloud services, platform operators, and federated applications.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt RFC 8417 SETs as the universal wire format for all security and lifecycle telemetry distributed between the super-app core, identity providers, and mini-app enterprise backends.
Enforce strict validation of `typ: secevent+jwt` and cryptographic JWS signatures before routing security event tokens through the platform message bus.
Maintain an in-memory distributed cache of SET `jti` identifiers with a 24-hour expiration window to prevent event replay and duplicate processing.

title: OpenID RISC 1.0: Account Security Event Types, Credential Compromise & Incident Coordination
category: Security Events, Incident Response & Distributed Governance
standard_reference: OpenID RISC Profile of IETF Security Events 1.0 Section 2 (Event Types) & Section 3 (RISC Event Definitions)
key_takeaways: OpenID RISC (Risk and Incident Sharing and Coordination) defines standard security event types enabling coordinated incident response across ecosystem participants.

Core standardized event types include `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/risc/event-type/account-credential-change-required`, `account-purged`, `account-disabled`, `account-enabled`, and `sessions-revoked`.
When the super-app or an identity provider detects a credential leak, account takeover attempt, or brute-force attack, it transmits a RISC event to all relying mini-apps.
Allows mini-apps to immediately terminate local user sessions, clear sensitive cached documents, or force step-up biometric re-authentication without waiting for access token expiration.
Crucial for containing cross-application contamination in multi-tenant super-app ecosystems where one compromised third-party service could otherwise compromise user trust.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated RISC event emission from the super-app Security Operations Center (SOC) to all active mini-app backends upon detecting compromised user credentials or device malware.
Require enterprise mini-apps handling financial or healthcare transactions to subscribe to RISC feeds and immediately invalidate active session tokens upon receiving `sessions-revoked` events.
Broadcast `account-purged` events when a user exercises their GDPR/PDPA right-to-erasure in the super-app, mandating that mini-apps purge local persistent records within 72 hours.

title: OpenID RISC 1.0: Privacy-Preserving Subject Identifiers, RFC 9493 & Anti-Correlation Protections
category: Security Events, Incident Response & Distributed Governance
standard_reference: OpenID RISC Profile 1.0 Section 2.2 (Subject Identifiers) & IETF RFC 9493 (Subject Identifiers for Security Event Tokens)
key_takeaways: RISC leverages RFC 9493 Subject Identifiers to reference affected user accounts without exposing unnecessary Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to unauthorized third parties.
Supports diverse standardized format identifiers: `iss_sub` (issuer and subject URI), `email`, `phone_number`, `opaque_id`, and `did` (decentralized identifier).

Mandates the use of Pairwise Pseudonymous Identifiers (PPID) in `iss_sub` format for third-party mini-apps, preventing different mini-app vendors from colluding and correlating user activities via security events.
Transmitters MUST evaluate recipient permissions and only send subject formats the specific receiver is authorized to process, upholding privacy-by-design standards.
Ensures that broadcasted security signals coordinate incident response across hundreds of ecosystem participants while strictly complying with global data protection laws.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce pairwise pseudonymous subject identifiers (`iss_sub` with app-scoped salt) when broadcasting RISC events to third-party mini-app developers.
Strictly prohibit transmitting plaintext email or phone subject identifiers to untrusted or low-tier mini-apps, using opaque alias mappings maintained by the super-app platform.
Audit all subject identifier schemas against RFC 9493 during mini-app store security compliance reviews.

title: IETF RFC 8935: Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Over HTTP & Webhook Resiliency
category: Security Events, Incident Response & Distributed Governance
standard_reference: RFC 8935 Section 2 (Delivery Protocol) & Section 3 (Error Handling)
key_takeaways: RFC 8935 specifies the standardized push delivery protocol for transmitting SETs from an event transmitter to a receiver via HTTP POST webhooks.
The transmitter issues an `HTTP POST` request to the receiver's delivery endpoint with `Content-Type: application/secevent+jwt` carrying the compact serialized SET in the request body.
Receivers validate the SET and respond with `HTTP 202 Accepted` on success, or an explicit JSON error document (e.g. `err: invalid_key`, `invalid_issuer`, `authentication_failed`).
Mandates strong mutual authentication: transmitters and receivers must authenticate via mutual TLS (mTLS) or OAuth 2.0 Bearer/DPoP tokens to prevent spoofed event injection.
Defines resilient delivery behavior: transmitters MUST implement exponential backoff and persistent retry queuing to handle temporary network partitions or receiver downtime.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy RFC 8935 push-based webhooks as the default distribution mechanism for delivering real-time security events to tier-1 enterprise and financial mini-app cloud backends.
Require mTLS certificate authentication (per RFC 8705) on all push delivery webhook endpoints registered in the mini-app developer console.
Implement a resilient dead-letter queue (DLQ) with exponential backoff retries for up to 72 hours when delivering critical account compromise SETs.

title: IETF RFC 8936: Poll-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Over HTTP & Air-Gapped Resiliency
category: Security Events, Incident Response & Distributed Governance
standard_reference: RFC 8936 Section 2 (Polling Interface) & Section 3 (Event Acknowledgement)
key_takeaways: RFC 8936 defines a poll-based delivery protocol allowing receivers behind NATs, firewalls, or strict inbound security perimeters to pull SETs from an event transmitter.
Receivers issue `HTTP POST` requests to the polling endpoint with JSON requests specifying `maxEvents` and `returnImmediately` flags, supporting long-polling patterns for low-latency event delivery.
Features built-in acknowledgement tracking: poll requests include `ack` arrays confirming receipt of previous `jti` event IDs, enabling the transmitter to reliably advance the queue.
Provides error-signaling mechanisms (`setErrs`) allowing receivers to report specific validation failures (e.g. signature error, unknown subject) without stalling overall queue processing.
Essential for enterprise, government, or on-premise partner mini-apps that cannot expose public inbound HTTP webhook endpoints to the super-app cloud.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide an RFC 8936 polling endpoint on the super-app event gateway for enterprise mini-app backends operating behind corporate firewalls or strict security zones.
Support HTTP long-polling with a 30-second hold window to minimize network overhead while ensuring sub-second delivery of security alerts.
Mandate explicit `ack` confirmation from polling clients before purging security events from the transmitter's outbound buffer.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance (OID4VCI 1.0): Architecture & Credential Issuer Metadata Standards
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance 1.0 Section 11.2 (Credential Issuer Metadata) & Section 5 (Credential Offer)
key_takeaways: OID4VCI 1.0 establishes an OAuth 2.0-based protocol for issuing Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and Verifiable Attestations across mobile apps and wallets.

Defines the standardized metadata discovery endpoint at `/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer`, returning a JSON object declaring `credential_issuer`, `credential_endpoint`, `batch_credential_endpoint`, and supported formats.

Specifies `credential_configurations_supported` which catalogues distinct credential types (e.g. mso_mdoc, jwt_vc_json, ldp_vc, sd_jwt_vc) along with their cryptographic binding requirements, supported cryptographic suites, and claim display definitions.
Enables localization via multi-lingual `display` arrays containing name, locale, logo, and theme color for dynamic rendering within the super-app wallet.
Decouples the Credential Issuer from the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server (AS) through the `authorization_servers` metadata array, supporting distributed enterprise architectures.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement the OID4VCI discovery endpoint `/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer` on the super-app identity gateway to allow mini-apps to publish verifiable credentials into the host wallet.
Require all credential issuers in the mini-app store to declare exact cryptographic binding algorithms (ES256, Ed25519) within `credential_configurations_supported`.
Enforce strict schema validation on mini-app credential metadata during the automated store onboarding review.

title: OID4VCI 1.0: Credential Offer Protocol, Pre-Authorized Code Flow & Transaction Code Security
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OID4VCI 1.0 Section 4 (Credential Offer) & Section 4.1.1 (Pre-Authorized Code Grant)
key_takeaways: The Credential Offer initiates issuance either by value (`credential_offer` query param) or by reference (`credential_offer_uri`), passing metadata and grant capabilities to the wallet.
Supports two issuance authorization modes: the standard Authorization Code Flow (with PKCE RFC 7636) and the Pre-Authorized Code Flow for streamlined cross-channel issuance.

In the Pre-Authorized Code Flow, the issuer generates an ephemeral `pre-authorized_code` out-of-band (e.g., in a mini-app checkout or customer support chat) that the wallet redeems directly for an access token.
Mandates a Transaction Code (`tx_code`) mechanism when using pre-authorized codes to protect against credential interception: the user must input an out-of-band PIN/OTP.
Specifies granular constraints within the offer, including `credential_configuration_ids` specifying exactly which credentials the wallet is permitted to request.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt OID4VCI Credential Offers via deep-links (`superapp://credential-offer?credential_offer_uri=...`) for instant credential issuance from mini-apps into the super-app secure enclave wallet.
Mandate `tx_code` entropy (minimum 6 digits numeric or 8 characters alphanumeric) and maximum 5 retry attempts whenever pre-authorized code flows are utilized by mini-apps.
Prohibit passing raw `credential_offer` payloads exceeding 2KB via URL query parameters, requiring signed HTTPS `credential_offer_uri` endpoints instead.

title: OID4VCI 1.0: Cryptographic Proof of Possession, Ephemeral C-Nonces & Client Key Binding
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OID4VCI 1.0 Section 7.2 (Proof Types) & Section 7.2.1 (JWT Proof)
key_takeaways: OID4VCI strictly mandates Proof of Possession (PoP) in credential requests to cryptographically bind issued credentials to the wallet's private key held in secure hardware.
The wallet signs a Proof object (typically a JWT or CWT) using its private key, asserting possession of the public key to be embedded in the issued credential.

To prevent replay attacks across issuers and sessions, the issuer provides an ephemeral cryptographic nonce (`c_nonce`) via the token or credential response, which MUST be embedded in the proof's `nonce` claim.
Specifies mandatory proof claims: `aud` (matching the Credential Issuer identifier), `iat` (issuance timestamp), and `nonce` (the valid, unexpired `c_nonce`).
Integrates seamlessly with DPoP (RFC 9449) and mTLS (RFC 8705) to ensure sender-constrained access token delivery at the `/credential` endpoint.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require all wallet issuance requests in the super-app container to generate PoP signatures within the device's Hardware Security Module (iOS Secure Enclave / Android StrongBox).
Enforce a strict 60-second validity window for `c_nonce` tokens generated by super-app credential issuance gateways.
Validate that the public key included in the PoP proof matches the `cnf` (confirmation) claim of the resulting issued Verifiable Credential.

title: OID4VCI 1.0: Synchronous, Asynchronous (Deferred) & Batch Credential Issuance Endpoints
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OID4VCI 1.0 Section 7 (Credential Endpoint), Section 8 (Batch Credential Endpoint) & Section 9 (Deferred Credential Endpoint)
key_takeaways: The `/credential` endpoint receives authenticated POST requests containing the credential format, requested claims/identifier, and cryptographic proof of possession.
Supports immediate synchronous issuance returning the credential directly in the JSON response, or deferred asynchronous issuance when manual enterprise approval or background vetting is required.
In deferred issuance, the endpoint responds with an opaque `transaction_id` and `acceptance_token`; the wallet polls the `/deferred_credential` endpoint until the credential is ready.
Defines the `/batch_credential` endpoint allowing mobile wallets to request multiple distinct credentials (e.g. driver's license + employee ID + loyalty pass) in a single atomic round-trip.
The response contains fresh `c_nonce` and `c_nonce_expires_in` values to enable immediate subsequent requests without re-authenticating.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide native super-app bridge APIs (`superapp.wallet.requestCredential`) abstracting both synchronous and deferred OID4VCI issuance flows for mini-app developers.
Implement exponential backoff polling (starting at 2s up to 30s) in the super-app client when handling deferred issuance `transaction_id` responses.
Enforce rate-limiting on the `/batch_credential` endpoint (maximum 10 credentials per batch request) to prevent denial-of-service on cryptographic signing hardware.

title: OID4VCI 1.0: Notification Endpoint, Issuance Acknowledgement & Audit Lifecycle
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OID4VCI 1.0 Section 10 (Notification Endpoint)
key_takeaways: OID4VCI includes an optional `/notification` endpoint enabling the wallet to report the final storage or user acceptance status of an issued credential back to the issuer.
When the credential response includes a `notification_id`, the wallet MUST send an HTTP POST notification after successfully storing or rejecting the credential.
Standardized notification event types include: `credential_issued` (credential successfully received and persisted in wallet) and `credential_deleted` (user refused or discarded the credential).
Enables issuers to maintain accurate lifecycle records, trigger downstream business processes, and invalidate temporary transaction contexts.
Provides an audit trail essential for regulatory compliance (eKYC, AML, GDPR) without exposing wallet keys or browsing behavior.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that the super-app wallet automatically dispatches OID4VCI notifications upon persisting credentials to the device keychain.
Log all issuance and deletion notifications in an immutable append-only ledger for enterprise auditing and dispute reconciliation.
Ensure that failure to deliver a notification does not revoke the issued credential unless explicitly required by the credential issuer's regulatory profile.

title: IETF OAuth Token Status List: Data Model, Bitstring Representation & Status Bit Semantics
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-status-list Section 4 (Status List Data Model) & Section 4.2 (Status List JWT)
key_takeaways: The OAuth Token Status List specification defines a scalable, privacy-preserving mechanism to convey the revocation and suspension status of tokens and verifiable credentials.

Represents status entries as a compact, fixed-size bitstring encoded in a `status_list` JSON object containing `bits` (number of bits per entry) and `lst` (byte array representing the bitstring, base64url-encoded).

Supports 1, 2, 4, or 8 bits per entry: 1-bit allocation provides binary status (0x00 = valid, 0x01 = revoked); 2-bit allocation supports 4 states (0x00 = valid, 0x01 = revoked, 0x02 = suspended, 0x03 = reserved).
The entire bitstring is encapsulated within a signed JWT (`typ: statuslist+jwt`), ensuring cryptographic integrity, issuer authentication, and tamper resistance.
Enables checking the revocation status of millions of credentials with a payload size orders of magnitude smaller than traditional CRLs or OCSP responses.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize on 2-bit status list representation (0 = valid, 1 = revoked, 2 = suspended) across the super-app token issuance and verifiable credential infrastructure.
Require all status list JWTs issued by the platform to be signed using ES256 or Ed25519 with public keys published in the super-app JWKS.
Integrate bitstring index extraction into the core super-app runtime security layer to validate mini-app session tokens.

title: IETF OAuth Token Status List: Status Claim Reference, Index Pointers & Credential Binding
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-status-list Section 5 (Referencing a Status List) & Section 5.1 (Status Claim)
key_takeaways: Issued tokens and verifiable credentials reference their status by including a `status` claim containing a `status_list` JSON object.

The `status_list` object contains two mandatory elements: `idx` (the zero-based integer index pointing to the credential's entry in the bitstring) and `uri` (the HTTPS URL where the status list JWT is hosted).
Allows multiple status checks in a single credential: an issued mini-app license can reference both an ecosystem-wide suspension list and a vendor-specific revocation list.
The `idx` value MUST be within the bounds of the total bit capacity defined by the referenced status list (length of `lst` bytes * 8 / `bits`).
Ensures complete decoupling between the credential issuance lifecycle and real-time status publication.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that all high-assurance OAuth tokens, developer API keys, and enterprise mini-app licenses carry the `status.status_list` claim structure.
Enforce that `uri` attributes within the status claim resolve exclusively to verified HTTPS domains declared in the mini-app developer manifest.
Implement automated range-checking during credential parsing to reject tokens where `idx` exceeds the advertised bit capacity of the target status list.

title: IETF OAuth Token Status List: Deflate Compression, HTTP Caching & Verifier Privacy Guarantees
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-status-list Section 4.2.1 (Compression) & Section 7 (Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: To maximize transport efficiency, the bitstring `lst` can be compressed using the DEFLATE algorithm (RFC 1951) prior to base64url encoding, signaled by the `c` claim (`c: 'DEF'`).
A compressed status list for 1,000,000 credentials requires only ~120KB of payload data, enabling fast mobile downloads over low-bandwidth cellular networks.

Leverages standard HTTP Caching (RFC 9111): status list endpoints provide `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, must-revalidate` and strong `ETag` headers for conditional validation (`304 Not Modified`).

Critical Privacy Guarantee: Verifiers download the aggregate status list once and cache it; the issuer CANNOT track individual credential verifications or user browsing destinations (solving the fundamental OCSP tracking flaw).
Protects users from correlation attacks by ensuring that the verifier performs status lookups entirely in local memory.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enable Deflate compression (`c: 'DEF'`) on all super-app status list distribution endpoints to minimize mobile client bandwidth consumption.
Implement a local in-memory status list cache with 5-minute TTL inside the super-app client container to avoid network overhead on repeated mini-app launches.
Audit all third-party mini-app verifiers to ensure they use cached aggregate status lists rather than making per-verification network requests to the issuer.

title: IETF OAuth Token Status List: Multi-Tenant Partitioning, Sharded Buckets & Zero-Bottleneck Updates
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-status-list Section 6 (Operational Considerations) & Section 8 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Large-scale ecosystems must avoid a monolithic single status list, which creates high write contention and forces unnecessary cache invalidation across the entire ecosystem.
Defines partitioning into shards or tenant-specific buckets (e.g. 100,000 entries per list allocated by tenant ID, credential category, or issuance month).
When a status list reaches capacity, a new list is allocated; existing entries remain immutable except for status changes (revocation/suspension).
Issuers batch bit updates into atomic transactions to minimize cryptographic resigning overhead on hardware security modules (HSMs).
Enables isolated maintenance: revoking a compromised mini-app vendor's batch of tokens only invalidates that specific shard, leaving unrelated platform credentials fully cacheable.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Partition super-app status lists into 65,536-entry shards indexed by mini-app category (fintech, telco, ecommerce, utility).
