Implement an asynchronous bit-mutation pipeline that coalesces status changes over a 10-second aggregation window before re-signing and deploying shards to the edge CDN.
Isolate developer testing and staging tokens into dedicated status list shards to prevent development churn from invalidating production cache entries.

title: IETF OAuth Token Status List: Store Compliance Verification Pipeline & Offline Grace Windows
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-status-list Section 7.2 (Stale Status Information) & Section 8.3 (Denial of Service)
key_takeaways: Mini-app platforms verifying third-party credentials must implement a deterministic, fail-safe status verification pipeline.

Verification steps: 1) Extract `status.status_list` from credential; 2) Fetch status list JWT from `uri` (or retrieve from local cache); 3) Validate JWT signature, issuer, and expiration (`exp`); 4) Check index bounds; 5) Extract target bit value.
Addresses network partition scenarios: defines maximum acceptable stale status window (`stale_age`) during temporary client offline periods.
For high-assurance transactions (payments, biometrics, access control), fresh status list validation is mandatory (fail-closed if unreachable).
For low-assurance read-only operations, platforms may permit a grace period (e.g. up to 1 hour) using cached status lists while logging an audit event.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Integrate automated status list verification into the super-app runtime bridge prior to executing privileged mini-app APIs (`superapp.payment`, `superapp.auth`).
Enforce a strict fail-closed policy (reject credential) if the status list is unreachable and the cached copy is older than 15 minutes for financial transactions.
Include automated status list validation conformance tests in the mini-app store review pipeline to verify partner SDK compliance.

title: IETF SD-JWT: Data Architecture, Disclosures Anatomy & Cryptographic Salt Digests
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt Section 5 (Disclosures) & Section 5.1 (Creating Disclosures)
key_takeaways: IETF SD-JWT defines a standardized mechanism enabling selective disclosure of individual claims in JSON Web Tokens without breaking issuer cryptographic signatures.

Each selectively disclosable claim is transformed into a Disclosure: a base64url-encoded JSON array `[salt, claim_name, claim_value]` where `salt` is a cryptographically secure random string (minimum 128 bits entropy).
The Issuer calculates the SHA-256 digest of each Disclosure string and includes these digests in the `_sd` array claim within the issued JWT body instead of the plaintext claims.
The Issuer signs the JWT containing the digests; the user (holder) receives both the signed JWT and the set of separate Disclosure strings.
Enables user-mediated data minimization: the user can selectively present only the required Disclosures to a verifier while withholding sensitive or irrelevant attributes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt the IETF SD-JWT format for all user identity profile tokens and verifiable credentials issued by the super-app platform.
Require minimum 128-bit cryptographic salt generation via WebCrypto `getRandomValues` for all client-side disclosures.
Enforce that mini-app permission manifests explicitly declare which selective disclosure claim names are requested (e.g. `over_18` instead of full birthdate).

title: IETF SD-JWT: Key Binding JWT (KB-JWT), cnf Confirmation Claims & Anti-Replay Nonces
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt Section 6 (Key Binding) & Section 6.2 (Holder-of-Key Proof)
key_takeaways: To prevent an unauthorized party or malicious verifier from stealing disclosed claims and replaying them, SD-JWT defines Key Binding via a Key Binding JWT (KB-JWT).
The Issuer binds the credential to the holder's public key by including a `cnf` (confirmation) claim (RFC 7800) in the signed SD-JWT.
When presenting the credential, the holder creates an ephemeral KB-JWT signed with their private key, proving possession of the key bound in `cnf`.
The KB-JWT includes an `aud` (verifier audience URL), `nonce` (fresh challenge from the verifier), `iat` (timestamp), and `sd_hash` (the cryptographic digest of the exact presented disclosures).
The complete presentation format is serialized as: `<Issuer-Signed-JWT>~<Disclosure 1>~...~<Disclosure N>~<KB-JWT>`, separated by tilde (`~`) characters.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate Key Binding (KB-JWT) with hardware-backed keys for all high-value transactions and age verification presentations across mini-apps.
Verify the `sd_hash` in the KB-JWT to ensure the holder signed precisely the set of disclosures provided and not an altered subset.
Require third-party mini-apps acting as verifiers to generate cryptographically random nonces (valid for maximum 60 seconds) for each presentation request.

title: IETF SD-JWT: Complex Data Structures, Nested Objects & Array Element Selective Disclosure
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt Section 5.2 (Selective Disclosure for Array Elements) & Section 5.3 (Recursive Disclosures)
key_takeaways: SD-JWT supports selective disclosure within hierarchical and complex data structures, including nested JSON objects and multi-element arrays.
For nested objects, each child object can contain its own `_sd` array of digests, allowing disclosures to be nested recursively.
For JSON arrays (e.g. lists of nationalities, degrees, or roles), selective disclosure is achieved using array element disclosures `[salt, element_value]` (omitting the claim name).
In the array container, undisclosed elements are replaced by an object containing a single `...` (ellipsis) property mapped to the digest string (`{"..." : "<digest>"}`).
Allows holders to selectively reveal individual items in a list (e.g., proving membership in an authorized group) while hiding all other entries without altering array order.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt recursive SD-JWT structures for complex business entities (e.g. corporate registration with multiple directors or bank account lists).
Utilize array element disclosures (`...`) when handling multi-value claims such as loyalty club memberships or academic credentials in mini-app profiles.
Ensure the mini-app presentation engine validates that disclosed array elements maintain their deterministic structural ordering.

title: IETF SD-JWT: Verifier Processing Rules, Digest Verification & Anti-Tampering Defenses
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt Section 7 (Verification)
key_takeaways: The SD-JWT verification process follows a strict 7-step cryptographic pipeline to guarantee non-repudiation and structural authenticity.
Step 1: Parse the compact tilde-separated string into the Issuer-Signed JWT, individual Disclosures, and optional KB-JWT.
Step 2: Validate the Issuer JWT signature against the Issuer's trusted JWKS and ensure expiration and not-before claims are valid.
Step 3: For each disclosure, compute the SHA-256 digest and verify that it matches an entry in the JWT's `_sd` array or array `...` elements.
Step 4: Detect and reject duplicate disclosures, unreferenced disclosures, or malformed JSON payloads.
Step 5: If KB-JWT is present, verify its signature using the key in `cnf`, confirm `aud` and `nonce`, and check that `sd_hash` matches the hash of all disclosure strings.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide a secure, sandboxed SDK verification module within the super-app client container that performs the full SD-JWT verification algorithm locally.
Reject any SD-JWT presentation where extraneous or unreferenced disclosure strings are detected, mitigating injection and padding attacks.
Log verification telemetry (claims verified, issuer ID, latency) in the super-app runtime analytics without logging cleartext claim values.

title: IETF SD-JWT: Super-App Identity Wallet Integration, Data Minimization & Privacy Consent UI
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt Section 8 (Privacy Considerations) & Section 9 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: In a super-app ecosystem, third-party mini-apps frequently request user profile attributes; SD-JWT enables user-centric, privacy-preserving disclosure mediation.
When a mini-app requests user data, the super-app native host displays a system-level consent dialog showing the exact claims requested.
The user can selectively toggle which optional claims to reveal; the host wallet releases only the corresponding Disclosures and computes a fresh KB-JWT.
Completely shields sensitive attributes (national ID number, home address, medical info) from the mini-app unless legally mandated and explicitly consented.

Prevents tracking across mini-apps: because each disclosure utilizes a unique random salt, two mini-apps receiving the same attribute value receive different digests unless the same disclosure is shared.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize the super-app system consent sheet for mini-app data requests based on SD-JWT selective disclosure toggles.
Prohibit mini-apps from demanding full credential disclosure when only a subset of attributes (e.g. proof of majority >= 18) is functionally required.
Incorporate automated privacy compliance scanners in the mini-app store pipeline to audit third-party mini-app claim request scopes.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP 1.0): Protocol Architecture, Authorization Request & vp_token Negotiation
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 Section 5 (Authorization Request) & Section 5.1 (Request Parameters)
key_takeaways: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP 1.0) extends OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization frameworks to allow Verifiers (relying parties or mini-apps) to request Verifiable Presentations from End-User Wallets.
The Verifier initiates the request using `response_type=vp_token` (or combined `response_type=id_token vp_token`) directed to the Wallet authorization endpoint.

The authorization request specifies requested credential types and claim requirements via the `presentation_definition` parameter (or referenced remotely via `presentation_definition_uri` / Digital Credentials Query Language `dcql_query`).

The Wallet evaluates the requested credentials against its internal cryptographic credential store, prompts the user with a privacy-preserving consent sheet, and generates the requested verifiable presentation.
Enables standardized, interoperable credential verification across diverse formats including SD-JWT VC, W3C Verifiable Credentials, and ISO/IEC 18013-5 mdoc.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement OID4VP 1.0 protocol endpoints directly within the native super-app identity runtime to handle mini-app verifiable credential verification requests.
Expose an asynchronous JavaScript API (`superapp.identity.requestPresentation({ dcqlQuery: ... })`) to third-party mini-apps that triggers native system wallet presentation flows.
Enforce that `presentation_definition` queries issued by mini-apps are statically declared in mini-app store manifests and validated during catalog security audit.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations: Response Modes, direct_post.jwt & Out-of-Band Transport
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 Section 6 (Response Mode 'direct_post') & Section 6.2 (Response Mode 'direct_post.jwt')
key_takeaways: OID4VP defines the `direct_post` and `direct_post.jwt` response modes to transmit large cryptographic presentations directly from the Wallet to the Verifier's `response_uri` via HTTP POST.
Direct POST completely circumvents URL length limitations and HTTP query string data leakage associated with traditional browser redirects.

Under `direct_post.jwt`, the Wallet encapsulates the response inside a cryptographically signed and encrypted JSON Web Token (JARM RFC 9101 alignment), guaranteeing confidentiality and integrity across untrusted network hops.

The response payload contains the `vp_token` (which may be a single presentation string or a JSON array of presentations) and `presentation_submission` mapping each presentation to the requested input descriptor.
Provides nonces and state validation within the response object, protecting the Verifier against token substitution and injection attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate `direct_post.jwt` with AES-GCM payload encryption for all inter-app and cross-domain verifiable credential presentations within the super-app ecosystem.
Configure the super-app API gateway to validate `response_uri` domains against the registered and TLS-pinned origin of the requesting mini-app.
Provide zero-copy bridge serialization in the super-app container to pass encrypted JWT presentation tokens without string concatenation overhead.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations: Verifier Trust, client_id Schemes & OpenID Federation Metadata
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 Section 5.3 (Verifier Metadata) & Section 8 (Verifier Authenticity & client_id Schemes)
key_takeaways: To establish Verifier authenticity before the Wallet releases sensitive credentials, OID4VP specifies unambiguous `client_id` schemes: `redirect_uri`, `entity_id`, `did`, and `x509_san_dns`.
Under the `entity_id` scheme, Verifier identity is cryptographically validated using OpenID Federation 1.0 Trust Chains originating from an accredited Trust Anchor.
Under `x509_san_dns`, the Verifier's public key and identity are bound to an X.509 certificate whose Subject Alternative Name matches the Verifier's DNS host domain.
The Wallet parses and cryptographically verifies the Verifier's signed Request Object (`request` parameter) or fetches it securely via `request_uri`.
Shields users against malicious phishing mini-apps attempting to pose as trusted banking or government relying parties to harvest digital identity attributes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement the `entity_id` scheme anchored in the super-app operator's root Trust Anchor for all internal mini-app presentation verification.
Reject presentation requests from any mini-app whose `client_id` scheme cannot be cryptographically verified against the store's developer identity registry.
Display an authenticated Trust Badge in the native wallet consent sheet showing the verified legal entity name and trust rating of the requesting mini-app.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations: Cross-Device Presentation, Dynamic QR Codes & request_uri Security
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 Section 5.2 (Cross-Device Flow) & Section 9 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: OID4VP natively supports cross-device credential presentation where the Verifier runs on a desktop, terminal, or POS kiosk, while the Wallet runs on the user's mobile device.
The Verifier renders a dynamic QR code containing an `openid4vp://` deep-link URI with a short-lived, single-use `request_uri` parameter.
When scanned by the mobile super-app wallet, the device fetches the signed Request Object via HTTPS from the `request_uri`, displays the consent UI, and posts the presentation via `direct_post`.
To prevent cross-site request forgery and session fixation, the authorization request must include an ephemeral cryptographic `nonce` generated by the Verifier with at least 128 bits of entropy.
The Verifier polls its backend session (or receives a server-sent event / WebSocket notification) and validates that the `vp_token` matches the issued `nonce` and session state.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement standardized QR code scanning in the super-app camera bridge to automatically parse and route `openid4vp://` requests to the native wallet.
Enforce a maximum TTL of 60 seconds on cross-device `request_uri` handles and invalidate them immediately upon first retrieval.
Bind cross-device presentations to the authenticated user's biometric confirmation prompt in the native super-app before transmitting credentials.

title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations: Verifier Verification Pipeline, Input Evaluation & Anti-Replay Guardrails
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 Section 7 (Verification Process) & Section 7.1 (Cryptographic Checks)
key_takeaways: The Verifier must execute an immutable verification pipeline upon receiving a `vp_token` and `presentation_submission`.
Step 1: Parse the `presentation_submission` and verify that each requested input descriptor in the `presentation_definition` is satisfied by a valid credential.
Step 2: Verify the cryptographic signature of each credential against the authoritative Issuer's public key (fetched from trusted discovery or status lists).
Step 3: Validate the cryptographic proof-of-possession (holder binding) ensuring the presentation was generated by the legitimate key holder matching the credential's `cnf` claim.
Step 4: Check the credential's status list (RFC Token Status List) to confirm the credential has not been revoked or suspended by the issuing authority.
Step 5: Verify the freshness of the `nonce` and timestamp boundaries (`exp`, `nbf`, `iat`) to reject replayed presentations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide a serverless verification utility in the super-app cloud runtime for mini-app backends to execute standardized OID4VP checks without bespoke cryptography.
Mandate real-time Token Status List checking for all high-assurance identity presentations (KYC, legal sign-off, ticketing) in mini-app workflows.
Log verification outcomes with redacted attribute hashes in the platform security audit stream to ensure non-repudiation and dispute resolution readiness.

title: IETF SD-JWT-based Verifiable Credentials (SD-JWT VC): Credential Profiling, vct Identifiers & Type Metadata
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc Section 3 (SD-JWT-based Verifiable Credential Structure) & Section 3.2.2.1 (vct Claim)
key_takeaways: IETF SD-JWT VC profiles the general-purpose SD-JWT specification specifically for digital identity and verifiable credentials ecosystems.
Mandates the `vct` (verifiable credential type) claim as an absolute URI or collision-resistant identifier uniquely denoting the credential schema and semantics.
Specifies Type Metadata endpoints where verifiers and wallets can retrieve JSON Schema definitions, display properties, and localized claim names for each `vct`.
Requires the `iss` (issuer) claim to be an HTTPS URL or DID uniquely identifying the credential issuing authority.
Standardizes the JOSE header typ parameter as `vc+sd-jwt` (or `dc+sd-jwt` for dynamic credentials), preventing credential substitution attacks with regular access tokens.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt `vc+sd-jwt` as the official container format for all super-app issued credentials (such as digital membership, employee badges, and driver permits).
Maintain a centralized, cached Type Metadata catalog in the super-app store repository to validate credential schemas during mini-app deployment.
Enforce strict schema validation on the `vct` claim before presenting credential values to mini-app runtime contexts.

title: IETF SD-JWT VC: Revocation Referencing via status Claim, Status List Sharding & Validity Intervals
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc Section 3.2.2.2 (status Claim) & Section 5 (Trust and Validation)
key_takeaways: SD-JWT VC standardizes credential revocation and suspension via the top-level `status` claim pointing directly to an OAuth Token Status List structure.
The `status` object includes `status_list` with `uri` and `idx` (bit index), enabling sub-millisecond, privacy-preserving cryptographic revocation lookups.
Mandates temporal validity boundaries: credentials must define `iat` (issued at) and `exp` (expiration timestamp), with recommended maximum lifetimes aligned with risk profiles.
Allows optional `nbf` (not before) claims for scheduled future-active credentials (e.g. event passes, seasonal contractor permits).
Because revocation state is externalized in compressed bitstrings, issuers do not learn when, where, or by which mini-app a credential is being verified.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Incorporate automated Token Status List evaluation into the super-app client SDK during credential verification calls.
Mandate that all high-risk mini-app credentials (e.g. financial credentials, access control badges) include an active `status` pointer with <= 1 hour cache TTL.
Reject any SD-JWT VC presentation whose expiration timestamp (`exp`) has elapsed or whose status bit indicates revocation.

title: IETF SD-JWT VC: Holder Key Binding, Hardware Enclave Attestation & Biometric Confirmation
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc Section 4 (Key Binding) & Section 4.1 (Holder-of-Key Presentation)
key_takeaways: SD-JWT VC enforces holder-of-key presentation by binding the credential to a cryptographic key declared in the `cnf` (confirmation) claim of the SD-JWT body.
Supported `cnf` formats include JWK (`cnf.jwk`) and key thumbprints (`cnf.jkt` RFC 7638 SHA-256 digests).
During presentation generation, the holder wallet constructs a fresh Key Binding JWT (`kb+jwt`) signed by the private key corresponding to `cnf`.
The `kb+jwt` binds the verifier's audience (`aud`), fresh verifier `nonce`, timestamp (`iat`), and `sd_hash` (the digest of the exact subset of disclosures revealed).
Enables cryptographic verification that the presenter is the genuine holder and that an eavesdropping or replay attacker cannot present intercepted disclosures.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Generate SD-JWT VC holder key pairs inside hardware-backed secure elements (Android Keystore StrongBox, iOS Secure Enclave) within the super-app native container.
Require biometric user confirmation (Touch ID / Face ID / Android BiometricPrompt) before releasing holder key signatures for credential presentations.
Audit third-party mini-app presentation verification logic to confirm strict verification of `cnf`, `aud`, `nonce`, and `sd_hash`.

title: IETF SD-JWT VC: Identity Assurance, Verification Evidence & eIDAS/Regulatory Trust Mapping
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc Section 6 (Privacy and Security Considerations) & Section 6.2 (Selective Disclosure Trust)
key_takeaways: SD-JWT VC integrates with OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance (IDA) to express identity verification processes, trust frameworks, and verification evidence.
Issuers can attach verified evidence claims (`evidence` array containing document verification records, electronic ID checks, or biometric face-match confidence scores).

Each evidence claim can be placed into its own Disclosure, allowing users to prove that their identity was formally verified (e.g. High Assurance level) without revealing raw identity document images or passport numbers.
Provides seamless alignment with regulatory frameworks such as EU eIDAS 2.0 (European Digital Identity Wallet) and ISO/IEC 18013-5 mobile driving licenses.
Guarantees that verifiers can automate KYC compliance checks programmatically while minimizing data exposure.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Structure identity assurance claims within super-app digital credentials using standardized IDA evidence schemas.
Allow users to selectively present proof of verified KYC tier (e.g. `assurance_level: high`) to financial mini-apps while keeping identity documents undisclosed.
Enforce that mini-app stores record issuer trust framework certifications in the catalog metadata registry.

title: IETF SD-JWT VC: Unlinkability, Anti-Correlation & Pairwise Pseudonymous Identifier Strategies
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc Section 6.1 (Unlinkability and Tracking) & Section 6.3 (Salt Entropy)
key_takeaways: A core privacy threat in verifiable credential ecosystems is verifier correlation: colluding verifiers comparing credential signatures or public keys to track user behavior across apps.
SD-JWT VC mitigates correlation by ensuring all Disclosures utilize cryptographically random salts with at least 128 bits of entropy.
If the Issuer signature over the SD-JWT body is presented to multiple verifiers, the verifiers could potentially correlate the user via the static issuer signature.

To achieve true unlinkability, the standard recommends: (a) issuing batch credentials with single-use presentation capability, or (b) combining SD-JWT with pairwise pseudonymous holder keys (`sub` and `cnf` unique to each relying party).
Issuers can issue multi-credential batches where each credential has an identical set of claims but unique salts and keys, allowing single-presentation usage.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated batch issuance in the super-app wallet for frequently presented credentials (e.g. transit passes, age verification tokens), preventing cross-app tracking.
Generate unique, pairwise pseudonymous holder keys per mini-app when creating Key Binding JWTs (`kb+jwt`).
Prohibit mini-apps from storing or exchanging raw issuer signatures across third-party analytics gateways.

title: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance (OIDC IDA): verified_claims Structure, Trust Frameworks & Evidence Data Model
standard_reference: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance 1.0 Section 4 (Data Structures) & Section 4.1 (verified_claims)
key_takeaways: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance (IDA 1.0) standardizes the representation of legally verified identity data and electronic Know-Your-Customer (eKYC) evidence in OpenID Connect ID Tokens and UserInfo responses.
Defines the top-level `verified_claims` object comprising `verification` metadata and `claims` payload.

The `verification` container specifies `trust_framework` (e.g. `de_aml`, `eidas_ial_high`, `nist_800_63A_ial_3`, or custom enterprise frameworks), `time` of verification, and `verification_process` identifier.

The `evidence` array details the exact verification mechanisms utilized: `id_document` (passport, national ID, residence permit), `electronic_record` (banking or tax registries), `utility_bill`, or `vouch`.
Eliminates ambiguity regarding the provenance, legal strength, and freshness of user identity claims consumed by relying parties.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Structure the super-app eKYC verification service around OIDC IDA `verified_claims` schemas to provide legally robust identity tokens to mini-apps.
Require banking, insurance, and telecommunications mini-apps to request specific `trust_framework` criteria through standard OIDC query claims parameters.
Store verified claims in encrypted local vaults within the super-app container, exposing only validated subsets via the native JS bridge.

title: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance: id_document Evidence, Document Types & Biometric Anti-Spoofing Records
standard_reference: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance 1.0 Section 4.1.1.1 (id_document Evidence) & Section 4.1.1.3 (check_details)
key_takeaways: OIDC IDA defines granular metadata schemas for physical and electronic identity documents inside `evidence` of type `id_document`.
Captures document classification: `type` (e.g., `idcard`, `passport`, `driving_permit`), `document_number`, `issuer` jurisdiction, `date_of_issuance`, and `date_of_expiry`.
Standardizes `method` of inspection: `physical_in_person`, `supervised_remote`, `unsupervised_remote` (AI-based optical recognition), or `electronic_signature`.
Includes `check_details` reporting specific validation outcomes: optical security feature verification, cryptographic chip reading (NFC ICAO 9303), and biometric facial liveness match scores.
Allows relying parties to verify that identity documents were checked for tampering, synthetic spoofing, and validity before authorizing high-risk transactions.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Include `check_details` metadata in the super-app KYC attestation payload to assure mini-app partners of optical and NFC chip authenticity.
Standardize camera-based document capture guidelines and NFC passport chip reading protocols within the super-app device bridge.
Enforce that mini-apps cannot mandate raw document photocopies when verified `id_document` metadata has already been attested by the super-app host.

title: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance: electronic_record Evidence, Government Registries & Source Validation
standard_reference: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance 1.0 Section 4.1.1.2 (electronic_record Evidence)
key_takeaways: OIDC IDA specifies the `electronic_record` evidence type for identity verification verified against external authoritative databases and government registries.
Captures `type` of record (e.g., `banking_record`, `credit_agency_record`, `government_registry`, `telecom_operator_record`), `source` registry name, and registry transaction ID.
Specifies `check_details` detailing whether the authoritative registry confirmed identity attributes synchronously via official API gateways.
Enables telco-backed super-apps (such as Viettel) to integrate SIM ownership registry and national citizen database verification into mini-app identity tokens.
Provides an auditable provenance chain proving that user attributes were sourced directly from authoritative institutional databases.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement telco and national registry integrations as authoritative `electronic_record` providers within the super-app identity gateway.
Provide signed verification receipts referencing the authoritative registry transaction timestamp for enterprise mini-app onboarding.
Redact internal registry identifiers before transmitting electronic record claims to third-party mini-app verifiers.

title: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance: Dynamic Claims Request Syntax, Essential Claims & Assurance Filtering
standard_reference: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance 1.0 Section 5 (Requesting Verified Claims)
key_takeaways: OIDC IDA defines how relying parties request specific verified claims and required assurance levels using the standard OpenID Connect `claims` request parameter.

Relying parties can specify constraints inside `verified_claims`: requiring a specific `trust_framework` (e.g. `{"value": "eidas_ial_high"}`), minimum verification freshness, or acceptable `evidence` types.
Claims can be designated as `essential: true` or optional, allowing the OpenID Provider to determine whether user interaction or step-up verification is required.
The OpenID Provider metadata at `/.well-known/openid-configuration` advertises supported features via `verified_claims_supported`, `trust_frameworks_supported`, and `evidence_supported`.
Enables mini-apps to initiate seamless step-up KYC flows only when an unverified user attempts to access a restricted financial or telecommunications service.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Advertise supported identity assurance capabilities in the super-app identity provider discovery endpoint (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`).
Allow mini-apps to declare required KYC tiers in their manifest, triggering automated in-app eKYC verification when required claims are missing.
Implement granular client authorization policies ensuring that only accredited mini-apps can request high-assurance verified claims.

title: OIDC IDA & Decentralized Verifiable Presentations: Super-App eKYC Synthesis & Cross-Format Interoperability
standard_reference: OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance 1.0 Section 6 (Privacy Considerations) & Section 7 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Synthesizes OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance (OIDC IDA), OID4VP 1.0, and IETF SD-JWT VC into a unified, privacy-preserving digital identity architecture for super-apps.
OIDC IDA provides the standardized legal vocabulary, evidence hierarchy, and trust framework taxonomy for verifying identities.
SD-JWT VC packages IDA verified claims into cryptographically salt-digested, selectively disclosable verifiable credentials.
OID4VP provides the secure runtime request/presentation protocol for mini-apps to verify credentials across in-app WebViews, native bridges, and cross-device POS terminals.

Delivers an end-to-end zero-trust architecture: users retain absolute control over their identity attributes, mini-apps obtain cryptographically verifiable proof of compliance, and platforms enforce data minimization by design.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Establish a unified Super-App Identity Architecture combining OIDC IDA semantic data models, SD-JWT VC packaging, and OID4VP presentation protocols.
Enforce strict data minimization rules across all mini-app store categories: mini-apps must never receive full identity credentials if a zero-knowledge or selective disclosure claim suffices.
Provide developer tooling and mock wallets in the super-app developer sandbox to accelerate compliance testing of decentralized identity flows.

title: W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Integrity 1.0: Cryptographic Proof Architecture & Proof Graph Model
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Integrity 1.0 Section 2 (Overview) & Section 3 (Data Integrity Proofs)
key_takeaways: W3C Data Integrity 1.0 defines a standard mechanism for expressing cryptographic authenticity and integrity proofs across linked-data and JSON-based credential graphs.

Each cryptographic proof is structured as an explicit proof object containing: `type` (e.g. DataIntegrityProof), `cryptosuite` (naming the specific cryptographic suite), `verificationMethod` (URI pointing to the cryptographic key), `proofPurpose` (such as assertionMethod, authentication, or capabilityInvocation), `created` (ISO 8601 timestamp), and `proofValue` (encoded cryptographic signature).

Separates the payload envelope from cryptographic metadata, enabling multiple independent proofs (e.g. co-signatures, notary attestations, countersignatures) over the identical claim graph without altering root data structures.

Unlike legacy Linked Data Signatures (LDS), Data Integrity 1.0 enforces standardized, modular cryptosuite identifiers and strict verification algorithms to prevent ambiguity and signature malleability.
Enables decentralized verifiers (including super-app native runtimes) to inspect and validate publisher assertions deterministically.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize on W3C Data Integrity 1.0 for all developer manifest and mini-app code bundle cryptographic signing within the super-app catalog.
Implement multi-proof verification in the super-app ingestion pipeline to support both publisher assertion signatures and store automated security scan counter-signatures.
Enforce strict schema validation on incoming `proof` objects, rejecting any proof missing mandatory `cryptosuite`, `verificationMethod`, or `proofPurpose` fields.

title: W3C Data Integrity: Canonicalization Pipeline, RDF Dataset Canonicalization & JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity 1.0 Section 4 (Proof Configuration) & Section 5 (Proof Verification)
key_takeaways: Deterministic canonicalization is fundamental to cryptographic integrity across distributed environments where serialization, whitespace, and key order vary.

Data Integrity supports dual canonicalization architectures: RDF Dataset Canonicalization (RDFC-1.0 / canonical RDF-N-Quads via URDNA2015 algorithm) for semantic graph data, and JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS, IETF RFC 8785) for compact, web-native JSON objects.

The proof generation and verification algorithm canonicalizes the document payload and the proof configuration object (containing all proof properties except `proofValue`), generates SHA-256 or SHA-512 cryptographic digests, and concatenates them into a canonical byte sequence for signing.

JCS-based cryptosuites (e.g., `eddsa-jcs-2022`, `ecdsa-jcs-2019`) eliminate the computational overhead and complex RDF graph parsing dependencies, providing sub-millisecond execution ideal for mobile runtimes.
Guarantees bit-for-bit reproducible byte arrays across heterogeneous operating systems, mobile WebViews, and backend ingestion clusters.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate JCS (RFC 8785) canonicalization for all client-side and mobile container mini-app signature verifications to minimize bundle overhead and CPU usage.
Prohibit custom or non-deterministic serialization formats; strictly validate that canonical JSON strings adhere to RFC 8785 sorting rules prior to cryptographic hashing.
Incorporate hardware-accelerated SHA-256 digest routines in the super-app native container bridge to process code bundle hashes at wire speed.

title: W3C Controller Documents & Verification Methods: Cryptographic Key Dereferencing & Purpose Matching
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Controller Documents 1.0 Section 2 (Data Model) & Section 3 (Verification Methods)
key_takeaways: A Controller Document (such as a DID Document or HTTPS-hosted JSON-LD Web Document) expresses the cryptographic verification methods and authorized capabilities of an entity.

The `verificationMethod` URI in a Data Integrity proof must be dereferenced by the verifier to extract the public key material (represented via `publicKeyMultibase` or `publicKeyJwk`) and the authorized controller URI.

The verifier must strictly validate that the dereferenced key is explicitly listed under the required `proofPurpose` relationship (e.g. `assertionMethod` for verifiable credentials/manifests, `authentication` for sessions, `capabilityInvocation` for administrative RPCs).
Prevents key substitution attacks and privilege escalation: a key authorized only for authentication cannot be used to forge valid credential assertions.
Specifies secure key lifecycle practices, key revocation status checks, and support for multi-controller governance models.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement a secure Controller Document resolver inside the super-app gateway that enforces strict URI scheme validation (restricting schemes to `did:web:`, `did:jwk:`, or HTTPS pinned origins).
Enforce strict purpose verification: reject any mini-app deployment package signed with a verification method not explicitly bound to the `assertionMethod` relationship.
Cache resolved Controller Documents locally within the super-app container using HTTP ETag / Cache-Control validation and an immutable developer key database.

title: W3C Data Integrity: Cryptosuite Modularity, Extension Architecture & Secure Suite Negotiation
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity 1.0 Section 6 (Cryptosuite Specifications) & Section 8 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Data Integrity 1.0 decouples proof structure from cryptographic algorithms through an extensible cryptosuite registry model.

A conforming cryptosuite specification must define three mandatory algorithmic interfaces: (1) Transformation/Canonicalizer algorithm, (2) Hashing algorithm, and (3) Signature generation/verification cryptographic primitives.
Cryptosuite identifiers are formally registered in the W3C Cryptosuite Registry or identified by dereferenceable URIs, preventing algorithmic confusion and downgrade attacks.

Verifiers must operate on a strict allowlist of cryptosuites, immediately rejecting unknown, unvetted, or deprecated suites (such as RSA-based legacy LD suites) without evaluating arbitrary dynamic code.
Ensures forward compatibility: newer zero-knowledge or post-quantum cryptosuites can be integrated seamlessly without breaking the underlying credential schema.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Define an explicit, vetted cryptosuite allowlist in the super-app mini-app store standard (e.g. allowing only `eddsa-jcs-2022`, `ecdsa-jcs-2019`, and `bbs-2023`).
Prohibit runtime loading of arbitrary cryptosuite plugins; compile trusted cryptosuite implementations directly into the native mobile SDK.
Establish an automated deprecation timeline for cryptographic suites within the store governance framework to transition away from obsolete algorithms before vulnerabilities arise.

title: W3C Data Integrity for Super-Apps: Publisher Manifest Verification, Offline Sandboxing & Store Trust Anchoring
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity 1.0 Section 5 (Verification Algorithm) & Architectural Guidance
key_takeaways: Applying W3C Data Integrity proofs to mini-app deployment packages enables end-to-end cryptographic supply-chain security from developer workstation to user device.
The mini-app manifest (`manifest.json`) and resource bundle digest table are packaged as an attested Data Integrity document, signed with the publisher's decentralized assertion key.

The super-app store review system verifies the developer's proof upon submission, runs automated AST and sandboxing checks, and attaches a secondary `DataIntegrityProof` endorsing the bundle for public distribution.

The mobile super-app container SDK can verify both proofs offline prior to execution without contacting external identity servers, leveraging cached publisher certificates and the store's embedded root public key.
Guarantees that third-party mini-app code has not been tampered with in transit or modified by malicious CDNs, caching proxies, or compromised storage nodes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Architect the mini-app store packaging specification around W3C Data Integrity dual-proof envelopes (Developer Signature + Store Verification Endorsement).
Implement instant pre-launch cryptographic verification in the super-app WebView loader: fail closed if either proof signature fails or does not match bundle content digests.
Expose proof verification metadata to users via a security trust sheet in the mini-app header bar, displaying verified publisher identity and audit timestamps.

title: W3C Data Integrity Ed25519 Cryptosuites: eddsa-rdfc-2022 & eddsa-jcs-2022 Cryptographic Architecture
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity Ed25519 Cryptosuites v1.0 Section 2 (The eddsa-rdfc-2022 Cryptosuite) & Section 3 (The eddsa-jcs-2022 Cryptosuite)
key_takeaways: Defines two standard cryptosuites based on the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) using the Curve25519 curve and SHA-512.
`eddsa-rdfc-2022` utilizes RDF Dataset Canonicalization (RDFC-1.0) and SHA-256 to hash document statements prior to Ed25519 signing.
`eddsa-jcs-2022` uses the lightweight JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS RFC 8785) with SHA-256, optimized for JSON-native execution environments without RDF parsing requirements.
Public keys are formatted using Multicodec (`0xed` for Ed25519 public key) and encoded in Multibase base58btc (`z6Mk...` prefix), ensuring compact, self-describing key strings.

Ed25519 provides deterministic signatures (eliminating random number generator failures during signing), constant-time execution protecting against timing side-channels, and exceptional verification throughput on mobile processors.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the primary standard cryptosuite for developer code bundle signing and offline super-app mini-app manifest verification.
Embed high-performance Ed25519 assembly or native Rust/C++ primitives into the super-app mobile runtime to achieve sub-millisecond manifest verification times.
Enforce Multibase `z6Mk...` key representation across the developer portal and reject uncompressed raw hexadecimal or proprietary key representations.

title: W3C Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites: ecdsa-rdfc-2019 & ecdsa-jcs-2019 Enterprise Hardware Alignment
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites v1.0 Section 2 (ecdsa-rdfc-2019) & Section 3 (ecdsa-jcs-2019)
key_takeaways: Specifies standardized ECDSA cryptosuites over NIST elliptic curves P-256 (secp256r1) and P-384 (secp384r1) using SHA-256 or SHA-384 hashing.
`ecdsa-rdfc-2019` operates over RDF canonicalized quads, whereas `ecdsa-jcs-2019` applies JCS canonicalization over structured JSON objects.
Supports key representations using Multibase Multicodec (`0x1200` for P-256, `0x1201` for P-384) or JSON Web Keys (JWK RFC 7517) with explicit `crv: P-256` properties.
Directly compatible with native mobile hardware security modules (Apple Secure Enclave on iOS, Android StrongBox / KeyStore, and enterprise HSMs such as FIPS 140-2 Level 3 appliances).
Enables non-exportable hardware-bound key pairs for high-assurance enterprise mini-app publishers and regulated financial service providers.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement `ecdsa-jcs-2019` (P-256) support in the super-app platform to allow enterprise developers to sign mini-app updates directly using HSMs or cloud KMS services.
Leverage native OS APIs (SecKey on iOS, KeyStore on Android) for hardware-accelerated signature validation during mini-app package decompression.
Enforce strict DER-encoded ASN.1 signature parsing or canonical 64-byte IEEE P1363 (r, s) validation to prevent ECDSA signature malleability exploits.

title: W3C Data Integrity: ecdsa-sd-2023 Selective Disclosure & HMAC-Blinded Statement Verification
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites v1.0 Section 4 (The ecdsa-sd-2023 Cryptosuite)
key_takeaways: `ecdsa-sd-2023` introduces selective disclosure capabilities to the standard ECDSA curve ecosystem without requiring complex pairing-friendly zero-knowledge cryptography.
The issuer canonicalizes the RDF graph into individual N-Quads, generates an HMAC secret key, and computes HMAC digests for each discrete quad statement.
The issuer signs a master hash constructed from the combined HMAC digests and issues the credential along with the blinded statement map.

When presenting credentials to a verifier (such as a third-party mini-app), the holder discloses only selected statements alongside the specific HMAC keys for those statements and the original ECDSA signature.
The verifier can verify the authenticity of the disclosed attributes against the master signature without learning any information regarding the undisclosed/blinded attributes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Integrate `ecdsa-sd-2023` in the super-app identity engine as a lightweight, widely supported selective disclosure mechanism for mobile web runtimes.
Provide native mini-app bridge methods (`superapp.identity.presentSelectiveClaims({ claims: [...] })`) that execute HMAC disclosure filtering client-side.
Audit memory handling in container WebViews to ensure HMAC disclosure keys and unrevealed statements are scrubbed immediately from heap memory post-presentation.

title: W3C Data Integrity: Cryptographic Agility, Deterministic Nonces & Side-Channel Mitigation
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity 1.0 Section 8 (Security & Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: Data Integrity specifications establish rigorous security requirements to prevent cryptographic agility vulnerabilities, such as algorithm substitution and cross-curve attacks.
The cryptosuite name and verification method URI are hashed directly into the proof configuration digest, ensuring that an attacker cannot transpose a signature from one curve/suite to another.

For ECDSA implementations, specifications mandate deterministic nonce generation according to RFC 6979 to mitigate catastrophic private key recovery caused by biased or compromised pseudo-random number generators.
Constant-time arithmetic must be enforced across all signature verification and hashing routines to eliminate timing side-channel attacks on shared mobile processor cores.

Canonicalization routines (JCS and RDFC-1.0) specify unambiguous handling of numeric limits (IEEE 754 float64), negative zero, NaN, and Unicode normalization (NFC) to prevent parser desynchronization exploits.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Incorporate automated cryptosuite binding checks in the super-app review pipeline, rejecting any credential where the proof object suite does not match the key curve parameter.
Enforce deterministic RFC 6979 signature generation in developer CLI tools distributed by the super-app developer portal.
Execute automated fuzz testing on the super-app JCS canonicalizer implementation to ensure resilience against malformed numeric encodings and Unicode canonicalization drift.

title: Super-App Container Security: Native Cryptosuite Hardware Acceleration & Sandboxed Bridge API
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity Framework & Native Container Architecture Guidelines
key_takeaways: Executing complex cryptographic canonicalization, hashing, and signature verification inside pure JavaScript WebViews introduces latency and degrades mini-app startup performance.
The native super-app container provides hardware-accelerated cryptographic primitives via an isolated IPC bridge (`superapp.crypto.verifyDataIntegrityProof`).

The bridge transfers the raw credential JSON and proof descriptor across memory boundaries using zero-copy structured clones, verifies the proof in native C++/Rust/Java/Swift, and returns a verified identity token.
Verified publisher identities, verification keys, and status list bitstrings are cached in native secure storage with cryptographic integrity tags.
Isolates cryptographic keys from mini-app DOM access, completely mitigating XSS-based key exfiltration and memory scraping attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement the `superapp.crypto.verifyDataIntegrityProof` native bridge in both Android and iOS container SDKs to offload Data Integrity verification from the JS thread.
Maintain an in-memory cache of verified mini-app package hashes in the native host process to enable instant, zero-latency re-launches of verified mini-apps.
Restrict access to native cryptographic bridge functions based on mini-app permission tiers declared in the mini-app manifest.

title: W3C Data Integrity BBS+ Cryptosuites: Pairing-Friendly Cryptography & Multi-Message Zero-Knowledge Proofs
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity BBS Cryptosuites v1.0 Section 2 (BBS Cryptosuites Overview) & Section 3 (The bbs-2023 Cryptosuite)
key_takeaways: The `bbs-2023` cryptosuite leverages pairing-friendly elliptic curves (specifically the BLS12-381 curve) to enable multi-message digital signatures with advanced zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) properties.
An issuer generates a single BBS signature over a vector of cryptographic messages (derived from canonicalized RDF N-Quads or JCS attribute statements).
The credential holder can derive a cryptographic Proof of Knowledge of the signature without revealing the original signature or the unrevealed messages.

Enables true selective disclosure: a user can disclose only specific claims (such as nationality or verified employment) while cryptographically proving that all attributes originate from a single valid issuer signature.
Eliminates the need for pre-computed HMAC keys or pairwise salted digests required by ECDSA selective disclosure schemes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy BBS+ (`bbs-2023`) support in the super-app identity runtime for maximum privacy in sensitive user attribute verification (e.g. KYC, legal age verification, regulatory licenses).
Embed optimized BLS12-381 pairing libraries (such as blst or native WebAssembly bindings) into the container engine to support fast zero-knowledge proof generation on mobile hardware.
Provide developer tooling and sandbox environments for mini-app developers to test BBS+ credential verification without touching live user identity data.

title: W3C Data Integrity BBS+: Unlinkable Presentations, Anti-Tracking Proofs & Predicate Verification
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Data Integrity BBS Cryptosuites v1.0 Section 4 (Proof Derivation) & Section 6 (Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: Traditional digital signatures and hashed credentials allow colluding relying parties (or mini-apps) to correlate a user's cross-app activities by comparing static signature bytes or persistent identifiers.
BBS+ proofs are dynamically randomized on every presentation: the holder blinds the signature using fresh cryptographic randomness, generating a mathematically unique proof for each presentation.
Two distinct mini-apps receiving BBS+ derived proofs from the same underlying credential cannot correlate or determine whether they originated from the same user or separate users.
Supports cryptographic predicate proofs (zero-knowledge range and inequality proofs), allowing a user to prove `age >= 18` or `credit_score > 700` without disclosing the exact numerical value.
Provides mathematical immunity against cross-app user tracking and commercial behavioral profiling within multi-service super-app platforms.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate BBS+ unlinkable presentations for all third-party mini-app identity verification flows where persistent user identification is not legally required.
Implement standardized zero-knowledge predicate evaluation in the super-app wallet (`superapp.identity.provePredicate({ field: 'age', operator: 'gte', value: 18 })`).
Prohibit mini-apps from storing raw presentation bytes as identifiers; audit mini-app backend data practices to enforce anti-correlation principles.

title: DIF Presentation Exchange 2.1: Presentation Definitions, Input Descriptors & Mini-App Query Matching
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF) Presentation Exchange v2.1.1 Section 4 (Presentation Definition) & Section 6 (Presentation Submission)
key_takeaways: DIF Presentation Exchange (PEX) 2.1 specifies a declarative, interoperable query syntax for verifiers to express credential requirements and for wallets to articulate presentation responses.

A `presentation_definition` object defines one or more `input_descriptors`, each specifying constraints on credential schema (`fields.path`), acceptable cryptographic formats (`format`), and predicate filters (`filter.type`, `filter.minimum`).
`submission_requirements` allow the verifier to specify combinatorial logic (e.g., require credential A AND (credential B OR credential C)).

The wallet's matching engine evaluates available credentials against the input descriptors, generates the matching `vp_token`, and attaches a `presentation_submission` object mapping fulfilled descriptor IDs to specific paths within the presentation.
Decouples mini-app identity querying logic from specific credential implementations, enabling seamless query reuse across SD-JWT, W3C Data Integrity, and mdoc credentials.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Integrate the DIF Presentation Exchange 2.1 evaluation engine into the super-app wallet core to automatically match mini-app credential queries against user wallet contents.
Require mini-apps to declare static `presentation_definition` templates in their store manifest, enabling automated permission scoring and privacy impact analysis during store review.
Provide a declarative visual prompt to users that highlights exactly which fields from which credentials will be shared with the mini-app based on the PEX query.

title: W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0: Compressed Status Bitstrings, Privacy-Preserving Revocation & Local Caching
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0 Section 2 (Data Model) & Section 3 (Status Verification Algorithm)
key_takeaways: W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0 defines a scalable, privacy-preserving standard for checking the status (revoked, suspended, valid) of verifiable credentials.

The status list represents millions of credentials in a single compact bitstring where each credential is assigned a specific bit index (`statusListIndex`) in a status list credential (`statusListCredential`).
Supports 1-bit status (e.g. `statusPurpose: 'revocation'`) and multi-bit status allocations (2-bit or 4-bit, enabling granular states such as valid, suspended, revoked, or compromised).
The bitstring is compressed using Gzip or Deflate and encoded in base64url, allowing 1,000,000 credential statuses to be represented in approximately 120 KB of data.

Crucially protects user privacy: the verifier downloads and caches the entire compressed bitstring (using standard HTTP cache headers), checking the user's index locally without querying the issuer about specific individual credentials.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0 parsing and verification in the super-app credential engine for sub-millisecond local status checks.
Maintain a background synchronization daemon in the super-app client that fetches and updates cached status list bitstrings using conditional HTTP GET (If-None-Match with ETag).
Fail closed on credential presentation if the relevant Bitstring Status List credential cannot be fetched or verified within the defined store cache TTL.

title: Super-App Privacy-Preserving Architecture: Harmonized BBS+ ZKP, DIF PEX & Bitstring Status List Pipeline
category: Decentralized Identity, Credential Issuance & Verifiable State
standard_reference: Super-App Decentralized Identity Synthesis & Architectural Standards
key_takeaways: Synthesizes W3C Data Integrity BBS+ proofs, DIF Presentation Exchange 2.1, and W3C Bitstring Status List v1.0 into a unified, zero-trust digital identity verification pipeline for super-app ecosystems.
When a mini-app requests user verification, it submits a DIF PEX 2.1 `presentation_definition` via the super-app JavaScript bridge.

The super-app native wallet matches user credentials, validates that none are revoked via the locally cached W3C Bitstring Status List, and derives a fresh, unlinkable BBS+ zero-knowledge presentation disclosing only approved attributes and predicate proofs.
The presentation is returned to the mini-app alongside a cryptographic verification attestation signed by the native container.

Achieves the gold standard in privacy: zero correlation across mini-apps, zero disclosure of unrequested attributes, zero phone-home tracking to issuers, and sub-100ms end-to-end presentation latency.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize this tri-part identity architecture (BBS+ ZKP + DIF PEX + Bitstring Status List) as the target Level 3 privacy profile for high-trust enterprise and governmental mini-apps.
Provide native mini-app SDK helpers (`superapp.auth.verifyPrivacyPreservingPresentation`) to abstract cryptographic verification complexity for mini-app developers.
Incorporate automated privacy audits in the super-app app store console to reward mini-apps implementing zero-knowledge predicate proofs with enhanced catalog discovery ranking.

title: W3C DID Core 1.0: Decentralized Identifier Architecture, Uniform Syntax & Graph Model
category: Decentralized Identity, Cryptographic Anchors & Verifiable Credentials
standard_reference: W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0 Section 2 (Core Concepts) & Section 3 (Identifier Syntax)
key_takeaways: W3C DID Core 1.0 standardizes globally unique, cryptographically verifiable identifiers that do not require a centralized registration authority, identity provider, or registry.

A standard DID URI conforms to the syntax `did:<method-name>:<method-specific-id>`, where the method specifies the precise cryptographic and protocol rules for resolution, key material binding, and document updates.

Each DID resolves deterministically into a DID Document conforming to JSON-LD/JSON schemas containing cryptographic public keys, authentication suites, service endpoints, and verification relationships.

Decouples subject identity from administrative control: the DID subject is the entity represented by the DID, while the DID controller is the entity authorized to introduce changes to the DID document.
Eliminates dependency on centralized DNS/domain registries or enterprise identity silos, creating self-sovereign roots of trust across federated mini-app systems.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt W3C DID Core URIs as canonical decentralized publisher and developer identifiers across the super-app store ecosystem.
Establish strict DID syntax validation in the mini-app submission gateway, ensuring all developer identities parse cleanly under RFC 3986 URI and W3C DID Core grammar.
Maintain explicit separation between the developer organization (DID Subject) and authorized enterprise release bots (DID Controllers) in the store publisher console.

title: W3C DID Core: Verification Methods, Cryptographic Suites & Explicit Verification Relationships
category: Decentralized Identity, Cryptographic Anchors & Verifiable Credentials
standard_reference: W3C DID Core v1.0 Section 5.3 (Verification Methods) & Section 5.4 (Verification Relationships)
key_takeaways: Defines explicit verification relationships separating cryptographic privileges: `authentication` (proving control in interactive protocols), `assertionMethod` (issuing verifiable credentials and signing release manifests), `capabilityInvocation` (authorizing actions on behalf of the subject), `capabilityDelegation` (delegating authorization to downstream delegates), and `keyAgreement` (performing ECDH key exchanges).
A single cryptographic key MUST NOT be assumed valid for all operations; it is valid solely for the verification relationships explicitly enumerating it in the DID document.
Supports diverse multibase/multicodec cryptographic encodings (such as Ed25519VerificationKey2020, JsonWebKey2020, and Multikey) to encapsulate public key material cleanly.
Enforces that verification method IDs are fully dereferenceable URIs matching `did:<method>:<id>#<key-fragment>`.
Prevents key cross-contamination and purpose confusion attacks where an ephemeral communication key is deceptively leveraged to assert legal contracts or software releases.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that mini-app code bundle signatures and release manifests strictly reference public keys listed under the publisher's `assertionMethod` verification relationship.
Configure native container Web Crypto and runtime security bridges to reject any mini-app signature if the referenced key is only authorized for `authentication` or `keyAgreement`.
Require explicit verification method URI fragments (e.g. `did:web:developer.example.com#signing-key-1`) in all mini-app package metadata manifests.

title: W3C DID Core: Service Endpoints, Privacy Containment & Controller Document Governance
category: Decentralized Identity, Cryptographic Anchors & Verifiable Credentials
standard_reference: W3C DID Core v1.0 Section 5.5 (Services) & Section 8 (Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: DID Documents express verifiable service endpoints (such as DIDComm messaging nodes, credential issuance endpoints, or developer support gateways) via the `service` property.
Each service entry comprises `id`, `type` (registered or URI-specified protocol), and `serviceEndpoint` (which may be a URI string, object, or URI array for redundant discovery).

Privacy considerations require strict minimization: DID documents must avoid personally identifiable information (PII) or unhashed identifiers, as public DID records create persistent correlation vectors.
Specifies controller governance where one or multiple external DIDs can be declared in the `controller` field, allowing decentralized multisig consortiums to govern enterprise identities.
Prevents trackability by encouraging pairwise or ephemeral DIDs when communicating across untrusted third-party services.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Permit mini-app developers to declare official API and customer support endpoints within their DID document `service` section for automated super-app service discovery.
Enforce a zero-PII policy on published developer DID documents, scanning and rejecting any DID Document containing email addresses, raw phone numbers, or unhashed personal metadata.
Support enterprise multi-controller models (`controller` array) for regulated mini-apps requiring joint sign-off by parent financial institutions or compliance auditors.

title: W3C DID Method Web (did:web): HTTPS Web-Anchored Resolution & Production DNS Governance
category: Decentralized Identity, Cryptographic Anchors & Verifiable Credentials
standard_reference: DID Method Web Specification (W3C CCG) Section 2 (Target System) & Section 3 (Operations)
key_takeaways: `did:web` bridges traditional DNS/Web infrastructure and decentralized identity by transforming a standard domain name or URL path into a resolved DID Document.

A DID of `did:web:example.com` resolves deterministically to `https://example.com/.well-known/did.json`, while a scoped sub-path `did:web:example.com:apps:miniapp1` resolves to `https://example.com/apps/miniapp1/did.json`.
Replaces blockchain transactions with TLS/HTTPS transport security, providing zero-gas, high-performance, and instantly updateable identity documents suitable for web-scale enterprises.
Requires mandatory TLS 1.2+ (strictly recommending TLS 1.3), valid X.509 certificate chains, and HTTP 200 responses with `application/json` or `application/did+ld+json` Content-Type.
Security vulnerability surface is bound to DNS and TLS CA security: DNS hijacking or compromised Web PKI certificates enable malicious DID document substitution unless pinned or anchored.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Support `did:web` as the primary decentralized developer identity method for verified enterprise mini-app publishers possessing verified corporate domains.
Implement automated HTTP cache header compliance (`Cache-Control: max-age=...`) and Certificate Transparency log inspection when resolving `did:web` documents during app ingestion.
Mandate CAA DNS records and DNSSEC validation in the super-app resolver pipeline to mitigate DNS spoofing and unauthorized TLS certificate issuance.

title: W3C DID Resolution: Abstract Architecture, Dereferencing Functions & Resolution Metadata
category: Decentralized Identity, Cryptographic Anchors & Verifiable Credentials
standard_reference: Decentralized Identifier Resolution (W3C Candidate Recommendation Draft) Section 4 (Resolution) & Section 5 (Dereferencing)
key_takeaways: W3C DID Resolution formalizes the abstract `resolve(did)` and `dereference(didUrl)` interfaces, standardizing interoperable resolution across heterogenous DID methods.

The `resolve()` function produces a 3-part tuple: `didDocument` (the core JSON/JSON-LD data model), `didResolutionMetadata` (containing `contentType`, error codes, and resolution timing), and `didDocumentMetadata` (containing `created`, `updated`, `deactivated`, and version tags).
`dereference()` handles DID URLs containing paths, queries, and fragments (e.g. `did:web:example.com?versionId=1#key-1`), retrieving discrete cryptographic keys or services directly.
Specifies standardized error codes: `invalidDid`, `notFound`, `representationNotSupported`, and `methodNotSupported` to enable robust client-side error handling.
Provides the foundational abstraction layer allowing super-app runtimes to resolve developer keys across web, blockchain, and peer-to-peer methods uniformly.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Embed a standardized DID Resolver client in the super-app core gateway and developer CLI, implementing the `resolve()` and `dereference()` interfaces.
Evaluate `didDocumentMetadata.deactivated` during every package download and background sync; immediately suspend execution of mini-apps whose publisher DID is flagged deactivated.
Log `didResolutionMetadata` latency and caching metrics in super-app APM to detect degraded resolver endpoints and DNS propagation bottlenecks.

title: DIF DIDComm Messaging v2.0: Message Framing, Plaintext Model & Cryptographic JWM Signatures
category: Decentralized Messaging, Agent Protocol & Secure Inter-App Comm
standard_reference: DIDComm Messaging Spec v2.0 Section 2 (Message Anatomy) & Section 3 (Message Formats)
key_takeaways: DIDComm Messaging v2.0 standardizes secure, private, transport-agnostic communication between decentralized identities (DIDs) utilizing JSON Web Messages (JWM / RFC 7515/7516).

A standard DIDComm message envelope contains: `id` (unique message UUID), `type` (protocol URI identifier, e.g. `https://didcomm.org/issue-credential/2.0/offer-credential`), `body` (protocol payload), `from` (sender DID URI), `to` (array of recipient DID URIs), `created_time`, and `expires_time`.

Defines three core envelope formats: Plaintext (unencrypted, debug/routing only), Signed (cryptographically non-repudiable JWS using the sender's assertion/authentication key), and Encrypted (authenticated end-to-end encryption).
Signatures are formatted as JSON Web Signatures (JWS) where the protected header declares `typ: application/didcomm-signed+json` and `kid` matching the sender's DID verification method.
Enables decentralized peer-to-peer messaging between mini-apps, host apps, and enterprise backends across heterogenous networks without persistent IP connections.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize on DIDComm v2.0 message framing for asynchronous, cross-origin communication between independent mini-apps and external agent services.
Mandate cryptographic signature verification on all administrative or policy notification messages dispatched from mini-app developer backends to the super-app container.
Reject unsigned plaintext DIDComm messages in production mini-app runtime environments, strictly enforcing Signed or Encrypted envelopes.

title: DIF DIDComm Messaging v2.0: Authenticated Encryption (authcrypt vs anoncrypt) & ECDH Key Agreement
category: Decentralized Messaging, Agent Protocol & Secure Inter-App Comm
standard_reference: DIDComm Messaging Spec v2.0 Section 3.3 (Encrypted Message) & Section 3.4 (Algorithms)
key_takeaways: DIDComm v2 Encrypted Messages wrap inner payloads within JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structures using standardized cryptographic curves: X25519 (ECDH-1PU / ECDH-ES) or NIST P-256 / P-384.

Specifies two distinct encryption modes: `authcrypt` (authenticated encryption providing sender authenticity, confidentiality, and non-repudiation between known DIDs) and `anoncrypt` (anonymous encryption hiding sender identity while preserving recipient confidentiality).

Leverages ECDH-1PU (One-Pass Unified Diffie-Hellman) for authenticated multi-recipient encryption, generating a shared key from the sender's private key, recipient's public key, and ephemeral keypair.
Content encryption utilizes AEAD algorithms: `A256CBC-HS512` or `A256GCM` to guarantee integrity, ciphertext authenticity, and resistance against padding oracle attacks.
Prevents eavesdropping and metadata analysis by intermediaries (such as push notification brokers or cloud relays).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement `authcrypt` with X25519 / A256GCM in the super-app native crypto container bridge for all sensitive inter-mini-app data exchange (e.g. KYC token transfers, payment tickets).
Expose a sandboxed JS API (`superapp.didcomm.encrypt` and `decrypt`) ensuring ephemeral keys and hardware-backed private keys never leak into the mini-app WebView execution context.
Enforce strict sender DID validation upon `authcrypt` decryption, rejecting messages where the authenticated sender does not match declared manifest permissions.

title: DIF DIDComm Messaging v2.0: Multi-Hop Routing, Forward Protocol & Onion Encryption
category: Decentralized Messaging, Agent Protocol & Secure Inter-App Comm
standard_reference: DIDComm Messaging Spec v2.0 Section 5 (Routing) & Section 5.1 (Routing Protocol)
key_takeaways: DIDComm v2 multi-hop routing enables secure message transit across intermediary mediators, edge gateways, and push relays without decrypting payload content.
Employs nested onion encryption (`Forward` protocol): the original encrypted message is nested within a `https://didcomm.org/routing/2.0/forward` message envelope targeted at the next hop relay.
Each intermediate mediator can only decrypt its immediate outer layer to discover the `next` recipient DID/URI, possessing zero visibility into internal message content or downstream recipients.
Accommodates mobile edge devices that lack static IP addresses or are behind NAT/firewalls through mediator inboxing and push pickup protocols.
Prevents network-level tracking, traffic correlation, and IP address harvesting of mobile mini-app users by third-party services.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy a high-availability Super-App Mediator Gateway service implementing the DIDComm Forward protocol to buffer incoming messages for offline mini-apps.
Enforce multi-layer onion encryption when routing messages between third-party mini-app microservices and the host super-app.
Strip internal network IP headers and telemetry metadata at the super-app edge mediator before forwarding messages to mini-app endpoints.

title: DIF DIDComm Messaging v2.0 & v2.1: HTTP/WebSocket Transport Bindings & Protocol Lifecycles
category: Decentralized Messaging, Agent Protocol & Secure Inter-App Comm
standard_reference: DIDComm Messaging Spec v2.1 Section 6 (Transports) & Section 7 (Protocols)
key_takeaways: Standardizes transport bindings for HTTP/HTTPS POST requests (`application/didcomm-encrypted+json`) and full-duplex WebSocket connections.
HTTP binding requires HTTP 200/202 status codes: 200 with an encrypted DIDComm response body for synchronous reply flows, or 202 Accepted for asynchronous out-of-band delivery.
Defines protocol state machine primitives including `thid` (thread ID to correlate multi-turn request-response conversations) and `pthid` (parent thread ID for nested workflows).
Supports standard protocol lifecycles: Discover Features (`https://didcomm.org/discover-features/2.0`), Issue Credential, Present Proof, and Trust Ping.
Decouples application logic from physical transport, permitting the same protocol conversation to seamlessly hop between Bluetooth, WebSockets, and HTTPS.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement bidirectional WebSocket transport bindings in the super-app native container to support real-time DIDComm messaging with sub-100ms latency.
Enforce thread tracking (`thid`) in the inter-mini-app IPC bridge to prevent message reordering, dropped RPCs, and race conditions during multi-step credential exchanges.
Expose the Discover Features protocol to allow mini-apps to dynamically negotiate protocol capabilities and supported versions prior to initiating transactions.

title: DIF DIDComm Messaging: Out-of-Band (OOB) Invitations, Deep-Linking & Super-App QR Bridging
category: Decentralized Messaging, Agent Protocol & Secure Inter-App Comm
standard_reference: DIDComm Messaging Spec v2.0 Section 8 (Out-of-Band Protocols)
key_takeaways: Out-of-Band (OOB) invitations establish initial contact, channel discovery, and goal negotiation between two entities that do not share an existing connection.

An OOB message includes: `goal_code` (e.g. `issue-vc`, `request-proof`, `p2p-chat`), `accept` (array of supported message MIME types and versions), `handshake_protocols`, and `services` (array of DID or inline service endpoints).
Easily encoded into compact URLs or high-density 2D QR codes (e.g. `https://superapp.example/oob?_oob=<base64url-encoded-oob-message>`).
Eliminates preliminary key negotiation friction, allowing instant one-click or scan-to-connect onboarding between physical merchants and mobile mini-apps.
Protects users against malicious connection injection by requiring human-in-the-loop confirmation before establishing persistent agent relationships.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Integrate native camera QR scanning and deep-link routing for DIDComm OOB invitations directly into the super-app top-level shell.
Display a standardized security consent card showing the target developer's verified DID, domain name, and requested `goal_code` before launching the target mini-app.
Prevent malicious mini-apps from silently parsing OOB payloads without explicit user permission and camera gating.

title: FIDO Alliance CTAP 2.1: Client-to-Authenticator Protocol Architecture & Framing
standard_reference: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Proposed Standard Section 5 (Protocol Details) & Section 6 (Framing)
key_takeaways: FIDO CTAP 2.1 defines the low-level binary protocol governing communication between a client platform (super-app host OS) and a hardware authenticator (USB/NFC/BLE security keys or on-chip secure enclaves).

All commands and responses are serialized using Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR / RFC 8949) over structured packet frames, minimizing wire overhead and parsing complexity on constrained microcontrollers.

Core command set includes `authenticatorMakeCredential` (0x01), `authenticatorGetAssertion` (0x02), `authenticatorGetInfo` (0x04), `authenticatorClientPin` / `authenticatorBioEnrollment` (0x06), `authenticatorCredentialManagement` (0x07), and `authenticatorSelection` (0x0B).

Framing layer handles packet fragmentation and reassembly across raw HID, ISO 7816 smart card APDUs (NFC), and BLE GATT characteristics, guaranteeing reliable transmission of large cryptographic attestations.
Establishes physical proof of possession and tamper resistance that cannot be intercepted by rogue WebView scripts or compromised operating system memory.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Leverage CTAP 2.1 primitives via the super-app native container to authenticate high-value transactions and enterprise administrative approvals.
Implement CBOR message boundary validation in the native hardware bridge to protect against malformed framing payloads from untrusted external USB/BLE peripherals.
Query `authenticatorGetInfo` prior to issuing authentication requests to verify authenticator version, supported algorithms, and hardware security certifications.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.1: User Verification, PIN/UV Auth Protocol v2 & Ephemeral ECDH Key Agreement
standard_reference: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Section 5.5 (PIN/UV Auth Protocol v1 and v2)
