key_takeaways: CTAP 2.1 introduces PIN/UV Auth Protocol v2 to securely establish user presence and user verification (PIN or biometrics) over untrusted physical buses without exposing raw PINs or biometric templates to the client platform.
Employs ephemeral ECDH key exchange using NIST P-256 or COSE algorithm -7, deriving a shared encryption key (`sharedSecret`) via HKDF-SHA-256.

The client platform sends an encrypted PIN hash or requests biometric verification; upon success, the authenticator issues an encrypted, time-limited token (`pinUvAuthToken`) bound to specific permissions (`mc` for makeCredential, `ga` for getAssertion, `cm` for credentialManagement).
Mitigates eavesdropping and replay attacks across shared USB/NFC connections through mandatory message authentication codes (HMAC-SHA-256) on every privileged command.
Guarantees that mini-apps cannot brute-force PINs or capture user biometric secrets.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce PIN/UV Auth Protocol v2 in the super-app hardware security module, strictly prohibiting deprecated v1 implementations.
Scope derived `pinUvAuthToken` permissions strictly to the active mini-app transaction, immediately clearing tokens from platform RAM upon completion.
Trap and handle authenticator error codes (`CTAP2_ERR_PIN_BLOCKED`, `CTAP2_ERR_PIN_AUTH_BLOCKED`) gracefully within the super-app UI shell.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.1: Credential Management API, Discoverable Credentials & Enterprise Attestation
standard_reference: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Section 5.8 (authenticatorCredentialManagement)
key_takeaways: CTAP 2.1 formalizes the Credential Management API (`authenticatorCredentialManagement`), enabling platforms to enumerate, inspect, and delete resident/discoverable credentials stored inside hardware authenticators.

Credentials can be queried by Relying Party ID hash (`rpIdHash`), returning public credential metadata (`user.id`, `user.name`, `user.displayName`, `credId`) while keeping private keys strictly sealed.
Enables seamless account chooser UI in client platforms without requiring preliminary username entry, drastically streamlining passkey sign-in experiences.

Supports Enterprise Attestation, allowing managed authenticators to return uniquely identifiable attestation certificates to enterprise relying parties while preserving consumer privacy in public contexts.
Includes storage reporting capabilities, allowing clients to query remaining discoverable credential slots on hardware tokens.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement a secure Credential Management panel within the super-app account settings, allowing users to view and revoke hardware passkeys associated with individual mini-apps.
Isolate credential queries strictly by mini-app origin: prevent mini-app A from enumerating or discovering passkeys registered to mini-app B or the super-app host.
Utilize Enterprise Attestation for internal corporate mini-apps to bind developer and operator access exclusively to organization-issued security keys.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.1: Large Blob Storage (largeBlobs), Bio Enrollment & Authenticator Config
standard_reference: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Section 5.10 (authenticatorLargeBlobs) & Section 5.7 (authenticatorBioEnrollment)
key_takeaways: CTAP 2.1 introduces `authenticatorLargeBlobs`, providing an authenticated storage partition on hardware tokens to persist arbitrary data blobs (e.g. encrypted encryption keys, identity certificates, session tickets).
Large blobs can be read or written either during standard `authenticatorGetAssertion` / `authenticatorMakeCredential` calls or via dedicated `largeBlobs` command sub-operations.
`authenticatorBioEnrollment` standardizes on-authenticator fingerprint and biometric sample enrollment, sample quality feedback, and template revocation directly via platform UI.
`authenticatorConfig` enables toggleable hardware options, such as enterprise attestation enforcement and minimum PIN length configuration.
Provides an ultra-secure, hardware-bound persistence mechanism for cryptographic credentials that survive device operating system reinstalls.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Leverage `largeBlobs` to store encrypted DID private recovery seeds and offline session tokens on supported FIDO authenticators.
Provide native progress dialogs in the super-app UI during biometric sample registration using `authenticatorBioEnrollment` status codes.
Enforce hardware PIN policy controls (e.g. minimum 6 digits) via `authenticatorConfig` for enterprise-grade mini-app deployments.

title: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Extensions: hmac-secret, PRF (Pseudo-Random Function) & Hardware Vault Synthesis
standard_reference: FIDO CTAP 2.1 Section 9 (Extensions) & FIDO Registry Section 3 (Extension Identifiers)
key_takeaways: CTAP 2.1 defines standardized extensions: `hmac-secret` and `prf` (WebAuthn Pseudo-Random Function extension) to derive symmetric cryptographic secrets directly from hardware authenticators.

The client provides salt inputs (`salt1`, optional `salt2`); the authenticator processes the salt through HMAC-SHA-256 using an internal secret associated with the specific credential ID, returning output MACs.
Crucially, the raw hardware master secret is never exposed to the client platform; derived output changes deterministically based solely on the credential and salt provided.
Enables client-side encryption of offline databases (IndexedDB/OPFS), local secure enclaves, and decentralized identity wallets using passkey authentication.
Forms the cryptographic backbone for zero-knowledge end-to-end encrypted mini-app state synchronization across multi-device ecosystems.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose a sandboxed WebAuthn PRF bridge to mini-apps for deriving client-side AES-GCM database encryption keys directly from hardware authenticators.
Standardize salt management in the super-app container to prevent cross-app key derivation collisions and rainbow table attacks.
Enforce strict user verification (`uv=required`) whenever a mini-app invokes the PRF extension to retrieve sensitive cryptographic keys.

title: OpenID Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2): Protocol Architecture, Discovery & Self-Issued OP Metadata
category: Decentralized Identity, SIOPv2 & Direct Wallet Authentication
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2) Section 5 (Self-Issued OpenID Provider Discovery)
key_takeaways: SIOPv2 defines an OpenID Connect deployment profile where the OpenID Provider (OP) runs locally on the user's personal device (e.g. mobile wallet, super-app identity vault) rather than on a remote third-party server.

Enables decentralized, peer-to-peer authentication directly between a Relying Party (mini-app or web application) and the end-user's device wallet without introducing central IdP tracking or single points of failure.
Self-Issued OP metadata can be statically known or dynamically discovered; SIOPv2 defines the standard issuer identifier 'https://self-issued.me/v2' or decentralized identifier (DID) representations.

The Self-Issued OP exposes supported cryptographic signing algorithms ('id_token_signing_alg_values_supported': ES256, EdDSA), subject syntax types ('subject_syntax_types_supported': 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:jwk-thumbprint', 'did:key', 'did:peer', 'did:web'), and presentation formats.
Eliminates dependency on third-party identity servers, ensuring high availability, offline authentication capabilities, and sovereign identity control for mobile clients.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Embed an RFC-compliant SIOPv2 Self-Issued OP runtime directly inside the super-app identity engine, allowing mini-apps to authenticate users locally via standard OIDC protocols.
Publish supported subject syntax types and cryptosuites in the super-app container discovery profile, mandating hardware-backed curves (ES256, EdDSA).
Standardize discovery and client metadata negotiation to ensure mini-apps can query container wallet authentication capabilities without network overhead.

title: SIOPv2 Authorization Request Negotiation, Client Metadata & Direct Presentation Handshakes
category: Decentralized Identity, SIOPv2 & Direct Wallet Authentication
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2) Section 6 (Authorization Request) & Section 9 (Client Metadata)
key_takeaways: Relying Parties initiate SIOPv2 flows by sending an authorization request specifying 'scope=openid', 'response_type=id_token', and explicit 'client_metadata' containing the RP's JWKS or jwks_uri.

Supports client identifier schemes including 'redirect_uri', 'entity_id' (OpenID Federation), and 'did' (e.g. did:web, did:peer), enabling mutual cryptographic authentication between mini-app and wallet.

Standardizes 'response_mode=direct_post' and 'direct_post.jwt', routing the authentication assertion directly from the device wallet to the RP's backend endpoint over HTTPS, preventing token interception in front-channel browser history.
Mandates fresh, cryptographically random 'nonce' and 'state' parameters with high entropy (>= 128 bits) to eliminate replay attacks across asynchronous wallet handshakes.
Allows the RP to convey required subject syntax types via 'client_metadata', ensuring the wallet generates an ID Token matching the RP's supported cryptographic identifier schemes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose an in-process native bridge method ('superapp.auth.requestSIOPAssertion') allowing mini-apps to dispatch SIOPv2 requests directly to the host container without HTTP redirection latency.
Enforce 'direct_post.jwt' response mode for all mini-app SIOPv2 interactions to encrypt responses via JARM directly to the mini-app's verified public keys.
Implement strict origin and client_id validation in the super-app wallet dialog, preventing rogue mini-apps from impersonating legitimate enterprise relying parties.

title: Self-Issued ID Token Cryptographic Generation, Subject Syntax Types & Key Binding
category: Decentralized Identity, SIOPv2 & Direct Wallet Authentication
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2) Section 10 (ID Token)
key_takeaways: The Self-Issued ID Token is a cryptographically signed JSON Web Token (JWS) issued and signed directly by the user's device wallet using an asymmetric private key held in secure hardware.
The 'iss' claim must match 'https://self-issued.me/v2' or the user's Decentralized Identifier (e.g. 'did:key:z6M...', 'did:peer:2...').

When using JWK Thumbprints, the 'sub' claim contains the base64url-encoded SHA-256 thumbprint of the user's public key (RFC 7638), and the ID Token includes the public key in the 'sub_jwk' header or claim.

The Relying Party verifies the ID Token signature against the public key declared in 'sub_jwk' (or dereferenced from the DID document in 'iss') and re-calculates the thumbprint to verify subject identity.
Enforces tight temporal constraints ('exp' <= 5 minutes from 'iat') and checks the 'aud' claim matches the RP's client_id and 'nonce' matches the request, guaranteeing freshness and non-repudiation.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Bind the Self-Issued ID Token signing keys directly to the device's hardware enclave (Apple Secure Enclave or Android Keystore StrongBox) with biometric authentication prompts.
Generate pairwise pseudonymous keys per mini-app origin when using JWK thumbprint syntax to prevent cross-app user tracking within the super-app ecosystem.
Provide client-side verification SDKs in the mini-app runtime to validate self-issued ID Tokens locally in sub-millisecond execution cycles.

title: SIOPv2 Integration with OID4VP Verifiable Presentations, dcql_query & Holder-of-Key Attestation
category: Decentralized Identity, SIOPv2 & Direct Wallet Authentication
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2) Section 12 (Cross-Device Flows) & OID4VP Annex A
key_takeaways: SIOPv2 converges seamlessly with OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP 1.0) by allowing the authorization request to include 'response_type=id_token vp_token'.
Enables a single transaction to execute both identity authentication (self-issued ID Token) and verifiable credential presentation (e.g. mDL, SD-JWT VC, W3C VC).

The authorization request specifies query criteria via 'presentation_definition' or Digital Credentials Query Language ('dcql_query'), requesting targeted credentials with attribute-level selective disclosure.
The self-issued ID Token includes the 'vp_token' in its response, cryptographically binding the presented verifiable claims to the holder's ephemeral authentication key.
Provides an end-to-end decentralized trust model where relying parties can verify government-issued or enterprise-certified credentials without contacting the issuing authority at presentation time.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Support joint 'id_token vp_token' response types across mini-app authentication bridges to streamline eKYC, onboarding, and access control flows into a single user gesture.
Implement DCQL query parsing in the super-app wallet engine to resolve and present matching credentials from local storage with minimal latency.
Enforce holder-of-key cryptographic binding between the presented vp_token and the self-issued ID Token to prevent credential replay and relay attacks.

title: SIOPv2 Security Architecture: Phishing Defense, Origin Isolation & Super-App Wallet Consent Mediation
category: Decentralized Identity, SIOPv2 & Direct Wallet Authentication
standard_reference: OpenID Connect Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2 (SIOPv2) Section 13 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Self-Issued OPs face unique attack vectors: malicious mini-apps can spoof RP client metadata, trick users into signing arbitrary payloads, or intercept responses via modified URI schemes.

Mitigates phishing and clickjacking by mandating that the wallet UI present a clear, un-spoofable consent dialogue showing the verified identity of the relying party, requested scopes, and target endpoints.
Direct post responses must enforce TLS 1.3 with valid CA certificates or mTLS; plain HTTP endpoints are strictly prohibited to prevent credential sniffing.
Pairwise pseudonymous identifier generation is essential to protect user privacy: sharing a static global public key across all relying parties would create an immutable correlation identifier.
The wallet must isolate private key operations within isolated security domains, ensuring mini-app sandbox code cannot access raw private keys or execute unprompted signatures.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement a mandatory out-of-process system consent sheet in the super-app container that displays verified mini-app store identity and requested claims before dispatching SIOPv2 responses.
Mandate pairwise key derivation: automatically derive distinct Ed25519/P-256 keypairs per mini-app app_id using HKDF with a hardware-protected master seed.
Audit all mini-app SIOPv2 requests against store verification metadata, instantly flagging and revoking mini-apps attempting to spoof third-party domains.

title: DIF Peer DID Method (did:peer): Architecture, Zero-Cost Scaling & Sovereign Bilateral Trust
category: Decentralized Identity, Peer DIDs & Ephemeral Trust Sandboxing
standard_reference: DIF Peer DID Method Specification Section 1 (Introduction) & Section 2 (Core Concepts)
key_takeaways: The `did:peer` method specifies completely decentralized, off-ledger, zero-cost Decentralized Identifiers designed specifically for peer-to-peer and bilateral communication contexts.

Unlike ledger-based DIDs (e.g. did:ion, did:indy) or web-anchored DIDs (did:web), `did:peer` requires zero external registry transactions, eliminating network latency, gas/transaction fees, and availability bottlenecks.

Enables sovereign, pairwise-unique identity relationships: Alice and Bob (or a mini-app and a host service) can establish a mutually private DID relationship with zero external visibility or third-party tracking.
Cryptographically binds public keys, key agreements, and service endpoints directly into the identifier or bilateral synchronizations, adhering strictly to the W3C DID Core 1.0 abstract data model.
Provides an optimal trust primitive for mobile super-apps where hundreds of ephemeral or domain-isolated mini-apps interact with host services without polluting public blockchains or DNS domains.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize `did:peer` as the default identifier format for mini-app internal service bindings and inter-app communication channels.
Generate unique pairwise `did:peer` instances per mini-app installation to eliminate cross-app identity correlation and leakage.
Eliminate central registry queries for local container interactions by resolving `did:peer` documents in-memory via deterministic algorithmic decoders.

title: did:peer Inception Algorithms: Method 0 (Inception Key Fingerprint) & Method 1 (Genesis Document Hash)
category: Decentralized Identity, Peer DIDs & Ephemeral Trust Sandboxing
standard_reference: DIF Peer DID Method Specification Section 3.1 (Method 0: Inception Key) & Section 3.2 (Method 1: Genesis Doc)
key_takeaways: Method 0 (`did:peer:0<multibase-key>`) encodes a single public signing key directly in the identifier using Multicodec and Multibase base58btc or base64url encoding (identical to `did:key`).
Method 0 generates an immutable DID Document containing a single verification method for authentication and assertion, requiring zero state synchronization or network communication.
Method 1 (`did:peer:1<multibase-hash>`) derives the identifier from the cryptographic SHA-256 hash of an initial genesis DID Document, establishing an immutable cryptographic root of trust.
In Method 1, the full genesis DID Document is communicated once out-of-band or during protocol handshake; the recipient validates that the hash of the document strictly matches the DID string.

Method 0 provides minimal overhead for static signing keys, while Method 1 allows rich multi-key configurations, custom service endpoints, and complex verification relationships established at inception.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Use Method 0 for lightweight, short-lived mini-app worker threads and ephemeral background tasks needing basic signature verification.
Leverage Method 1 during mini-app initial installation handshakes to establish a multi-key bilateral contract with the host container.
Provide zero-allocation native parsers in the super-app runtime to unpack Method 0 and verify Method 1 genesis hashes with zero heap fragmentation.

title: did:peer Method 2: Inline Multi-Key Encoding, Service Endpoint Abstraction & Self-Contained Resolution
category: Decentralized Identity, Peer DIDs & Ephemeral Trust Sandboxing
standard_reference: DIF Peer DID Method Specification Section 3.3 (Method 2: Multiple Keys Inline)
key_takeaways: Method 2 (`did:peer:2.<element>.<element>...`) encapsulates multiple public keys, key agreement keys, and service endpoints directly within the DID string itself using compact dot-delimited elements.

Element prefixes standardize capabilities: `.V` specifies verification keys (e.g. Ed25519 for authentication/assertion), `.E` specifies encryption/key-agreement keys (e.g. X25519 for ECDH), and `.S` specifies service endpoints.
Service endpoints are encoded using compact JSON or base64url serialization, mapping directly to message routing protocols (e.g. DIDComm Messaging URIs, WebSocket endpoints, internal bridge schemes).
Enables 100% self-contained resolution: any party receiving a Method 2 DID can reconstruct the complete W3C-compliant DID Document deterministically without requesting external data.
Eliminates the 'genesis document discovery' phase required by Method 1, allowing instant, authenticated, end-to-end encrypted communication upon receiving the identifier.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt Method 2 (`did:peer:2...`) as the primary identifier format for inter-mini-app service routing and host bridge messaging.
Encode both Ed25519 authentication keys and X25519 key-agreement keys into the mini-app's Method 2 identifier to support simultaneous signing and encryption.
Embed internal URI schemes (e.g. `superapp://bridge/mini-app-channel`) into the `.S` service element to route inter-app messages through native IPC queues.

title: did:peer Method 4: Dynamic State Evolution, Key Rotation & Delta CRDT Synchronization
category: Decentralized Identity, Peer DIDs & Ephemeral Trust Sandboxing
standard_reference: DIF Peer DID Method Specification Section 3.5 (Method 4: Dynamic State) & Section 4 (State Machine)
key_takeaways: Method 4 standardizes long-term dynamic evolution for peer DIDs, enabling key rotation, service endpoint updates, and capability additions over an established bilateral channel.
State transitions are represented as cryptographically signed delta records (patches) chained sequentially from the genesis state, verified using authorization rules defined in the prior state.
Does not require a consensus blockchain; synchronization occurs strictly between the two bilateral peers using Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDT) or linear micro-ledgers.
Enforces strict anti-forking rules: every state transition must reference the cryptographic hash of the immediate prior state and must be signed by currently authorized key material.

Enables robust enterprise key hygiene: compromised keys can be rotated out, algorithms upgraded (e.g. classical to post-quantum curves), and endpoints modified without breaking existing relationship trust.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Support Method 4 state updates for long-lived enterprise mini-app partnerships, allowing seamless key rotation without requiring mini-app re-installation.
Maintain a sandboxed append-only state ledger in the host container's encrypted storage to record verified did:peer state delta transitions.
Enforce automatic revocation and channel termination if a peer presents an invalid delta signature or attempts a state bifurcation.

title: did:peer & DIDComm Messaging v2.0: Zero-Trust Inter-App Channels & Cryptographic Leak Sandboxing
category: Decentralized Identity, Peer DIDs & Ephemeral Trust Sandboxing
standard_reference: DIF Peer DID Method Specification Section 5 (Security Considerations) & DIDComm Messaging v2.0
key_takeaways: Pairing `did:peer` with DIDComm Messaging v2.0 creates a complete zero-trust, end-to-end encrypted application-layer security boundary between mini-apps and host services.
Messages are framed as JSON Web Messages (JWM) encrypted using Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD A256GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) over ephemeral Diffie-Hellman shared secrets (X25519).
Eliminates dependency on underlying transport security: messages remain encrypted and signed even if intercepted in WebView bridge logs, IPC buffers, or proxy routers.
Guarantees forward secrecy: ephemeral key agreements ensure that compromise of an authenticator's long-term root key cannot decrypt past conversation history.

Provides strict isolation against malicious mini-apps: a mini-app cannot impersonate another app because the recipient decrypts and verifies messages using keys strictly bound to that specific bilateral peer DID.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy DIDComm v2.0 authenticated encrypted messaging over internal postMessage and bridge channels for all high-risk financial and identity transactions.
Enforce ephemeral key exchange per session to guarantee forward secrecy for inter-mini-app communications.
Isolate DIDComm private key operations within native host cryptographic worker processes, strictly prohibiting raw private key access from JavaScript sandboxes.

title: ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL Security Architecture: MobileSecurityObject (MSO), CBOR & COSE Signatures
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 Section 9.1 (mDL Data Structure & Mobile Security Object)
key_takeaways: ISO/IEC 18013-5 standardizes the Mobile Driving Licence (mDL) digital document format and security architecture, implemented across state and national mobile identity deployments worldwide.
The data model is encoded using Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR, RFC 8949) and signed using CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE, RFC 9052) structures, specifically COSE_Sign1.

The root cryptographic artifact is the MobileSecurityObject (MSO), issued and signed by the issuing authority; it contains metadata, cryptographic algorithms, validity periods, and digests of all individual data elements.
Each namespace (e.g. 'org.iso.18013.5.1') contains a digest mapping: the MSO holds a map of element identifiers to their SHA-256 digests rather than cleartext values.

Enables non-repudiable issuance integrity: the verifier verifies the COSE_Sign1 signature over the MSO against the issuer's public key (retrieved via trusted ICAO Master List or national PKI), ensuring data has not been modified.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Embed a high-performance native CBOR/COSE parsing and verification engine in the super-app container to handle ISO 18013-5 mDL credentials without third-party web polyfills.
Maintain an authoritative issuer certificate cache within the super-app identity manager, synchronized with certified trust registries for off-line verification.
Validate MSO signature status, validity dates ('validityInfo.signed', 'validityInfo.validUntil'), and revocation status before accepting mDL presentations.

title: ISO/IEC 18013-5 Selective Disclosure: Digest-Based Attribute Masking & Data Minimization
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 Section 9.1.2 (IssuerSignedItem & Value Digestion)
key_takeaways: ISO/IEC 18013-5 implements zero-knowledge-like data minimization through digest-based selective attribute disclosure: users can disclose specific attributes while keeping others cryptographically hidden.

Each attribute is wrapped in an `IssuerSignedItem` structure containing a digest ID, a cryptographically secure random salt (random bytes), the element identifier (e.g. 'age_over_18'), and the element value.
The holder's wallet releases ONLY the requested `IssuerSignedItem` objects; unrequested items are completely omitted from the presentation payload.
The verifier re-computes the SHA-256 hash of each disclosed `IssuerSignedItem` and matches it against the corresponding digest recorded in the issuer-signed MSO.

Eliminates over-disclosure: a mini-app requiring proof of majority receives only 'age_over_18: true' along with its MSO digest proof, with zero disclosure of birthdate, full name, address, or document number.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce strict attribute-level permission scoping in the mini-app store review process: prohibit mini-apps from requesting full mDL profiles when boolean flags (e.g. age_over_18) suffice.
Render an explicit data minimization confirmation UI in the super-app wallet sheet showing exactly which mDL attributes are being shared with the requesting mini-app.
Reject presentation requests that attempt to harvest non-essential mDL identity attributes in regulated banking and commerce mini-apps.

title: Device Engagement, Ephemeral Session Key Derivation & Reader Mutual Authentication
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 Section 8 (Device Engagement & Session Establishment)
key_takeaways: ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines device engagement protocols for establishing secure communication channels across NFC, QR code, BLE, and online HTTP/OID4VP transports.

The mDL holder and reader execute an ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange (e.g. over NIST P-256 or Brainpool curves), deriving fresh symmetric session encryption keys (`SKDevice`, `SKReader`).

Device Authentication ensures the mDL presentation was authorized by the genuine device hardware: the holder device generates a MAC (`DeviceMac`) or digital signature (`DeviceSignature`) using a hardware-bound private key.
Reader Authentication enables the mDL holder to cryptographically verify the reader's identity: the reader presents an X.509 certificate and signs the ephemeral session parameters.

Protects the user against skimming and unauthenticated readers: the super-app wallet will not disclose any sensitive mDL items unless the reader proves authorization through a valid reader certificate.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement Reader Authentication verification in the super-app container: mini-apps must present store-verified reader credentials before triggering mDL presentations.
Bind the mDL Device Authentication key to the hardware secure element (StrongBox / Secure Enclave), requiring biometric confirmation prior to signing.
Generate unique ephemeral session keys for every mini-app presentation transaction to guarantee forward secrecy and prevent replay attacks.

title: Bridging ISO/IEC 18013-5 into W3C Digital Credentials API & OID4VP Presentation Protocols
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL
standard_reference: W3C Digital Credentials API / OID4VP ISO 18013-5 Profile (Annex B)
key_takeaways: While ISO/IEC 18013-5 was originally designed for in-person proximity interactions (NFC/BLE), modern standards bridge mDL into web and mini-app contexts via OID4VP and W3C Digital Credentials API (`navigator.identity.get`).
In OID4VP, an mDL presentation request is conveyed using `format: mso_mdoc`, specifying required doctypes (`org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL`) and requested element namespaces in the presentation definition.
The response delivers the CBOR-encoded `DeviceResponse` inside the `vp_token`, base64url-encoded or directly nested within JARM direct_post payloads.
W3C Digital Credentials API provides a standardized JavaScript interface for mini-apps to request mDL presentations natively without triggering external application switching.
Unifies identity verification: developers write standard web queries for mDL credentials while the super-app container handles secure element retrieval, user consent, and CBOR payload construction.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose a standardized `navigator.identity.get()` implementation in the mini-app WebView runtime that bridges directly to native mDL wallet storage.
Support `format: mso_mdoc` and ISO 18013-5 namespace querying within the super-app OID4VP verification framework.
Ensure full interoperability between mDL binary CBOR formats and JSON-based SD-JWT VC credential representations via automated container transformation layers.

title: Hardware Enclave Protection, Biometric Gating & Regulated eKYC Compliance for mDL in Super Apps
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 Section 10 & FIDO CTAP 2.1 Hardware Security Integration
key_takeaways: Deploying mDL within a mobile super-app in regulated sectors (banking, telecom, government) requires strict hardware-backed key protection meeting FIPS 140-3 Level 2/3 or Common Criteria EAL4+.
Private keys bound to the `DeviceKey` must be generated and stored inside the host device's Secure Enclave, StrongBox, or eSIM, preventing key extraction even on compromised/rooted operating systems.
Every mDL presentation transaction must be gated by local biometric user verification (FaceID, fingerprint) with anti-spoofing and liveness guarantees.
Cryptographic nonces and transaction-specific reader ephemeral keys must be signed into the `DeviceSignature`, strictly preventing credential replay across sessions.
Provides an unforgeable, legally binding digital identity verification pipeline that satisfies stringent Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (eKYC) regulatory mandates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate biometric user authentication (`UserVerification = required`) for all mini-app transactions requesting mDL identity verification.
Anchor mDL device keys exclusively in hardware security modules (Android StrongBox Keystore or iOS Secure Enclave) with attestations checked at provisioning.
Generate cryptographically sealed, tamper-evident eKYC audit records containing verifier certificate hashes, disclosed attribute digests, and timestamps for regulatory compliance.

title: RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata (PRM): Discovery Protocol, Well-Known Suffix & Resource Binding
category: OAuth 2.0 Security, Protected Resource Metadata & RFC 9728
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9728 Section 1 (Introduction) & Section 3 (Obtaining Protected Resource Metadata)
key_takeaways: RFC 9728 defines a standardized JSON metadata format enabling OAuth 2.0 clients and authorization servers to obtain configuration parameters needed to interact with an OAuth 2.0 protected resource server (RS).

Establishes structural symmetry with OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) and Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414), creating a complete triad of machine-readable OAuth metadata standards.
Metadata is discovered by inserting the well-known URI string `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` into the resource identifier between the host component and path/query components.
The `resource` parameter in the metadata response is REQUIRED and MUST match the exact resource identifier queried; mismatch MUST result in immediate rejection to thwart impersonation.
Eliminates hardcoded resource endpoint configurations in client applications and enables automated, dynamic discovery of resource boundaries across distributed API meshes.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that all enterprise and third-party backend microservices exposed to mini-apps publish RFC 9728 PRM at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.
Implement automated PRM discovery and validation inside the super-app API Gateway to dynamically bind resource identifiers to incoming mini-app requests.
Strictly enforce the `resource` identity equality check in the mini-app runtime network client before utilizing any discovered endpoints.

title: RFC 9728 Core Metadata Parameters: Authorization Servers, Scopes, Bearer Methods & DPoP Binding
category: OAuth 2.0 Security, Protected Resource Metadata & RFC 9728
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9728 Section 2 (Protected Resource Metadata) & Section 8.1 (Metadata Registry)
key_takeaways: Standardizes core PRM parameters: `resource` (REQUIRED), `authorization_servers` (RECOMMENDED list of issuer URLs trusted by this RS), `jwks_uri`, `scopes_supported`, and `bearer_methods_supported`.
Introduces `dpop_bound_access_tokens_required`: a boolean flag signaling whether the resource server mandates sender-constrained Demonstrating Proof of Possession (RFC 9449) tokens.
Defines `bearer_methods_supported` with standardized values ['header', 'body', 'query']; modern security profiles restrict this to ['header'] to prevent query parameter token leakage.
`resource_signing_alg_values_supported` and `resource_encryption_alg_values_supported` advertise cryptographic algorithms when the RS returns signed/encrypted resource responses (JARM/JWE).
Enables clients to dynamically determine which Authorization Server to contact, what scopes to request, and whether sender-constrained DPoP proofs must be generated.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require high-privilege financial and user-data resource servers in the super-app ecosystem to set `dpop_bound_access_tokens_required: true` in their PRM.
Prohibit `query` in `bearer_methods_supported` across all store APIs, restricting access token presentation exclusively to the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer` or `DPoP` headers.
Use `authorization_servers` lists to dynamically guide mini-apps to the correct tenant Authorization Server in federated multi-carrier super-app deployments.

title: RFC 9728 Signed Metadata: JWS Bundling, Issuer Attestation & Cryptographic Tamper Defense
category: OAuth 2.0 Security, Protected Resource Metadata & RFC 9728
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9728 Section 2.2 (Signed Protected Resource Metadata)
key_takeaways: In addition to plain JSON elements, PRM may be provided as a `signed_metadata` value consisting of a complete JSON Web Token (JWT) signed with JSON Web Signature (JWS).
The signed JWT MUST contain an `iss` (issuer) claim identifying the attesting authority (either the RS itself or a central governance entity) and encapsulates configuration parameters as claims.
When signed metadata is present and supported by the consumer, values inside `signed_metadata` MUST take precedence over plain JSON elements in the surrounding object.
Recipients MUST cryptographically verify that the JWS signature validates against trusted public keys belonging to the declared issuer.
Guarantees integrity and non-repudiation: intermediate proxies, caches, or malicious networks cannot tamper with declared authorization servers, public keys, or DPoP mandates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate `signed_metadata` for all partner mini-app resource servers operating in regulated fintech, healthcare, and telecommunications categories.
Configure the super-app platform to sign partner RS metadata using the super-app root governance key, providing cryptographic proof of store approval.
Enforce immediate client rejection in the mini-app WebView runtime if `signed_metadata` fails signature verification or is signed by an unrecognized issuer.

title: RFC 9728 WWW-Authenticate Discovery: 401 Challenge, resource_metadata Parameter & Step-Up Routing
category: OAuth 2.0 Security, Protected Resource Metadata & RFC 9728
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9728 Section 5 (Use of WWW-Authenticate for Protected Resource Metadata)
key_takeaways: An unauthenticated or under-scoped client request to a protected resource triggers an HTTP 401 Unauthorized response with a `WWW-Authenticate` header containing the `resource_metadata` parameter.
Example header: `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"`.

Enables zero-configuration client bootstrapping: a mini-app can attempt a call to an API endpoint without pre-configured OAuth parameters, receive the 401 challenge, retrieve PRM, and initiate authorization.
Crucial validation rule: the `resource` value inside the retrieved metadata MUST match the URL that the client used to make the initial request, defeating redirection/spoofing attacks.
Works seamlessly with OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication (RFC 9470), signaling changed security requirements, fresh scopes, or updated authorization servers dynamically.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated 401 challenge interception in the super-app mini-app fetch/HTTP bridge SDK, parsing `resource_metadata` to trigger automatic token acquisition.
Validate that the `resource` URI returned from the challenge URL strictly matches the request origin and path prefix before executing OAuth authorization flows.
Combine `resource_metadata` with RFC 9470 `error="insufficient_user_authentication"` to provide a friction-free, dynamic step-up authentication experience for mini-apps.

title: RFC 9728 Cross-Validation: AS protected_resources, Anti-Impersonation & Architecture Synthesis
category: OAuth 2.0 Security, Protected Resource Metadata & RFC 9728
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9728 Section 4 (Authorization Server Metadata) & Section 7 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Defines the `protected_resources` parameter in Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414), explicitly listing the valid resource identifiers the AS is authorized to issue tokens for.
Mandates bidirectional cross-validation: the client checks that the RS metadata lists the AS in `authorization_servers`, AND the AS metadata lists the RS in `protected_resources`.
Thwarts rogue resource server attacks where a compromised or malicious API points the client to a legitimate AS to steal broad user tokens (mix-up attack mitigation).
Eliminates audience confusion: tokens are issued strictly with `aud` claims matching the validated `resource` identifier, preventing token forwarding to unauthorized third parties.
Provides the foundational discovery substrate for Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, open banking APIs, and decentralized mini-app microservices in 2026.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure the super-app Authorization Server to publish `protected_resources` enumerating all authorized mini-app backend APIs.
Enforce strict bidirectional cross-checking in the super-app security proxy before relaying user access tokens to mini-app backends.
Ensure that all tokens minted for mini-app backends include explicit RFC 8707 `resource` indicators and RFC 9728-validated audience bindings.

title: OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication: Architecture, Roles & Public Client Integrity
category: Client Attestation, Mobile App Integrity & OAuth 2.0 Security
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth Section 1 (Introduction) & Section 2 (Protocol Overview)
key_takeaways: Extends OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) to enable public client instances (mobile super-apps, native apps, embedded runtimes) to prove their genuine software authenticity and execution integrity.
Solves the fundamental mobile security flaw where public clients cannot securely protect embedded static client secrets, transforming them into cryptographically verifiable client instances.

Defines four key architectural roles: Client Instance (super-app mobile container), Client Attester (OS/hardware platform service, e.g. Play Integrity, App Attest, StrongBox), Authorization Server (AS), and Resource Server (RS).

Crucial privacy design: the client instance obtains an attestation statement from the Client Attester without disclosing its target Authorization Server, preventing attester tracking of user activities.
Allows the Authorization Server to verify that requests originate from an unmodified, store-certified application binary executing in a secure, non-compromised runtime environment.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy Attestation-Based Client Authentication as the mandatory authentication standard for mobile super-app containers requesting OAuth tokens.
Eliminate all embedded static client secrets in mini-app SDKs and mobile builds, replacing them with dynamic key-bound client attestation statements.
Implement attester-privacy preserving isolation in the super-app container to prevent OS attesters from logging downstream mini-app identities.

title: Client Attestation Tokens: Hardware Public Key Binding (cnf/jwk) & Cryptographic Statements
category: Client Attestation, Mobile App Integrity & OAuth 2.0 Security
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth Section 3 (Client Attestation Statement)
key_takeaways: The Client Attestation statement is a digitally signed security token (typically a JWT) issued by the Client Attester certifying the integrity of the client instance.
The statement contains an `iss` (Client Attester identifier), `sub` (unique instance or app identifier), `exp`, and a `cnf` (confirmation) claim containing or referencing a public key (`jwk`).
The public key bound in `cnf` belongs to an asymmetric key pair generated locally by the client instance inside a hardware security module (Secure Enclave / StrongBox Keystore).
Binds the software integrity verdict directly to hardware cryptographic key material, ensuring the attestation cannot be extracted, duplicated, or used on an unauthorized device.
Enables the Authorization Server to establish a trusted cryptographic communication channel bound directly to the hardware-verified client instance.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that the super-app client container generate its instance key pair inside hardware-backed storage (Android StrongBox or iOS Secure Enclave) using NIST P-256 or Ed25519.
Require Client Attestation tokens to encapsulate the hardware public key in the `cnf.jwk` claim before submission to the enterprise Authorization Server.
Enforce strict token lifetime limits (e.g. 5–15 minutes) on Client Attestation statements to minimize the window of compromise for stolen assertions.

title: Attestation Proof-of-Possession (PoP): Nonce Binding, Request Signing & Anti-Replay Security
category: Client Attestation, Mobile App Integrity & OAuth 2.0 Security
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth Section 4 (Client Attestation PoP)
key_takeaways: To prove possession of the private key corresponding to the public key certified in the Client Attestation, the client generates a Client Attestation PoP token.
The PoP token is a short-lived JWT signed by the client's private key and presented in the `OAuth-Client-Attestation-PoP` HTTP header alongside `OAuth-Client-Attestation`.
The PoP JWT includes an `aud` claim (Authorization Server token endpoint), `iat`, `exp` (lifetime <= 60 seconds), and a cryptographic `nonce` provided by the AS.
If the request includes an HTTP body or specific headers, the PoP token incorporates a cryptographic digest (`htm`, `htu`, `ath`) or signature of the request elements.
Guarantees that an intercepted Client Attestation statement cannot be replayed by a man-in-the-middle or malicious proxy to obtain unauthorized access tokens.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated challenge-response nonce management at the super-app Authorization Server token endpoint for attestation verification.
Require client instances to sign the exact HTTP request method, target URL, and fresh server nonce inside the Client Attestation PoP JWT.
Enforce a maximum PoP validity window of 60 seconds and maintain an ephemeral replay detection cache for processed PoP identifiers (`jti`).

title: Threat Mitigation: Cloned Binaries, Emulators, Bot Farms & Rogue Mini-App Execution
category: Client Attestation, Mobile App Integrity & OAuth 2.0 Security
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth Section 7 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Addresses severe mobile threat vectors: modified client binaries (re-packaged APKs/IPAs), instrumentation frameworks (Frida, Xposed), emulator bot farms, and API scraping.
Hardware-backed attesters verify OS boot state (Verified Boot), kernel integrity, application signing certificate hash, and genuine hardware device signals.
Prevents automated credential stuffing and financial fraud botnets from masquerading as legitimate super-app mobile client instances.
Extends integrity guarantees to mini-app execution: the super-app host asserts its own verified state before granting bridge access to third-party mini-app bundles.
Provides non-repudiable audit logs of device security posture at the exact moment sensitive financial or personal data transactions are authorized.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Gate access to high-value mini-app categories (banking, investments, digital payments) behind verified hardware attestation verdicts (`MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY`).
Automatically revoke active user sessions and clear OPFS local data if the host platform reports a compromised boot state or runtime hooking.
Incorporate client attestation verdicts into the store's automated risk scoring and fraud prevention telemetry pipeline.

title: Super-App Host Attestation: Multi-Tenant Mini-App Verification & Enterprise Token Issuance
category: Client Attestation, Mobile App Integrity & OAuth 2.0 Security
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth Section 5 (Token Request) & Section 6 (Token Response)
key_takeaways: In a super-app architecture, the host mobile container acts as a local attester and cryptographic bridge for embedded mini-apps.
When a mini-app requires direct access to an external enterprise Authorization Server, the host container attaches its hardware-backed Client Attestation to the mini-app's request.
The host container binds the mini-app's unique manifest ID and package cryptographic hash into the attestation claims, asserting both container and mini-app provenance.
The Authorization Server verifies the two-tier trust hierarchy: genuine super-app host container + unmodified, store-certified mini-app package.
Enables decentralized third-party mini-apps to attain enterprise-grade client authentication without exposing long-lived credentials or API keys in client-side code.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement a native Attestation Bridge API in the super-app runtime, enabling mini-apps to request container-signed attestation tokens for enterprise OAuth flows.
Embed the mini-app's store package hash and developer DID within the attestation context presented to the enterprise Authorization Server.
Provide Authorization Server reference plugins supporting two-tier validation of both host super-app integrity and embedded mini-app package certificates.

title: ISO/IEC 18013-7 & OpenID4VP Remote Architecture: Online Verification, Transports & Trust Frameworks
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-7 Remote mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-7 (Mobile Driving Licence - Add-on online presentation) & OpenID4VP mDL Profile
key_takeaways: ISO/IEC 18013-7 standardizes mechanisms for presenting mobile driving licences (mDL) and mobile documents (mdoc) in remote/online scenarios, complementing proximity standards (ISO/IEC 18013-5).
Defines OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP) as the primary normative online transport protocol for mDL verification over HTTPS and RESTful web architectures.
Supports diverse engagement models: in-app browser/mini-app presentation, cross-device engagement via dynamic QR codes, and native wallet app-to-app redirection.
Eliminates proximity hardware dependencies (NFC/BLE), enabling remote digital onboarding, age verification, and high-assurance identity verification across digital services.
Aligns international driving licence specifications with the European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Incorporate ISO/IEC 18013-7 and OID4VP remote presentation protocols into the super-app digital identity wallet architecture.
Provide native mini-app SDK APIs to trigger remote mDL verification flows without requiring custom developer cryptographic implementations.
Support both in-app WebView presentation and cross-device QR code workflows to accommodate desktop-to-mobile and kiosk interactions.

title: Session Transcript Binding in ISO/IEC 18013-7: Nonce, client_id & Man-in-the-Middle Defense
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-7 Remote mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-7 Annex B / OID4VP Section 6 (SessionTranscript Construction)
key_takeaways: In remote mDL verification, preventing Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) and presentation replay is paramount: the device authentication signature must be cryptographically bound to the specific online session.
ISO/IEC 18013-7 constructs an ephemeral `SessionTranscript` structure combining the verifier's `client_id`, the verifier's fresh `nonce`, and the response URI or TLS channel binding parameters.
The mobile wallet hardware enclave signs a CBOR structure containing the SHA-256 hash of this `SessionTranscript` during the `DeviceSignature` generation.
Any tampering with the verifier identity, redirect URI, or intercepted response invalidates the hardware signature immediately.
Guarantees that an mDL presentation generated for one mini-app or merchant cannot be intercepted and forwarded to authenticate against another service.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Construct standard-compliant `SessionTranscript` structures inside the super-app secure container before invoking hardware signing keys.
Inject verifier-specific cryptographically strong nonces and verified store client IDs into all remote mDL requests initiated by mini-apps.
Reject any mini-app mDL presentation if the session transcript binding hash fails validation against the initial request parameters.

title: ISO/IEC 18013-7 Privacy: Selective Disclosure, Age Verification Predicates & Namespace Sandboxing
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-7 Remote mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-7 / ISO/IEC 18013-5 Section 7.2 (Data Elements & Namespaces)
key_takeaways: mDL data elements are partitioned into standardized namespaces (e.g. `org.iso.18013.5.1` for global driving privileges and `org.iso.18013.5.1.aamva` for regional attributes).
Supports privacy-preserving boolean predicate elements such as `age_over_18`, `age_over_21`, or `age_in_years` without disclosing the exact date of birth, legal name, or home address.
The Issuer signs attribute digests in the `MobileSecurityObject` (MSO); the holder selectively discloses only the requested attribute-digest pairs, withholding all others.
Prevents online tracking and over-collection: merchants verifying age for restricted goods or services receive cryptographically certified truth without personal profiling data.
Complies with stringent data minimization principles mandated by GDPR, CCPA, and regional personal data protection regulations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Restructure mini-app store permission requests to mandate boolean age verification predicates (e.g. `age_over_18`) instead of requesting full birth dates.
Display an itemized, user-comprehensible consent sheet in the super-app container highlighting exactly which mDL attributes are requested.
Enforce strict namespace sandboxing in the store review process, rejecting mini-apps that request disproportionate or unneeded mDL identity fields.

title: EUDI Wallet ARF Alignment: High-Assurance Cross-Border Identity & Trust Registries
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-7 Remote mDL
standard_reference: European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) v1.4 / ISO 18013-7
key_takeaways: The EU Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet ARF establishes ISO/IEC 18013-7 and OID4VP as core technical standards for cross-border digital identity presentation across EU member states.
Defines Level of Assurance (LoA) High requirements: mDLs must be provisioned and signed within Qualified Signature Creation Devices (QSCD) or hardware Secure Elements (eSE/SIM/eUICC).
Establishes trusted issuer lists and Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) registries for cryptographically validating document signer certificates across sovereign borders.
Provides an interoperable blueprint for commercial super-apps to serve as compliant Digital Identity Wallets in regulated financial, healthcare, and public sector ecosystems.
Standardizes relying party authentication: verifiers must register and obtain verified digital certificates before being permitted to request wallet presentations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Architect the super-app digital identity wallet to adhere to EUDI ARF and ISO/IEC 18013-7 specifications for international compliance readiness.
Integrate national/regional trust list validation into the super-app verification engine to check issuer root certificates in real time.
Establish relying party verification gates in the mini-app store developer portal, ensuring third parties hold certified reader credentials before requesting identity data.

title: Super-App Container mDL Bridge: Native JavaScript APIs, Enclave Isolation & Audit Trails
category: Mobile Security, Digital Credentials & ISO/IEC 18013-7 Remote mDL
standard_reference: ISO/IEC 18013-7 / W3C Digital Credentials API Mini-App Integration
key_takeaways: Synthesizes ISO/IEC 18013-7 remote mDL protocols into a clean, sandboxed JavaScript API exposed to authorized mini-apps via the super-app native container bridge.
Mini-apps invoke `superapp.identity.requestMdocPresentation({ docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', elements: ['age_over_21'] })`, completely abstracting underlying CBOR/COSE complexity.
The native container executes all cryptographic operations (session transcript hashing, device signature generation, ECDH key agreement) inside the hardware secure enclave.
Generates cryptographically sealed, immutable local audit records containing the transaction timestamp, mini-app ID, disclosed attribute names, and verifier certificate hashes.
Enables enterprise super-apps to provide banking-grade, legally compliant digital identity verification while guaranteeing complete client-side data isolation.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose a standardized `superapp.identity.requestMdocPresentation()` API in the mini-app runtime environment with strict Permissions Policy gating.
Execute all CBOR parsing, COSE signature generation, and session transcript bindings within isolated native code outside the WebView JavaScript context.
Maintain a user-accessible audit log in the super-app settings allowing users to inspect every historical mini-app mDL data disclosure.

title: RFC 9711 Entity Attestation Token (EAT): Attestation Claims Set, CWT/JWT Envelopes & RATS Architecture Alignment
category: Mobile Security, Hardware Attestation & RFC 9711 EAT
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9711 Section 1 (Introduction), Section 1.3 (RATS Alignment) & Section 3 (Top-Level Token Definition)
key_takeaways: RFC 9711 defines the Entity Attestation Token (EAT), a standardized format for transferring signed claims describing the security state, hardware configuration, and runtime environment of an entity.

Operates strictly within the IETF RATS (Remote ATtestation procedureS, RFC 9334) architecture: Attester produces Evidence (EAT), Verifier appraises Evidence against Reference Values, and Relying Party consumes Attestation Results (also an EAT).
Supports dual serialization envelopes: CBOR Web Token (CWT, RFC 8392) secured with COSE (RFC 9052) for binary efficiency, or JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) secured with JOSE (RFC 7515).

Differentiates attestation keys from authentication keys: attestation keys are bound to device hardware/manufacturers and protected by hardware security enclaves, preventing extraction even by root/jailbroken software.
Freshness is strictly enforced using the `eat_nonce` claim (single string or byte array for multistage processing) or cryptographically synchronized epoch timestamps.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt RFC 9711 EAT as the normative payload format for device integrity reports generated by the super-app native container.
Implement a cloud-based EAT Verifier within the super-app gateway that evaluates mobile client evidence before granting access to high-risk mini-app APIs.
Mandate nonce-based freshness checks (`eat_nonce`) for all high-value transactions (financial transfers, eKYC verifications) to thwart attestation replay attacks.

title: RFC 9711 Hardware Identity & Environment Claims: UEID, OEMID, Hardware Model & Boot Status Verification
category: Mobile Security, Hardware Attestation & RFC 9711 EAT
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9711 Section 4.2 (Claims Describing the Entity: ueid, sueids, oemid, hwmodel, oemboot, dbgstat)
key_takeaways: Defines canonical hardware identification claims: `ueid` (Universal Entity ID, globally unique hardware serial), `sueids` (semi-permanent UEIDs for privacy rotation), and `oemid` (hardware manufacturer identifier).
`hwmodel` and `hwversion` precisely identify the physical chip and handset architecture, enabling server-side risk engines to evaluate known hardware vulnerability profiles.
`oemboot` (OEM Authorized Boot) verifies that the operating system was cryptographically verified and launched through an unbroken hardware root of trust (Verified Boot).
`dbgstat` (Debug Status) indicates whether hardware/software debug interfaces (e.g. JTAG, USB debugging, ADB, kernel debuggers) are active, providing authoritative tamper signals.
Allows relying party servers to mathematically confirm that a connecting mobile super-app is operating on genuine OEM hardware without unauthorized bootloader unlocking.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce a mandatory store policy rejecting or sandboxing mini-app execution if `oemboot` is false or `dbgstat` reveals active runtime debugging on production user devices.
Use privacy-preserving `sueids` or salt-hashed device identifiers to track compromised device clusters without violating GDPR/PDPA device fingerprinting restrictions.
Incorporate `hwmodel` into capability negotiation to enable advanced hardware-accelerated WebAssembly and WebGPU features only on verified hardware platforms.

title: RFC 9711 Software Measurements, Manifests & Results: Runtime Hashing, Golden Images & Verification Reporting
category: Mobile Security, Hardware Attestation & RFC 9711 EAT
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9711 Section 4.2.15 (manifests), Section 4.2.16 (measurements) & Section 4.2.17 (measres)
key_takeaways: `manifests` claim carries the developer-signed software inventory and build artifacts originally packaged with the application (e.g. mini-app package hashes, version manifests).
`measurements` claim contains runtime cryptographic measurements (hashes of memory segments, executable code blocks, dynamic libraries) recorded by hardware or hypervisor measurement agents.

`measres` (Software Measurement Results) provides a standardized comparison matrix ('success', 'failure', 'not run', 'absent') contrasting live measurements against expected Golden Image reference values.
Enables runtime detection of code injection, hook frameworks (Frida, Xposed, Substrate), and dynamically modified JavaScript assets inside the host WebView.
Separates the entity that defines the software specification (developer manifest) from the runtime measurement engine (container/OS security agent), creating objective evidence.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure the super-app container to generate cryptographic `measurements` of loaded mini-app code bundles prior to executing Web Worker or WebView threads.
Implement automated `measres` evaluation on the super-app gateway, instantly revoking API tokens if client runtime measurements deviate from store-approved bundle hashes.
Include third-party SDK binary hashes in the container's `manifests` claim to maintain complete software supply-chain visibility on client devices.

title: RFC 9711 Composite Devices & Submodules: Sandboxed Runtime Hierarchy & Multi-Tenant App Attestation
category: Mobile Security, Hardware Attestation & RFC 9711 EAT
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9711 Section 4.2.18 (submods - Submodules Claim) & Section 5 (Detached EAT Bundles)
key_takeaways: The `submods` (Submodules) claim enables hierarchical representation of complex entities comprising multiple independent cryptographic domains (e.g. host OS, TEE, eSE, and app sandboxes).
Each submodule can contain its own independent claims set, measurements, public keys, and even nested EAT tokens signed by distinct subsystem keys.
Perfect architectural fit for super-apps: the top-level EAT attests to the physical phone and OS, while nested `submods` attest to the super-app host container and individual mini-app sandboxes.
Detached EAT bundles allow separating the cryptographic attestation envelope from bulky claims sets or detached evidence blobs while maintaining verifiable integrity.
Isolates multi-tenant mini-app attestation: one mini-app's security status does not invalidate or compromise the attestation verification of neighboring mini-apps.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Model the super-app client architecture as a composite entity using RFC 9711 `submods`, with dedicated submodules for 'native_host', 'webview_runtime', and active 'mini_apps'.
Generate nested EAT tokens where each active mini-app possesses its own submodule claims set documenting its origin, bundle version, and runtime permission grants.
Use detached EAT bundles to transmit high-assurance hardware proof headers alongside standard HTTP API requests without duplicating device attestation payloads.

title: RFC 9782 EAT Media Types & Profiles: Standardized MIME Headers, Content Negotiation & Gateway Dispatching
category: Mobile Security, Hardware Attestation & RFC 9711 EAT
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9782 Section 2 (EAT Types), Section 3 (Media Type Parameter for EAT Profiles) & Section 6 (IANA Considerations)
key_takeaways: RFC 9782 standardizes official media types for EAT: `application/eat+cwt` (CBOR/COSE binary), `application/eat+jwt` (JSON/JOSE 8-bit text), and detached bundle formats `application/eat-bun+cbor` and `application/eat-bun+json`.
Introduces the `eat_profile` media type parameter, allowing API endpoints and gateway routers to inspect the attestation profile in HTTP `Content-Type` headers without parsing token payloads.
`eat_profile` carries an OID or URI matching the token's internal `eat_profile` claim, defining mandatory claims, supported cipher suites, and verification rules for specific industries.
Unprotected claims sets are designated as `application/eat-ucs+cbor` (UCCS) and `application/eat-ucs+json` (UJCS) when transport-layer security (mTLS) provides channel-bound protection.
Enables RESTful API gateways to automatically route incoming client attestation payloads to specialized verification hardware (e.g. HSM clusters or TEE verification engines).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize API Gateway ingest headers to accept `application/eat+jwt; eat_profile="https://superapp.com/profiles/v1/client-attestation"` for standard web requests.
Use `application/eat+cwt` for high-throughput mobile binary channels and IoT device integrations to minimize mobile data consumption and battery overhead.
Define a formalized Super-App EAT Profile URI in the store developer portal detailing required claims (`ueid`, `oemboot`, `dbgstat`, `measurements`) for store certification.

title: RFC 9553 JSContact: Standardized JSON Data Model, Card Architecture & Privacy Context Scoping
category: Data Governance, Address Book Privacy & RFC 9553 JSContact
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9553 Section 1 (Introduction), Section 2 (Card) & Section 2.1 (Context Property)
key_takeaways: RFC 9553 defines JSContact, an unambiguous, extensible JSON data model for contact cards, replacing legacy line-based vCard (RFC 6350) and cumbersome jCard (RFC 7095) formats.
The top-level entity is the `Card` object, containing typed properties for identification (`uid`), names, organizations, titles, communication channels, addresses, and crypto material.
Introduces the `contexts` property on granular contact attributes (emails, phones, addresses), explicitly scoping data into `'personal'` and `'private'` vs `'work'` environments.

Solves impedance mismatches in modern web/mobile APIs by natively representing complex contact hierarchies, preferred contact channels, and localized script representations without custom X-properties.
Provides an ideal, standardized schema for mobile super-app contact sharing APIs, eliminating proprietary JSON schemas across third-party mini-apps.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt RFC 9553 `Card` as the canonical JSON payload format for the super-app Contact Picker API bridge.
Expose context filtering parameters (`contexts: ['work']` or `contexts: ['personal']`) in the contact picker bridge to allow users to enforce privacy boundaries when sharing cards with mini-apps.
Reject proprietary mini-app contact serialization formats in favor of strict RFC 9553 validation in the store runtime SDK.

title: RFC 9553 Name Decomposition, Phonetics & Multilingual Scripts: Internationalized Contact Identity
category: Data Governance, Address Book Privacy & RFC 9553 JSContact
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9553 Section 2.2 (Name Properties: name, nicknames, phonetic)
key_takeaways: Defines granular name components within `Name`: `components` (array of typed segments: 'prefix', 'personal', 'surname', 'suffix', etc.) and `full` formatted display string.
Natively accommodates diverse cultural naming orders (e.g. Eastern surname-first order in Vietnamese, Chinese, Japanese, Korean vs Western given-name first) without parsing ambiguity.
Includes first-class `phonetic` properties specifying pronunciation, phonetic script systems (e.g. IPA, Pinyin, Hiragana), and transcription phonetics for voice-assisted super-apps.
Supports multilingual localized representations via `localizations`, mapping BCP 47 language tags to script-specific name overrides on the same contact card.
Guarantees that mini-apps receive accurately rendered, culturally respectful contact names across international super-app user bases.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Utilize RFC 9553 structured `components` and `full` name attributes in super-app contact synchronization to preserve Vietnamese and regional Southeast Asian naming conventions.
Leverage the `phonetic` property in AI voice assistant and accessibility screen-reader bridges to ensure correct pronunciation of merchant and contact names.
Enforce BCP 47 language tag validation on all localized contact overrides exchanged between the host and mini-app contexts.

title: RFC 9553 Digital Communication Channels: Emails, Phones, Online Services & URI Sandboxing
category: Data Governance, Address Book Privacy & RFC 9553 JSContact
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9553 Section 2.3 (Contact Properties: emails, phones, onlineServices)
key_takeaways: Standardizes communication maps: `emails` (RFC 5322 addresses), `phones` (E.164 normalized phone URIs: `tel:+84...`), and `onlineServices` (messaging handles, social profiles, WebRTC endpoints).
Each communication entry incorporates a `pref` integer attribute (1 to 100), explicitly defining the user's preferred contact priority across multiple numbers or emails.
The `onlineServices` object modernizes contact sharing by standardizing `service` identifiers (e.g. 'Telegram', 'WhatsApp', 'Zalo') and authenticated account handles.
Features property-level `label` attributes, allowing user-customized identifiers (e.g. 'Customer Support', 'Warehouse Delivery') without corrupting structural data.
Provides strict sanitization boundaries: URI schemes are restricted to verified protocols (`tel:`, `mailto:`, `https:`), preventing URI injection attacks in mini-app WebViews.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Normalize all phone numbers exported through the mini-app contact bridge to standard E.164 `tel:` URIs within RFC 9553 `phones` objects.
Enable users to selectively share only preferred communication channels (`pref = 1`) with third-party mini-apps to minimize sensitive data exposure.
Validate and sanitize all `onlineServices` URI schemes at the container boundary to prevent malicious intent filter hijacking on mobile OS platforms.

title: RFC 9553 Geographic & Delivery Addresses: Structured Components, Geocoding & Logistics Privacy
category: Data Governance, Address Book Privacy & RFC 9553 JSContact
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9553 Section 2.5 (Addresses: addresses, coordinates)
key_takeaways: Defines structured `Address` objects breaking locations into discrete components: `street`, `locality` (city), `region` (state/province), `country`, and `postcode`.
Supports `coordinates` via WGS 84 `geo:` URIs (RFC 5870), enabling high-precision mapping and logistics dispatch without relying on brittle freeform address string parsing.
Introduces address `contexts`: categorizes locations into `'billing'`, `'delivery'`, `'work'`, and `'private'`, directly solving multi-address selection in e-commerce mini-apps.
Accommodates international postal standards and non-standard address formats through the `full` unparsed fallback and component-level `type` discriminators.

Prevents address harvesting: allows the super-app host to share coarse locality information (city/district) during initial mini-app browsing and reveal full street details only upon final checkout confirmation.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Structure the super-app user delivery address book according to RFC 9553 `addresses` specifications.
Implement two-stage address disclosure in e-commerce/delivery mini-apps: disclose only `locality` and `region` for catalog browsing, and full `street` only after explicit user purchase confirmation.
Validate that geographic coordinates shared with ride-hailing/delivery mini-apps conform to standardized RFC 5870 `geo:` URIs.

title: RFC 9555 JSContact to vCard Bi-directional Mapping: Legacy Migration & Lossless Preservation
category: Data Governance, Address Book Privacy & RFC 9553 JSContact
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9555 Section 1 (Introduction), Section 2 (Mapping Rules) & Section 4 (Preserving Unknown Properties)
key_takeaways: RFC 9555 defines normative bidirectional conversion algorithms between RFC 9553 JSContact and RFC 6350 vCard 4.0, ensuring full backwards compatibility with legacy OS address books.
Specifies exact parameter mapping rules: converts vCard `TYPE`, `PREF`, and `LANGUAGE` parameters into native JSContact object properties and context enumerations.
Introduces property preservation mechanisms (`JSCard` extension parameters) to retain unrecognized vCard extensions without data loss during round-trip conversions.

Enables super-app mobile clients to seamlessly ingest native iOS (Contacts framework) and Android (ContactsContract) address book entries and transform them into clean JSContact JSON for mini-app consumption.
Eliminates encoding bugs (e.g. folded lines, escaping errors, character set mismatches) that historically plagued line-delimited vCard parser implementations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement RFC 9555 conversion pipelines in the super-app native container to ingest device contacts into standardized JSContact format.
Perform automated property scrubbing during vCard-to-JSContact transformation to strip sensitive device-internal metadata before bridge delivery.
Provide developer SDK utilities for converting incoming JSContact payloads into vCard files when mini-apps require contact export functionality.

title: W3C Payment Request API: Architecture, Lifecycle State Machine & Native Sheet Presentation
category: E-Commerce, Container Payment Mediation & W3C Web Payments
standard_reference: W3C Payment Request API (W3C Proposed Recommendation / Working Group Note) Section 4 (PaymentRequest Interface)
key_takeaways: W3C Payment Request API eliminates brittle, customized checkout forms by standardizing a native, container-mediated payment sheet presentation across mobile and desktop browsers.
Constructed via `new PaymentRequest(methodData, details, options)`: decouples payment method negotiation from merchant transaction details (items, totals, modifiers) and user data collection options.
Execution is mediated via the `show()` promise lifecycle: requires transient user activation, validates merchant data, presents the native UI, and resolves to a `PaymentResponse` upon user approval.
`canMakePayment()` and `hasEnrolledInstrument()` enable merchants to proactively query whether a compatible payment instrument is configured without exposing user account identifiers.

The lifecycle concludes deterministically via `response.complete('success' | 'fail')`: signals the browser/container that backend settlement finalized, releasing UI locks and dismissing modal overlays.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize the super-app mini-app payment bridge on the W3C Payment Request API interface, replacing proprietary checkout APIs with `window.PaymentRequest`.
Enforce mandatory transient user activation (touch/click gesture) before permitting a mini-app to invoke `PaymentRequest.show()`, eliminating spontaneous payment modal spam.
Guarantee container UI responsiveness by enforcing a strict 30-second timeout on unfinalized `PaymentResponse` promises, automatically releasing frozen resources.

title: W3C Payment Method Identifiers: Standardized PMIs vs URL-Based Scoping & Ecosystem Interoperability
category: E-Commerce, Container Payment Mediation & W3C Web Payments
standard_reference: W3C Payment Method Identifiers Section 2 (Payment Method Identifier Syntax) & Section 3 (URL-based Payment Method Identifiers)
key_takeaways: Defines two categories of Payment Method Identifiers (PMIs): Standardized Short PMI strings (governed by W3C registries) and URL-based PMIs (scoped under absolute HTTPS URLs).
URL-based PMIs (e.g. `https://superapp.com/pay`, `https://google.com/pay`, `https://vietqr.net/pay`) decentralize payment innovation by anchoring payment method ownership to DNS domains.
Prevents PMI collision and namespace spoofing: only the domain owner of the URL-based PMI has the cryptographic authority to define the payment method specification and authorized apps.
A mini-app indicates accepted instruments by passing an array of `PaymentMethodData` objects: `{ supportedMethods: 'https://superapp.com/pay', data: { merchantId: '...', orderId: '...' } }`.
Allows a single super-app container to arbitrate between platform-native wallet rails, domestic banking networks (NAPAS/VietQR), and international schemes within one unified call.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish an official URL-based PMI for the super-app payment gateway (e.g. `https://<superapp-domain>/payments/v1`) with full public documentation.
Validate all `supportedMethods` strings in the container bridge, rejecting malformed URIs, non-HTTPS protocols, or unwhitelisted third-party schemes in regulated environments.
Implement standardized method data serialization allowing mini-apps to seamlessly pass order tokens and digital signatures to underlying banking adapters.

title: W3C Payment Method Manifest: Machine-Readable JSON Discovery & Authorized Web/Native Payment Handlers
category: E-Commerce, Container Payment Mediation & W3C Web Payments
standard_reference: W3C Payment Method Manifest Section 2 (Format) & Section 3 (Payment Method Manifest Discovery)
key_takeaways: The Payment Method Manifest specification establishes a machine-readable JSON format hosted at the PMI URL or linked via HTTP `Link: <...>; rel="payment-method-manifest"`.
Defines two key authorization dictionaries: `default_applications` (array of web app manifests authorized to handle the payment method) and `supported_origins` (origins allowed to host payment apps).
Protects users against rogue payment applications: a browser or super-app container will only invoke a payment handler if its origin is explicitly authorized in the PMI manifest.
Enables decentralized payment app distribution: independent financial institutions can launch dedicated payment handler mini-apps without modifying the host super-app binary.
Integrates with mobile OS native apps by cross-referencing Android package names and signing certificate SHA-256 fingerprints directly within the manifest structure.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy a validated `payment-method-manifest` on the super-app payment domain to cryptographically enumerate authorized payment handler mini-apps.
Incorporate automated manifest fetching and signature verification into the super-app store review pipeline when vetting external banking mini-apps.
Restrict payment invocation rights exclusively to origins and native application IDs cryptographically verified through the published manifest.

title: W3C Secure Payment Confirmation (SPC): FIDO/WebAuthn Cryptographic Assertion & PSD2/SCA Compliance
category: E-Commerce, Container Payment Mediation & W3C Web Payments
standard_reference: W3C Secure Payment Confirmation (SPC) Candidate Recommendation Section 4 (Data Model) & Section 5 (Browser Processing Model)
key_takeaways: Secure Payment Confirmation (SPC) extends the Payment Request API to provide low-friction, highly secure WebAuthn-based cryptographic payment authentication.
Invoked using the standardized payment method `secure-payment-confirmation`: passes credential IDs, challenge, rpId, payeeOrigin, and structured transaction `instrument` details.
