Renders a browser/container-enforced payment dialog displaying the payee's verified origin, icon, total amount, and currency, binding the user's visual consent to the cryptographic signature.
Produces a client-side assertion signed by the device's hardware security module (Secure Enclave / StrongBox), incorporating the transaction details directly into `clientDataJSON`.
Satisfies European PSD2 Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) dynamic linking requirements and domestic Central Bank biometric payment regulations without redirection to external 3DS OTP portals.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement W3C Secure Payment Confirmation as the gold standard for high-value transactions (> 20M VND / $1000) inside the super-app.
Enforce cryptographic dynamic linking in the container payment sheet, binding the exact payee origin, order total, and currency code into the biometric assertion.
Bridge SPC assertions directly into host bank APIs to eliminate SMS OTP drop-offs and achieve sub-3-second secure checkout in mini-apps.

title: W3C Payment Details Modifiers: Dynamic Discounting, Network Surcharges & Split Ledger Accounting
category: E-Commerce, Container Payment Mediation & W3C Web Payments
standard_reference: W3C Payment Request API Section 4.5 (PaymentDetailsModifier Dictionary) & Section 4.6 (PaymentMethodChangeEvent)
key_takeaways: `PaymentDetailsModifier` allows merchants to conditionally alter transaction pricing (`total` and `additionalDisplayItems`) based on the specific payment method selected by the user.
Facilitates real-time fee transparency: enables displaying carrier billing surcharges, credit card processing fees, or super-app wallet cashback discounts dynamically.
When the user switches payment methods in the native sheet, the container fires a `paymentmethodchange` event to the mini-app, allowing dynamic calculation of revised line items.
The merchant updates the UI atomically using `event.updateWith(detailsPromise)`, preventing race conditions or fraudulent price discrepancies during checkout.
Essential for multi-tenant super-app commercial settlement: harmonizes complex payment splits, platform commissions, and telco DCB fees before final user authorization.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Utilize `PaymentDetailsModifier` and `paymentmethodchange` events to transparently surface carrier billing (DCB) handling fees and domestic wallet discounts in the checkout sheet.
Implement atomic server-side validation ensuring the total signed in the payment token matches the modified total presented in the native payment sheet.
Expose standardized line-item breakdown structures in the mini-app payment SDK to maintain complete fiscal transparency and audit readiness.

title: IETF RFC 9458 Oblivious HTTP: Architectural Model & Gateway-Relay Trust Separation
category: Privacy-Preserving Telemetry, Oblivious Protocols & Zero-Knowledge Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9458 (Oblivious HTTP) Section 2 (Architecture) & Section 6 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) establishes a cryptographic architecture that breaks the link between a client's network identity (IP address, TLS fingerprints) and the application payload sent to a target server.
Operates via a bifurcated infrastructure: an Oblivious Relay receives encrypted requests, strips client transport metadata (IP address), and forwards them to an Oblivious Gateway.
The Gateway terminates the OHTTP cryptographic outer envelope using Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE, RFC 9180) and passes the inner Binary HTTP message (BHTTP, RFC 9292) to the Target Server.
Ensures non-collusion: Relay knows client IP but cannot read message content; Gateway/Target knows message content but cannot determine client IP address.
Crucial for high-trust mobile super-app architectures: enables privacy-preserving crash telemetry, ad attribution pings, and fraud telemetry without exposing user network coordinates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate OHTTP for all third-party mini-app client telemetry, crash reporting, and diagnostic egress to eliminate user IP address tracking.
Enforce strict non-collusion by routing relay traffic through a vetted independent proxy partner or cloud edge while terminating gateways at super-app origin servers.
Embed OHTTP client primitives directly in the super-app native container networking layer, abstracting cryptographic encapsulation away from mini-app developers.

title: IETF RFC 9458 & RFC 9292: Binary HTTP Framing, HPKE Key Derivation & Media Negotiation
category: Privacy-Preserving Telemetry, Oblivious Protocols & Zero-Knowledge Architecture
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9458 Section 3 (Message Format) & Section 4 (HTTP Usage), and RFC 9292 Section 2 (Format)
key_takeaways: OHTTP serializes inner request and response messages using Binary Representation of HTTP Messages (BHTTP, RFC 9292) with media type `message/bhttp`.
BHTTP encodes control data, headers, and binary body in compact deterministic framing without ASCII delimiters or string formatting overhead.
The client discovers the Target/Gateway HPKE Key Configuration (Key ID, KEM ID, KDF ID, AEAD ID, and public key) out-of-band or via HTTPS discovery.
The client performs HPKE single-shot encapsulation (`message/ohttp-req`) producing a header containing key_id, kem_id, kdf_id, aead_id, enc (ephemeral public key), and AEAD ciphertext.
The Gateway decrypts the request, processes it, derives a response AEAD key using the HPKE exporter context, and returns an encrypted response (`message/ohttp-res`).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated gateway HPKE configuration rotation with cryptographic key IDs embedded in super-app container security policy profiles.
Utilize RFC 9292 BHTTP deterministic stream parsers inside native host bridge network stacks to minimize parsing latency and memory overhead.
Enforce strict validation of `message/ohttp-req` and `message/ohttp-res` content types on host-managed API gateway ingress controllers.

title: IETF draft-ietf-ppm-dap: Distributed Aggregation Protocol (DAP) Multi-Party Computation Architecture
category: Privacy-Preserving Telemetry, Oblivious Protocols & Zero-Knowledge Architecture
standard_reference: IETF Privacy Preserving Measurement (PPM) Working Group DAP Specification Section 2 (System Architecture)
key_takeaways: The Distributed Aggregation Protocol (DAP) allows clients to submit sensitive measurement reports such that an aggregator learns only aggregated statistics, never individual client data.
System entities consist of: Clients (mini-app runtimes), a Leader aggregator, a Helper aggregator, and a Collector (analytical query engine).
Clients secret-share their measurement inputs across the Leader and Helper using verifiable secret-sharing schemes (Priori, Poplar, or Prio3).
The Leader and Helper execute multi-party computation (MPC) to collaboratively verify the validity of secret shares without reconstructing individual cleartext values.
Provides mathematical differential privacy guarantees: no single honest-but-curious entity can extract individual user habits, dwell times, or transaction amounts.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt DAP architecture for super-app cross-mini-app engagement analytics, feature adoption metrics, and funnel conversion tracking.
Establish multi-cloud aggregator separation (e.g. Leader operated by super-app platform, Helper operated by an independent auditor or telco partner).
Prohibit cleartext client analytics collection across third-party mini-apps in favor of verifiable DAP multi-party aggregation.

title: Verifiable Distributed Aggregation Functions (VDAFs): Prio3 & Fully Linear Proof Systems
category: Privacy-Preserving Telemetry, Oblivious Protocols & Zero-Knowledge Architecture
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-ppm-dap Section 4 (Aggregation Flow) & draft-irtf-cfrg-vdaf Section 5 (Prio3 Framework)
key_takeaways: VDAFs allow aggregation servers to verify that each client input belongs to a valid domain (e.g., a boolean 0/1 or bounded integer) using zero-knowledge Fully Linear Proofs (FLPs).
Prio3 supports diverse measurement types: Prio3Count (boolean hit counters), Prio3Sum (bounded integers), and Prio3Histogram (categorical bucket counters).
Clients generate an encoded input vector, split it into additive secret shares over a finite field, and generate an FLP proof share.
Aggregators verify proofs via single-round interactive protocols: invalid shares are rejected before aggregation, preventing malicious poisoning of platform metrics.
Combined with OHTTP transport framing to simultaneously guarantee network layer anonymity and cryptographic data confidentiality.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize on Prio3Sum and Prio3Histogram algorithms in the super-app client SDK for mini-app crash frequency and performance latency metrics.
Incorporate finite field proof verification checks into the platform Leader service before aggregating batch telemetry.
Implement automated batch size thresholds (minimum batch size K >= 1000 clients) to ensure k-anonymity and differential privacy.

title: Super-App Privacy-Preserving Telemetry Governance: Anti-Collusion, Key Rotation & Batch Policies
category: Privacy-Preserving Telemetry, Oblivious Protocols & Zero-Knowledge Architecture
standard_reference: RFC 9458 Section 6.2 (Operational Considerations) & DAP Section 7 (Privacy and Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Operational security for OHTTP and DAP hinges on strict organizational and administrative isolation between Relay and Gateway, and between Leader and Helper.
Platform operators must publish signed transparency manifests containing public HPKE gateway keys and DAP task definitions.
Anti-collusion audits: independent legal and technical auditors verify that traffic logs, IP tables, and MPC state are isolated and cryptographically wiped.
Differential privacy budgeting: collectors must enforce strict privacy loss parameters (epsilon and delta) across aggregate queries to prevent reconstruction attacks.
Protects regulated super-app operators from regulatory penalties under GDPR, Vietnam PDPD (Decree 13/2023, Law 91/2025/QH15), and CCPA.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish public transparency audit reports demonstrating physical and logical separation between OHTTP relay proxies and internal gateway endpoints.
Configure automated 24-hour HPKE gateway key rollover policies and distribute public key digests via signed application config bundles.
Incorporate strict differential privacy budget tracking on the platform analytics query interface to prevent iterative extraction of mini-app user telemetry.

title: IETF RFC 9497: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRFs) & Blinded RSA Token Primitives
category: Anti-Fraud, Trust Tokens & Cryptographic Proof Protocols
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9497 (Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions Using Prime-Order Groups) Section 3 (Protocol Overview) & Section 4 (OPRF Schemes)
key_takeaways: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRFs) allow a client to compute f(k, x) where x is the client's input and k is the server's private key, without revealing x to the server or k to the client.
Standardizes Two-Party OPRF protocols: Hash-to-Curve mapping, client-side blinding (scalar multiplication with random blinding factor r), server evaluation, and client unblinding.
Defines Verifiable OPRF (VOPRF) using discrete logarithm equality proofs (DLEQ) to prove the server evaluated the token with the correct public key.
Supports Partially Oblivious PRF (POPRF) incorporating public metadata (e.g. key identifier, token epoch, or trust level) into the cryptographic evaluation.
Forms the exact mathematical and cryptographic foundation underpinning Privacy Pass (RFC 9576 - RFC 9578) and W3C/WICG Private State Tokens.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement VOPRF prime-order curve operations (ristretto255 / NIST P-256) inside the super-app crypto core for anti-fraud trust token generation.
Utilize POPRF public metadata tags to embed issuance epoch and store tier classifications without sacrificing client anonymity.
Verify server DLEQ proofs inside native mobile client bridges before caching unblinded redemption tokens.

title: WICG Private State Token API: Architecture, Trust Token Issuance & Blinded Signing Lifecycle
category: Anti-Fraud, Trust Tokens & Cryptographic Proof Protocols
standard_reference: WICG Private State Token API Section 2 (System Overview) & Section 3 (Issuance Protocol)
key_takeaways: The Private State Token (PST) API enables a trusted top-level context (e.g., super-app identity provider) to issue cryptographically signed, unlinkable tokens to a verified user.
Issuance invocation: executed via `fetch(issuerUrl, { privateToken: { version: 1, operation: 'token-request' } })`.
Client blinds random nonces and transmits `Sec-Private-State-Token: ...` header to the issuer; issuer signs blinded nonces with its private key and returns them.
The browser/container unblinds the signature, validates issuer proofs, and stores the resulting Private State Tokens in origin-partitioned local storage.
Tokens are unlinkable: the issuer cannot correlate the identity or session at token issuance time with the session where the token is subsequently redeemed.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Serve as an authoritative PST Issuer for all embedded mini-apps: issue trust tokens to users who successfully complete KYC or biometric authentication.
Expose `privateToken: { operation: 'token-request' }` hooks through the host WebView container to facilitate silent trust token issuance.
Enforce token quotas (e.g., maximum 500 active tokens per user device) to optimize local storage and prevent hoard-and-replay attacks.

title: Private State Token Redemption: Redemption Records (RR), Cryptographic Binding & Cross-App Anti-Fraud
category: Anti-Fraud, Trust Tokens & Cryptographic Proof Protocols
standard_reference: WICG Private State Token API Section 4 (Redemption Protocol) & Section 5 (Redemption Record Sharing)
key_takeaways: Token redemption converts an unblinded token into a time-limited Redemption Record (RR) bound to a specific origin via `operation: 'token-redemption'`.
Client sends `Sec-Private-State-Token: ...` containing the token to the issuer; issuer validates token signature, records redemption against double-spend database, and returns signed RR.
A mini-app can then send the cached RR to third-party resource servers via `operation: 'send-redemption-record'`, including the `Sec-Redemption-Record` header.
Enables a merchant or advertising mini-app to verify that a user is human and trustworthy without knowing the user's super-app user ID, phone number, or real identity.
Mitigates bot farms, ad fraud, ticket scalping, and synthetic account creation across the super-app ecosystem in a privacy-compliant manner.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enable third-party mini-apps to request PST redemption records during high-risk actions (flash sales, ticket booking, voucher claims) to block bot manipulation.
Maintain a distributed double-spend redemption log across platform edge clusters to prevent token reuse across concurrent sessions.
Implement container-level rate-limiting on token redemption calls to mitigate timing analysis and side-channel deanonymization.

title: Private State Token Security: Storage Partitioning, Rate Limits & Tracking Prevention
category: Anti-Fraud, Trust Tokens & Cryptographic Proof Protocols
standard_reference: WICG Private State Token API Section 6 (Privacy and Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: PST incorporates rigorous defenses against tracking: an origin cannot query whether a token exists without attempting redemption.
Enforces origin-partitioned token storage: tokens issued for Issuer A cannot be inspected or redeemed by Issuer B.
Restricts the number of redemption attempts per top-level site per time window (rate limiting) to prevent binary search and entropy extraction.
Token redemption yields binary trust signals (trusted vs untrusted) or very low-entropy metadata (e.g. 2-3 bits), preventing high-entropy user fingerprinting.
Provides mathematical immunity against cross-app tracking while equipping mini-app developers with enterprise-grade anti-bot attestation.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce strict token metadata bit limits (maximum 3 bits / 8 distinct trust classifications) in the super-app issuer configuration.
Partition PST storage across mini-app appIDs in the native container database to prevent cross-mini-app fingerprinting attacks.
Log token issuance and redemption volumes per mini-app in security audit logs to detect abusive patterns and token draining attacks.

title: Super-App Enterprise Architecture: Centralized PST Issuance & Decentralized Mini-App Verification
category: Anti-Fraud, Trust Tokens & Cryptographic Proof Protocols
standard_reference: WICG Trust Token API / Private State Token Architecture Section 7 (Deployment Considerations)
key_takeaways: Enterprise super-apps act as natural root-of-trust identity anchors: they possess rich fraud detection signals (device attestation, SIM tenure, biometric login, transaction history).
By translating rich platform trust signals into lightweight Private State Tokens, the super-app empowers thousands of mini-apps without leaking user privacy.
Mini-apps integrate trust checks into checkout workflows with zero server-to-server API overhead or PII sharing.
Architectural pattern: Native container exposes `superapp.trust.requestToken()` / `superapp.trust.getRedemptionRecord()` bridging standard WICG fetch semantics.
Reduces platform-wide chargebacks and bot-driven inventory depletion by over 90% in high-volume retail and gaming mini-app ecosystems.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement native container bridge methods mimicking standard Private State Token fetch APIs for transparent cross-platform compatibility.
Establish automated risk scoring engines that dynamically grant PSTs based on hardware attestation (EAT/Play Integrity/DeviceCheck) and user account maturity.
Provide mini-app developers with lightweight open-source server SDKs to verify `Sec-Redemption-Record` signatures with zero external API calls.

title: W3C MiniApp Standardization White Paper: Dual-Process Architecture, View/Logic Separation & Container Model
category: W3C MiniApp Architecture, Runtime Isolation & Core Standards
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Standardization White Paper version 2 Section 2 (MiniApp Core Architecture) & Section 3 (Design Principles)
key_takeaways: The W3C MiniApp White Paper formalizes the industry-standard dual-process runtime architecture: strict physical separation between the View thread (UI rendering) and the Logic thread (Service Worker / JavaScript engine).
View thread: runs inside an isolated WebView/renderer, handles DOM/CSS layout, animation, and user input rendering.
Logic thread: executes business logic, data models, and API handling in a sandboxed JavaScript runtime (e.g. V8 isolate, JavaScriptCore) without direct access to the DOM.
Communication between View and Logic is mediated exclusively via asynchronous MessageChannel / IPC bridge through the Native Host Container.
Eliminates DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS) privilege escalation: malicious scripts injected into HTML cannot invoke privileged native device APIs.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate the dual-process View/Logic isolation architecture across all super-app mini-app execution runtimes (Android, iOS, desktop).
Strip direct `window`, `document`, and DOM manipulation APIs from the Logic thread runtime environment.
Enforce asynchronous message validation and parameter sanitization on the native IPC bridge mediating View and Logic communication.

title: W3C MiniApp Manifest Specification: Metadata, Page Routing, Window Decorators & Capability Scopes
category: W3C MiniApp Architecture, Runtime Isolation & Core Standards
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Manifest Candidate Recommendation Section 4 (Manifest Structure) & Section 5 (Window and Page Properties)
key_takeaways: W3C MiniApp Manifest standardizes the declarative configuration file (`manifest.json` / `app.json`) governing mini-app metadata, execution structure, and window behaviors.

Extends W3C Web App Manifest with mini-app specific primitives: `pages` array (declarative routing table), `window` settings (navigation bar style, background color, pull-to-refresh), and `tabBar` navigation.
Supports capability scoping and permission declarations: developers declare required device capabilities (e.g. bluetooth, camera, location) directly in manifest.
Defines `subpackages` architecture: allows splitting large mini-apps into independent code packages dynamically loaded on demand, cutting initial cold launch latency.
Enables deterministic static analysis by the super-app store review pipeline before approving or distributing packages.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt W3C MiniApp Manifest schema validation as a mandatory automated gate in the mini-app store submission pipeline.
Require declarative `subpackages` configuration for all mini-apps exceeding 4MB package size to ensure cold start launch under 800ms.
Enforce exact matching between declared manifest permission scopes and runtime bridge capability invocations.

title: W3C MiniApp Packaging Specification: Zip Container Structure, Digest Manifests & Cryptographic Integrity
category: W3C MiniApp Architecture, Runtime Isolation & Core Standards
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Packaging Candidate Recommendation Section 4 (Package Structure) & Section 5 (Integrity Verification)
key_takeaways: W3C MiniApp Packaging standardizes the physical archive format (`.zip` container) used to distribute, verify, and store mini-apps.
Standard container structure: root contains `manifest.json`, compiled view templates, packaged scripts, static assets, and a root digital signature manifest.
Specifies per-file SHA-256 digest validation: manifest indexes every included asset with its expected cryptographic hash.
Mandates container-level cryptographic signatures: packages must be signed by the developer and counter-signed by the super-app store platform.
Protects against tampering, man-in-the-middle content corruption, and malicious sub-resource injection during OTA distribution.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize package distribution on W3C MiniApp Packaging format with dual digital signatures (developer ECDSA signature + super-app store platform signature).
Validate per-file SHA-256 digests upon container extraction before staging files into local application sandboxes.
Reject and purge any package bundle exhibiting signature verification failures, unexpected file paths, or directory traversal (`../`) vulnerabilities.

title: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle Specification: Application & Page State Transitions, Hooks & Memory Reclamation
category: W3C MiniApp Architecture, Runtime Isolation & Core Standards
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle Specification Section 4 (MiniApp Lifecycle Model) & Section 5 (Page Lifecycle Model)
key_takeaways: W3C MiniApp Lifecycle establishes deterministic state machines for both the overall MiniApp instance and individual MiniApp Pages.
Application Lifecycle states: Initialization -> Launch -> Foreground (Active) -> Background -> Destroy.
Page Lifecycle states: Load -> Show -> Ready -> Hide -> Unload, paired with standardized callbacks (`onLaunch`, `onShow`, `onHide`, `onError`, `onPageNotFound`).
Background resource throttling: container automatically pauses timers, throttles network, and suspends high-frequency sensors when an app transitions to Background.
Deterministic memory eviction: specifies graceful destruction hooks and state serialization before low-memory termination by host OS.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement strict lifecycle callback dispatch in host container bridges, ensuring synchronous delivery of `onHide` and `onDestroy` events.
Automate immediate suspension of background media, camera streams, and location subscriptions upon `onHide` transition.
Provide structured `saveState()` and `restoreState()` lifecycle APIs enabling frictionless state restoration after process termination.

title: W3C MiniApp Addressing Specification: miniapp:// URI Scheme, Deep Linking & Parameter Serialization
category: W3C MiniApp Architecture, Runtime Isolation & Core Standards
standard_reference: W3C MiniApp Addressing Recommendation Section 4 (MiniApp URI Syntax) & Section 5 (Resolution Model)
key_takeaways: W3C MiniApp Addressing defines the standardized URI syntax for identifying, locating, and deep-linking into mini-apps and specific pages.
URI scheme syntax: `miniapp://<miniapp-id>/<page-path>?<query>#<fragment>`, where `miniapp-id` is an unambiguous registered identifier (e.g. domain-based or UUID).
Supports inter-app navigation: enables one mini-app to invoke or navigate to another mini-app via standardized declarative URI resolution.
Integrates query parameter passing and fragment routing, ensuring consistent deep-link routing from web browsers, SMS, and QR codes.
Defines security boundaries: host container enforces navigation authorization policies and origin checks before resolving target miniapps.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt `miniapp://` URI scheme resolution across native platform intent filters and universal link handlers.
Implement declarative inter-app invocation permission checks in the host container to prevent unauthorized cross-app data exfiltration.
Sanitize all query parameters and deep-link payload data before passing them into the target mini-app's `onLaunch` / `onShow` lifecycle arguments.

title: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1: JUMBF Manifest Store Encapsulation & Provenance Tree Architecture
category: Digital Media Provenance, C2PA Standards & Content Authenticity
standard_reference: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1 Section 6 (Assertions), Section 7 (Data Boxes) & Section 11 (Manifests)
key_takeaways: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) Technical Specification v2.1 defines an interoperable, open standard for binding cryptographically verifiable provenance metadata to digital media (images, video, audio, and documents).

Manifest encapsulation is based on ISO/IEC 19566-5 (JPEG Universal Metadata Box Format - JUMBF): packages manifest assertions, claims, and signature boxes inside standard JUMBF superboxes (`c2pa` box type).

Establishes a hierarchical provenance tree architecture: the 'Active Manifest' represents the most recent state/transformation of the asset, while 'Ingredient Manifests' cryptographically link upstream parent assets.

Supports dual manifest storage topologies: Embedded Manifests (placed directly in file format chunks/atoms such as JPEG APP11 markers, MP4 moov/c2pa boxes, or PNG eXIf/iTXt chunks) and External/Remote Manifests referenced via URI/HTTP link headers.

Ensures non-destructive provenance tracking: downstream edits (crops, filters, transcodings, AI generation) append a new active manifest referencing prior ingredients without corrupting earlier provenance history.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Integrate C2PA JUMBF manifest parsing into the super-app media ingestion pipeline to automatically detect and display content provenance on user-uploaded media.
Mandate that media generation mini-apps (AI image/video synthesizers) embed an active C2PA v2.1 manifest declaring model provenance, training metadata, and generation parameters.
Preserve embedded JUMBF metadata boxes during media compression and resizing pipelines on the super-app client and edge proxy servers.

title: C2PA Claims, Assertions Taxonomy & Provenance Graph: Actions, Hash-Data, Exif & AIGC Metadata
category: Digital Media Provenance, C2PA Standards & Content Authenticity
standard_reference: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1 Section 10 (Claims) & Section 6 (Assertions Taxonomy)
key_takeaways: A C2PA Manifest contains a Claim consisting of an ordered set of cryptographic assertions: actions assertions (`c2pa.actions`), hash-data bindings (`c2pa.hash.data`), ingredient references (`c2pa.ingredient`), and contextual metadata (`c2pa.metadata.exif`).

The `c2pa.actions` assertion standardizes a finite dictionary of provenance actions (e.g. `c2pa.created`, `c2pa.edited`, `c2pa.cropped`, `c2pa.filtered`, `c2pa.color_adjustments`, `c2pa.placed`, `c2pa.watermarked`, `c2pa.ai_generated`).

AI-Generated Content (AIGC) metadata is formally standardized via `c2pa.ai_generated` action and software agent descriptors (model name, version, training cutoff, prompt hashes), establishing transparent AI disclosure.

Ingredients assertions (`c2pa.ingredient`) provide the edges in the provenance directed acyclic graph (DAG): each ingredient contains the ingredient's JUMBF URI, title, format, relationship (`parentOf`, `componentOf`), and validation status.
Enables fine-grained provenance audit trails: Relying parties and viewers can traverse the complete edit history from camera sensor capture to final publishing.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated badge rendering in the super-app newsfeed and social channels displaying standardized C2PA icons for verified cameras vs AI-generated content.
Require third-party mini-apps submitting media for news, journalism, and public broadcast to include complete `c2pa.actions` provenance records.
Expose standardized JavaScript bridge APIs (`superapp.provenance.getManifest(mediaUri)`) allowing mini-apps to inspect parent ingredients and transformation actions.

title: C2PA Cryptographic Signature Standards: COSE_Sign1, X.509 Certificate Chains & RFC 3161 Timestamping
category: Digital Media Provenance, C2PA Standards & Content Authenticity
standard_reference: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1 Section 13 (Cryptography), Section 14 (Signatures) & Section 15 (Validation)
key_takeaways: C2PA manifest claims are cryptographically secured using CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE, RFC 9052) wrapped in a `COSE_Sign1` structure embedded in the manifest JUMBF signature box.
Supports modern asymmetric signing algorithms: Ed25519 (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm), ECDSA over NIST P-256 / P-384, and RSA with PSS padding (minimum 2048-bit keys).

Trust anchoring relies on X.509v3 PKI: signing certificates are conveyed via the COSE header parameter `x5chain`, linking the signer to a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) compliant with the C2PA Trust List.

Enforces mandatory RFC 3161 cryptographic timestamping: includes a signed Time-Stamp Token (TST) from an authorized Time Stamping Authority (TSA) inside the COSE signature uncompressed attributes to prove manifest creation time before certificate expiration.

Validation algorithm mandates strict revocation checks: the verifier evaluates Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP, RFC 6960) responses or Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) anchored at the time certified by the RFC 3161 token.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Anchor super-app media verification against an automated C2PA Trust List distribution service maintained within the platform gateway.
Enforce mandatory RFC 3161 timestamp verification on all incoming C2PA manifests to prevent post-expiration signing and backdated fraud.
Reject COSE signatures using deprecated hash algorithms (SHA-1, MD5) or weak RSA keys (< 2048-bit) during store review and runtime media upload.

title: C2PA Content Binding Mechanics: Hard Byte-Range Hashing, Soft Watermarking & Assertion Redaction Governance
category: Digital Media Provenance, C2PA Standards & Content Authenticity
standard_reference: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1 Section 9 (Binding to Content) & Section 6.8 (Redaction of Assertions)
key_takeaways: Content binding guarantees that the C2PA manifest cannot be detached and fraudulently applied to a different asset: supports Hard Bindings and Soft Bindings.
Hard Bindings compute cryptographic SHA-256/SHA-384 hashes across exact byte ranges of the media payload (excluding the JUMBF manifest box itself) specified in the `c2pa.hash.data` assertion.
Soft Bindings accommodate lossy distribution channels (social media recompression, format transcoding, screenshotting) using robust perceptual hashes or embedded steganographic watermarks.
Assertion Redaction: allows downstream publishers to redact sensitive assertions (e.g. GPS coordinates, creator biometrics, face embeddings) while preserving cryptographic integrity.

Redaction mechanics: the redacted assertion's byte box is replaced with a `c2pa.redacted` assertion containing the target JUMBF URI and salt digest, ensuring the root claim signature remains cryptographically valid.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement privacy-preserving assertion redaction in the super-app client SDK: automatically redact exact GPS coordinates from user media before public timeline display.
Combine Hard Bindings with container-level soft watermarking to maintain provenance integrity when users share media across third-party chat and messaging mini-apps.
Enforce strict validation of byte-range exclusion tables in `c2pa.hash.data` to prevent header injection attacks in multipart media files.

title: Super-App C2PA Runtime Integration: Financial eKYC Anti-Spoofing, Camera Binding & Store Integrity Gating
category: Digital Media Provenance, C2PA Standards & Content Authenticity
standard_reference: C2PA Technical Specification v2.1 Section 16 (User Experience) & Section 17 (Security and Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: Integrating C2PA provenance into super-app mobile architecture transforms identity verification (eKYC) and high-value transactions by eliminating presentation attacks and synthetic deepfakes.

Camera Hardware Binding: native super-app camera captures capture images directly into secure hardware buffers, generating a hardware-signed C2PA manifest (using Secure Enclave / StrongBox attestation keys) before passing to the mini-app WebView.

Financial eKYC Gating: banking and loan mini-apps verify that national ID photos and selfie video streams contain unbroken hardware-rooted C2PA manifests, rejecting gallery uploads and virtual camera emulators.

Store Submission Compliance: the super-app app store validates that mini-app promotional assets, screenshot bundles, and video trailers include valid C2PA author assertions signed by the registered developer.
Provides an unforgeable evidentiary chain for regulatory compliance under EU AI Act transparency rules and national financial security directives.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement a hardware-anchored C2PA signing pipeline in the native camera module (`superapp.camera.takeVerifiedPhoto()`) returning media with embedded root manifests.
Require all financial, fintech, and banking mini-apps to mandate C2PA hardware camera manifests for biometric onboarding and document scans.
Display an unambiguous, native verification drawer when users tap C2PA provenance badges in the UI, rendering signer identity, timestamp, and edit history.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0): Legal Framework, European Digital Identity Wallet & Mandatory VLOP Acceptance
category: Decentralized Identity, European Digital Identity Wallet & eIDAS 2.0
standard_reference: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 & European Commission Digital Strategy on eID
key_takeaways: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0), enacted in 2024, establishes a comprehensive legal and technical framework for cross-border electronic identification and trust services across all 27 EU Member States.
Mandates that each EU Member State must provide at least one certified European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet to all citizens, residents, and businesses by 2026.

Imposes mandatory acceptance obligations: Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs, as designated under the Digital Services Act) and private entities legally required to strongly authenticate users (banks, airlines, telcos, utilities) must accept the EUDI Wallet for user identification and login.
Establishes legal equivalence: Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES) created via the wallet have equivalent legal standing to handwritten signatures across the European Union.
Prohibits commercial wallet providers and state issuers from using identity transactions to track user habits, monetize telemetry, or profile behavior without explicit legal basis.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Architect the super-app identity core to act as an authorized Relying Party compliant with eIDAS 2.0 EUDI Wallet integration standards.
Incorporate certified Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) invocation flows into enterprise contract and loan disbursement mini-apps.
Prepare the super-app store review guidelines to mandate EUDI Wallet acceptance for all commercial mini-apps operating within European economic jurisdictions.

title: EUDI Wallet Architecture & Reference Framework (ARF): Four-Party Trust Model & Common Secure Cryptographic Applications
category: Decentralized Identity, European Digital Identity Wallet & eIDAS 2.0
standard_reference: EUDI Wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) Section 2 (EUDI Wallet Ecosystem) & Section 3 (Roles and Trust Model)
key_takeaways: The EUDI Wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) outlines the functional building blocks, cryptographic primitives, and interaction protocols across the European digital identity ecosystem.

Operates a decentralized Four-Party Trust Model: User/Holder (citizen managing the wallet), Issuer (public authorities or accredited entities issuing credentials), Relying Party / Verifier (super-app or service consuming credentials), and Wallet Provider (technical entity operating the wallet application).

Defines Common Secure Cryptographic Applications (CSCA) and Secure Cryptographic Devices (QSCD): requires hardware-backed private key protection meeting Common Criteria EAL4+ (or equivalent high-level assurance).
Separates wallet application logic from cryptographic key storage: supports device-bound hardware enclaves (eSE / UICC / StrongBox) as well as certified remote HSM / cloud trust services.
Standardizes interaction flows for both Proximity (in-person NFC / BLE / QR presentation) and Remote (online HTTPS / REST / Web-redirect presentation).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Align super-app native wallet architecture with the EUDI ARF role definitions to ensure seamless interoperability between local mini-apps and sovereign identity wallets.
Enforce QSCD-equivalent hardware security (Android StrongBox, iOS Secure Enclave) for wallet key generation within the native container.
Implement standardized relying party verification logic to validate signed trust marks issued by accredited Member State Supervisory Bodies.

title: EUDI ARF Person Identification Data (PID) & QEAA: Data Models, OpenID Protocols & Status Lifecycle
category: Decentralized Identity, European Digital Identity Wallet & eIDAS 2.0
standard_reference: EUDI Wallet ARF Section 4 (Credentials and Attestations) & Section 5 (Protocols: OID4VCI and OID4VP)
key_takeaways: The EUDI Wallet handles two primary credential types: Person Identification Data (PID, the official sovereign identity containing legal name, birth date, unique identifier) and Qualified Electronic Attestation of Attributes (QEAA, educational diplomas, professional licenses, medical certificates, bank authorizations).
PID and QEAA support dual verifiable credential data models: ISO/IEC 18013-5 mDL binary CBOR/COSE structures and IETF SD-JWT VC (Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token Verifiable Credentials).
Credential Issuance Protocol: standardizes on OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance (OID4VCI 1.0) with mandatory Proof of Possession (c_nonce) and DPoP sender-constraining.
Credential Presentation Protocol: standardizes on OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP 1.0) using response_mode `direct_post.jwt` and cryptographic SessionTranscript binding.

Status management and revocation: utilizes privacy-preserving W3C Bitstring Status Lists or IETF OAuth Token Status Lists (draft-ietf-oauth-status-list) to check validity without tracking verification events.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize the super-app credential bridge to natively parse both SD-JWT VC and ISO 18013-5 mDL credential formats returned by EUDI Wallets.
Implement OID4VP presentation exchange in the super-app native container to allow mini-apps to request specific QEAA claims (e.g. valid driving license, university diploma).
Incorporate automated status list parsing to ensure revoked PIDs or commercial attestations are instantly invalidated across all mini-app sessions.

title: EUDI ARF Privacy Engineering: Unobservability, Selective Disclosure & Anti-Correlation Protections
category: Decentralized Identity, European Digital Identity Wallet & eIDAS 2.0
standard_reference: EUDI Wallet ARF Section 6 (Privacy and Data Protection) & Annex C (Cryptographic Requirements)
key_takeaways: A core pillar of eIDAS 2.0 and the EUDI ARF is Unobservability: neither the Wallet Provider nor the Credential Issuer can observe or log where, when, or to whom the user presents their credentials.
Issuer Blindness: achieved by separating credential issuance from presentation; once a credential is issued, the issuer receives no telemetric callbacks during subsequent verification events.

Selective Disclosure & Predicate Verification: users disclose only minimal required attributes (e.g. boolean age verification `age_over_18 = true`) without revealing their birth date, address, or full legal name.

Anti-Correlation & Pseudonymity: enforces pairwise pseudonymous identifiers (PPID) and unique ephemeral device keys per Relying Party, preventing multiple super-apps or mini-apps from colluding to track user activity across services.
Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP): ARF specifies migration paths toward cryptographic ZKP cryptosuites (BBS+ / anonymous credentials) for unlinkable multi-show presentations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce zero-knowledge predicate requests in the mini-app permission model (e.g. requesting `age_over_21` instead of full date of birth for alcohol and gaming mini-apps).
Isolate relying party client identifiers across individual mini-apps to ensure the host super-app prevents cross-merchant tracking.
Audit all super-app telemetry pipelines to strictly guarantee that identity presentation payloads are never transmitted to platform analytics servers.

title: Super-App EUDI Integration: Cross-Border Onboarding, e-Commerce Age Gating & Regulated API Delegation
category: Decentralized Identity, European Digital Identity Wallet & eIDAS 2.0
standard_reference: EUDI Wallet ARF Section 7 (Integration and Interfaces) & Section 8 (Security Architecture)
key_takeaways: Integrating EUDI Wallet capabilities into commercial super-apps provides a frictionless, high-assurance digital onboarding gateway across regulated industries (banking, healthcare, transport, government).
Cross-Border Interoperability: allows a citizen from any EU Member State to onboard onto a foreign super-app instantly without manual paper passport scanning or brittle third-party OCR pipelines.

Native Container Delegation: the host super-app exposes a standard `navigator.identity.get({ digital: { providers: [...] } })` JavaScript interface, allowing mini-apps to request verified claims via OS-native credential sheets.

Transaction Binding & Dynamic Linking: high-value transactions combine EUDI authentication with PSD2-compliant cryptographic consent, binding the transaction amount and recipient to the user's electronic confirmation.

Store Compliance Gating: the super-app marketplace validates that mini-apps handling regulated services (financial leasing, crypto assets under MiCA, prescription medication) possess accredited QEAA verifier certificates.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement W3C Digital Credentials API hooks in the super-app WebView container, bridging directly into the native EUDI Wallet subsystem.
Require all mini-apps dealing with age-restricted goods to mandate EUDI privacy-preserving age attestation before checkout.
Establish an automated verification gateway that checks relying party registration and digital trust marks before permitting mini-apps to request user PID data.

title: IETF SCITT Architecture: Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency and Trust Model & Core Roles
category: Supply Chain Security, Notarization & IETF SCITT Transparency Ledgers
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-scitt-architecture Section 1 (Introduction), Section 2 (Terminology) & Section 3 (System Architecture)
key_takeaways: The IETF Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT) architecture establishes a decentralized, verifiable standard for publishing, auditing, and querying claims about software artifacts and supply chains.

Deconstructs supply chain auditing into four fundamental roles: Issuer (creates and signs statements about an artifact), Transparency Service / Notary (validates statements, records them in an append-only ledger, and issues receipts), Ledger (the immutable append-only data store), and Verifier (evaluates statements and receipts).

Decouples statement creation from registration: an Issuer signs an assertion offline; the Transparency Service anchors it onto an append-only cryptographic log, making it globally discoverable and immutable.
Eliminates reliance on vendor trust alone: all claims (build provenance, security scans, vulnerability disclosures, release approvals) become auditable public or consortium records.
Directly addresses modern supply chain attacks (code tampering, compromised developer credentials, dependency confusion, silent backdoors) by providing non-repudiable audit trails.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Deploy an internal SCITT Transparency Service within the super-app platform infrastructure to record all mini-app submission, review, and deployment events.
Mandate that third-party developers register their signed build statements with the super-app SCITT service before initiating store submission review.
Enforce that client devices verify SCITT notarization receipts before executing downloaded mini-app packages.

title: SCITT Signed Statements: COSE_Sign1 Envelopes, Feeds & Canonical Payload Binding
category: Supply Chain Security, Notarization & IETF SCITT Transparency Ledgers
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-scitt-architecture Section 4 (Statements and Envelopes) & Section 5 (Abstract Statement Syntax)
key_takeaways: SCITT statements are encapsulated using CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE, RFC 9052 / RFC 9053) formatted as `COSE_Sign1` structures.

Defines the `feed` parameter: a string identifier in the protected header that groups sequential statements related to a specific product, package, or artifact lifecycle (e.g. `miniapp.com.merchant.food/releases`).
The payload carries an opaque, typed assertion: can encapsulate CycloneDX/SPDX SBOMs, OpenVEX vulnerability triage sheets, SLSA provenance attestations, or custom security audit reports.
Protected header parameters mandate issuer key identification (`kid` or `x5chain`), signing algorithm (e.g. Ed25519, ES256, ES384), content type, and registration parameters.
Provides canonical binary serialization via CBOR Canonical Encoding Rules (RFC 8949 Section 3.9), ensuring deterministic hashing across distributed notarization systems.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize mini-app release manifest envelopes on SCITT `COSE_Sign1` structures with dedicated `feed` identifiers bound to each mini-app's unique bundle ID.
Require developer CI/CD pipelines to output SCITT-compliant signed statements containing package SHA-256 digests and Git commit hashes.
Enforce strict validation of protected header parameters during store review, rejecting any submission with unauthenticated or malleable metadata.

title: SCITT Transparency Receipts: Merkle Tree Inclusion Proofs, Tree Head Signing & draft-ietf-cose-merkle-tree-proofs
category: Supply Chain Security, Notarization & IETF SCITT Transparency Ledgers
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-cose-merkle-tree-proofs Section 3 (Receipt Structure) & draft-ietf-scitt-architecture Section 6 (Receipts)
key_takeaways: When a Transparency Service accepts a signed statement, it appends the statement to a Merkle tree and generates a cryptographically verifiable SCITT Receipt.

The SCITT Receipt contains two components: an Inclusion Proof (demonstrating the statement exists at a specific leaf index in the tree) and a Signed Tree Head (STH, the tree root signed by the transparency service's private key).
Inclusion proofs are encoded in standardized COSE structures defined by `draft-ietf-cose-merkle-tree-proofs`, allowing offline verification without querying the live ledger.

Auditors and verifiers can mathematically prove that: (1) the statement was recorded at a specific tree height, (2) the log has remained strictly append-only without historical modification, and (3) all clients observe a consistent ledger view.
Enables instant detection of 'split-world' attacks where a rogue actor attempts to serve malicious mini-app builds to targeted users while hiding them from public audit.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Package SCITT Merkle tree inclusion proofs directly into mini-app distribution bundles (`.zip` container root receipt) for offline client-side validation.
Implement high-performance Merkle inclusion proof verification in the super-app client container runtime during package unpack.
Maintain an independent consistency auditor service that continuously monitors Transparency Service STHs to detect log forks and unauthorized tampering.

title: SCITT Supply Chain Attestation Gating: SBOMs, OpenVEX Exploitation Status & SLSA Provenance Binding
category: Supply Chain Security, Notarization & IETF SCITT Transparency Ledgers
standard_reference: IETF draft-ietf-scitt-software-use-cases Section 3 (Software Supply Chain Use Cases) & Section 4 (Attestation Types)
key_takeaways: SCITT serves as the unifying trust layer for heterogeneous supply chain attestations: connects Software Bill of Materials (SBOMs), vulnerability triage, and build provenance into a single audit graph.

Dynamic Vulnerability Tracking: developers and automated security scanners register OpenVEX statements directly on the artifact's feed, asserting whether a newly discovered CVE affects the production mini-app (`not_affected`, `affected`, `fixed`, `under_investigation`).

Hermetic Build Provenance: embeds OpenSSF SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) build provenance proofs, cryptographically certifying that binaries were produced by hermetic GitHub Actions / GitLab CI builders.

Cryptographic Revocation: when an exploit or compromised dependency is discovered, the vendor registers a revocation statement on the SCITT log, providing an immutable record that triggers automated remediation across consumers.
Eliminates friction in regulatory audits: provides enterprise security teams with immediate, cryptographically verifiable answers regarding third-party mini-app dependencies and exploitability.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate that all submitted mini-app packages include a SCITT-registered CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM and SLSA Build Provenance attestation.
Configure super-app store review engines to automatically verify OpenVEX status on SCITT feeds before approving version updates.
Implement automated vulnerability alerting that scans SCITT feeds and flags mini-apps containing unmitigated critical vulnerabilities for immediate quarantine.

title: Super-App SCITT Release Pipeline: Transparent Store Notarization, Instant Revocation & Zero-Trust Client Execution
category: Supply Chain Security, Notarization & IETF SCITT Transparency Ledgers
standard_reference: IETF SCITT Architecture Section 7 (Deployment and Operational Considerations) & Section 8 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: Deploying a SCITT-based release pipeline establishes a zero-trust distribution architecture for the super-app mini-app marketplace.

Two-Phase Notarization: (1) Developer registers signed package statement on their private feed; (2) Store review system audits the package and registers a signed Approval Statement on the platform's public endorsement feed.

Client Enforcement Policy: the super-app client container enforces a strict admission policy: a mini-app package is executed only if it contains valid inclusion proofs for both the developer statement and the store approval statement.

Global Kill-Switch & Revocation: if a zero-day exploit or malicious backdoor is detected in an active mini-app, the security team registers a Revocation Statement on the log; client containers syncing the log instantly refuse execution.

Completely eliminates insider threat and rogue administrator risks: no platform engineer can silently publish an unauthorized mini-app version without generating an immutable, publicly auditable log entry.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement the Two-Phase Notarization pipeline requiring dual SCITT receipts (developer build receipt + store certification receipt) for all public mini-app releases.
Equip the native super-app container with a local SCITT receipt verification engine and cached log consistency checks.
Establish an automated emergency revocation broadcast system that streams SCITT revocation events to active mobile clients via WebPush and WebSocket bridges.

title: IETF RFC 9470: OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication Challenge Protocol & WWW-Authenticate Gating
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9470 Section 3 (Protocol Flow) & Section 4 (The insufficient_user_authentication Error Code)
key_takeaways: RFC 9470 defines a standardized interoperable challenge protocol enabling protected resources (Resource Servers / Microservices) to demand step-up authentication when an incoming access token has insufficient authentication strength or freshness.
Introduces the 'insufficient_user_authentication' error code returned in HTTP 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate Bearer response headers.
Includes 'acr_values' indicating acceptable Authentication Context Class References required for high-risk operations (e.g. biometric authentication, hardware token, FIDO2/WebAuthn).
Includes 'max_age' indicating the maximum allowable elapsed time in seconds since the end-user was actively authenticated, preventing session replay on sensitive actions.
Eliminates proprietary error conventions between mini-app microservices and the super-app authorization server, streamlining in-app re-authentication flows.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Adopt RFC 9470 across all super-app resource gateways and mini-app partner APIs executing sensitive financial transfers, security settings changes, or biometric activations.

Implement client-side interception in the super-app WebView bridge to detect 401 'insufficient_user_authentication' challenges and automatically trigger native step-up prompts (e.g., FaceID/Biometrics or passkey prompt) without breaking user session state.

title: RFC 9470 AS Discovery Metadata (acrs_supported) & Authorization Request acr_values/max_age Negotiation
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9470 Section 6 (Authorization Server Metadata) & Section 5 (Client Handling)
key_takeaways: RFC 9470 Section 6 defines the 'acrs_supported' metadata element published at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, declaring the array of ACR values the AS can satisfy.

When a client receives a 401 with 'insufficient_user_authentication', it initiates a new authorization flow transmitting the challenged 'acr_values' and/or 'max_age' parameters directly to the AS /authorize or /par endpoints.
Enables dynamic escalation without forcing global session termination or re-authenticating for low-risk operations.
Provides cryptographic proof in the resulting access token or ID token via 'acr' and 'auth_time' claims validating that the step-up challenge was fulfilled.
Guarantees that resource servers can verify token freshness and credential strength deterministically using standard JWT introspection or local verification.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish 'acrs_supported' in the super-app OAuth 2.0 authorization server metadata catalog (e.g. ['urn:superapp:auth:pwd', 'urn:superapp:auth:bio', 'urn:superapp:auth:fido-hw']).
Support standard 'max_age' and 'acr_values' in Pushed Authorization Requests (RFC 9126 PAR) to prevent URL query parameter manipulation during step-up elevation.

title: RFC 9470 Token Claims Verification: 'acr' and 'auth_time' Compliance Verification in Resource Gateways
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9470 Section 3.2 (Resource Server Validating Access Tokens)
key_takeaways: Resource servers must inspect the 'acr' claim in the access token or introspection response to ensure it matches or exceeds the required security policy tier.

Resource servers enforcing freshness must calculate (current_time - auth_time) and reject requests where elapsed time exceeds the operation's policy limit (even if the access token lifetime 'exp' is still valid).

Distinguishes access token expiration ('exp') from user presence/authentication age ('auth_time'), resolving a major security vulnerability where long-lived tokens execute high-risk actions without fresh consent.
Provides clear separation between authentication context (how the user proved their identity) and authorization scopes (what resources the client can access).
Ensures zero-trust policy enforcement across distributed microservices without centralizing business authorization logic.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure API gateway policies to reject financial transactions if (now - auth_time) > 300 seconds (5 minutes) or if 'acr' does not denote hardware-backed biometric verification.
Standardize error responses so mini-apps can handle step-up prompts transparently via container SDK helpers.

title: RFC 9470 Security Considerations: Anti-Looping Defenses, Downgrade Attack Prevention & Privacy Protections
standard_reference: IETF RFC 9470 Section 7 (Security Considerations) & Section 8 (Privacy Considerations)
key_takeaways: RFC 9470 warns against infinite redirection/challenge loops: clients must limit consecutive step-up attempts (maximum 2-3 retries) and abort if an AS returns a token that still fails the RS's criteria.
Mitigates downgrade attacks: malicious clients cannot bypass 'acr' requirements by omitting requested ACRs, as the resource server unconditionally enforces its internal baseline policy.
Protects user privacy by restricting the granularity of ACR definitions to coarse-grained capabilities rather than exposing detailed biometric or physical sensor telemetry to third-party mini-apps.
Requires HTTPS and mutual authentication or sender-constrained tokens (DPoP / mTLS) to prevent interception and injection of step-up challenge headers.
Addresses session desynchronization: clients must invalidate older, lower-privilege tokens upon acquiring step-up tokens if policy dictates single active session tokens per client.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement loop detection in the super-app native container bridge to break infinite step-up cycles and surface user-friendly recovery UI.
Enforce RFC 9449 DPoP or mTLS binding on all step-up access tokens to prevent theft of high-privilege credentials.

title: Super-App Native Step-Up Orchestration: Automated WebView Interception & Native Biometric Sheet Mediation
standard_reference: RFC 9470 Implementation Architecture for Super-App Containers & Hybrid Mini-Apps
key_takeaways: When a mini-app issues an AJAX/Fetch request to its backend or super-app Open API that yields a 401 'insufficient_user_authentication', the request interceptor delegates to the host container.

The container parses 'acr_values' and 'max_age', displays the OS-native biometric verification sheet (Face ID, Touch ID, Android BiometricPrompt), and contacts the super-app OAuth server with the biometric assertion.
The AS issues a fresh sender-constrained token with updated 'acr' and 'auth_time', which the container silently injects into the pending request before retrying.
The end-user experiences a seamless native biometric verification without full-page navigation, URL flickering, or losing their shopping cart or input state.
Third-party mini-app JavaScript code never touches user biometrics, master credentials, or raw authentication keys, strictly adhering to zero-trust privacy boundaries.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Expose 'superapp.auth.requestStepUp({ acrValues, maxAge })' in the mini-app JS SDK, backed by native container handling of RFC 9470 challenges.
Enforce mandatory step-up challenges for transactions exceeding threshold values (e.g. payment > 500,000 VND or high-risk administrative operations).

title: Cross-Origin Embedder Policy: 'credentialless' Header Semantics & No-Credential Subresource Isolation
category: Web Security, Cross-Origin Isolation & Subresource Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C / WHATWG HTML Specification Section 4.12 & WICG COEP Credentialless
key_takeaways: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP): 'credentialless' allows a document to achieve cross-origin isolation without requiring every cross-origin subresource to explicitly send a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP) header.
Cross-origin requests triggered from a 'credentialless' environment are made without ambient credentials (cookies, client certificates, HTTP authorization headers).
If the cross-origin server responds without credentials, the browser safely permits loading and rendering the subresource, eliminating Spectre cross-origin read attack vectors.

Substantially lowers the developer friction of enabling high-performance APIs (SharedArrayBuffer, performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory, high-resolution timers) for mini-apps incorporating third-party media or CDN assets.
Prevents malicious mini-apps from probing internal intranet or authenticated user resources via side-channel timing attacks.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Configure the super-app WebView container runtime to serve 'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless' alongside 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin' for high-performance mini-apps requiring WebAssembly threads and SharedArrayBuffer.
Document clear migration paths for mini-app developers transitioning from legacy insecure embeddings to COEP credentialless.

title: HTMLIFrameElement 'credentialless' Attribute & Ephemeral Child Frame Isolation
category: Web Security, Cross-Origin Isolation & Subresource Sandboxing
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML Specification Section 4.8.5 (The iframe element: credentialless attribute)
key_takeaways: The boolean 'credentialless' attribute on <iframe> elements instructs the user agent to load the framed document in an ephemeral, partitioned, credential-less storage and network context.
The credentialless iframe cannot access the ambient cookies, storage, or cache of its origin, and outgoing network requests omit cookies and credentials unless explicitly opted in.

Any storage created by the credentialless iframe (IndexedDB, localStorage, CacheStorage) is isolated to a temporary, non-persistent partitioned storage partition destroyed upon navigation or destruction.
Allows a parent mini-app to safely embed untrusted third-party interactive widgets, ads, or partner content without allowing them to leak user credentials or access tracking state.
Acts as a major browser-native sandbox capability complementing traditional iframe 'sandbox' attributes with automatic cryptographic and storage boundaries.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce mandatory 'credentialless' attribute injection on all dynamic third-party web content or affiliate partner widgets embedded inside super-app mini-apps.
Verify that mini-app container policies prohibit embedding unvetted third-party frames without either 'sandbox' or 'credentialless' flags.

title: WICG Anonymous Iframe Architecture: Enabling Cross-Origin Isolation in Legacy-Heavy Mini-Apps
category: Web Security, Cross-Origin Isolation & Subresource Sandboxing
standard_reference: WICG Anonymous Iframes Specification & Cross-Origin Isolation Compatibility Explainer
key_takeaways: The Anonymous Iframe specification (originating in WICG and upstreamed into WHATWG HTML credentialless iframe) addresses the challenge where COEP: require-corp broke third-party iframe integrations.
By loading frames in a completely anonymous context, cross-origin documents do not have access to shared ambient state, so they cannot be weaponized to read sensitive user information across origins.
Enables super-app host pages running under Cross-Origin Isolation to embed third-party payment gateways, customer support chats, or partner widgets that have not yet deployed CORP headers.
Establishes a double-partitioning model ensuring that the iframe's network requests cannot be linked to the user's primary browsing session in external mobile browsers.
Provides granular control over window.postMessage communication between parent mini-apps and anonymous child frames, validating event origin and payload schemas.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Leverage anonymous/credentialless iframe support to allow legacy mini-app partner integrations to run within high-security cross-origin isolated super-app runtime shells.
Audit all iframe communication channels to ensure postMessage contracts enforce strict validation of event.origin and structured cloning types.

title: Cross-Origin Isolation APIs (SharedArrayBuffer, High-Res Timers) & Spectre Hardware Security Gates
category: Web Security, Cross-Origin Isolation & Subresource Sandboxing
standard_reference: WHATWG HTML / ECMAScript Specification & MDN Cross-Origin Isolation Guide
key_takeaways: High-performance browser features—specifically SharedArrayBuffer (shared memory multithreading) and sub-millisecond performance.now() timers—are gated behind cross-origin isolation (window.crossOriginIsolated === true).

To activate crossOriginIsolated, the host document must deliver both 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin' (or same-origin-allow-popups) and 'Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp' or 'credentialless'.
Prevents transient execution / speculative execution side-channel attacks (Spectre / Meltdown) from extracting memory contents across untrusted origins running in the same process.
Mini-apps employing 3D gaming engines (Unity, Unreal WebGL/WebGPU) or heavy audio/video DSP algorithms require SharedArrayBuffer for real-time parallel computing across Web Workers.
The super-app platform must ensure that isolating the mini-app does not prevent legitimate OAuth bridge redirects or parent-child communication.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Provide an automated opt-in configuration in the mini-app manifest ('cross_origin_isolated: true') that instructs the native container proxy to inject COOP: same-origin and COEP: credentialless headers.
Perform automated static analysis during app store submission to verify that mini-apps using SharedArrayBuffer declare valid isolation headers and handle isolation degradation gracefully.

title: The CORP, COOP, and COEP Triad: Comprehensive Defense-in-Depth Container Sandboxing Architecture
category: Web Security, Cross-Origin Isolation & Subresource Sandboxing
standard_reference: W3C Web Application Security Working Group: Post-Spectre Web Development & Container Security Architecture
key_takeaways: Security architecture requires orchestrating three interrelated policies: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP), Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP), and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP).
CORP ('same-origin', 'same-site', 'cross-origin') protects server resources from being read by unauthorized origins via media, script, or image elements.
COOP ('same-origin', 'same-origin-allow-popups', 'unsafe-none') isolates browsing contexts, preventing cross-window DOM manipulation and window.opener abuse.
COEP ('require-corp', 'credentialless') prevents a document from loading any resource that does not explicitly permit it or that carries ambient credentials.

Together, this triad transforms the traditional permissive web security model into an explicit, zero-trust boundary essential for enterprise-grade super-apps running multiple third-party financial and commercial applications.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Formulate a mandatory container header policy establishing CORP: same-site on all internal super-app API endpoints, preventing unauthorized mini-app resource scraping.
Audit all third-party mini-app submissions to ensure proper configuration of the CORP/COOP/COEP triad before granting access to sensitive platform APIs.

title: W3C JSON-LD 1.1 Core Syntax: Context Mapping, IRIs, Node Objects & Semantic Interoperability
category: Semantic Web, Data Architecture & Structured Catalog Metadata
standard_reference: W3C Recommendation 16 July 2020: JSON-LD 1.1 - A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data Section 3 (Basic Concepts) & Section 4 (Syntax Tokens)
key_takeaways: JSON-LD 1.1 provides a standardized JSON-based syntax for serializing Linked Data, mapping plain JSON keys to unambiguous Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs) using the '@context' keyword.
Defines core syntax keywords: '@id' for global subject identification, '@type' for class taxonomy, '@vocab' for default vocabulary scoping, and '@graph' for multi-node graph containers.
Allows disparate mini-apps, partner catalogs, and super-app search indexes to exchange structured data without schema collision or ambiguous property naming.
Maintains 100% syntactic backward compatibility with standard JSON, allowing existing REST APIs and client SDKs to consume payloads without specialized RDF parsers.
Enables super-app marketplace catalogs to ingest rich structured schemas (Schema.org SoftwareApplication, Product, Organization, Offer) for semantic discovery and federated search.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Mandate JSON-LD 1.1 metadata annotations in mini-app store manifests ('manifest.jsonld') and in-app content sharing payloads to enable rich indexation and conversational AI search indexing.
Adopt Schema.org vocabularies (@context: 'https://schema.org') for mini-app store catalog entries, including pricing, developer identity, and content classifications.

title: JSON-LD 1.1 Processing Algorithms: Expansion, Compaction & Flattening Canonical Normalization
category: Semantic Web, Data Architecture & Structured Catalog Metadata
standard_reference: W3C Recommendation: JSON-LD 1.1 Processing Algorithms and API Section 4 (Algorithms)
key_takeaways: JSON-LD 1.1 API defines deterministic transformation algorithms: Expansion, Compaction, Flattening, and RDF conversion.
Expansion removes the '@context' and transforms all properties and types into fully qualified IRIs, providing a canonical representation ideal for security verification and policy audits.
Compaction applies a target '@context' to an expanded document, producing a concise, developer-friendly JSON format optimized for network transmission and mobile client consumption.
Flattening ensures every entity in the graph is represented as a top-level node with flattened '@id' references, eliminating deeply nested cyclic dependencies.
Guarantees that disparate data payloads submitted by independent mini-app developers can be normalized into deterministic data structures before indexing or digital signing.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Implement automated JSON-LD expansion during mini-app package ingestion to normalize and validate third-party manifest metadata against the super-app platform schema.
Use compacted JSON-LD representations in mobile client catalog feed APIs to minimize bandwidth usage and parsing overhead on constrained cellular networks.

title: JSON-LD 1.1 Framing Specification: Deterministic Tree-Shaping for Mobile UI Components & Search Feeds
category: Semantic Web, Data Architecture & Structured Catalog Metadata
standard_reference: W3C Recommendation 16 July 2020: JSON-LD 1.1 Framing Section 4 (Framing Algorithm)
key_takeaways: JSON-LD 1.1 Framing allows developers to impose a specific hierarchical tree layout on a flat, interconnected graph of linked data.
Uses a 'frame' document containing matching criteria ('@type', property inclusion, '@requireAll', '@explicit') to extract and structure subgraphs into predictable nested objects.

Solves the primary challenge of consuming linked data in mobile frontend frameworks (React Native, Flutter, Swift, Kotlin), where components require deterministic object hierarchies rather than graph traversals.
Supports '@embed' controls ('@always', '@once', '@never') to prevent duplicate object representations or circular graph references in mobile memory buffers.
Enables the super-app store UI to dynamically project complex federated catalog graphs into clean, component-ready view models.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Standardize official JSON-LD frames for common super-app views: Store Homepage Carousel, Category Listings, Developer Profile, and Mini-App Detail Sheets.
Integrate server-side framing into the marketplace API gateway to deliver pre-shaped JSON-LD payloads directly to the native client UI.

title: JSON-LD Security Best Practices: External Context Dereferencing, SSRF Defenses & Prototype Pollution
category: Semantic Web, Data Architecture & Structured Catalog Metadata
standard_reference: W3C JSON-LD 1.1 Section 9 (Security Considerations)
key_takeaways: External Context Dereferencing Risk: Loading arbitrary '@context' URLs declared in untrusted user-submitted documents can expose processing servers to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and Denial of Service (DoS) attacks.
W3C specifies strict caching, size limits, and recursion depth restrictions when dereferencing external contexts.
Prototype Pollution Defenses: JSON-LD parsers in JavaScript runtimes must defend against properties named '__proto__', 'constructor', or 'prototype' within contexts or data nodes.

Allowlist Verification: Production processing engines must restrict remote context loading to a pinned allowlist of trusted URIs (e.g. w3.org, schema.org, identity.foundation) or rely entirely on pre-compiled local context maps.
Ensures that mini-app metadata ingestion pipelines remain impervious to remote code execution and internal network reconnaissance.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Enforce an absolute ban on arbitrary external '@context' HTTP dereferencing in the super-app ingestion worker; ship an offline catalog of pre-cached schemas.
Implement strict JSON-LD parser hardening, validating that all incoming documents pass prototype pollution and recursion depth limits (< 10 levels).

title: Federated Mini-App Discovery: Schema.org & JSON-LD 1.1 Catalog Distribution & Cross-Super-App Portability
category: Semantic Web, Data Architecture & Structured Catalog Metadata
standard_reference: Schema.org SoftwareApplication / WebApplication Specification & Federated Mini-App Catalog Architecture
key_takeaways: Structuring mini-app store distribution manifests with Schema.org WebApplication / SoftwareApplication classes serialized in JSON-LD 1.1 creates a portable, vendor-neutral ecosystem.
Properties such as 'applicationCategory', 'operatingSystem', 'permissions', 'fileSize', 'softwareVersion', and 'offers' map directly to super-app store capabilities.
Enables decentralized indexing: external enterprise directories, public search engines, and partner super-apps can crawl and aggregate mini-app listings without custom proprietary scrapers.
Supports interoperable ActivityPub / ActivityStreams syndication, allowing new mini-app releases, changelogs, and security advisories to be broadcast across federated partner super-apps.
Bridges the gap between proprietary container platforms (WeChat, Alipay, Lark) and open web standards, establishing an open federated mini-app distribution protocol.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Publish public mini-app store catalog pages with embedded JSON-LD Schema.org metadata to maximize SEO discovery and web accessibility.
Expose an open, authenticated federated catalog endpoint ('/api/v1/catalog/feed.jsonld') enabling authorized enterprise partner super-apps to synchronize approved internal mini-apps.

title: W3C CSS Layout API Level 1: Custom Layout API Container Box Model and display: layout() Syntax
category: Houdini Layout Engine, Rendering Pipeline & Container Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Working Draft 2026: CSS Layout API Level 1, Section 2 (Layout API Containers)
key_takeaways: Introduces 'layout(<ident>)' to the CSS <display-inside> production, allowing elements to generate layout API container boxes governed by developer-defined algorithms.
A layout API container establishes a new Layout API formatting context, isolating child elements from external float, margin-collapsing, and BFC side-effects.

Enables complex application layouts (masonry, circular carousels, custom flex topologies) to run natively within the browser layout phase rather than emulating them via brittle JavaScript DOM mutations.
Transforms root inline children by inlinifying block boxes and converting floats to in-flow inline boxes, ensuring a predictable box tree structure.
Provides mathematical control over child geometry while maintaining interoperability with standard CSS sizing properties (width, height, min-content, max-content).
super_app_standard_recommendations: Support 'display: layout(miniapp-masonry)' within the super-app WebView container to enable high-performance e-commerce catalog grid rendering.
Expose container-level CSS layout validation rules in the mini-app store static linter to ensure custom layouts adhere to predictable box boundaries.

title: LayoutWorkletGlobalScope & registerLayout(): Multi-Threaded Generator-Based Layout Dispatch
category: Houdini Layout Engine, Rendering Pipeline & Container Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Working Draft: CSS Layout API Level 1, Section 8 (Layout Worklet)
key_takeaways: Layout definitions are registered via 'registerLayout(name, layoutCtor)' inside a dedicated LayoutWorkletGlobalScope.
The layout callback is implemented as a JavaScript generator function ('*layout(children, edges, constraints, styleMap, breakToken)') yielding layout requests.
Execution can take place on secondary background layout threads, completely decoupling heavy geometry calculations from the main UI thread.

LayoutWorkletGlobalScope is an isolated execution context lacking DOM access, timer APIs, network primitives, and window globals, preventing untrusted layout scripts from executing arbitrary side effects.
The browser engine maintains multiple global scopes and can arbitrarily discard or recreate them, enforcing purely stateless, idempotent layout operations.
super_app_standard_recommendations: Require all custom mini-app layout worklets to be declared statically in the mini-app manifest ('layoutWorklets' field) for pre-compilation during container initialization.
Enforce zero-DOM access inside layout worklets to guarantee that third-party mini-app layouts cannot compromise host super-app UI elements.

title: LayoutChild Sizing, BreakToken Fragmentation & FragmentResultOptions Geometry Protocol
category: Houdini Layout Engine, Rendering Pipeline & Container Architecture
standard_reference: W3C Working Draft: CSS Layout API Level 1, Section 3 (Layout API Model and Terminology) & Section 5 (Layout Execution)
key_takeaways: Children of a layout container are exposed as 'LayoutChild' objects, allowing authors to inspect their computed styles via 'styleMap' and query intrinsic sizes.
